steps.text: To judge an attack on a castled king, **count at the weak square**: how many of your pieces attack it, and how many of his defend it, the king included. The weak square is usually part of the pawn cover, such as h2 or h7. More attackers than defenders is a reason to look further, not a proof.

steps.text: The count only helps if every counted piece really reaches the square: a piece standing in its way blocks a line and removes an attacker. steps.text: A king still in the centre is a target when lines can be opened toward him and his pieces cannot cover them in time. To attack him you need **open lines** and attackers that arrive first. The lines usually come from a pawn break (a pawn push that attacks an enemy pawn and opens a line) or a sacrifice. Before you sacrifice, name the lines it opens and the checks or forks that follow. Without a follow-up the sacrifice is a gift.

steps.text: A direct attack is a commitment. After the first sacrifice you cannot take it back, and his replies are mostly forced. steps.text: The **Greek gift** is the bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2). Bxh7+ Kxh7 drags the king out; then the knight checks from g5 and the queen joins on h5. It asks for a bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, a knight that can reach g5, and a queen (or another piece) that can join on h5. It is a pattern with conditions, not a trick that always works.

Along the engine's best-defence line White ends at least 2 points ahead.

Only the king defends h7.

steps.text: Check these before you play it, as a **rule of thumb**: the bishop reaches h7 with check; a knight can check from g5 and no black piece can safely take it (a bishop on e7 can; a queen can if g5 is unguarded); a queen can join on h5; no black knight on f6 covers h7. If one is missing the sacrifice may lose a piece. The engine check decides.

title: How fast to attack: forcing now or calm first
outcomes: Chooses between forcing play now and a calm strengthening move, and gives the reason (king in the centre, or sound cover)
Explains why a calm move that adds an attacker is not passive
Tests whether a defender's piece already in place changes the right pace
Recognises a position with no attack to pace because material is simply free

steps.text:
How fast should an attack go? Two speeds.
**Quick:** forcing moves now (checks, captures, sacrifices), because the king is still in the centre or the defenders are not yet near.
**Moderate:** a calm move that brings one more piece to bear, because forcing moves would only trade your attackers away.
A calm move that adds an attacker is not passive.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's king is still on e1 and has not castled.

line.say: Check at once, while the king is still in the centre.
White takes the bishop with the queen.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: Bxf2+ is the engine's best move.
Along the engine line Bxf2+ nets Black at least 4 points.
The white king is in the centre.
The calm Qd5 is far worse.

steps.text: **Moderate pace.** When the king is sheltered behind pawns, forcing moves often run out of pieces. A calm move that adds one more attacker can beat a check. Ask: which of my pieces is not yet attacking? This is a *rule of thumb*. Whether to attack at all is the lesson 'Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no'.

**Conditions.** Quick when the king is still in the centre or open files point at it. Moderate when the king is sheltered and you can add an attacker.
**Fails.** A slow move while the king can still castle gives him time. A calm plan fails when the defender's piece is already in place: test that before trusting the plan.

steps.text: A **pawn storm** pushes pawns at a castled king to open a file or diagonal for your pieces. It belongs mainly to **opposite-side castling** (the two kings castle on different wings), where pawns are cheap and speed counts. A **lever** is a pawn move that attacks one of the pawns shielding the king. Before pushing, count the pieces standing ready behind the pawns.

steps.text: **Conditions.** A storm works when many of your pieces can join before the defender's pieces arrive, and the pawn barrier can be broken. It fails when the barrier is intact and defenders are near. Call a storm *practical* unless you calculated it to be *sound*.

steps.text: **Calculating without moving pieces:** play the line in your head and look at the board only at the end. You need no photographic memory, only the list from the lesson *Track the line: what moved, what is gone, what is attacked*, kept current: *what moved, what is gone, what is attacked now.* Moving pieces while you think is a different skill; it hides whether you can hold the position. Six plies is a first target, a rule of thumb.

Qxe5: queen takes queen. Gone: the black queen. The pawn on f6 now attacks the White queen.
fxe5: the f-pawn takes the queen. Gone: the White queen. A black pawn now stands on e5.

Rxf7: rook takes rook. The rooks on f1 and f7 now face each other, and neither has a defender.

title: How deep, and when to stop: a time budget for a whole set
outcomes: Splits a stated time budget over six positions before solving any of them, giving more time to the critical ones

steps.text: In **Where the depth goes: sort the candidates before you calculate** you sorted the moves inside one position. Now sort the **positions**. Given a set and a budget, say 12 minutes for six positions, decide before you start where the minutes go. A forcing line that keeps going gets the most; a position where the first move ends the game gets seconds. Equal shares are the usual mistake.

**When a budget split holds.** It needs a decision that matters and a clock. Rule of thumb: critical positions (checks, a long forcing line, a tempting capture) get about half the time; routine ones get what is left. It fails when you cannot tell which is which in advance, and a sort made after you have solved proves nothing. Stopping is justified by a forced result or a quiet position, not by tiredness.

steps.title: Where the minutes go
steps.prompt: The first position shows a move that works. Then solve the next two. For each of the three, write down in your own words how much of a 12-minute set it would deserve, and what made you say so.

steps.text: **Check your sort.** The first (a mate in 3 by sacrifice) is **critical**: a long forced line, so it earns a lot. The second (a mate in 2, with a tempting rook capture that loses) deserves a **short look**. The third (a queen mate in one) is **routine**: seconds. These three differ in several ways, not one, and its prompt gives the mate away on purpose. In a real set the prompt will not.

Success means the long plans took the long times and the totals stayed near the budget. Six positions are a rough look, not a measurement. Overspending on a position you marked routine suggests the sort may have been wrong, or that you hesitated; look at which.

steps.text: In **Long lines late in the session: measure it on yourself** you compared a fresh set with a late set. D2 asks for more: across a two-hour set, the **second half stays flat**. Split the two hours into four blocks of the same size and the same kind of line. The aim is not a perfect fresh block; it is that block four has no more than one error above block three. title: The analysis tree: fill each cell once
outcomes: Lays out a table of candidates, replies and one-word verdicts for a forcing position

steps.text: A **tree** is a table you fill once. Rows are your candidates. For each, write the opponent's best replies (two is a start) and follow every branch about four plies to its end. At the end write **one word**: *mates, wins, even* or *loses* (judge by material). Fill each cell once, in order, and do not jump back. A candidate is only as good as its worst cell for you.

steps.caption: White to move. Three candidates, each followed against the best defence. A) Rh1+ : every reply loses to mate, so its cell says mates. B) Nxf7+ : White ends at least two points down, so loses. C) Rg4 : no net material change, so even. The best row is A.

After Rg4 and the best defence White's net material change is zero.

steps.text: **Next: a longer exercise.** This one asks you to enter a whole line, five plies, instead of a verdict word. Fill your table on paper first. A miss here is information, not failure.

**When a tree works.** It works when branches end in a clear verdict within about four plies: checks, captures, threats. It fails in two ways. A reply you never listed (the table looks complete and is not), and going back over a branch you already judged. In a quiet position few branches reach a verdict; a tree finds little. Four plies and two replies are rules of thumb.

title: Track the line: what moved, what is gone, what is attacked
outcomes: Writes what moved, what left the board and what is attacked after a two-ply line, with no piece moved

steps.text: Calculating is not taking a mental photograph. It is **updating a short list** after every move: *what moved, what left the board, what is attacked now.* Start small: one candidate and one reply, so two plies, with the board in front of you and nothing moved. Then ask one question: **which piece is attacked now, and does anything defend it?**

steps.caption: Black to move. Follow the two moves without touching a piece, and update the list after each one. A piece is loose when it is attacked and nothing defends it.

line.say: Rxd2+: the d7 rook, which defended d8, leaves and takes White's rook with check.
Rxd2: White retakes. Black's rook is gone. White's d2 rook now faces the undefended d8 rook down an open file.

claims.statement: The rook on d7 defends the rook on d8.
Before the moves exactly one black piece defends d8.
After the two moves no black piece defends the rook on d8.
After the two moves one white piece attacks it.
Black's only loose piece is the rook on d8.
White has no loose piece.

steps.text: **Where tracking breaks.** A capture does two things: the capturing piece lands somewhere new, and the captured piece stops attacking and defending. A capture can also open a line behind it (a discovered attack). So ask again after every capture: *who defended what, and what is open now?* Two plies is a first size, a rule of thumb. Accuracy after the first capture matters more than length.

Tracking covers routes too. On paper, write every square a knight lands on when it travels from a1 to h8 on an empty board, then count. Counting by eye is where an extra move hides.

title: Counter-attack or defend: count both races

steps.text: A **counter-attack** answers a threat with a bigger threat of your own. It works only if your own position survives the first reply and your threats arrive first. Count both races: how many moves does the opponent need, how many do you need, and are yours checks? A half-hearted mix of defending and attacking is often the weakest choice (a rule of thumb from the source idea, not a theorem).

steps.text: **It holds** when your checks or mate threats come with tempo and the opponent's king has no spare move. **It fails** when you are one move slower, or when the opponent can capture your attacker. *Rule of thumb:* if you cannot write down your whole forcing line, defend. 'The best defence is attack' is a slogan, not a theorem.

A counter-attack is right when your threat is faster than his and comes with a check or a threat he must answer. Do not drift into the **half-hearted third option**: a move that neither defends properly nor threatens something bigger. At each move say one word aloud before you play: counter or defend.

It **fails** when it is one move slower or loses the supporting piece. steps.text:
Four questions for the side that is worse.
1. What is my **chief weakness**?
2. What is the opponent's **chief threat**?
3. Is his advantage big enough to win by force?
4. Will it be settled in the middlegame or the ending?

steps.text:
A **fortress** is a set-up the stronger side cannot break, even when it is ahead. Here both sides have a bishop, on opposite colours, and White has one extra pawn, yet White cannot win.
In these examples the defender has a king beside the square the pawn needs next and a bishop with safe waiting moves. The tablebase confirms each example; it does not prove the same holds for other pawns or bishop colours.

steps.text:
**When it holds.** In these examples the draw holds while the black king stays next to the square in front of the pawn (or on it) and the bishop has waiting moves; moving the king two files away from the pawn's file, as in Kd7 or Kd8, loses by the tablebase.
**Rule of thumb:** Before you trust a fortress, name the square the extra pawn needs and which of your pieces guards it; then check with a tablebase or engine rather than assuming.

title: Can I hold it? Can he break it?
outcomes: Decides whether a worse position can be held by a fortress

steps.text: In **Ahead in material, still unable to win** you built a fortress from a given imbalance. Now judge any position. Behind in material, ask: can I set up something he cannot break? Ahead, ask: can he? Three questions: is there an entry square or a breakthrough? Does the weaker side always have a safe waiting move? Can the stronger side force a zugzwang?

**Rule of thumb:** more material does not always win. A fortress holds when the stronger side has no entry square and no breakthrough, and the defender always has a safe waiting move. In the next three positions the black pawn is one step from queening, and where the draw holds it rests on stalemate: the queen leaves Black no legal move. Change the pawn's file, or move a piece, and see which change matters. The tablebase gives the verdicts.

title: A defender's resources: meet the chief threat, nothing more
outcomes: Names the chief threat before choosing a defensive move

steps.text: A defender has several resources: move the piece, defend it, block, capture the attacker, make a bigger threat, vacate a weak square before supporting it, give material back. 'Five ways to meet an attack' teaches the first five. The skill here is the order: **name the chief threat first**, then choose the resource that meets it, and nothing more.

steps.caption: White to move. Black threatens Qxg2 mate (the rook on g8 backs the queen up). The pawn steps to g3.

g3 is the engine's best move.

steps.text:
**Vacate, then support** (a rule of thumb, not tested in this lesson). If your important piece stands on the weak square, move it off first, then support the square; supporting it while the piece stands there can leave both stuck.
**Unneeded defence.** If nothing is threatened, a defensive move is a lost move. Whichever resource you pick must stop the chief threat in the position as it is now.

title: Pawn cover: what a pawn push in front of your king gives away
outcomes: Names the pawns that form the cover in front of a castled king

steps.text: A castled king hides behind his **pawn cover**: the pawns in front of him, on his file and either side of it. A pawn that steps forward stops guarding the squares diagonally ahead of it. A **hole** is a square on your third to fifth rank that no pawn of yours attacks now or can attack later: an enemy piece can sit there and no pawn can chase it away.

steps.caption: Black to move. His king stands on g8 behind the pawns f7, g7 and h7.

line.say: The g-pawn steps to g6. It no longer guards f6 or h6, and no other pawn can.
The white queen lands on h6. No black pawn attacks that square, now or later.

claims.statement: Before the move the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6.
After g6 the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6, f6, h6.
After g6 the queen on e3 attacks h6.
No black pawn attacks h6 once the queen is there.

steps.text: A hole matters when an enemy piece can reach it and your pieces cannot cover it, so a push is a warning sign, a **rule of thumb**, not a ban. Some pushes create no hole, and a push on the other wing leaves the king's cover alone. Before a pawn move near your king, name the squares it stops guarding and the enemy pieces that could land there.

title: Trade off the piece doing the damage
outcomes: Names the most dangerous attacking piece and the exchange that removes it
Checks that an exchange removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace

steps.text:
When you are under attack, one **exchange** can do more than any quiet defensive move: it takes away the attacker's most dangerous piece.
Ask two questions. Which enemy piece is doing the damage? Which of my pieces can trade for it?
The rest of the lesson is about when this works and when it does not.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight and queen are aimed at the white king and queen.

line.say: The knight takes the knight on f4, the piece that attacks the queen on e2.
Black recaptures with the queen. One pair of knights is off the board.
White has traded off the knight that was aimed at the king and queen.

claims.statement: Nxf4 is the engine's first choice.
If White passes, Black has a forced win of material or mate.
The knight on f4 attacks the queen on e2 and the pawn on g2.
Ignoring the knight with g3 is at least two pawns worse.

steps.text:
**What to check.** An exchange helps when it removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace. Before you trade, ask: is a second attacker ready to take its place?
Then ask the reverse question: which of my pieces guards my king, and does this trade take it away?
**Rule of thumb:** fewer pieces usually help the defender, but only when the trade takes away the piece doing the damage.

title: Trade, hold or leave it: choosing the defence
outcomes: Asks what the opponent threatens before choosing a defensive move
Counts the attackers before deciding that one exchange answers the attack

steps.text: In **Trade off the piece doing the damage** you took away an attacker by exchanging. Now the harder question: is a trade the right answer at all? Under attack you can **trade** an attacker, **hold** by moving or guarding the target, or **counter-attack** with a bigger threat of your own. Start with the threat question: if I pass, what can he do? Then count his attackers.

**When a trade works.** It works when it removes an attacker he cannot replace. It fails when a second attacker is left: one exchange cannot answer two threats. **Rule of thumb:** count the attackers before you trade. A counter-attack is a third option only if your threat comes first and is bigger; no exercise here proves one.

**Defence by economy:** when the opponent has no clear way forward, do not change your set-up without a reason. Needless pawn moves, king walks and rook shuffles give him free tempi. Hold the best post you have and make him commit first.

steps.text: A **breakthrough** gives up one or two pawns so that a pawn is left with no enemy pawn in front of it. It needs pawns facing pawns; the classic case is three against three on neighbouring files, and the middle pawn moves first. Look for it when your pawns are further advanced and the kings are far away. Watch one, then find it yourself.

steps.text: The breakthrough is **not a rule**. Here it works because White's pawns are further advanced, the kings are far from the pawns, and White moves first. Change one of these and the same skeleton may be level. Counting who queens first, and where the kings stand, decides. Having the same number of pawns, or more, does not guarantee it.

steps.text: *The pawn breakthrough: giving pawns to make a passed pawn* taught you to find the sacrifice. Now the question is **who wins** before you try. Look at two things: which side's pawns are nearer to queening, and who is to move. In these positions (a pawn "skeleton": only pawns and kings) both kings are far away, so the pawns decide. Predict the first one.

**Rule of thumb.** With both kings far from the pawns, the side whose pawns are nearer to queening can break through, and the move matters too. Push the same skeleton back down the board and the result can flip, even with the same number of pawns. A breakthrough that works in one position is not a rule for the next. Having the extra pawn is not enough by itself.

steps.text: A **fortress** is a set-up that the stronger side cannot break, even with extra material. The weaker side keeps its pieces protecting one another, covers the squares the enemy could enter, and keeps a harmless waiting move. For the best-known case, a wrong-coloured bishop with a rook pawn, see the lesson *The wrong bishop: a rook pawn that cannot win*.

steps.caption: Black to move: king, rook and a pawn against a queen. Natural moves such as Ra5 and Rc6 lose; Rb6 holds. The tablebase says the position is a draw; one line is shown.

steps.text: **Ask three questions.** (1) Is every square the queen could enter, or check from, covered? (2) Do the defenders protect each other, and is none forced to move away? (3) Is there a waiting move that breaks nothing? Rule of thumb: the set-up fails if some defender is attacked more often than it is protected, or if the stronger side can force a defender off its post so that an entry square is uncovered.

Now someone claims one, and you must **prove or break it**. Look for a loose piece (attacked and not defended), an entry square nobody covers, and a check that attacks a second piece. If you find a break, name the move. Start with a position where a black piece is loose.

steps.text: *The king as a fighter: pawn endings the active king decides* showed the king winning races in pawn endings. Most positions are mixed. Before you step the king forward ask two things: **are the queens (or rooks) still on**, and **could the opponent give a check after my step**? If heavy pieces are off and nothing can check the king, the step towards the centre is usually right.

**Rule of thumb, not a law.** Bring the king out when the queens are off and no check or mating threat exists. Before a king step, look for checks and skewers on its new square. steps.text: You know when the king should come out (*The king as a fighting piece: bring it out only when it is safe*). Now a race: a passed pawn against a king that may catch it. **Count** the pawn's moves and the king's moves to the queening square. Then ask what a bishop or rook can do: a check costs a move.

**Push first.** In these positions only the pawn push wins; any king move gives the bishop or rook time to get in front of the pawn, and the result drops to a draw. A king step onto the piece's line can even come with a check, which costs another move. Before a king step ask: does the pawn queen by force right now? steps.text: Knights are slow. A knight needs up to six moves to cross the board, and every move changes the colour of its square. steps.text: **Lucena.** The pawn is on the seventh rank and your king stands in front of it, on the queening square, so the pawn cannot move. The enemy king is cut off: your rook holds a file it may not cross. If your king steps aside, the enemy rook starts checking. You win by moving the king out and sheltering it behind your own rook. It is a plan with conditions, not a reflex.

The king steps off the file.
Black's rook checks again, now along the e-file.
The king steps toward the rook.
Black checks along the d-file.
The king steps up the board, next to the fourth rank.
Black checks along the e-file again.
The rook blocks on e4 and the king defends it, so Black's rook cannot take it with a win. This shelter is the bridge.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Lucena needs a pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it and the enemy king cut off. Two moves often spoil it: promoting while the enemy rook can take the new queen, and blocking a check with a loose rook (one your king does not defend). The bridge is a block by your own rook, on a square your king defends. Before you count on the win, ask what else about the arrangement matters.

steps.text: **The question.** A queen can check a king in many ways, but only some checks end the game. steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Mate with king and queen: the supported check. This part covers Why it works, and when it fails; Set it up. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Count the squares.** A mate must settle the king's own square (the check) and every neighbour it could step to: up to eight, fewer at an edge. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*, lectures 7 and 8) frames mating as counting squares, with the checking piece safe (checked in our notes). [V] All 364 mating positions of king and queen against a bare king, enumerated here, have the lone king on the edge. [I] In the middle, one queen and one king cannot cover eight neighbours and stay safe.
steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

steps.text: **Three questions for any queen check.** 1. Can the king take her? 2. Is any neighbouring square free? 3. If it is not check at all, does Black still have a legal move? Ask them in this order before every queen move, and the draw traps disappear. Driving the king to the edge is the next skill: see the lesson 'King and queen against king: shrink the box'.

steps.caption: Black to move and checkmated. The five squares around the king are marked. The queen and the white king between them cover all five; f7 and h7 are covered twice.
The same black king, but the white king stands on e6, two files away from the corner squares.

line.say: A check along the back rank, but the king on e6 is too far away to cover g7 or h7.
The king simply steps off the rank. A check is not yet a mate.

steps.caption: Same position again. This check looks more forceful, because the queen goes right beside the king.

line.say: The queen lands beside the king, and nothing protects her.
The king takes the queen. Only two bare kings remain: a draw.

steps.caption: Same position, third try. Quiet king moves also keep the win; one of the neatest is the king step to f6.

line.say: The patient move: the king steps nearer, so that it covers g7 and the squares beside it.
Suppose Black steps into the corner.

Now the queen lands beside the king on a protected square: checkmate. If Black goes to f8 instead, the queen's check on the back rank is mate, because the king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7. [V: search here] This mates in two; several other quiet moves win more slowly.

steps.text: **Who needs protection?** A king can capture only on a square beside it. So a check from far away needs no protector; it needs every flight square covered. A check from beside the king must be protected, or the king takes the queen. [I] 'Protect the queen' is a good slogan up close and a poor one at long range: ask *can the king take her, and where else can it go?*

steps.caption: A king in the middle has up to eight neighbours, and here five legal replies, so no single check can mate it. Mate happens at the edge, so the king must first be driven there. [V]
Black to move, not in check, with no legal move. This position came from the kings-facing position, one queen move away from mate.

steps.text: **The stalemate trap.** The last queen move can leave the lone king with no legal move and no check: a draw, not a win. [H] It happens when attention jumps from the king's squares to the squares the queen covers, so the 'tighter' move feels better. Ask: does it give check? If so, can the king take her and is any square free? If not, does Black still have a legal move?

**The quiet move.** Often the queen cannot give mate yet, so you first take away the king's last squares. A quiet move works when every reply loses. Count Black's legal moves after yours: when one is left, the mate usually shows. The king helps by covering squares, and by standing ready to protect the queen. [H] Learners may like the close check because it feels nearer the kill; it also needs a protector.

steps.caption: Black's king on d8 has several squares. No check is mate yet.

line.say: A quiet move: the queen covers the whole c-file and checks nothing.
The king goes to e8, its only free square.
The queen checks along the back rank, with the kings facing each other. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Here a king move comes first. Whatever Black replies, a queen check follows on the first rank.

line.say: The king covers a2, b2 and c2, so the black king cannot come up the board.
Black chooses a1. The other choice, c1, also loses to a queen move.
The queen checks along the first rank. The king on b3 covers the second rank. Checkmate.

steps.caption: The king steps in front of the black king and the queen waits on the side. One careless queen move later would be stalemate.

line.say: The king steps up, covering g7 and h7. Only g8 is left for the black king.
The king goes to g8.
The queen checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers f7, g7 and h7. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Sometimes the first move is itself a check that forces the king to one square.

line.say: A check that covers g8 and g7. Only h7 is left for the king.
The king goes to h7.
The queen lands beside the king, protected by the white king. Checkmate.

steps.text: **Recap.** Three questions for any queen check: can the king take her, is a neighbouring square free, does Black still have a legal move? A check beside the king needs a protector. From far away, the king and the edge must cover the flight squares. Quiet moves prepare it. No check and no move is a draw. steps.text: Two bishops on **opposite-coloured squares** can mate a lone king, but only with their own king close by. Your king takes away flight squares (squares the lone king could step to), the bishops attack squares of both colours near the corner, and a quiet bishop move (a waiting move) or a check forces the last steps. Watch one finish, then find the first move yourself.

steps.caption: White to move mates in three. Black's king is in the corner a8; White's king covers b7 and b8.

Black's king goes back to a8.
The light bishop checks on the long diagonal. Mate: the king covers b7 and b8, the other bishop a7.

Before Be2 the black king already has exactly one legal move.

steps.text: Three conditions. The bishops must stand on **opposite colours**: two bishops on one colour only draw. Your king must come close; bishops alone do not mate. And count Black's moves before any quiet move: if the king has no legal move and is not in check, the game is **stalemate**, a draw.

steps.text: The count is arithmetic. The halfmove clock counts half-moves since the last capture or pawn move, and at 100 either player may claim a draw. The tablebase tells how many more half-moves the win needs at best. **The win holds if the clock plus that number is at most 100.** First the sum: one move by each side adds two half-moves.

steps.prompt: The clock reads 64. How many more moves of his own can White make before the clock reaches 100?

steps.text: Now test the sum on a real position. The win needs 57 half-moves, so the clock is the only thing that changes in the first two positions below; the third is reflected left to right. Predict each result.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb:** when the sum is close to 100, every move must be among the fastest. A move that looks as good can still cost the win. In the next two positions the clock leaves almost no spare time, so find the move that loses none. The third position is a different question: can the count be met at all?

No short method finds the fastest move. When the clock is high, prefer the move that keeps both pieces and the king together and cuts the king's escape squares, and check it with the tablebase after you answer.

title: Mating without stalemating
outcomes: Tells checkmate, stalemate and neither apart at a glance
Counts the lone king's legal moves before every move that is not mate

steps.text: A winning side can throw the game away in one move. If the lone king is **not in check** and has **no legal move**, the game is a draw by stalemate, however much material you have. So before every move that is not checkmate, ask one question: **after my move, can Black still make a legal move?** The danger is highest on an edge or in a corner.

steps.caption: White to move. Qh3 is checkmate. Qg3 takes away every square without giving check, so it is stalemate and a draw.

line.say: Check along the h-file; the white king covers g1 and g2, so Black has no legal move and is in check: checkmate.

Black's king steps to h5.
Another quiet queen move. The white king stays on f3.
Black's king steps to h4.

steps.text: **Count the king's moves after your move.** Check and a legal reply: play on. Check and no reply: checkmate. No check and no reply: stalemate. This holds for queen and rook alike. *Rule of thumb:* a quiet queen move a knight's jump from the cornered king often takes the last square, so count first. title: Mating without stalemating: the quick move is the trap
outcomes: Finds the mate in queen and rook positions near the edge when the quickest-looking move is a stalemate

steps.text: *Mating without stalemating* taught you to count the lone king's legal replies. Now the positions are mixed: queen and rook, kings near an edge. The trap is the move that looks quickest. It takes away the king's last square but gives no check. Find the mate first. Then name the decoy and count replies after it too. Stalemate is a draw, however much you are ahead.

steps.caption: The decoy from that position: Qd6 takes the last squares but gives no check. Black has no legal move, so it is stalemate.

steps.text: **When it holds, and when it fails.** Counting replies after a quiet move settles it every time, because stalemate needs two things: no check, and no legal move. It fails to help if you stop at the first move that boxes him in. *Rule of thumb:* near a corner the quickest-looking move is suspect; if it leaves no square and no check, look again. steps.text: Part 2 of 4: King and rook against king: fence, approach, check on the edge. This part covers Fence and approach. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: Job one: fence. The rook on a4 closes the whole fourth rank, so the black king may only stay above it. Count its squares.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these five squares.
Black is not in check.

steps.text: **Fence from far away.** A rook shuts a whole file or rank, and the king may not cross it. Keep the rook where the king cannot reach it, or where your own king guards it. A fence must also move: slide it one line closer to the king and the area he lives in shrinks. That is the whole idea. Watch the fence move in the next three boards.

steps.caption: Fence, part one: the rook slides from file to file, and the black king is driven to the left. White wins by force in at most seven moves.

line.say: The rook closes the e-file from the far end of the board. The black king cannot cross it, and cannot attack the rook.
Black stays on the left of the fence.
The fence moves one file closer. Now the d-file is closed too, and Black has three moves, all to the left.
Black keeps going left, towards the edge.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part two: now a check drives the king off the seventh rank and the white king steps up.

line.say: A check along the seventh rank from a square the king cannot reach. Black must leave that rank.
Black steps to the back rank. Ka6 was also legal; this is the engine's line.
The white king steps up. It covers b7 and c7 while the rook holds d7 and d8, so Black has one move.
Forced.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most six moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part three: the net closes in the corner. One quiet move, then the last check. Mate in at most three moves.

line.say: A check along the back rank. Only a7 is left.
Forced again.
A quiet rook move, not a check. It covers the whole back rank and leaves Black one square, a6.
The only move.
The rook checks along the a-file. The king on c6 covers b5, b6 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.text: **A rule for the fence [I].** Put the rook on the file next to the black king's file, as far from the king as the board allows. When the king steps away from the fence, bring the fence one file closer. When the king comes next to the rook, move the rook away along its line. A rook left near the king is lost, as the next board shows.

steps.prompt: Before the next card: in the long line you just stepped through, how many of White's eight moves were checks? Write your guess.

steps.caption: The wrong way to fence: the rook stands next to the black king with no guard. It is Black's move.

line.say: The king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left: a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on e4 is attacked and undefended.
With Black to move, this is only a draw.

steps.text: **Job two: bring your king.** Capablanca's *Chess Fundamentals* (our notes on it) says the rook confines the enemy king to a strip, but only your own king can finish the job. With the enemy king in the centre, he advises walking your king up first, and putting it on the file next to the black king's, towards the centre, not the same file.

steps.caption: If it were Black's move here, the king would have five squares and could walk sideways. Who has the move decides what a check can do.

claims.statement: With Black to move the king has these five squares.

steps.caption: The squeeze, part one. It is White's move and the kings face each other with a gap, so the rook check cannot be answered by stepping forward. Mate in at most nine moves.

line.say: The check comes along the seventh rank from the far side. Black must go back to the last rank.
Black steps back.
The white king walks forward and takes c7, d7 and e7. Black can only slide along the last rank.
Black slides to the other side.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most nine moves.

steps.caption: Part two: the rook waits, the king follows, and the black king is herded toward the corner. Mate in at most seven moves.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook slides along the seventh rank to a square nobody can attack, and Black has to move again.
Black moves toward the corner.
The king follows, covering d7, e7 and f7. Black has two moves, both on the back rank.
Black goes toward the corner.
The rook steps next to the black king, which is safe only because the king on e6 guards f7. Black has one move, h8.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Part three: the king closes in step by step, and the rook gives the last check.

line.say: The king closes in. Black has one move, g8.
Forced.
The white king takes a position facing the black king, and h8 is the only square left.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers g7 and h7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.text: **Count the checks.** [V] In this line 2 of White's 8 moves are checks; the rest are quiet king steps and rook moves that keep the fence closed. [I] So the king does more of the squeezing, and the rook shuts lines. [H] Beginners overrate checks, because a check feels like progress. A check next to an unguarded rook loses it: see the contrast below.

steps.caption: A quiet rook move can be the strongest move. The white king covers e7, f7 and g7; Black has the d-file left.

line.say: No check. The rook closes the d-file from far away, and Black has exactly one move, f8.
Forced.

steps.title: A check next to the king
steps.prompt: White can also check at once with Rg8+. Predict first: does that work as well as the best move? Then find the best move.

steps.text: **Why it works.** [I] Mate needs an edge: a king in the middle has eight squares, on an edge five, in a corner three. The check pushes the king back only when the kings face each other with one square between **and it is White's move**. Three things break the win: a rook within the king's reach, a quiet move that leaves Black no legal move, a check when the kings do not face.

steps.title: The rook is attacked
steps.prompt: The black king attacks the unguarded rook and it is White's move. Predict first: does the king move Kb2 keep the win as well as the best move? Then find a move that keeps the win.

The king steps forward to f6, which the white king does not guard. The squeeze has failed, and White must begin again.

White still wins from here, but not by that check.

steps.caption: The kings face each other with a gap, but it is White's move, so a check would not help. A waiting rook move passes the turn.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook stays far away, nothing is attacked, and Black must now give up the facing position.

claims.statement: Ra2 keeps the win.

steps.text: **The waiting rule [I].** Check only when the kings face each other with one square between and it is White's move. Otherwise make a safe waiting move with the rook, far from the king, and let Black come to you. The boards above are checked with the tablebase; the rule is a teaching summary, not a theorem for every position.

steps.title: Mate or stalemate?
steps.prompt: Both Rg7 and the best move take the king's last square. Predict first: is Rg7 as good as the best move? Then find checkmate in one.

steps.caption: A rook beside the king, with nothing guarding it, is simply lost. It is Black's move.

line.say: The black king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left, and the game is a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on d2 is attacked and undefended.
The position is a draw with Black to move.

steps.text: **Stalemate, the quiet disaster.** If every square is taken away but the king is not in check, the game is drawn. It happens near the end, when the king is boxed in and White plays a quiet rook move. Before any move that is not a check, count Black's legal moves. If the count is zero, find another move.

steps.caption: Two rook moves take away the king's last squares. Only one of them is mate.

line.say: The rook checks along the a-file while the king on c8 covers b8 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Before the move the black king has only a7.
Ra4 is checkmate.
The other rook move, Rg7, is only a draw.

steps.caption: The other move, Rg7: the rook takes a7 and b7, the king on c8 takes b8, and Black has no move and is not in check.

claims.statement: Black is stalemated.

steps.text: **Three questions before every move.** One: is my rook out of the king's reach, or guarded? Two: after my move, does Black still have a legal move, or is it mate? Three: does this move take away a square or a line that Black had? [I] These questions catch the two errors this lesson showed, a lost rook and a stalemate; they do not choose the best move.

steps.text: In an ending of **bishop against knight**, the pawns often decide who stands better. A bishop reaches both wings in one move; a knight needs several. So pawns on **both wings** tend to favour the bishop, and pawns on **one wing** give the knight better chances to hold. This is a rule of thumb: test it on one position first.

steps.text: **When it holds.** The bishop's side has pawns on both wings, so the bishop can switch between them faster than the knight. **When it fails.** All the pawns on one wing: the knight can hold, as the next pair shows. Rule of thumb: count the wings before you count anything else. Opposite-coloured bishops follow other rules, so do not use this on them.

steps.text: A bishop only ever travels on squares of one colour. If the two bishops run on **opposite colours**, they can never attack or trade each other, and neither can chase the other away. A pawn up is usually a big advantage; here it often is not. Test the idea on the first position before you trust it.

**Material often draws.** Even two pawns up can be a draw. The reason is the **blockade**: the defending king stands in front of the pawn, on a square of the colour that the attacker's bishop cannot touch. The attacker's bishop cannot drive it away, and the defender's bishop guards the rest.

steps.text: **The defender's king is the key piece.** Far from the pawn, it loses the race. In front of the pawn, the blockade holds. When the attacker has more than one pawn, the blockade has to cope with both. Check this on three more tablebase positions: some win, some draw. Look at the pawns first, then the king.

**Rooks change the picture.** With only bishops, the blockade is a draw. Add a rook for each side and the attacker gets checks, skewers and a second piece to attack with. That does not make every case a win: the next two positions add rooks to the same blockade. Predict each.

steps.text: **Three ways to explain the same thing.** Capablanca taught the opposition as a rule about the move. Edward Lasker named the moment the pawn reaches its sixth rank as critical and showed that a spare pawn move can take the opposition back. Nimzowitsch thought the usual account vague and preferred forcing the enemy king to yield. [S] All three are paraphrased from our reading sheets. [I] They look like one idea seen from three sides: the king not on the move owns the better squares.

steps.text: **Distant opposition.** Kings can also face each other from farther away: on one file or rank with an odd number of empty squares between them, such as three. steps.text: **What to remember.** The opposition is a position plus a turn: the kings face with one square between and the other side must move. It wins when the attacking king is ahead of the pawn and the defender is near. It fails for a king level with the pawn, an edge pawn or a faraway defender, and on the sixth rank it can reverse. Always ask whose move it is.

**Self-check before you write.** Did you say when the opposition works? Did you say when it fails and name at least one failing look-alike? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did you name one mistake, such as pushing the pawn too early? The app does not grade this; you are the judge.

steps.text: **Opposition**: the kings face each other and the player who must move gives way (see the lesson *Opposition: one tempo between a win and a draw*). **Distant opposition** is the same fight from afar: the kings stand on one file or rank with an **odd number of squares** between them (3 or 5), and the player who just moved holds it. steps.text: A pawn race is a **counting problem**. Count each pawn's moves to the last rank: one move per rank, except that a pawn on its starting square may move two squares in its first move. A king's distance to a square is the larger of the file gap and the rank gap. And ask **whose move it is**: the side to move spends its first move first. A pawn that arrives with no king in reach queens.

**When counting works**: both pawns are free to run and no king is near enough to interfere. **When it fails:** a king close to a pawn changes the count (a king that can reach the pawn's path in time can stop it), and the first queen may be captured or checked at once. If the first queen has no check or capture, the other pawn queens one move later and the race may be only a draw.

steps.text: Can a lone king catch a runaway pawn? Count the pawn's steps to the eighth rank (for a black pawn, count towards the first rank) and draw a square with that many squares on a side, starting at the pawn. If the defending king is inside the square, or steps into it on his move, he catches the pawn. This **rule of the square** is a heuristic: it counts only the pawn and the defending king.

steps.text: **The square rule has limits.** (1) Your own king can escort the pawn, so a king inside the square may still lose. (2) A pawn on its second rank can move two squares, so draw the square from the square it will reach after the double step. Both are limits of a rule of thumb: the square counts only the pawn and the defending king, so check the position before you trust it.

steps.text: A queen usually beats a lone pawn. But when the pawn is one step from queening and its own king stands beside it, a **stalemate** trap can save it: a careless queen move leaves the weaker side with no legal move. The pawn's **file** decides whether the trap exists. Watch one trap first, then compare files.

steps.text: **When the draw works.** Take a pawn on the seventh, the weaker king on or next to the queening square, and the stronger king far away. Then the rook and bishop pawns (a, c, f, h files) can often hold by stalemate, while the knight and central pawns (b, d, e, g files) are lost for the pawn's side. 'Often' matters: the exact squares still decide, so the next positions are checked one by one. The nearer the stronger king, the less this holds.

steps.text: The lesson *Queen against a pawn on the seventh: when it is only a draw* gave a rule of thumb: with the stronger king far away, a rook or bishop pawn can draw by stalemate. Here you **test the verdict**: say win, draw or loss for the side to move, then compare with the tablebase, which is exact for seven pieces or fewer. Then see what **one king step** does.

**One step can flip a draw.** In the tested set-ups, one step closer turned a draw into a win. A step to a square no nearer (a4 to b3) left the draw standing. Rule of thumb for a pawn on the seventh with its own king beside it, not a law: the tablebase decides each position.

steps.text: A passed pawn **far from the kings** is a *remote passed pawn*. The enemy king cannot catch it in time, so it ties his king down while your own king does the other work. Push it too early and his king can take your other pawns and come back in time. Watch Black: king first, then the pawn.

steps.text: In rook endings an active rook checks, cuts the king off, or stands behind the passer; a passive rook only guards. That is a rule of thumb, not a law: the tablebase decides each position. Before a rook captures a pawn, ask what it gives up. In the next positions a rook can capture a pawn. Predict first, then check.

**Pawn or position?** An extra pawn does not win a rook ending by itself (rule of thumb). Before a rook captures a pawn, ask whether the pawn is defended and what the rook gives up: a check, a file, the cut-off. Sometimes a safe capture only draws, and sometimes the capture simply loses the rook. The tablebase decides.

steps.text: Two slogans: *always keep the rook active* and *never defend passively*. Neither works every time. The lesson *Active rooks: the pawn or the rook's position?* compared a capture with an active move. Now the defender must find the **only draw**: sometimes a passive rook move, sometimes an active one. Test the moves instead of trusting a slogan. For passive defence as a method see *Philidor: the passive defence that works*.

**A tied rook** is one for which only a few moves hold. Here Black's rook cannot capture the pawn or check from the side: those moves lose. Rule of thumb: when the king is next to the pawn's file and the pawn is far advanced, the defender's rook may be tied to a rank. Move the king one file and the draw can vanish.

Before you choose, list the rook's checks, its attacks and its quiet moves, and ask which of them keep the draw.

title: Rook endings: four habits and where they fail
outcomes: Puts the rook behind a passed pawn and predicts how the result changes when the rook stands in front of it
Checks which side of the rook's file the enemy king stands on, and predicts how the result changes when the king is not cut off
Predicts win or draw with the rook on the seventh rank, and names a position where the seventh rank is not enough
Finds the defender's far check instead of a close one, and spots a position with no passed pawn, where the rook-behind habit does not apply

steps.text:
Four rook-ending habits.
**Behind:** put the rook behind a passed pawn.
**Cut off:** keep the enemy king away along a file or rank.
**Seventh:** a rook on the seventh rank can shut the enemy king on the back rank.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away.
Each is a *rule of thumb* with exceptions. A **tablebase** (exact results for few pieces) checks every position.

steps.caption: White to move wins. The rook stands on e4, behind the passed pawn on e5. One line is shown.

line.say: The pawn advances. The rook on e4 defends it from behind along the open file.
Black's rook runs to the far end of the board.
The pawn reaches e7. The rook still defends it from behind, across more squares.
Black's rook takes the square in front of the pawn.
White's king steps up the board towards the pawn.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.
1.e6 keeps the win.
The pawn on e5 is passed.
White's rook is on e4.
After e6 the rook defends the pawn.
After e7 the rook still defends the pawn.

steps.text: **Why behind?** From behind, the rook defends the pawn along the file after every push, and each push gives the rook more open squares behind the pawn. In front of the pawn it blocks the pawn's path and loses a square with each push. This is a *rule of thumb*: some positions need a passive rook instead. First test the habit: predict each position, then check.

steps.title: Behind or in front?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook is behind its passed pawn. In the second it stands on g7, in front of the pawn; in the third Black's rook is on c6. Predict the second and the third, then check.

steps.text: **Cut off, and when it fails.** A rook on a file keeps the enemy king on the far side of that file, away from your pawn. If the king is already on the pawn's side of the file, there is nothing to cut off, and the win can vanish. A *rule of thumb*: check which side of the rook's file the king stands on, then predict.

steps.title: Is the king cut off?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook on e1 keeps Black's king on the far side of the e-file from the pawn. In the second the king stands on c7, on the pawn's side; in the third Black's rook is on b8, not a8. Predict the second and the third, then check.

steps.text:
**Seventh rank:** a rook there attacks the whole rank if it is open, keeping the enemy king on the back rank. It is strongest with an advanced passed pawn, but no guarantee.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away, where the king cannot attack it. A check right next to the king can simply lose the rook.
Both are *rules of thumb*. Predict, then check.

steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook is on the seventh rank and Black's king is shut in on a8. In the second Black's king stands on a6; in the third White's king is on e3, not d3. Predict the second and the third, then check.

outcomes: Counts the pawn's moves to queen (with the double step from the second rank) and the defending king's steps to the queening square

steps.text: In **The rule of the square: can the king catch the pawn?** you drew a square. Now count. n: the pawn's moves to queen (from the second rank use the double step: b2 and b3 give 5). k: the king's steps to the queening square (the bigger of the file gap and the rank gap). King to move: he stops the pawn if k is at most n + 1; pawn to move: if k is at most n.

steps.text: **The extra step, and when the count holds.** The extra step is the new queen: a king beside it takes it. The count uses only the pawn and the defending king, so it holds when the pawn's own king is far away (*rule of thumb*; the tablebase checks every position here). It fails when that king is near the pawn or near the queening square: he can escort the pawn or guard the new queen. The double step adds nothing: b2 and b3 both give 5.

title: The tablebase lab: test a claim, do not just quote it
outcomes: States what a tablebase result is (exact for the side to move, seven pieces or fewer) and what it does not say
Decides whether a position can be looked up at all
Tests a conjecture with a position where it should hold and one where it should fail, predicting each result first

steps.text:
A **tablebase** stores every position with few pieces (seven or fewer, kings included) and its exact result under the usual rules for the side to move: win, draw or loss with best play. It is not an engine's opinion.
It gives the result, not the reason. The Analysis page can look a position up in an online tablebase if you tick the box (it sends only the position); the lab itself is a paper routine, and any online tablebase will do.

The lab routine:
**1.** Write the conjecture as one sentence, with its conditions.
**2.** Write two positions that differ by one feature: one where it should hold, one where it should fail.
**3.** Predict both results before you look.
**4.** Query the tablebase.
**5.** Record the result and a reason a person could check by hand.
One failure refutes a conjecture. Many successes do not prove it.

steps.title: When can the lab answer?
steps.prompt: A seven-piece rook ending, the same ending with one more pawn, and an opening position. For each, decide whether a tablebase can answer, then check.

steps.text:
Conditions. A tablebase answers only for seven pieces or fewer. It names a result and never a reason, so 'win' needs your own checkable explanation before you teach it to anyone.
Rule of thumb: if you cannot state a reason another person could check, you hold a fact, not an understanding.

steps.prompt: Run steps 1 to 3 of the lab now on a claim from a book, a video or your own games (seven pieces or fewer). Save the note, then do the lookup later in any online tablebase and write the result and a reason beside it on paper; the app cannot reopen a saved note.

title: Spare moves: mutual zugzwang and the catch in the count
outcomes: Predicts the result of a locked pawn ending from the count of free squares and checks it against the tablebase

steps.text: The lesson *Spare moves: who runs out first?* counted free squares between two h-pawns. Now look at the same position with **either** side to move. In a **mutual zugzwang** whoever has the move is worse off. Predict first, then check: the tablebase gives the exact result. Start with White to move.

**Count, then check.** With no free square between the pawns, the side to move loses here. With one free square, the side to move wins. Rule of thumb: an even number of free squares means the mover gives way, an odd number means the mover wins. It holds only while both kings are tied to their squares and no pawn can still double-step. Change any of that and recount, or look the position up in the tablebase.

title: Two knights cannot mate alone, but a pawn can change that
outcomes: Says that two knights cannot force mate against a bare king
Explains that a defender's pawn gives the defender spare moves, which can turn some two-knight positions into wins
Classifies two-knight positions as win or draw instead of assuming the extra knight always wins

steps.text: Two knights and a king look strong against a bare king. They are not: with best play they **cannot force checkmate**. Mate only appears if the defender helps. Test it before you read on: predict the result of the next position, then check.

**Result:** two knights against a bare king are a draw with best play. The knights can corner the king, but they cannot take away every square and still give check, so the defender can always avoid being forced into mate (or is stalemated). This position is checked by the tablebase. Now give the defender a pawn and see what changes.

**Why a pawn can help the knights:** a pawn that can still move gives the defender spare moves, so there is no stalemate. **Conditions:** bare king, draw. With a pawn on the board there are three outcomes: the knights can win (spare moves for the defender), the position can stay drawn (a blockaded pawn can leave the defender short of moves), or the pawn side can win by queening. Do not assume; classify each position.

title: Two knights and a pawn: find the win, spot the draw
outcomes: Finds the winning first move for the knights in a position with two knights against a king and a pawn
Recognises positions where the knights cannot win
Keeps in mind that removing the pawn turns a won position into a draw

steps.text: In *Two knights cannot mate alone, but a pawn can change that* you learned that two knights cannot force mate against a bare king, and that the defender's pawn can change the result. Now the positions come without labels: find the winning move where there is one. Ask what the black pawn can do, then which squares the knights can take from the black king. Find the move.

**Rule of thumb:** the pawn changes the result, so never treat these as two knights against a king. Taking the pawn can throw the win away. Not every position with a pawn is won either. Predict the three positions: the second is the first with the black pawn removed, and the third is the first reflected left to right.

steps.text: This lesson teaches no new ending. It is a **checklist** built from the endgame lessons in this course. Each lesson teaches a principle, positions that win, and a look-alike that fails. Rate yourself honestly first, then test yourself on positions with no label: nothing tells you which lesson applies.

title: Queen against rook: force the king away from its rook
outcomes: Finds the check that starts a forced win of the rook in a queen-against-rook position
Checks for a rook fork, a stalemating capture and an advanced pawn before playing a check
Predicts win or draw for queen against rook, including when the rook's side is to move

steps.text:
A queen is stronger than a rook, but it does not win by size alone. It wins by **forcing**: a check makes the king move, then one queen move attacks the king and the rook together (a fork), or attacks the king with the rook behind it on the same line (a skewer): when the king steps away, the rook falls.
In the first positions below the rook falls. Your job: find the check that separates the rook from its king.

steps.caption: White to move. Look for a check that makes the black king stand in front of its rook.

line.say: Qa1+ is check along the first rank. Black must answer it.
The king steps to c2, onto the same rank as its rook on h2.
Qa2+ checks along the second rank. The king stands between the queen and the rook.
The king must leave the rank to escape the check.
Now the queen takes the rook.

claims.statement: White to move wins.
Qa1+ wins the rook along the engine's best defence.
After Qa1+ Kc2 the king stands on c2.
The rook stands on h2 on the same rank as the king.
After Qa2+ and Kd3 the queen attacks the rook on h2.

steps.text: A **tablebase** is a stored list of exact results for positions with few pieces. It gives the result with best play by both sides: win, draw or loss. It does not say how many moves a person needs, or how hard the defence is to find; that is not measured here. Read 'the queen wins' as a statement about perfect play, then practise the method until it is routine.

Check three things before a check.
**1. Who moves?** The rook's side to move may fork king and queen and draw.
**2. Stalemate.** Taking the rook can leave a lone king with no legal move: a draw.
**3. Pawns.** An advanced pawn can change the result; this method is for queen against rook alone.
Before each check, ask: can the rook then check and hit the queen?

steps.caption: White to move. The capture looks natural. Watch the black king after it.

line.say: Qxb1 wins the rook. Black's king on a8 now has no legal move.

claims.statement: White wins from here.
After Qxb1 the position is a draw.

steps.caption: The position after Qxb1, Black to move. The king is not in check and has no legal move: stalemate, so the game is drawn.

claims.statement: Black has no legal move and is not in check.

steps.prompt: Predict each result, then check. The next position changes the side to move; a third changes something that does not matter.
Which check would you most likely forget in a game: whose move it is, the stalemate capture, or a pawn on the board? Write one sentence on how you would remind yourself.

title: Queen against rook: win or fortress?
outcomes: In an unlabeled queen-against-rook position, predicts win or draw and finds the winning move where one exists
Recognises the verified drawn setup with the rook on a7, a pawn on b7 and the king beside them, and the changes that break it
Does not assume the extra queen wins by itself

steps.text: In **Queen against rook: force the king away from its rook** you separated rook and king. The new question comes first: can the queen win at all? The general fortress test is in **Fortresses: when more material cannot break through**. Here we only meet one queen-against-rook case where the tablebase says draw, and the changes that break it.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook on a7, the pawn on b7 and the king on c8 stand together. The tablebase says draw; Qh8+ keeps the draw.

line.say: Qh8+: check along the eighth rank.
Kd7: the king steps off the rank.
Qh3+: check along the diagonal to d7.
Kc7: the king steps next to the pawn.

claims.statement: With best play the position is a draw.
Qh8+ keeps the draw.
Qh3 keeps the draw.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The extra queen does not win by itself. In the verified examples the draw holds with the black king on c8 beside its rook and pawn and the white queen far away from them (on h1, d1 or e1). Put the king on b8 or far away, or the queen where it attacks the rook, and White wins. Rule of thumb: before you plan the separating check, ask whether rook, pawn and king stand together. These results are verified for these positions only.

steps.prompt: White is to move in each position. Predict the result, then check. Only one piece differs from the first.
Before each answer: did you ask if rook, pawn and king stand together, or did you start looking for checks? Which change surprised you?

title: Queen against rook: play it out within a budget
outcomes: Plays out queen against rook within a move budget against the tablebase, as the queen side
Holds the draw as the rook side when a check hits the queen and a king stands ready to recapture
Predicts win, draw or loss for the unlabeled position, including positions where the rook side wins or the queen wins despite the rook moving first

steps.text:
In **Queen against rook: force the king away from its rook** you learned the method. Here you **play it out** against the tablebase, where every move costs. A tablebase gives the result with best play, not how many moves a person needs, so you set a move budget yourself.
The extra queen does not win by itself: the rook's side has one trick besides the fortress of the last lesson, shown next.

steps.caption: Black, the side with the rook, to move. The queen is stronger, yet this is a draw. Step through the one resource: a check that skewers king and queen.

line.say: Ra3+ is check along the third rank. The queen stands behind the king on that rank, so when the king steps off the rank, the rook attacks the queen (a skewer).
The king steps off the rank to c2. The rook now attacks the queen, but the king stands next to it. Any king move that is not next to d3 loses the queen.
The rook takes the queen.
The king takes the rook. Only the two kings are left.

claims.statement: Black to move draws.
After Ra3+ the position is still a draw.
After Ra3+ Kc2 Rxd3 the white king recaptures on d3.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The rook's side draws when it has the move and gives a check that hits the queen, directly or after the king steps aside, leaving only bare kings. That needs the queen's king next to the capture square, so it can retake (as on the previous board). **When it fails:** the king does not cover that square, so the rook takes the queen for nothing; or no check hits the queen, so the queen's side keeps winning. Before each queen move, look for such a check.

steps.title: Same pieces, one change
steps.prompt: Predict each result, then check. The next position changes who moves; the third only reflects the board left to right.

steps.text: Now play against full-strength defence. **Plan before move one:** list the rook's checks, then pick a check that does not leave your queen where the rook can fork it. **Budget:** the move count shown is more than the tablebase's own distance to mate. If you have spent a third of it without winning the rook, stop and look for the check you missed.

steps.prompt: Which of your play-outs used most of its budget? Name the move after which the win became slow, and the check you would try first next time.

title: Which ending to enter: check the trade first
outcomes: Names the ending that a trade leads to and says whether it is a win, a draw or a loss
Sees that a winning position can turn into a draw by a trade into the wrong ending
Checks the ending that follows a trade before making it

steps.text: Before you trade, ask which ending you are entering. A trade is a choice of ending, not a safe default. Trade queens into a king-and-pawn ending and the result depends on where the kings stand. The question is not whether you are ahead, but whether the ending that follows is won. Here is a trade that works.

steps.caption: White to move. White trades queens and enters a king-and-pawn ending. The trade wins.

line.say: White takes the queen with check.
Black's king recaptures. Only kings and the e-pawn are left.
White's king goes to f6, ahead of the pawn.
Black's king goes to e8.
White's king goes to e6.
Black's king goes to f8.

claims.statement: Before the trade the tablebase result for White is a win.
After Qxd8+ the tablebase result for White is still a win.

steps.text: **Conditions.** A trade into a known ending is only as good as the ending. Rule of thumb: before simplifying, name the ending, find the kings and the pawn, and check the result. Misconceptions to drop: exchanging is not always safe, and it does not always kill winning chances. Predict: the same trade with the white king one step away, and with the black king elsewhere.

title: Which ending to enter: keep, avoid or force the queen trade
outcomes: In an unlabeled queen ending, names the ending the queen trade leads to and checks it before choosing
Separates three cases: the trade wins, the trade only draws, no move wins
Finds a move that keeps the win when the trade does not

steps.text: In **Which ending to enter: check the trade first** the trade was handed to you. Now nobody says it is there. Look for every queen trade, name the ending each leads to, check that ending, and compare it with keeping the queens on. The result is one of three: the trade wins, the trade only draws, or nothing wins at all.

steps.caption: White to move, with an extra pawn on f6. The trade Qxe6+ looks natural, but the ending after it is only a draw; f7 keeps the win.

line.say: Qxe6+: the queens come off with check.
Kxe6: Black recaptures with the king, next to the f6 pawn.

claims.statement: White to move wins.
The trade Qxe6+ gives up the win: the result is a draw.
f7 keeps the win.

steps.text: **The decision.** Rule of thumb: name the ending the trade leads to and check it first. If the trade wins, it is one winning move among others. If it only draws and another move wins, play the other move. If nothing wins, check that the trade does not lose. An extra pawn alone does not make a trade good; the king squares decided it. Verified for the positions shown.

title: Triangulation: a king detour that passes the move
outcomes: Explains triangulation: a king walk around three squares costs an odd number of moves and hands the move to the opponent
Finds the only winning first move in a king-and-pawn position and asks first whether the direct move already wins
Tells a position where the triangle wins from look-alikes where the defender has a spare move or where the move does not matter

steps.text: Sometimes the winning position is on the board, but the wrong player is to move. A king can pass the move. Stepping out and back takes **two** moves, and the opponent can answer with a two-move shuffle. Walking round a triangle of three squares takes **three**. That is **triangulation**: your king ends where it started and the opponent has to move.

steps.caption: Black to move, and Black loses: its king has one legal move. The same placement with White to move is only a draw (Ka5, Kb5 and Kb6 all let the win slip). Triangulation tries to reach a placement like this with the other side to move.

line.say: Black's only legal move: the king goes to b8.
Kb6 is the only winning reply for White. Ka5 and Kb5 would draw.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result is a loss for Black.
The black king on a8 has exactly one legal move.
After Kb8 Black is still lost.

steps.text: **When it works.** The three squares must be free and safe, and the defender must have no triangle or waiting move of his own. If he has one, he answers in kind and the draw is back. Rule of thumb: ask first whether the position would win with the opponent to move; if it would and you are to move, look for a triangle. Opposition stays the first tool.

title: Triangulation: decide before you walk the king
outcomes: Decides in a locked-pawn king ending whether the direct king step or a three-square detour keeps the win, by asking who would be to move

steps.text: In **Triangulation: a king detour that passes the move** you found the three-square detour when told to. Now decide *before* you move. Ask three questions. Which placement do I want, with the opponent to move? If I walk straight there, who is to move? Are the squares of a three-square walk free and safe? Next, a position where the direct step fails and the detour wins.

steps.caption: White to move; the pawns on f5 and f6 are locked. The direct step Ke6 loses, a quiet king move on d5 only draws, and Ke7 wins.

line.say: Ke7: the king steps away from e6 instead of onto it.
Black has to move its king; it cannot pass.
Ke6: the square of the direct step, now with Black to move.

claims.statement: White to move wins.
Ke7 keeps the win.
The direct step Ke6 loses.
Kd5 only draws.

steps.text: **When it works.** The detour wins only if the target placement exists, the three squares are free and safe, and the defender cannot also spare a move. Rule of thumb: first ask who is to move after the direct step; if that would be you in zugzwang, look for the detour. The tablebase results here are verified for these examples only. Why the drawn look-alikes draw is your question to answer: check whether Black has a move to spare. Opposition stays the first tool.

title: The wrong-coloured bishop: win or draw from the family
outcomes: In an unlabeled position with a rook pawn and a bishop, predicts win, draw or loss from the pawn file, the bishop's colour and the defender's king distance

steps.text: In **The wrong bishop: a rook pawn that cannot win** you learned why the corner draw exists. Now read an unlabeled position as a family. Check three features: the file of the pawn, the colour of the bishop against the queening square, and how far the defending king is from the corner. steps.caption: Black to move. A rook pawn on a5 and a bishop on c1 face the black king on d8. The tablebase says draw; Kc7 holds, Ke7 and Ke8 lose.

line.say: Kc7: the king heads for the queening corner.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The draw needs a rook pawn, a bishop that cannot cover the queening square, and a defending king near enough. Remove one and the result can change: a king one step further, or a bishop of the other colour. Rule of thumb: ask whether the defending king can reach b7 or b8 before the pawn reaches a7. In the board above the defender is to move, which gains him one move. Checked only on the examples here (Ke8 draws, Kf8 loses).

title: The wrong bishop: a rook pawn that cannot win
outcomes: Predicts win or draw for a rook pawn with a bishop, from the bishop's colour and the pawn's file
Names what can rescue a 'wrong bishop' win: another pawn file, or a defending king that cannot reach the corner
Tests a rook-pawn-and-bishop ending for the three conditions before predicting win or draw

steps.text: A bishop and a **rook pawn** (a- or h-file) do not always win. If the bishop cannot control the pawn's queening corner, a defending king that reaches that corner can draw. The colour of the bishop and the file of the pawn decide. Watch what the same set-up does with a different bishop or a different pawn.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop travels on dark squares; a8 is light. One line is shown.

line.say: The pawn advances.
Black's king steps next to the corner.
The pawn goes to a6.
Black's king goes back to the corner.
White tries a king move.

claims.statement: The position is a draw.

steps.text: **What decides it:** (1) the bishop's colour against the queening square, (2) the pawn's file, (3) whether Black's king can reach the corner in time. Change any one of them and the result can flip. Predict each look-alike first.

steps.title: Same bishop, other pawn
steps.prompt: The dark-squared bishop with a pawn on the b-file instead. Is it still a draw? Predict, then check.

steps.title: Same pawn, other bishop
steps.prompt: The a-pawn again, with a light-squared bishop. Is it still a draw? Predict, then check.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, and when it fails.** A rook pawn with a bishop that does not control the queening corner is a draw *if* the defending king can get to the corner. It fails when the defending king is cut off from the corner (the last position), when the pawn stands on another file, or when the bishop does control the corner. Check the king's distance before you trust the draw.

steps.text: **Zugzwang** means every move you have makes your position worse; you would rather pass. In some blocked pawn endings both sides are in zugzwang, so whoever has to move loses. Then the fight is about the move itself: the winner tries to reach that position with the other side to move.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Mutual zugzwang needs blocked pawns and no spare moves: only the kings can move. Then the side to move loses. It is a heuristic about such positions, not a law: when a king stands one step away, or has a detour that loses a move (**triangulation**), the move can be won back. Predict what changes.

steps.text: **What the lesson asks.** You will be able to say how a prepared line trades a wrecked pawn structure for active pieces, and why that can be fair. steps.text:
**Recap.**
- A pawn can buy time: pieces developed and pointed at a target.
- A defended pawn that attacks a piece can gain space, while the opponent has no pawn break to undermine it.
- Trade the piece that guards the key squares.
- Waiting is safe only if you know the break you are stopping.
- Being down in material is fine if their pieces cannot join the fight.
- Engine numbers move with depth: evidence, not proof.

steps.text: **What a quiet position looks like.** Neither side has a loose piece, a weak pawn or an open file to attack. When the engine reads a position as level, the player who wants more has to change something: the pawn structure, the piece placement or the number of pieces. Carlsen's game is a series of small changes of that kind, each rated close to level by the engine. [I]

In return, White's rooks get the half-open f-file, and Black has given up the bishop that had been aimed at f2. At depth 16 the engine reads the result as level, so the trade wins nothing yet; it only changes the structure. Before any trade, ask what it gives and what it costs.

This is not yet one side converting an edge: the engine rates each checked position up to move 31 as level or slightly better for one side. A common idea says the side that is ahead should trade, since a smaller army has fewer ways to counterattack [I]. The counter-case: trades also remove your attackers. Ask what is left after the last recapture.
