steps.text: **What the numbers say.** At depth 16 the engine reads the checked positions as level for long stretches: after the queen trade, around move 49 and at move 55. At that depth 55.Rf8 is at least a quarter-pawn below the best move, and 57.Rg8+ at least 0.3 pawns below it (claims above). So the win looks like a long squeeze of small slips, with Black's king and pawns gaining time while White's rook did not [I]. We checked only these moves, not every move.

**One plan for converting.** The last three decisions form a plan. First the king goes up to the pawns (58...Ke3). Then a pawn block stops White's rook attacking along the fourth rank (59...f4). Then a pawn break makes a passed pawn (60...h3, and the f-pawn runs). King up, rook free, passed pawn: ask which of the three is missing when you convert. [I]

steps.prompt: Write the one question you would ask before any trade. Then apply it to 23...Bxe3: what did the trade give, what did it cost, and what was left after the last recapture?

steps.text: **A model answer.** The question: what does this trade give me, what does it cost, and what does the position look like after the last recapture? Applied to 23...Bxe3: Black gave up the bishop aimed at f2 and got White's pawns doubled on e3 and e4, while White got the half-open f-file. The engine reads the result as level (depth 16), so the trade was fair, not a win. [I] Compare your own answer with this one.

**To remember.**
1. A level position changes only when someone changes the structure, the pieces or the trades.
2. Name what each trade gives and costs.
3. Trade only into an ending you have checked.
4. Count the pawns before you call a position better. A pawn up often needs activity, and usually a passed pawn, to win; the other side may win one back.
5. In rook endings, keep the rook active and bring the king forward.
6. Engine numbers are ratings at a depth, not proofs.

steps.text: **Two bishops, with conditions.** Capablanca held that two bishops nearly always beat two knights [V-sheet 8.3], and the usual advice is to open the position when you hold them [S]. Both are rules of thumb. [I] They work when lines are open, when the knights lack safe posts, and when pawns stand on both wings. They fail in locked positions, where a knight on a protected square can be the better piece.

steps.text: **The pair has a price.** Taking on f3 and recapturing with the g-pawn gives White the only pair of bishops, but also doubled f-pawns. Declining keeps Black's bishop and spares him the doubled pawns. Gain and cost roughly cancel, so the engine reads White as 0.4 to 1.1 pawns better either way [V]. That is why the bishop pair is a bonus to weigh against the pawn structure, not a verdict [I].

steps.text: **Recap.** Queens off does not mean nothing to do. Two bishops help most on open lines and when the knights have no safe posts. Count attackers and defenders on a square before you trade. An exchange up in a queenless position is a long task, not a finish. Next: Emanuel Lasker against Bauer, or Counting attackers and defenders.

steps.text: **Petrosian (White) against Spassky (Black)**, game 10 of the 1966 World Championship match in Moscow, 2 May 1966. Both kings castled kingside. In this lesson, the exchange means winning a rook for a bishop or knight, or losing one: you give about five points and get about three, so something on the board must pay the difference. You will play White at five moments and compare your move with the engine's first choice and the game. Engine numbers are evidence at a stated depth, not proof.

Black's g-pawn recaptures.
The knight goes back to d1.
The bishop goes to b2.
Black's bishop takes the bishop on b2.
White's queen takes it back.
White's g-pawn takes the pawn on f4.
Black's bishop on h3 attacks the rook on f1. Moving it is not forced. What would you lose if the bishop took it and your other rook took back?

line.say: The bishop goes to g4, on the diagonal through e6.
Black's knight takes the pawn on f4. It is attacked once and defended once.

After Bg4 exactly two white men attack e6 (the bishop and the pawn on d5).
At depth 16 the engine rates this position between 0.5 and 2 pawns better for White.

steps.caption: 24.Rxf4 Rxf4: the game move, and White has now given up both rooks.

line.say: The rook takes the knight on f4.

What did White get for the two rooks? Black's king has one pawn beside it, Be6+ is coming and White's pieces reach the king while Black's knight on a5 does not. That is the reason; the payoff is the attack, and it is not guaranteed.

At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 24.Rxf4 at least 2.5 pawns better for White.

Black's rook blocks on f7.

steps.text: **Count it the usual way.** After 25...Rf7, White has 23 points (queen, bishop, two knights, five pawns); Black has 27 (two rooks, queen, knight, five pawns). White is four behind, yet the engine at depth 16 rated the position before 25.Be6+ at least 2.5 pawns better for White. The count only adds up material, not where it stands. You can see Black's king with a single pawn beside it, and Black's knight on a5, far from the kingside. The engine weighs many such features; this lesson names two. Your move.

Black's rook takes the bishop.

steps.text: **What the game used.** **Counting attackers and defenders**: the bishop on e4 had two defenders, then one, then none. **Overloaded defender** (one piece guarding two things at once): after 22.g3 the queen on e2 defended both e4 and h2. **Removing a defender**: 22...Rxc3 took the knight. **Deflection**: 23...Rd2 attacked the queen, so taking the rook left e4 undefended. title: Which squares does a piece attack?
outcomes: Taps every square a rook, bishop, knight or pawn attacks when other pieces stand in the way
Stops a line at the first piece it meets

steps.text: A piece **attacks** a square if it could capture an enemy piece standing there. A rook, bishop or queen attacks along its line only up to the first piece it meets: it cannot see past it. The line stops at the first piece, friend or enemy. A square holding your own piece still counts as attacked: it means that piece is defended. Watch the rook.

steps.caption: The lit squares are every square the rook attacks. The pawn on d7 is one of them; d8 behind it is not.

line.say: The rook attacks d7, so it may capture the pawn. Nothing past the pawn is attacked.

claims.statement: The rook attacks exactly these 13 squares.
A black pawn stands on d7.
The rook can capture the pawn on d7.

steps.caption: The bishop's diagonal ends at the pawn on f6. The squares behind that pawn are not attacked.

line.say: The bishop captures on f6; g7 and h8 behind it were never attacked.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks exactly these nine squares, ending at f6.
The bishop can capture the pawn on f6.
The square g7 behind the pawn is not attacked.

steps.text: **Knights jump**, so nothing blocks them: they leap over the pieces beside them. **Pawns attack the two squares diagonally ahead**, even though they walk straight. The king attacks the squares around it, and the queen attacks like rook and bishop together.

steps.caption: A knight in the middle of an empty board attacks eight squares.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 attacks exactly eight squares.

steps.caption: The pawn can move only to e5, but it attacks d5 and f5.

claims.statement: The pawn can move only to e5.
The pawn attacks d5 and f5, not e5.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A pawn walks straight but attacks diagonally forward, so it attacks the two squares ahead on either side, whether or not it can move there. Move squares and attacked squares are the same only for pieces like the rook on an empty board; the pawn shows they can differ.

title: The board and its square names
outcomes: Taps a named square and names a square from its file and rank
Tells a file from a rank and says which one a name's letter and number stand for
Checks a board's orientation by square colour

steps.text: Every square has a name, like an address, so two players can talk about the same square. The board has eight columns called **files**, lettered **a** to **h** from White's left, and eight rows called **ranks**, numbered **1** to **8** from White's side. A name is the file letter first, then the rank number. The white king you just tapped stands on **e1**: the e-file, rank 1.

steps.caption: Worked example: where is the knight? Follow the f-file up from the bottom and rank 5 across from the left. They cross on **f5**. Letter first, then number.

On a physical board, is it the right way round? Square a1 is dark, so seen from White's side the light square is the bottom-right corner, h1. Dark in that corner means the board is turned the wrong way. (On screen the app draws it correctly for you.)

steps.prompt: Say it back. A friend asks you to find the square c6. In your own words, tell them where to look.

steps.text: **Compare with your answer.** Find the c-file, the third column from White's left, and rank 6, the sixth row up from White's side. The square where they cross is c6: letter first, number second. On a physical board, if the corner on your right is dark, turn the board first.

title: Naming squares fast, from either side
outcomes: Names a square pointed at on either side of the board without counting from the edge
Uses the square colour as a quick check on a name
Does not mirror squares when the board is turned

steps.text: In **The board and its square names** you learned that a square is its file letter, then its rank number. Now the aim is speed. Two habits replace counting. First, read the letter and number along the board's edge. Second, check the **colour** from the corner: a1 is dark, and colours alternate, so a square is dark when it is an even number of steps from a1 across and up added together (d4 is 3 across and 3 up, 6 steps, so dark). This holds on every square.

steps.caption: Naming squares by colour. The long line from a1 to h8 is all dark squares: a1, b2, c3, d4, e5, f6, g7, h8. Check d4: 3 steps across and 3 up from a1 is 6, even, so dark.

line.say: Now look at d4. It is dark, like a1: 3 steps across and 3 up is 6, even.

steps.text: Many boards and diagrams show letters and numbers, and many do not; this app's board can also be turned to Black's side. The skill is to name squares without needing the letters. The names stay with the squares, so only the picture changes. The common slip is to **mirror**: reading the square on screen as if White were looking, so b3 becomes g6. As a **rule of thumb**, find the letter on the edge first, then the number, and never copy the picture.

steps.title: One square, three ways of reading it
steps.prompt: The same white rook seen from White's side, seen from Black's side, and read by copying the picture as if White were looking. Predict first: which readings name the rook's square correctly?

steps.text: Limits of these checks. The colour test tells you a name is wrong, not which name is right: two dark squares both pass. It also cannot catch a board turned 180 degrees, because that keeps every square's colour, so use the corner check: a1 is dark at White's left, h1 is light at White's right. Both are **rules of thumb** for speed, so keep practising until naming is automatic.

steps.text: A **capture** is a move onto a square where an enemy piece stands: you remove it and your piece takes its place. Before you take, ask one question: **can the enemy take back?** A piece whose own side can take back on that square is called **defended**. Values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9.

steps.text: A piece is **defended** when a friendly piece could capture on its square and so take back. A piece nobody defends is **loose**, and taking it wins the piece unless the capture itself walks into something, so check that too. A black pawn captures down the board. The next board is the position you just tried: first the capture, then the answer.

steps.caption: The rook attacks the bishop on g5. The pawn on h6 defends it. The pawn on g6 stands in front of it but cannot capture on g5.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop for 3 points.
The h6 pawn recaptures. The g6 pawn could not have. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The bishop on e6 is loose: no black piece attacks that square. The knight can take it safely.

line.say: The knight takes the bishop and nothing can capture the knight there.
Nothing can retake here. White has won a bishop.

steps.text: A defender must be able to capture on that exact square, **using its own kind of move**. A pawn defends the two squares diagonally ahead of it. A knight defends by its jump, a bishop along its diagonals, a rook along its lines, and a queen both ways. A piece in the way blocks a line. Standing close counts for nothing. A **pinned** piece, one that cannot move without exposing its king, may be unable to recapture: check first.

steps.caption: A pawn defends diagonally forward. For Black, the pawn on d6 covers e5, so the knight is defended.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.

steps.text: You just **castled**: the king slid two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumped to the king's other side. Toward the h-file is **kingside** (written O-O), toward the a-file is **queenside** (O-O-O). Castling tucks the king away and brings a rook into play. It is never forced: you castle only when you want to.

steps.text:
Castling is allowed only when **all four** are true.
1. The king and that rook have never moved (a moved king ends castling on both sides; a moved rook only on its own side).
2. Every square between them is empty.
3. The king is not in check right now.
4. The king does not cross or land on an attacked square.
Squares only the rook crosses do not matter. Here is one failure of each.

steps.caption: The black rook on e8 looks straight down the e-file at the white king. Nothing stands between them, so White is in **check**.

steps.text: A king is in **check** when an enemy piece attacks it. You must answer at once, and there are exactly three ways: **move** the king to a safe square, **block** by putting a piece in between, or **capture** the checking piece. The king itself may capture the checker if nothing protects it. A knight's check cannot be blocked, since it jumps; then you must move or capture.

steps.text: When none of the three ways exists, it is **checkmate**: the game ends and the player in check loses. Look at the next board. White has a rook move that gives check.

steps.caption: Here White can win at once. Look at the black king and its own pawns.

steps.caption: The king's own pawns fill the squares in front of it, and the rook covers the rest of the back rank. No move for the king. Even h8 is covered: if the king stepped there, the rook would still see it along the row.

steps.text: Every position gets one of three labels. **Check**: the king is attacked, and it has a way out. **Checkmate**: the king is attacked and every way out is closed. **Neither**: the king is not attacked at all. steps.caption: Checkmate, questions in order. Attacked? Yes, by the rook along the eighth row. Can anything of Black's take the rook? No. Can anything step in the way? No. Does the king have a safe square? No: three pawns fill the front, and h8 is covered too, as the next board shows.

The king cannot step along the rook's line away from the rook. Once it leaves, the rook's line extends through its old square, so h8 is covered. Moving there is illegal. Learners often miss this and think the king has a flight square.

steps.text: These are the **four questions**, in this order. One: is the king attacked? If not, it is neither, and you stop. Two: can the checker be captured? Three: can something go in the way? Four: does the king have a safe square? Any yes after the first means only check. [I] The order runs from cheapest to dearest: a capture is one look, a block takes a search, king squares come last. It settles almost every position; double check is the exception.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Check, checkmate or neither?. This part covers When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Some positions look like check and are not. A piece beside the king is not always attacking it. A line with a piece in the way gives no check. A pawn attacks only diagonally forward. And a king that is not attacked but has no legal move is stalemate, also neither. Stalemate has its own lesson; in short, the side to move has no legal move and is not attacked, and the game is drawn.

steps.caption: The black knight stands right beside the white king, but a knight attacks by jumping to squares two and one away. It does not attack the king, so White is not in check.
This pawn stands straight in front of the king. Pawns attack the squares diagonally ahead of them, not straight ahead. Not check, and the king may even take it.

Two more look-alikes. The bishop is on the king's file, but a bishop attacks only along diagonals. The rook is on one of the king's diagonals, but a rook attacks only along rows and files. Neither attacks the king, so Black is not in check.
Black has no legal move, but the king is not attacked: the queen covers every square around it and does not attack it. That is stalemate, a draw. It is neither check nor checkmate.
Move the queen one square and the same pieces give checkmate instead of stalemate. Now the queen attacks the king, the white king guards her, and every other square is covered.

A gentler pin first. White is not in check, but the knight stands between the bishop and its king. A piece that cannot leave a line without exposing its own king is pinned. Every knight move is illegal.

Looks like check, not mate? The black queen can see the rook. But the white bishop looks along the diagonal at the king, with only the queen between. If she moves off it, the king would be attacked, so she may not take the rook. Checkmate.
Take the bishop away and the queen is free. She takes the rook and the check is over. Same check, a different answer.

line.say: The queen takes the checking rook. Nothing attacks the king now.

steps.text: A pinned piece is not free to move. It cannot take the checker, and it cannot block. So when you count ways out, count only legal moves. Check must be answered at once, and you may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked. The king obeys the same rule: it may not step onto an attacked square, nor take a guarded piece, nor go next to the enemy king.

steps.caption: Two kings can never stand next to each other, because each would attack the other. The white king cannot step to e2 or d2, beside the black king, though nothing else attacks those squares. Moving to f2 is fine.
A discovered check: White moves a piece, and the piece behind it gives check. Here the knight leaves the e-file, so the rook attacks the king. The knight need not give check itself.

steps.text: Picture a game where you leave a piece on a square and a pawn you never noticed takes it for free. Most lost pieces go this way: one attacker or defender was left uncounted. This lesson gives you a short habit that catches it.

steps.text: Every capture fight happens on one square. Count the **attackers**: the pieces that could capture there. Then count the **defenders**: the other side's pieces that could take back. Do both counts before you move anything. In the position above it is 2 against 1. The numbers alone do not give the answer, but without them you are guessing.
A **loose** piece is attacked and has no defender, so it can be taken for free. Count it as 1 against 0.

steps.title: Same count, different target and first capturer
steps.prompt: Again two attackers and one defender. This time the target is a pawn and the first attacker is a knight. Predict first: does the count still win?

steps.caption: One attacker, no defenders. This is the loose piece from earlier, seen as a count: 1 against 0.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Nothing can take back, so White wins 3 points.
Black cannot win the knight back. White is a knight ahead.

steps.caption: Count for your own piece too. Before the rook steps to d5, ask who attacks that square: the pawn on e6 does, and nothing of White's defends it.

line.say: The rook lands where a pawn attacks it and nothing defends it.
The pawn takes it for free. One look at the count would have stopped this.

steps.caption: Again 1 attacker, but now 1 defender, and the attacker is worth more than the target.

line.say: The rook takes a pawn: +1.
The defending pawn takes the rook: -5. White gave 5 points for 1.

steps.text: A fight on one square is a string of swaps: capture, take back, capture again. Each side may stop when the next capture would cost more than it wins. Add the points as you go, using the counting values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Those values are a rule of thumb [I], not the true worth of a piece.

steps.caption: Back to the opening position. The pawn goes first: the cheapest attacker.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: +3, and the cheapest White piece did it.
Black's pawn takes back: -1. White's running total is +2.
The knight takes the last pawn: +1. Total +3, and Black has no defender left.

steps.text: The first piece to capture is the one the defender takes. If it is worth more than what it captured, you start behind and need the last capture to win it back. So send your cheapest attacker first. [I] That is a rule of thumb; a pin or a hidden piece can change who is able to recapture.

steps.caption: The pawn on d5 is attacked by a pawn and a rook, and defended once. Start with the pawn.

line.say: The pawn takes a pawn: +1.
Black takes back: -1. Running total 0.
The rook takes the last pawn: +1. Nothing can take the rook, so White wins a pawn.

steps.caption: The same position, but the rook goes first. Same pieces, same squares, a different result.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn: +1, but now a rook stands where a pawn can take it.
Black's pawn takes the rook: -5. Running total -4.
White's pawn takes back: +1. Total -3. Two pawns won, a rook lost.

steps.text: Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, advised totalling what each side can capture with before starting, not playing the line out in your head. The boards here play it out so you can see each step; totals are the method to aim for. Znosko-Borovsky, in *The Middle Game in Chess*, counted attackers needed against defenders available around a king; the same habit of counting both sides first carries over to one square.

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting. This part covers Hidden helpers and false defenders; Stop in time. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: Two rooks doubled on the d-file. Only the front rook attacks the knight directly; the rear one waits behind it.

line.say: The front rook takes the knight: +3.
Black's rook takes back: -5. Total -2 for now.
The rear rook, which was hidden behind the first, takes again: +5. Total +3.

steps.caption: Take away the rear rook and nothing is left to take back. A lone rook against a defended knight loses.

line.say: The rook takes the knight: +3.
Black's rook takes back: -5. White is 2 points down and has no helper.

steps.text: A piece behind another on the same file, rank or diagonal can join in once the front one has gone, but only if it moves along that line: two rooks on a file, a queen behind a bishop on a diagonal. A rook behind a bishop on a diagonal does not. Count such pieces, and the same goes for the defending side.

steps.caption: Not a battery. The rook on a2 stands behind the bishop on the same diagonal, but a rook cannot move along a diagonal, so it never joins the fight on d5.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight: +3.
The pawn takes the bishop: -3. The rook behind could not take part.

steps.text: A defender only counts if it can really capture. A piece that is **pinned**, meaning it may not move because that would leave its own king in check, cannot take back. Edward Lasker warned in *Chess Strategy* that a defender can be an illusion for reasons like this. So after counting, ask about every defender: could it legally capture right now? A pin to the king makes a recapture illegal; a pin to a bigger piece only makes it costly.

steps.caption: The pawn on d7 looks like a defender of the knight. But the bishop on b5 pins it against the king.

line.say: The rook takes the knight with check. The d7 pawn cannot take back: moving would leave its king in check.
The king steps aside (Kf8 or Kd8). White has won a whole knight.

steps.text: The king can capture too, but never onto a square a defender guards. So a king is usually the last attacker or the last defender, and it counts only when nothing is left to take it back. Count it last.

steps.caption: The king touches the rook on d2, but the knight on b3 defends it. The king cannot take.

steps.text: You do not have to finish the swaps. After each capture, look at what is left and ask whether the next capture would give up more than it gains. If so, stop there. Counting well means knowing how many captures to make, not only how many are possible. Next: two attackers against two defenders, and White still comes out ahead.

steps.caption: Two attackers (pawn and rook), two defenders (pawn and rook). The target is a knight, and the pawn is the cheapest piece here.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: +3.
Black's pawn takes back: -1. White is 2 points up, and this is the place to stop.

steps.caption: Why stop? The pawn on d5 is attacked once and defended once, and White's attacker is a rook.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn: +1.
Black's rook takes back: -5. White would be 4 points down on this swap.

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Counting answers one question: what happens if captures start on this square? It says nothing about a threat elsewhere, such as an attack on your king. Check those separately. [H] My guess: most beginner counting errors come from forgetting one far-away attacker or defender, not from bad arithmetic. Test this on your own games and see if you agree.

**The method in four steps.** 1. Count the attackers and the defenders of the square, including pieces behind. 2. Check that each one could legally capture. 3. Add up the points, cheapest piece first. 4. Stop when the next capture makes the total worse. [I] The point values and cheapest-first are rules of thumb; they break with a pin, a king capture, or a rear piece that is not on the right line.

Next in this strand: removing a defender, where you chase off or capture the piece guarding a target so the count flips, and overloaded defenders, where one piece guards two things. Both start from the count you just learned. [H] My guess: once counting is automatic, spotting these two is the next jump in your tactics.

steps.prompt: In two sentences, tell a beginner how to decide whether to start captures on a square. Write it in your own words first. Then tick what you included.

fields.label: Count attackers and defenders, including pieces behind
Check each piece could really capture
Add points cheapest first and stop when it gets worse

steps.text: **Compare.** A model answer: to judge a fight over one square, I count the attackers and the defenders, including any hidden behind another piece. I check that each defender could really capture. Then I add up the swaps in points, cheapest piece first, and I stop when the next capture would lose more than it wins.

steps.prompt: Optional. Think of a capture you almost made in a recent game. Which piece was in danger, and what was the first thing you counted? Write one line.

steps.text: You just brought the rook home, and Black's king can do the same. Players sometimes shuffle without noticing. The rules answer with a **draw**: the game ends and nobody wins. Two situations lead there in this lesson: the *same position coming back*, and *a long stretch with no progress*. First, watch a shuffle on the board.

steps.caption: White is a rook ahead and could win, but shuffles instead. Watch where the pieces end up.

line.say: White moves the rook one step. Nothing is attacked; this is a waiting move.
Black's king steps sideways. It has little else to do.
The rook goes home.
The king goes home too. The starting position is back, White to move: its second appearance.

claims.statement: White to move wins in this position (tablebase).
The rook can step to a2.

steps.caption: The same four moves again. Count the appearances of the start: the beginning, after one round, after two.

line.say: The same waiting move.
The same reply.
Home again.
Second appearance of the starting position.
Once more, the rook steps out.
And the king answers.
The rook returns.
The starting position for the third time. White may claim a draw.

claims.statement: White to move wins in this position (tablebase).
The rook can step to a2.

steps.text: **Repetition:** when the same position appears for the third time, the player whose turn it is may **claim** a draw. To claim means to ask for it because the rules allow it; the game does not stop by itself. Here a claim comes once the count is reached. [R] Over a real board you may also claim on a move that would make it three; a reviewer is to check this against Article 9. At the fifth time the game ends on its own [S].

A repeat only counts when it is the **same position**. Three things must match: the pieces on the same squares, the same player to move, and the same **rights**. Rights are whether castling or capturing en passant is still allowed. Change any one and it is a new position. Watch each in turn.

steps.caption: Same squares, other player to move.

line.say: The rook steps out.
Black's king steps aside.
The rook goes a different way this time.
The king returns.
The rook is home. The pieces stand as at the start, but now Black must move: a different position.

claims.statement: After the five moves the rook is back on a1.
The rook can step to a2.

steps.caption: White may castle on the short side now. Watch what the rook's trip costs.

line.say: The rook leaves its corner. White can no longer castle on this side, even if the rook returns.
Black's king steps aside.
The rook comes home.
The king returns. The squares look like the start, but the right to castle is gone: a different position.

claims.statement: White can castle here, with the king moving to g1.
At the end the rook is back on h1.

steps.caption: A second right: capturing en passant. The white pawn jumps two squares past a black pawn.

line.say: The pawn jumps two squares and lands beside Black's pawn. Black may capture it in passing, but only on the very next move.
Black takes en passant. Had Black waited, the chance would be gone for good, and the position would then be different.

claims.statement: The pawn can jump two squares.
After the capture a black pawn stands on e3.
The white pawn is gone from e4.

steps.caption: Same pieces on the same squares twice. Only the first time can Black capture en passant.

line.say: The pawn jumps beside Black's pawn. Black may capture it in passing, right now. Remember this position.
Black declines, and the chance is gone for good.
White waits.
Black waits.
The same squares as after the jump, Black to move. But no capture exists now. The legal moves differ, so this is not the same position.

claims.statement: The pawn can jump two squares.
After the five moves the white pawn is still on e4.
The white king is back on e1.

steps.caption: Appearances do not need to follow one another. Here a different rook trip comes between the rounds.

line.say: The rook steps out.
The king steps aside.
The rook goes home.
Second appearance of the start.
Now a different trip: the rook slides along the first row.
Black's king takes another route.
The rook returns.
Third appearance, even with a detour in between. White may claim.

claims.statement: The rook can slide to b1.
At the end the king is back on e8.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Ways a game is drawn. This part covers The fifty-move clock. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The second way to a draw is **no progress**. Count in **half-moves**: one move by one player is one half-move. The count goes back to zero after any capture or any pawn move, because those change the game for good. When it reaches 100, which is fifty moves by each player, a player may claim a draw. This is the **fifty-move rule**.

steps.title: Does the clock go back to zero?
steps.prompt: Predict, then check.

steps.caption: Nothing is captured and no pawn moves, so every half-move adds one to the count. Say the clock aloud as you step.

line.say: Clock 1.
Clock 2.
Clock 3.
Clock 4. Even a changing position adds to the count when nothing is captured and no pawn moves.

claims.statement: The rook can step to a2.

steps.caption: The clock shows 40 here. Both kings walk, then the rook takes a loose pawn. Watch what the capture does to the count.

line.say: The white king steps. Clock 41.
The black king steps. Clock 42.
Clock 43.
Clock 44.
The rook takes the unprotected pawn. The count goes back to 0.

claims.statement: After the capture the rook stands on a5.
The king can step to d2.

steps.caption: The clock shows 0 after the capture. Black to move. A check is coming; does it reset the count?

line.say: Black's king steps. Clock 1.
The rook moves. Clock 2.
The king steps again. Clock 3.
The rook gives check. Clock 4: a check does not reset the count.

claims.statement: After the last move the black king on f6 is attacked, so it is a check.

steps.caption: The clock shows 30. Now a pawn moves. Watch the count.

line.say: A pawn move. The count goes back to 0.
Black's king steps. Clock 1.
The rook moves. Clock 2.
The king steps again. Clock 3.
The rook moves. Clock 4. Only the pawn move reset the count; nothing since has.

claims.statement: The pawn can advance to a4.
After the move the pawn stands on a4.

steps.text: At 100 half-moves a player whose turn it is **may** claim the draw. Until someone claims, play goes on. The player who is ahead may well prefer to play on. [S] At 150 half-moves the game ends without a claim, unless the last move is checkmate. A rules library agrees; a human reviewer still has to check the printed Laws.

**Claiming and agreeing.** To claim, you tell the arbiter or press the claim button on a screen. For agreement, one player offers and the other must accept; a declined offer changes nothing. [R] Details differ by event, and a reviewer is to check them against Article 9.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Ways a game is drawn. This part covers Use it or avoid it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The draw rules are tools. [H] A rule of thumb, not a law: the side that is **worse** asks 'can I make a position come back?', and the side that is **better** asks 'which different move improves my position?'. A side with a winning plan usually changes the plan; a side with no way to make progress may be happy to repeat. Watch a side that is behind use it.

steps.title: Can the checks go on forever?
steps.prompt: Predict, then check.

steps.caption: A lighter version first. Black's own pawns on g7 and h6 take squares from its king, so a single check leaves one square.

line.say: Check along the last row. The queen also covers g8, so only h7 is left.

claims.statement: After the queen checks, g8 is covered.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.caption: White is behind: three rooks against one queen. But the queen can check again and again. Checks that never end are called **perpetual check**.

line.say: Check along the last row. The queen also covers g8, so the king has one square: h7.
Black's king steps to h7.
Check again, along the diagonal. The king must move or block.
Black goes back to h8. The starting position has returned.
Check again.
Black steps to h7 again.
Check again.
The third appearance. White may claim a draw.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position as level, depth 16.
After Qe8 the queen attacks g8, so Black's king has only h7.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.caption: From the same start Black can also block with a pawn. The queen still has a new check each time.

line.say: Check on the last row.
The king steps.
Check on the diagonal.
Black blocks with the pawn.
A new check along the seventh row.
The king runs to g8.
Check again.
Back to h7.
Check again. In each line the queen finds a check [engine, depth 16].

claims.statement: The engine rates the starting position as level, depth 16.
After the block the queen checks on the seventh row.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.text: In these examples every reply Black has allows another check; the bishop on g8 took the checks away. [I] My reading, not a published rule. Perpetual check is not a separate rule: the draw comes from the repetition rule, or from a claim when the same position keeps returning.

steps.caption: Now the other side. White is the one ahead and wants to win. Repeating would allow a draw claim, so White changes the plan.

line.say: The rook takes the seventh row. Black's king is cut off from everything below it.
Black's king can only shuffle on the last row.
The white king starts walking up to help. Every move now creates a new position.
Black waits.
The king keeps walking.
Black waits again.
The king climbs further.
Nothing repeats. The king is on its way to help the rook finish the game.

claims.statement: White to move wins in this position (tablebase).
The rook can go to a7.
The white king can step to f2.

steps.text: Five ways to a draw, in one place. **Stalemate** and **too few pieces left to give mate**: the game ends by itself. **Agreement:** both players say yes. **Repetition** and the **fifty-move rule:** a player must claim. The next lesson on draws covers positions with too few pieces.

steps.caption: The first draw on the list needs no claim at all.

line.say: The queen takes the last escape square. Black is not in check and has no move: stalemate, and the game is over.

claims.statement: After Qc7 the black king has no legal move.
Qc7 is not checkmate.
After Qc7 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.caption: The same position, a different queen move. When you are winning, check before every move that the other king still has a move or is in check.

line.say: The queen checks along the last row and the king has nowhere to go: checkmate, not stalemate.

claims.statement: Qc8 is checkmate.
The queen can go to c8.

steps.text: **[H] A guess about why these rules exist.** Without a repetition rule, a worse side could shuffle for ever. Without a fifty-move rule, a side that cannot make progress could do the same. [I] Both rules seem to answer one question: how long may a game go on while nothing changes? Do you think they protect the stronger side or the weaker one? There is no checked answer.

steps.text: Part 4 of 4: Ways a game is drawn. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Say it back.** A position has repeated only when the pieces, whose turn it is and the rights all match, and the third time lets a player claim a draw. The half-move count resets after a capture or a pawn move, not after a check, and at 100 a player may claim. steps.prompt: Explain to a friend in three sentences why the third repeat lets you claim a draw, and why a check does not reset the 50-move count.

title: Sorting endings: won, drawn or play on
outcomes: Tells a position drawn at once for lack of material from one that is only drawn with best play
Recognises endings that look drawn but are won, such as king, bishop and knight against a king
Sorts a mixed ending into won, drawn now or play on

steps.text: **Ways a game is drawn** listed the ways a game ends drawn. This lesson sorts endings by material. There are three boxes. **Drawn now:** no sequence of legal moves can reach mate, so the game ends by rule. **Won:** the stronger side can force mate. **Play on:** mate is possible, but nobody can force it. Ask the questions in that order.

steps.caption: King and one bishop against a bare king.

claims.statement: With best play the position is a draw (tablebase).

steps.text: **What decides the box.** Pieces that cannot mate, like one bishop or one knight, give a draw at once. Bishops that all stay on one colour cannot mate either, but only when no knights, rooks, queens or pawns are on the board. But king, bishop and knight against a king is a **win**, and two knights against a king is not forced, yet not drawn by rule. Counting pieces is a **rule of thumb**: check colours and pawns.

line.say: The rook slides up the open file and attacks the king along the back row.

steps.text: **Checkmate** is a check that the king cannot escape. The game ends at once and the side giving it wins. In the last lessons you met the three ways out of check: move the king, capture the checker, or block. Checkmate is the case where all three are impossible. Next, the same mate frozen, so you can see why.

steps.caption: Frozen: Black to move and no legal move. Its own pawns fill the squares in front of the king. The rook's line runs through the king, so h8 is covered too.

steps.text: Before you say checkmate, ask three questions, in a good order. Can the king step to a safe square? Can the checking piece be captured? Can anything be put in between? If all three answers are no, it is checkmate. If two pieces give check at once, only a king move can answer. The mate you just saw is a **back-rank mate**: the back rank is the row where a side's pieces start, and the king's own pawns trap it there.

steps.caption: A second way out of a back-rank check: a block. The knight can jump between the rook and the king.

line.say: The rook checks along the back row.
The knight jumps in between. It is check answered, not mate.

steps.caption: A third way out: capture. Black has a rook on the back row, and the white rook is not defended.

line.say: The rook checks along the back row.
Black's rook takes it. The check is gone and White has lost its rook.

steps.caption: The queen checks from the square next to the black king. The white king also defends that square, so Black cannot take her.

line.say: The queen arrives next to the king. The white king defends her, so she cannot be taken.

steps.caption: Same queen move, but White's king is far away. Nothing defends the queen, so the black king captures her.

line.say: The queen checks, but she stands alone.

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Checkmate in one: finding the patterns. This part covers Two rooks; Queen and bishop; Knight mates. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Two rooks can mate with no help from pawns. One rook cuts off a whole row so the king cannot step onto it; the other checks along the edge row. Neither rook needs defending because the king cannot get near either.

steps.caption: Two rooks take turns. Whatever the king does on the back row, Ra8 is mate. Try Kh8 yourself.

line.say: The first rook takes the seventh row. This is not check, but the king cannot step onto that row.
The king can only shuffle along the back row.
The second rook checks. The first rook covers the row in front, so the king has no square.

steps.text: The queen can also be defended by a **bishop**. At the start of a game the pawn on f7 is guarded only by the king. If the queen and a bishop both aim there, the queen takes with check and the king cannot take back. Watch how a short game reaches that position.

steps.caption: A short game. The pawn on f7 is attacked twice by White and defended once, by the king.

line.say: White opens in the centre.
Black matches it.
The queen comes out and looks at the pawn on f7.
Black develops but does not notice the target.
The bishop comes out and aims at the same pawn.
Black attacks the queen and forgets about f7.

steps.caption: Now the queen takes. The bishop defends her, so the king cannot take her. d7, d8 and f8 hold Black's own pieces and the queen herself covers e7.

line.say: The queen takes with check. Checkmate: the bishop defends her.

steps.caption: Same idea, but the bishop is on b5 and does not aim at f7. The queen takes with check, and the king simply takes her.

line.say: The queen takes with check.
The king takes her. Nothing defended f7.

steps.caption: How does Black stop it? The queen and bishop both aim at f7. Defend it once more, or chase the queen away.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen, so she must move. The threat is gone.

steps.text: [I] Inference from the position: defend f7 once more (...Qe7 or ...Nh6) or chase the queen (...g6) and the mate disappears. Decent opponents do this, so treat the quick queen-and-bishop attack as a trap for careless players, not a plan.

A knight checks by jumping, so nothing can be put in its way. The defender may capture the knight or move the king. In a **smothered** mate the king's own pieces take away its squares and nothing can capture the knight: the king is boxed in by its own side.

steps.caption: The black king on a8 has a pawn on a7, a pawn on b7 and a rook on b8 around it.

line.say: The knight jumps to c7 and attacks the king. Its own pieces box the king in, and nothing can take the knight.

steps.caption: Remove the rook and the king has b8.

line.say: The knight checks.
The king steps to b8, the square the rook used to fill.

steps.text: When you look for mate, make a list of every check first. Then run the three questions on each. [H] My guess: most checks in a position are not mate, so listing them all beats stopping at the first. Next, one position with three checks: only one finishes the game.

Emanuel Lasker, in *Common Sense in Chess*, counted squares: a mate needs the king's own square and each neighbour controlled or blocked by the king's own pieces, up to nine, with the checking piece safe. [H] My guess, not a tested fact: beginners miss mates because they check one exit and stop. Say the three questions out loud every time.

steps.caption: White has three checks. The queen can go to e8, a8 or h7. Think about each before the next steps show it.
First check: a8. The black rook can block it.

line.say: The queen checks along the back row.
The rook blocks. Check answered, no mate.

steps.caption: Second check: h7. The queen takes a pawn, and the rook on h3 defends her. Still, the king has a square.

line.say: The queen takes on h7 with check. The white rook defends her.
The king steps away.

steps.caption: Third check: e8. The black rook cannot reach e8 or f8, and the pawns fill the king's squares.

line.say: The queen checks and the king has no square. Checkmate.

title: Is there a mate in one?
outcomes: Decides whether a mate in one exists in a mixed position, without being told
Lists the checks and tests each for king moves, capture and block

steps.text:
In **Checkmate in one: four patterns** you were told to look for a mate. Now nobody says whether one exists, and *no mate* is often the answer.

**Method.** 1) List every check you have: a move that is not a check cannot be mate. 2) Test each check on three escapes: the king moves, the checker is captured, the line is blocked. 3) If every check has an answer, say *no mate*.

steps.caption: Five checks, one mate. Test them one at a time.

line.say: Qc6 is the one check with no answer: the king's own pawns hold a7 and a5, and the queen covers the other squares.

steps.text:
*No mate* is a real answer. It is right when every check has an answer: a free square, a capture or a block.

**Rule of thumb:** if a mate looks easy but one defender stands next to the king, test again before you trust it. A piece that cannot reach the king's squares, the checking piece or the checking line does not change the answer.

title: Mates that need a closer look
outcomes: Finds a mate in one that uses a smothered king, a discovered or double check, or a promotion
Tests each check for king moves, capture and block before calling it mate
Rejects look-alikes that have a free square, a capture or a block

steps.text: In **Checkmate in one: four patterns** the mates were easy to see. Some need a closer look. First the **smothered mate**: a knight checks a king whose own pieces fill every neighbouring square. A knight's check cannot be blocked, so test two things: can the knight be captured, and does the king have a free square?

steps.caption: The king's own rook and pawns fill every square next to it.

line.say: Nc7 checks. Nothing captures the knight, and the king has no free square.

steps.text: **Discovered check:** a piece moves away and uncovers a check from the piece behind it. If the moving piece also checks, that is a **double check**, and only a king move answers it: capturing or blocking does not help. Test captures anyway: a knight that the king can simply take is no mate.

steps.caption: The knight stands on the bishop's diagonal.

line.say: Ng6 checks, and the bishop's diagonal is open too. Two checks; the king has no square.

steps.text: A **promotion** can be the checking move. The new piece decides whether it is mate, so test each choice: queen, rook, knight. A knight's check cannot be blocked and ignores pieces standing in the way, so a knight can mate where a queen does not.

steps.caption: The pawn can become a queen or a knight on f8.

line.say: The knight attacks h7 and nothing can take it. The king's own pieces fill g8, h8 and g7, and the white king covers g6 and h6.

steps.text:
These mates hold when, after the check, the king has no free square, the checker cannot be taken (for a double check, only a king move counts), and no piece can step in the way.

**Rule of thumb:** with a king boxed in by its own pieces, look first for a knight check, a discovered check or a promotion. It fails when one neighbouring square is open or a piece can interpose.

steps.text: You just played a written move. A **record** names two things: which piece moves, and the square where it lands. A pawn needs no letter, so a bare square name means a pawn moved there. The squares have the names you already know: file letter, then rank number. A game written as a list of records is a **score**.

steps.caption: A short score played from the start. Read each record first, then watch the move happen.

line.say: 1.e4: no letter, so a pawn moves, and it lands on e4.
1...e5: Black's pawn answers on e5. Still no letter, so still a pawn.
2.Nf3: N is the knight. It lands on f3 and now attacks the pawn on e5.
2...Nc6: Black's knight lands on c6 and defends the pawn on e5.
3.Bb5: B is the bishop. Its diagonal now points at the knight on c6.
3...a6: a pawn move again, so no letter. It attacks the bishop on b5 [I] and questions what White plans.

claims.statement: After Nf3 the knight attacks the pawn on e5.
After Bb5 the bishop attacks the knight on c6.
After a6 the black pawn attacks the bishop on b5.

steps.text: The other pieces get a capital letter in front of the square: **K** king, **Q** queen, **R** rook, **B** bishop, **N** knight. The knight borrows N because K is already the king. Try saying a record as a sentence: Nc3 is knight to c3. [H] Saying each record aloud this way may help you picture the move before you make it; test it on the next few.

Add an **x** when a piece is captured. For a piece, write its letter, then x, then the square: the bishop takes the knight on f6 is Bxf6. A pawn has no letter, so its capture starts with the file it came from. Two pawns may be able to take on the same square, and the file letter says which one.

steps.caption: Pawn captures start with a file letter. Watch which pawn takes each time.

line.say: 1.e4: a pawn to e4.
1...d5: Black's pawn answers and attacks the pawn on e4.
2.c4: a second white pawn. Now the pawns on c4 and e4 both attack d5.
2...e6: a second black defender of d5, so the pawn is guarded twice (pawn and queen).
3.cxd5: two pawns could take on d5, so the c says the c-pawn does it.
3...exd5: Black's e-pawn retakes. The record starts with the file it left, e.
4.exd5: now White's e-pawn takes. Same square, different file letter, different pawn.

claims.statement: After c4 two white pieces attack d5.
After e6 two black pieces defend d5.

steps.text: A **+** after a record means the move gives check. A **#** means checkmate, so the game ends. Neither mark changes which piece moves or where it lands; each only reports what the move did. Watch for the + on the next board, and for the # on the one after it.

steps.caption: A check is written with a +. Black must deal with it at once.

line.say: 1.e4: a pawn to e4. It opens the diagonal for White's queen.
1...f6: Black's f-pawn steps forward and opens the diagonal from e8 to h5.
2.Qh5+: the queen lands on h5 and attacks the king on e8. The + says check.
2...g6: Black answers the check by blocking with a pawn. A + asks for an answer.

claims.statement: After Qh5 the queen attacks the king on e8: check.

steps.caption: White to move, and one record ends the game. Read it piece by piece.

line.say: 4.Qxf7#: Q is the queen, x is the capture on f7, # is checkmate. The king has no escape.

claims.statement: Qxf7 is checkmate.

steps.text: Castling is one move that moves two pieces, so it has its own record. The king moves two squares and the rook goes to the square the king crossed. **O-O** means the short way, toward the h-file. **O-O-O** means the long way, toward the a-file. Use the capital letter O. It needs an unmoved king and rook and a safe path; the castling lesson covers that.

steps.caption: Short castling. Notice where the king and the rook end up.

line.say: O-O: the king moves two squares toward the h-file and the rook lands on f1, the square the king crossed. One record, two pieces.

claims.statement: White can castle toward the h-file.
The square g1 is empty before castling.

steps.caption: Long castling needs three empty squares between king and rook. Watch White clear them.

line.say: 1.d4: a pawn to d4. It opens a path for the queen and the bishop on c1.
1...d5: Black answers with a pawn to d5.
2.Nc3: the knight leaves b1, clearing one of the squares castling needs.
2...Nf6: Black's knight comes out toward the centre.
3.Bf4: the bishop leaves c1, clearing the next square.
3...e6: Black opens a path for the bishop on f8.
4.Qd2: the queen leaves d1, so b1, c1 and d1 are all empty.
4...Be7: Black's bishop steps out and Black will be ready to castle too.
5.O-O-O: castling the long way. The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1.

claims.statement: The first move, d4, is legal.
b1 is empty before castling.
c1 is empty before castling.
d1 is empty before castling.

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank it must become another piece. The record gives the landing square, an equals sign and the new piece's letter. So a8=Q means the pawn lands on a8 and turns into a queen. The record can name a queen, a rook, a bishop or a knight. A queen is usually strongest [H], but the choice is yours.

steps.caption: A pawn one step from the last rank. Read the record, then watch.

line.say: a8=Q: the pawn lands on a8 and becomes a queen. The =Q names what it turned into.

claims.statement: The pawn can promote to a queen on a8.

steps.text: A record must name exactly one move. When two pieces of the same kind can land on the same square, add where the mover starts: the file letter first, as in Nbd2. If both start on the same file, use the rank number instead, as in R1a3. Add the least that removes the doubt.

steps.text: One number covers White's move and Black's reply, as in 1.e4 e5. A score that starts with a Black move uses three dots. Marks such as **!** and **?** are a writer's opinion and never change the move. [R] Older books wrote moves another way, with phrases like king's knight to bishop three; today's books and apps use the file-and-rank style, which is in FIDE's rules, Appendix C.

line.say: 1...d5: three dots, because this score starts with Black's move. A pawn, so no letter.
2.c4: White attacks the pawn on d5 with a pawn.
2...e6: a pawn move, no letter. It defends d5 and opens a path for the bishop [I].
3.Nc3: N is the knight. Now two white pieces attack d5.
3...Nf6: Black's knight comes out and adds another defender of d5, three in all.
4.Bg5: the bishop comes out and attacks the knight on f6.
4...Be7: Black's bishop steps out; the knight on f6 stays defended.

steps.text: An **opening** is the first stretch of a game, roughly the first ten moves. Your pieces start boxed in behind the pawns, so most of them cannot move at all. The opening has one job: get your pieces out and your king safe before the fighting starts. The next board shows what is stuck at the start, and which single move frees two pieces.

line.say: One pawn move opens a diagonal for the bishop on f1 and another for the queen on d1.

steps.caption: After the centre pawn moves, the bishop on f1 reaches five squares and the queen on d1 reaches four.

steps.text: Part 2 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers The three habits. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The **centre** is the four middle squares: d4, e4, d5 and e5. Knights and bishops see the most squares from the middle (the next board shows a knight with eight against two). [I] That is why pawns and minor pieces are drawn there early. A pawn there also takes squares from the enemy and opens paths for your bishops and queen. That gives habit one: **start with a centre pawn**.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 reaches eight squares, the one on the h-file four, and the one in the corner two.

steps.text: What do the strongest players choose? Our own database holds 329,379 games between players rated 2500 or higher [V]. White's first move was e4 in 43% of them, d4 in 36%, Nf3 in 12% and c4 in 8%. The first two are centre pawns. [I] The other two fight for the centre from a distance, a second way to follow the same habit.

steps.caption: The d-pawn also opens a path, this time for the bishop on c1 and the queen on d1.

line.say: The bishop steps outside its own pawns to an active square instead of staying boxed in.

steps.text: To **develop** a piece means to bring it off its starting row to a square where it works. Habit two: bring out your knights and bishops, and bring out a new piece each time instead of moving one piece again and again. Capablanca (*Chess Fundamentals*) and Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*) both urged quick development, usually knights before bishops [S: our source sheets]. Treat it as a default.

steps.caption: Four moves, four pieces out. Each piece has a job.

line.say: The knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight too, and guards its pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black answers with the same idea and aims at f2.

steps.text: A **tempo** is one move of time. Count the moves, not just the pieces: if you spend two moves on one knight, your opponent has used the same two moves to bring out two pieces. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) treated development as teamwork, where the side ahead in it holds the initiative [S: our source sheet]. [I] Counting tempi is a rule of thumb, not a law: a second move is fine when it wins something or answers a threat. [H] Beginners notice lost tempi sooner when they count moves aloud.

steps.caption: Seven moves in. White has a knight, a bishop and a castled king working. Black has a pawn and one knight that went twice. Count the moves, not the pieces. [I] That gap is what players call losing time.

line.say: White opens with a centre pawn.
Black copies it.
A knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
A bishop comes out.
The same knight moves again. Black has used two moves on it.
White castles. Three pieces are working, against one for Black.

steps.title: Same knight, other square
steps.prompt: Both Nf3 and Nh3 bring the knight out. Predict first: do they work equally well?

steps.text: Part 3 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers Knights before bishops; Why castle; Black's side. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Knights before bishops** is a common default, with a reason. [I] A knight's good squares, such as f3 and c3, are clear early whatever your opponent does. A bishop's best diagonal depends on where the pawns end up, so it often pays to wait and see. In the next board the bishop has several plausible squares, and one reply with a pawn changes the question at once.

steps.caption: White's bishop can go to b5, c4 or e2, and Black's pawns decide which is best. After the bishop goes to b5, one pawn move asks it a question straight away.

line.say: The bishop attacks the knight that guards e5.
A pawn asks the bishop what it wants to do. The pawns have changed the question.

steps.text: The queen is strong, so it is tempting to send it out early. [I] A queen out alone often gets chased by smaller pieces, and each chase can cost you a move. An early queen is not refuted by force, though: it works if Black ignores the threat. The next boards show the chase, and then what happens when Black does ignore it.

steps.caption: White's queen moved twice. Black developed two knights, and a pawn push gained a tempo by attacking the queen. [I] Black is simply ahead in development. Queen to h5 is not refuted: it works only if Black ignores the threat.

line.say: White opens.
Black copies.
The queen comes out and eyes e5 and f7.
Black guards e5 and develops.
The bishop joins the queen against f7.
A pawn attacks the queen with tempo.
The queen retreats and still eyes f7. White has used the queen twice.
The knight develops and shuts the queen's line to f7.

steps.caption: White's queen and bishop both aim at the pawn on f7. Black has just developed a knight and ignored them.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn, protected by the bishop. The king cannot capture it and has no square: checkmate.

steps.caption: Black to move. Several moves hold: attack the queen (g6), or add a guard to f7 (Qe7, Nh6, Qf6). [V] Checked at depth 16.

line.say: A pawn attacks the queen, so White must move it.
The queen retreats and still aims at f7.
Now the knight develops and blocks the queen's line to f7.

steps.text: Habit three: **castle**. Castling is one move that does two jobs: the king goes two squares toward a corner, behind its pawn shelter, and the rook leaves the corner for the middle. It is allowed only if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check and does not cross or land on an attacked square. Castling toward the queen is slower [I].

steps.caption: White's knight is out but the bishop is still on f1, between the king and the rook.

line.say: The bishop leaves, so one blocker between king and rook is gone.
Black develops a bishop too.

steps.caption: Both squares between king and rook are empty now.

line.say: The king hops two squares to the corner and the rook lands next to it, closer to the centre files.

steps.text: The king hides best behind its pawns, but every pawn move in front of it is permanent and can open lines for enemy pieces. Before the next board, see if you can find the fastest checkmate there is. It works only because White moved the two pawns in front of its own king.

steps.caption: After 1.f3 e5 2.g4, Black plays Qh4 and it is checkmate.

line.say: The queen slides along the long diagonal and gives check. No piece can block or capture, and the king has no square.

steps.text: A king left in the middle is a target. In the next board Black has one piece out, the king is still on e8, and a bishop sacrifice has dragged it onto e7. A castled king sits behind three pawns, as in the model game later, and enemy pieces have to get past them first.

steps.caption: Black's king never castled and its pieces are undeveloped. The knight from c3 delivers checkmate. This is a well-known trap, usually called the Legal trap [R].

line.say: Checkmate: the knight on d5 gives check, and the bishop on f7 and knight on e5 cover every square.

steps.text: The same three habits work for Black; the pawns just point the other way. Against a queen-pawn start Black can answer with a centre pawn of its own, then develop knight and bishop, then castle. Against the king-pawn start Black often fights for the centre from the side with a c-pawn, which is the same habit seen from a distance [I]. The next board follows one calm Black game.

steps.caption: One calm game from Black's side: a centre pawn, a pawn to support it, a knight, a bishop, and castling.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn answers White's centre pawn.
White offers a pawn to pull the d-pawn away.
Black supports the pawn and opens the bishop on f8.
White develops a knight.
A knight comes out and watches the centre.
White pins the knight against the queen.
Black develops the bishop and unpins.
White opens the bishop on f1.
Habit three: Black castles.

steps.text: Part 4 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers When it does not apply; Put it together. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.title: Same move, different moment
steps.prompt: Black wants to play the developing move Bc5 in both cases. Predict first: is it equally good each time?

steps.text: A **threat** is a move your opponent could play next that wins material or gives checkmate. The three habits are for moments when nothing is threatened. When something is, deal with it first: capture the attacker, guard the target, move the target, or block the line. Here a threat appears in the middle of a normal opening.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop already aims at f7, which only the king guards.

line.say: The knight joins the attack. Now two White pieces aim at f7, and Black must respond.

steps.caption: If Black develops anyway, the knight takes the pawn on f7 and forks queen and rook. Black can win a pawn back with the bishop, but the position is difficult. [V] The engine calls it about -1.0 for Black at depth 16.

line.say: Black develops the bishop and ignores the threat.
The knight takes f7 and attacks the queen and the rook.
Black wins a pawn back with check, but the king and queen are both stuck.

steps.text: Habits have conditions. A piece that is attacked has to move, and moving a piece twice is fine when it saves the piece or keeps a strong diagonal. [I] The rule serves you; you do not serve the rule. The next boards follow one bishop that moves three times and loses nothing.

steps.caption: White's bishop has moved once. Black's pawn now asks it a question.

line.say: The bishop retreats but stays on the same diagonal.
The pawn attacks the bishop again.
The bishop retreats to a safe square on a diagonal that aims at f7.

steps.caption: The bishop has moved twice. [V] At depth 16 the engine's first choice is the retreat.

line.say: A third bishop move, but forced and useful: nothing is lost.

steps.text: Nimzowitsch, in *My System*, warned: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" [S: our source sheet, quotation checked]. He allowed one exception, a centre pawn taken without great danger [S]. [H] Beginners may lose more games by grabbing pawns than by forgetting to castle; our own game data could test that. Next time you play, count the moves you spend before castling and note any pawn you grab early.

steps.prompt: White to move. The knight on b1 and the rook on f1 have not joined the game yet. Before the questions, name the move you would play and the habit behind it.

steps.text: Now watch all three habits work together in one calm game. Each step gives the reason, not only the move. Notice the order: a centre pawn, a knight, a bishop, a supporting pawn, then castling.

steps.caption: A quiet game of the Italian opening, move by move.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn takes space and frees the bishop and the queen.
Black copies the idea.
A knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black mirrors the move and aims at f2.
A modest pawn move supports the centre pawn and opens a path for the bishop on c1.
The second knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e4.
White castles: the king is safe in the corner and the rook is closer to the centre.
Black supports its centre pawn and opens the bishop on c8.
White gets ready to push the d-pawn, which would give it two centre pawns. [I]
Black castles too. Both kings are safe. White has one knight out and Black two; the knight on b1 still has to join. [I]

steps.caption: Black has two knights and a bishop out and has castled. White has one knight and a bishop out and has castled, so White is a move behind in development. [V] The depth-16 evaluation is about +0.2 for White.

steps.text: After castling comes tidying up. Bring the last pieces out, then connect the rooks, meaning nothing stands between them, and place a rook on a file that matters. [I] The castled king here sits behind three pawns. [V] The engine finds h3, Re1 and the knight to d2 equal. When several moves are equal, choose by plan, such as preparing a centre push. [H] Naming your plan aloud each move may build the habit faster.

steps.text: **One possible answer.** A centre pawn takes space and frees a bishop and the queen. title: The pawn
outcomes: Moves a pawn one square forward, or two from its starting row, to reach a target
Captures one square diagonally forward and knows a piece straight ahead blocks a pawn
Says in one sentence how a pawn's walk and its capture differ

steps.title: Grab the star
steps.say: Move the pawn forward onto the star.

steps.text: A **pawn** moves straight forward, one square at a time, never backward. From its starting row it may move two squares in one go. These are White's pawns; Black's walk down the board the other way. Promotion and en passant come in later lessons.

steps.title: Grab the star
steps.say: Use the two-square first move.

steps.text: A pawn **captures** differently: one square **diagonally forward**, onto an enemy piece. The enemy piece stands on a star in the next boards.

steps.title: Capture to reach the star
steps.say: Take the rook diagonally.

steps.text: A pawn **cannot capture straight ahead**. A piece directly in front blocks it, and the pawn cannot walk around it. This includes the two-square first move: both squares ahead must be empty.

steps.caption: A knight stands straight ahead of the pawn. The pawn cannot move at all.
Same block, but now a rook stands on the forward diagonal. The pawn can take it.
The pawn is on its starting row, but a piece stands on the square just ahead. The two-square move is blocked too.

steps.prompt: Say it back in three short parts: one fact about walking, one about capturing, one about blocking. Then compare with the model answer.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A pawn walks straight forward, two squares from its starting row, but captures one square diagonally forward. A piece straight ahead blocks it.

title: The bishop
outcomes: Taps every square a bishop can reach, including captures and blocked diagonals
Says why a bishop can never reach a square of the other colour

steps.say: Slide the bishop to the star.
Two slides this time.

steps.text: A bishop slides any distance along a **diagonal**: a slanting line of squares that touch at their corners.

steps.say: The king blocks the diagonal. Find a way round.

steps.text: Like the rook, a bishop cannot jump. Its own piece blocks it. It may take an enemy piece by landing there.

steps.say: Take the pawn, then slide on.

steps.text: A bishop always stays on the colour it started on.

steps.caption: Stepping sideways flips the colour, and stepping up flips it again. A diagonal step does both, so the colour never changes.

claims.statement: A white bishop stands on c1.
The bishop can step to d2.
From c1 the bishop reaches exactly these squares, all on its two diagonals.

steps.caption: The c1 bishop is dark, the f1 bishop light. Together they reach every square, so keeping both is usually good; one alone reaches half.

claims.statement: A white bishop stands on the dark square c1.
A white bishop stands on the light square f1.
The bishop on c1 reaches exactly these dark squares.
The bishop on f1 reaches exactly these light squares.

steps.say: Your pawns box the bishop in. Free it, then reach the star.

steps.prompt: Say it back: how does a bishop move, and why can the bishop that starts on c1 never visit a light square?

steps.text: **Model answer.** A bishop slides along diagonals. Each diagonal step flips the colour twice, so the c1 bishop only ever lands on dark squares.

steps.say: One star is light, one is dark. Which bishop can reach which?

steps.text: The piece on e3 is a **bishop**. In a game nobody names a piece for you, so the first job is to say its name to yourself; the name gives you the rule. A bishop slides along **diagonals**, the slanting lines of squares, and it has four of them. The next four boards follow one diagonal each. Compare each with the squares you tapped.

steps.caption: Up and to the right the diagonal is clear: three squares, then the edge.

line.say: The bishop slides three squares to the edge of the board. Empty squares do not stop it.

steps.caption: Up and to the left the diagonal meets a black pawn.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn and stops on c5. The square b6 behind it stays out of reach.

steps.caption: Down and to the left the diagonal runs into the corner.

line.say: The bishop slides back two squares. Backward is as good as forward for a bishop.

steps.caption: Down and to the right a white piece stands in the way.

line.say: The bishop can step to f2, but g1 holds White's own king, so it must stop one square short.

steps.text: Two stopping rules cover almost everything. A piece of **your own** blocks the line, and the bishop stops one square before it. A piece of **the enemy** blocks it too, but you may capture it and stop there. Squares behind the piece are out of reach this move. [I] A pinned bishop, or one whose king is in check, can have fewer legal moves; a later lesson covers that.

steps.caption: Count the squares before you look: in the middle the bishop reaches thirteen squares along four long lines.

line.say: The bishop crosses two empty squares to g7 in a single move.

steps.caption: Count first: in the corner it has one line, seven squares. The same piece, much less to do.

line.say: All the way across the board in one move, but only along that one line.

steps.text: A bishop in the middle sees four long lines; in a corner it sees one. [H] My conjecture, not a sourced rule: when a bishop reaches very few squares, first look for your own pawns on its diagonals. Test it on the next boards. It says nothing yet about threats.

steps.text: In a real game nobody tells you which piece to think about, and the board is full. You already know how a rook slides. This lesson is about reading a crowded board without mistakes. First watch one worked example, then try a quiet board yourself.

steps.caption: A busier board. The white rook is on d4. Walk outward from it, one direction at a time, and stop at the first piece you meet.

claims.statement: The piece on d4 is a white rook.

steps.caption: Up. d5 is empty, then White's own pawn stands on d6.

line.say: The rook may stop on d5. Its own pawn on d6 is the first piece, so d6 and beyond are closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d5.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: Down. Nothing stands on d3, d2 or d1.

line.say: Three empty squares and then the edge: the rook can stop on any of them, even the last.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d3.
The rook can go to d1.

steps.caption: Left. c4 is empty, then a black knight stands on b4.

line.say: The first piece is an enemy knight, so the rook may take it. The slide ends there, and a4 is out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can go to c4.
The rook can take on b4.
The rook cannot go past the knight to a4.
A black knight stands on b4.

steps.caption: Right. e4 and f4 are empty, then White's own pawn stands on g4.

line.say: Two free squares. The rook stops on f4, one short of its own pawn. h4 behind the pawn is closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to f4.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: All together: eight squares. One up, three down, two left (one of them a capture), two right. The bishop on e5 and the pawns on g7 and h7 are on none of the rook's lines, so they change nothing.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

steps.caption: For comparison, the same rook on an empty board reaches fourteen squares. Every blocker on a line removes squares, so a busy board gives a smaller number.

claims.statement: On an empty board the rook on d4 reaches exactly these fourteen squares.

steps.text: **Three questions, in this order.** What piece is it? Which lines does it travel on? What is the first piece on each line: nothing, one of yours, or an enemy? A piece standing on a line is a **blocker**. [I] Walking outward line by line probably works better than scanning the whole board, because each line ends at its first piece.
Nobody will tell you the piece is a rook. A different piece takes a different walk, so name the piece before you draw a single line. Here is the same board again, with other pieces on d4.

steps.caption: A bishop on d4. It travels on diagonals, so the squares it reaches are not the rook's squares at all. Its own bishop on e5 closes one diagonal at once.

line.say: Up and to the left along the diagonal to the edge: three squares, a move no rook can make.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the bishop on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white bishop.

steps.caption: A knight on d4. It jumps in an L, and jumping ignores blockers. Eight squares, and not one is on the rook's lines.

line.say: The knight leaps two squares up and one across. What stands in between does not matter.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the knight on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white knight.

steps.caption: A queen on d4 does both jobs: all the rook's squares and all the bishop's squares, fifteen in total here. Name the piece and you know which lines to walk.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white queen.
