steps.text: Part 2 of 4: The rook in a busy position. This part covers What stops a rook. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The first piece on a line ends it. If it is yours, the rook stops one square short. If it is an enemy, the rook may take it and then stops there. It never goes through, and a piece beside the line, not on it, blocks nothing.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: A white knight now stands on e3. Predict first: can the rook still reach g3?

steps.caption: The white knight on a4 is the first piece on the a-file.

line.say: The rook can come up to a3. The knight is its own piece, so a4 is off limits and a5 to a8 are out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can go to a3.
The rook cannot land on its own knight.
The rook cannot reach a8.
A white knight stands on a4.

steps.caption: Now the first piece on the file is an enemy knight, with a black pawn behind it on a6.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Taking ends the slide, so the pawn on a6 is not reachable this move.

claims.statement: The rook can take on a4.
The rook cannot go past the knight.
The rook cannot reach the pawn behind the knight.
A black knight stands on a4.

steps.caption: The first piece can be right next to the rook. The black pawn on d5 is an enemy, so the rook may take it at once.

line.say: The nearest square is a capture. The slide ends there, so d6 and beyond stay out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can take on d5.
The rook cannot go past the pawn.
A black pawn stands on d5.

steps.caption: The black knight sits on d4, on neither of the rook's lines. The a-file is clear, so the rook goes all the way up. Only a piece on the line counts.

line.say: Seven squares up the file in one move. The knight is beside the rook's route, so it does not matter.

claims.statement: The rook can go from a1 to a8.
A black knight stands on d4.

steps.caption: A far target behind an enemy piece. The black pawn on c3 is the first piece on the c-file.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and the slide ends. It cannot carry on to c8.

claims.statement: The rook can take on c3.
The rook cannot reach c8.
A black pawn stands on c3.

steps.text: **Counting moves without a board.** Is the target on my rank or file? Is any piece on the line between? If nothing, one move. If one blocker is all that stops it, look for another line that reaches the same square: that is often two moves. [H] Beginners may miss a blocker mostly because they scan the line too fast; naming each square aloud may help.

steps.caption: The white knight on a4 blocks the a-file, so the top row is not reachable in one move. The rook sidesteps to a clear file. [I] A second blocker, or blockers on the neighbouring files, can make it three moves or more.

line.say: Step sideways onto the b-file. The rook does not need a2 or a3.
Black moves the king. Nothing changes on the b-file.
The b-file is clear all the way. Here one blocker cost one extra move.

claims.statement: The rook cannot reach a8 in one move.
After the sidestep, the rook on b1 attacks the whole b-file up to b8.

steps.caption: A common slip: trying to take your own pawn. The pawn on d5 is white, like the rook. The square is off limits.

line.say: Down is free. Up, the first piece is a friend, so the rook goes nowhere on that side.

claims.statement: The rook cannot take its own pawn.
The rook can go down to d3.

steps.caption: Another slip: turning a corner. A rook goes in one direction per move, so f6 takes two moves, never one.

line.say: First slide right along the rank.
Black's king moves.
Then slide up the f-file. Two moves, two straight lines.

claims.statement: The rook cannot reach f6 in one move.
The rook can slide to f4 first.

steps.caption: Pieces on your own side block too. The rook on a1 can only come up to a3, because the other white rook on a4 is its first piece.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on a1 can move to.

steps.caption: Friends can shut a rook in on one line and leave it free on the other. Here the knight and the bishop close the first rank, so only the d-file is open.

line.say: Six squares up the open file in one move. The rank gave it nothing, but the file is clear.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d1 can move to.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: The rook in a busy position. This part covers Blockers and what they mean; When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**A blocker has a colour, and the colour matters later.** An own piece on the line ends the slide, and the rook stands guard over it. An enemy piece on the line ends the slide too, and the rook attacks it. Same stop, opposite meaning. Watch both on a board.

steps.caption: The knight on d3 is White's own. The rook cannot take it, but the rook protects it: if an enemy piece took the knight, the rook could take back. The black pawn on d5 is behind the knight and out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 covers d2 and the own knight on d3, and nothing beyond.
The rook cannot capture its own knight.

steps.caption: Now the knight on d4 is Black's. The rook attacks it and may take it. Same line, same stop, but the blocker is a target instead of a friend.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and the slide ends on d4.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 attacks the knight on d4 and nothing beyond it.
The rook can take the knight on d4.

steps.caption: A trap for the line-walker. The white rook on c1 stands between its king and the black rook on a1. If it left the first rank, its king would be in check, so up the c-file is closed to it. It may only slide along the rank. It still sees the c-file; it is not allowed to use it.

claims.statement: These are exactly the legal squares of the pinned rook on c1.
The rook on c1 still attacks the whole c-file, pins ignored.
The pinned rook cannot move up the c-file.

steps.text: **Attacked is not the same as allowed.** A rook attacks every square up to its first blocker. It may only go to those squares if the move leaves its own king safe. [I] Counting a rook's squares first by lines, then asking whether its king is in the way, probably avoids most slips here. Sometimes the right answer is *none*, and sometimes the rook's lines are the wrong lines altogether. Look at a rook boxed in by its own side. One piece moving changes everything.

steps.caption: The rook in the corner has a pawn above it and a knight beside it: no legal move at all.

line.say: The knight moves away, which opens the first rank.
Black moves the king.
Now the rook has room: one piece out of the way gave it a line.

claims.statement: The rook on a1 has no legal move.
The piece on a1 is a white rook.

steps.caption: A hint of why we care. On a file with no pawns, the rook crosses the board in one move. [I] An open file lets a rook cross the board in one move, which is probably why open lines matter so much to rooks. A later lesson looks at this.

line.say: Six squares in one move, from the first rank to the seventh, because nothing stands on the file.

claims.statement: The rook can go from e1 to e7.

steps.caption: On an empty board a rook reaches fourteen squares from any square, corner or centre. Mobility depends on what stands on its lines, not on where the rook stands.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on a1 can move to.

title: Promotion: a pawn on the last rank
outcomes: Promotes a pawn to a queen when told
Promotes by capturing when the square ahead is blocked
Says when a pawn cannot promote on this move
Notices that a queen is not always the best choice (preview only)

steps.text: You just **promoted**. A pawn that reaches the far edge, the **last rank**, cannot stay a pawn: in the same move it becomes a **queen, rook, bishop or knight** of its own colour, your choice (never a king). The queen is the usual pick because it is the strongest piece. Watch a pawn make the last of the trip.

steps.caption: A lone pawn marches to the last rank and changes into a queen.

line.say: One step puts the pawn next to the last rank.
Black's king is too far from d8 to stop it.
The pawn reaches the last rank and becomes a queen.

claims.statement: The pawn can step forward.
After the march a white queen stands on d8.

steps.text: A pawn reaches the last rank by moving **straight ahead** onto an empty square, or by **capturing one step diagonally forward**. It never captures straight ahead. When a piece blocks the square in front, look at the two diagonals: an enemy piece there lets the pawn promote by capturing.

steps.caption: The knight still blocks the way, but now an enemy rook stands diagonally ahead.

line.say: The pawn captures the rook and becomes a queen in the same move.

claims.statement: The capture and promotion is legal.
The straight move is blocked by the knight.

steps.caption: This pawn is still two steps from the last rank. It needs two moves.

line.say: One step: the pawn is now on the rank before the last, but it has not promoted yet.
Black's king moves.
Only now does the pawn reach the last rank and promote.

claims.statement: The pawn cannot jump two squares from here.
It can step to c7.

steps.caption: Preview, not a rule to learn yet: the queen is only the usual choice. Here a knight gives checkmate, because it checks the king and covers b6 while Black's own pieces fill the other squares. A queen on c8 is not mate: Black still has moves.

line.say: Checkmate: the knight gives check, and the king has no square and no capture.

claims.statement: c7c8n is checkmate.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight in the same move. It gets there by moving straight onto an empty square or by capturing one step diagonally forward. A pawn two or more steps away needs more moves first. The queen is usual; the knight mate was a preview of another choice.

title: Can this pawn promote now?
outcomes: Says whether a pawn can promote on this move, straight ahead or by capture
Spots a pawn that is blocked ahead but can still promote by capturing
Does not count a pawn that is not yet on the seventh rank, or a capture of its own piece

steps.text: **Promotion: a pawn on the last rank** showed what a pawn becomes. This lesson asks an earlier question: **can it promote on this move?** A pawn promotes only when it moves to the last rank. It gets there straight ahead if that square is empty, or by capturing an enemy piece one square diagonally ahead. Check the square ahead first, then both diagonals.

steps.caption: The white pawn on d7 has three ways to reach the last rank: d8, c8 and e8.

line.say: The pawn takes the rook on c8 and becomes a queen.

claims.statement: The pawn on d7 can reach exactly c8, d8 and e8.

steps.text: **Three questions.** Is the pawn on the seventh rank (the second, for Black)? Is the square straight ahead empty? Is an **enemy** piece on a diagonal square ahead? If the first is a yes, a yes to the second or third means it can promote. Your own piece on a diagonal does not count, and a piece standing far from these three squares changes nothing.

title: Choosing the promotion piece

steps.text: You know how to promote from **Can this pawn promote now?**. The queen is the usual choice, and a later lesson shows rare positions where a knight is better. Here you learn two checks to run **before** you pick the piece: does the queen leave the enemy king with **no legal move and no check** (stalemate), and does some other piece give **checkmate** at once?

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn is about to promote and the black king stands on h6.

line.say: A queen covers g6, g7 and h7, and the white king covers g5 and h5. Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate.

claims.statement: Promoting to a queen only draws (tablebase).
Promoting to a rook still wins (tablebase).
After Qg8 the black king has no legal move.
After Qg8 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.text: **Check list.** Count the enemy king's legal moves after each promotion, and ask whether it is attacked. If, after a promotion, the enemy king would have no legal move and no check, that promotion is a draw. Try another piece: a rook often still wins, but run the same count on it too. Also look for a promotion that gives checkmate immediately. **Rule of thumb:** with no stalemate and no mate in sight, the queen is the safe choice. A boxed-in king is the warning sign.

steps.caption: Black's pawn jumps two squares, past the square White's pawn attacks. White gets one chance to answer.

line.say: Black's pawn jumps two squares and lands beside White's pawn, past the square White attacks.
White captures as if the pawn had stepped one square: it lands on d6 and the pawn on d5 is removed.

claims.statement: The jump to d5 is legal.

steps.text: That is **en passant**, French for 'in passing'. When a pawn jumps two squares and lands right **beside** an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved only one square, landing on the square the jumper passed over. It is optional. Ask three things about the last move: a pawn? two squares? beside my pawn? Three yeses: it is available, if it leaves your king safe.

steps.caption: The same for Black: White's pawn jumps two squares, and Black answers by capturing it in passing.

line.say: White's pawn jumps two squares and lands beside Black's pawn.
Black captures en passant: the pawn lands on e3 and the white pawn on e4 is removed.

claims.statement: The jump to e4 is legal.

steps.text: **Only right now.** The chance lasts for one move. Play something else and it is gone for good, even if the pawns do not change. It also needs a real jump: a pawn that steps only one square gives no en passant, even beside your pawn.

steps.caption: White ignores the chance and moves the king. A move later the chance is gone.

line.say: White plays a different move and does not capture.
Black replies. The pawn on d5 now stands beside White's pawn in an ordinary way: the chance has passed.

claims.statement: Capturing en passant is legal in this position, right now.

steps.caption: Black steps one square and lands beside White's pawn. A step is not a jump.

line.say: Black's pawn takes one step and lands beside White's pawn.
White's pawn can only walk ahead. There is no capture, because Black did not jump.

claims.statement: The one-step move is legal.

steps.text: **Your king still comes first.** En passant is a move like any other, so it may never leave your own king in check. Rarely, both pawns leave the same rank at once and open a line to your king. Then the capture is illegal, even with all three yeses. Check the king before you take.

**Model answer.** En passant is an optional pawn capture that exists only on the move right after an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside your pawn. You capture it as if it had stepped one square. If you wait, if it only stepped once, or if it was not beside your pawn, the chance is gone.

steps.caption: Now give White the move in the same arrangement. The queen travels up the open file.

steps.text:
**Stalemate:** the player to move is **not** in check and has **no legal move** with any piece. The game ends at once as a **draw**: nobody wins.
One question tells it from checkmate: is the king attacked right now? Yes means checkmate, no means stalemate. A king may never step onto a square an enemy piece attacks, so a king can be stuck even when its neighbouring squares are empty.

steps.title: One square, opposite results
steps.prompt: Black's king is on h8 in both positions, but White's pieces are arranged differently. On the left the white king is on g6 and the queen on f8; on the right the king is on f8 and the queen on g6. Predict first: is the right-hand result still checkmate?

steps.text: **Both things must be true.** A boxed-in king is not stalemated if any other piece of its side can still move, even a lone pawn. A pawn blocked by an enemy pawn directly in front has no push, and it can still move if it can capture something diagonally. Here it has neither. Stalemates often happen when one side is far ahead and moves quickly, so count the king's squares, and the other pieces' moves, before a quiet move.

steps.caption: Black to move. The king has no square, and Black's only other piece is a pawn that White's pawn blocks.

Black has no legal move.

line.say: Black's only legal move.
A quiet waiting move: the queen keeps the cage and still leaves the king one square.

claims.statement: At the start the black king has one move.
After the waiting move the king still has exactly one legal move.

steps.caption: Black to move again. The king still has exactly one square, and then the queen mates.

line.say: Again Black's only legal move.
Now the queen gives check with the escape squares covered: checkmate.

claims.statement: The black king has one move.
At the end the king has no legal move.
At the end the king is attacked, so it is checkmate.

steps.text: **Model answer, to compare with yours.** Stalemate is when the player to move is not in check but has no legal move with any piece; it is a draw. It differs from checkmate by one question: is the king attacked? Before a quiet move near the enemy king, count its moves, and count its other pieces too.

steps.text: You found the pawn that two white pieces attack. This is how a **threat** begins: a move your opponent could play next that would win material or give checkmate. Black to move. Step through what happens if Black ignores it.

line.say: Black develops a knight and does not notice what White is aiming at.

steps.text: A threat is only worth what it would gain. Znosko-Borovsky observed that a threat can pay off even if carrying it out would gain nothing, because the opponent must spend a move answering it. [H] Real threats against beginners usually do gain material, so treat every threat as real until you have checked.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn has just reached e5 and attacks the knight on f6.

line.say: Black develops and ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
Black recaptures, but has traded a knight for a pawn.

claims.statement: If Black ignores the pawn, White comes out ahead.
The knight on f6 is defended, so it is not loose.

steps.text: Notice that the knight was defended and still in trouble. Count what each side gives and takes in the exchange. When the attacker is worth less than the target, a defender does not save you; when it is worth the same or more, a defender usually does. Values are a rule of thumb: pawn 1, knight 3. Next, see how to answer the threat by moving away.

There are five answers to a threat. **Move away** the piece in danger. **Defend** it. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line between them. **Counter-attack** with a bigger threat of your own. List them all, then pick the one that leaves nothing else attacked. [I] The safest answer is usually the one that changes least.

steps.caption: The knight needs a square that no white piece attacks. Two of its squares are covered by the queen. White can chase the knight next move, but nothing is lost.

line.say: The knight steps to d5. No white piece attacks it there, so the threat is gone.

Second question: which of my own pieces is **loose**, attacked and not defended? A loose piece is the easiest thing for an opponent to win. In the next board the bishop on e4 is loose. Step through it and see Black's mistake.

steps.text: A useful picture: every piece of yours has a number of attackers and a number of defenders. In this course, loose means attacked and undefended. Many players use the word for any undefended piece, attacked or not. If the attacker is worth less than the target, even a defended piece can be in trouble. Now find the loose piece in a new position.

Before you play a move, imagine it already made and ask what your opponent can now take. Three leaks: **1.** the moved piece lands on an attacked square. **2.** the moved piece was guarding something. **3.** the move ignores a threat already there. The next boards show the first two.

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Before every move: two questions. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Your routine before every move: **1.** What does the last move threaten? **2.** Which of my pieces are loose? **3.** After my move, what can be taken? Capablanca names, in the notes to his own games, a time he missed an opponent's threat entirely. [I] The check is for everyone.

**Say it back.** Before I move, I ask what my opponent's last move threatens and whether any of my pieces is loose. If something is threatened I list my answers: move away, defend, capture the attacker, block, counter-attack. Then I imagine my own move and check what it leaves attacked. If nothing is threatened and nothing is loose, I carry on with my plan. After a game, I mark one moment where I was unsure.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Piece values: counting what you win and lose. This part covers Add and subtract. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Most captures are not free, because the other side can capture back. To judge a capture, **add what you take and subtract what you lose**. The result is the points you gain or lose in the swap. A swap that leaves you ahead is usually a good one when nothing else is going on, even if you lose a piece. Watch three swaps next.

steps.caption: A bishop can take a rook, but a pawn guards it. Add and subtract.

line.say: The bishop takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the bishop back: 3 points out. Five minus three is plus two.

claims.statement: White comes out at least 2 points ahead.
One pawn guards the rook.

steps.caption: Now the other way round. A queen can take a pawn, but a pawn guards it.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn: only 1 point in.
The pawn takes the queen: 9 points out. One minus nine is minus eight.

claims.statement: White ends the swap 8 points down.
The capture is a serious mistake.
One pawn guards the pawn.

steps.caption: A rook can take a rook, and a pawn guards it. Equal pieces cancel out.

line.say: The rook takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the rook back: 5 points out. Five minus five is zero: an even swap.

claims.statement: The swap is even.
One pawn guards the rook.

steps.caption: A small piece can take a big one. A pawn can take a knight, even though the queen takes the pawn back.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: 3 points in.
The queen takes the pawn: 1 point out. Three minus one is plus two.

claims.statement: White nets two points.
One queen guards the knight.

steps.caption: Longer swaps work the same way: keep a running total. A pawn is guarded by a rook, and White has two rooks lined up.

line.say: The first rook takes the pawn: running total plus 1.
The black rook takes it: minus 5, so minus 4.
The second rook takes the rook: plus 5, so plus 1. Black has nothing left to take with.

claims.statement: White nets one point.
One white rook attacks the pawn directly; the other stands behind it.
One black rook guards it.

steps.caption: Count attackers and defenders. White attacks d5 three times and Black guards it twice. The knight goes first: it is the cheapest attacker.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn: 1 in.
The pawn takes the knight: 3 out, running total minus 2.
A rook takes the pawn: 1 in, minus 1.
The black rook takes it: 5 out, minus 6.
The last rook takes the rook: 5 in. White ends one point down.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack d5 directly; the second rook backs up the first.
Two black pieces guard d5.
The whole sequence ends one point down.

steps.text: **Count, then decide.** List the attackers and defenders of the square, cheapest first. Either side may stop at any moment, so before each capture ask whether it improves your running total; if not, leave the rest. Three attackers against two defenders sounds like a win, yet the board above ends a point down.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Piece values: counting what you win and lose. This part covers Points, not pieces; When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Count **points**, not pieces. Giving a rook (5) to win a bishop and a knight (3 and 3) leaves you one point ahead, although you lose one piece and win two. Giving a queen (9) for two minor pieces (6) loses three points, although you win more pieces than you lose. The next board shows how the **order** of the captures changes what you give up.

steps.caption: Two pieces for one. Add the points, not the number of pieces, and send the cheaper piece in first.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight first: 3 points in.
The black bishop takes it back: 3 points out.
The rook takes the bishop: 3 more in. Three minus three plus three is plus three.

steps.text: Where do the numbers come from? [H] A guess: players wanted a sum they could do in their head, and the table fits that, since a queen is close to a rook plus a minor piece plus a pawn (9 against 5, 3 and 1). [S] Capablanca (1921) compared pieces in pairs, for example a rook as a minor piece plus about two pawns. [S] Edward Lasker (1915) saw how freely a piece can move as its real value.

Two honest limits. [I] A bishop and a knight share a number but are not identical: a bishop tends to be stronger in open positions, a knight in closed ones. [I] A common habit is to trade pieces when ahead in points and avoid trades when behind, because the lead becomes a larger share of what is left.

steps.text:
**Games with the same pawn structure tend to share plans.** Group games by their pawns, not the opening's name. Here White's d4 and e5 face Black's d5 and e6. Each pawn but the base is protected by the one behind: a chain, head e5 in front, base d4 behind.
**Rule of thumb:** the owner plays where the chain points (here the kingside); the other side attacks the base.

White advances. The pawns d4 and e5 now form a chain.

White's d4 pawn is the base of the chain: it protects e5 and no pawn protects it.
Black's d5 and e6 pawns are protected by pawns: a chain pointing the other way.
After ...c5 a black pawn attacks d4, the base.
After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5, the head.

steps.caption: Game A, after 3...c5: the fight over d4, move by move.

line.say: White adds a defender to d4. The chain now runs b2-c3-d4-e5, so its base is b2.
Black adds an attacker: the knight.

Black's queen joins the queenside.
A third defender of d4.

White recaptures. The chain stands again, with a second protector on f4.

steps.text: **The plan holds while the structure holds.** If the base falls, the head is exchanged, or a lever opens the position, the plans stop fitting; read the position on its own. Ask first: is the chain still there? A family holds more than one plan: Black can hit the chain at d4 with ...c5, hit the head with ...f6, or take space with ...c4. Which fits depends on the pieces.

steps.text:
**When a chance counts.** A legal move that works was there at the time, and the engine agrees. A chance that stays on the board counts once, as used if taken before it goes. A fork that fails (the forking piece is captured at a net loss) does not count.

title: Annotate your own game before the engine
outcomes: Marks at most three critical moments in his own game, with what he saw, expected and planned, before consulting an engine

steps.text: **Annotate before the engine.** An engine says what was best. Only you know what you saw. After a game, replay it and mark at most three **critical moments**: where you were unsure, thought a long time, were surprised, or changed your plan. For each, write what you saw, what you expected and what you planned. Only then ask an engine.

steps.prompt: Think of your last game. Before looking anything up, write down up to three moments you would mark. For each: what did you see, what did you expect your opponent to do, and what was your plan?

steps.text: To check your marks, use three bands for what a move cost, measured by an engine at a fixed depth: **routine** (many moves about as good), **slip** (costs half a pawn to a pawn and a half), **blunder** (costs two pawns or more). The cut-offs are my own choice, not a law, and a move that falls between two bands is simply in between. The bands are a measuring stick for the move, not a verdict on you.

The engine can show where the swing is. Only you can say which of the five it was. Write the question you would ask yourself, not a verdict.

steps.text: **The gap sentence** has three parts: *I marked it as ...; the engine measures it as ...; so the gap is ...* For example: 'I marked it as nothing; the engine measures a slip; so I under-rated a quiet capture.' **A pattern is more than one bad game.** Keep a ledger, one line per game, with the box for each mistake. Then count GAMES, not mistakes: four mistakes in one game are one game.
**Rule of thumb:** a box that appears in three or more of ten games is worth checking. That is a lead for a test, not a verdict on you.

steps.text: **What is not a pattern.** One very bad game: many mistakes, one game. A thin spread: each box once or twice, which looks like noise. **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The Progress page counts every press of a cause button, so one bad game or a changed mind can fill a box. It does not count games, and My games forgets your presses when you reopen a game: write each game's boxes on paper. My plan takes skills, not boxes. A games-per-box count is planned.

steps.text:
**A mistake has a cause, and the cause decides what to practise.** Five boxes:
**Not seen:** you never looked at their reply.

steps.text: **What one match can and cannot show.** It shows that in May 1997 a machine built by a company, and prepared against this opponent, won a six-game match: three draws, one win for the human, two for the machine. It does not show that machines beat every human, or that the machine understood chess. Six games and one opponent are a small sample, the hardware was special, and IBM was a party to the match [S, I].

steps.prompt: Decide: 'The 1997 match proved computers play chess better than every human.' Is that supported, partly supported, or not supported, and what would you need to see?

steps.text: **A fair reading [H].** The 1997 loss mattered less for chess than for how people felt about computers. The match was a cultural turning point more than a technical proof. You may disagree: a match with fair terms could have been more convincing.

steps.prompt: Do you agree that the match was more a cultural turning point than a technical proof? Give one reason for and one against.

steps.text: **Software and open engines [S].** The 2006 Bonn match was won by Deep Fritz, a commercial program. Stockfish is an open-source engine. Its version 12, released on 2 September 2020, made NNUE (a neural-network evaluation) its default [Stockfish blog]. The project's own post says version 12 won far more game pairs than it lost against version 11.

**The neural era [S].** The paper Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play was first submitted to arXiv on 5 December 2017 (arXiv 1712.01815). Leela Chess Zero was announced on 9 January 2018 as an open project built on the same idea and adapted from the Go program Leela Zero; it won the engine championship TCEC season 15 in May 2019 (Wikipedia). We quote no AlphaZero match score: we read only the abstract page, and the score has one source.

steps.text: **Two ways to look.** An engine does two jobs: it searches (tries moves ahead) and it evaluates (judges the position it reaches). Early programs leaned on search speed. Neural evaluation lets a modern engine judge a position well after fewer lookups. [I] That is our reading of the sources above, not a measurement. The next two boards show what a search that is too shallow can miss.

steps.text: **Why the shallow score failed.** Depth 2 sees the pawn about to queen and counts it as won. The corner h8 is a dark square and this bishop is light, so it can never cover the corner: Black's king shuffles and stalemate follows. Depth 2 is far shallower than any 1997 machine, so this shows only that a shallow search misreads fortresses, nothing about Deep Blue [I]. Depth 16 gives about +0.7: better, yet not the true result, a draw. The contrast is score versus tablebase.

steps.text: **Using this.** When an engine score and your own sense disagree, ask what the score is blind to: a fortress, a stalemate, a position that needs a long plan. A score is a summary of a search; the board is the evidence. Later lessons use engines the other way round: engine last, after you have found the idea yourself.

**What a club player faces.** Deep Blue was a special IBM machine [S]. The engine in this app is Stockfish 19 lite, running in your browser [V]. How the two would score against each other we have not measured, so we make no claim [H]. What matters for you: a free engine is a tool in your hands, so the habits in this lesson (test the score, read the source) are yours to use.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you give a date and a source? Did you say what one match cannot show? Did you give an example a friend could set up on a board (the fortress works)? Did you mark one claim as your own guess? If you cannot answer one of these, reopen the matching board. The app grades none of this; you are the reviewer.

**Recap.** 1996: human won, 4-2. 1997: machine won, 3.5-2.5, under IBM's own organisation. 2006: Deep Fritz beat Kramnik. 2017 to 2020: neural ideas reached open engines. One match is a small sample. Scores are depth-limited evidence; fortresses and stalemates show why. Sources can disagree with an engine, and then you test, you do not pick a winner.

title: Engines and humans 2: what engines see and what they miss
outcomes: States which of win, draw or hard to hold a fortress position is, using the bishop's colour and the pawn's file, and checks it with a tablebase

steps.text: **The question.** An engine's number feels like a fact. This lesson asks when it misleads a person: a *fortress* that a short search does not see, a *horizon* that hides the truth, a defence with many *only-moves*, and sacrifices whose worth no count shows. By the end you can say win, draw or hard to hold, and explain why the number alone could not tell you.

**An honest wrinkle [V].** The next board is a different case. There the engine does not show a big number, and its score rises with depth: +0.01, +0.15, +0.35 and +1.09 at depths 4, 8, 16 and 30, while the tablebase says draw. So a draw can hide behind a small or rising score as well as a big one.

steps.text: **Two words.** A *rook pawn* stands on the edge file (a or h). A *wrong-coloured bishop* travels on squares whose colour differs from the pawn's promotion corner. Here the corner a8 is light and this bishop is dark, so it can never cover the corner.

**The condition [S].** With a rook pawn and a wrong-coloured bishop, the defender draws if the king reaches the corner. Textbook geometry [S]. The same pieces with Black's king far away, on h8, are a tablebase win [V]. So the file of the pawn, the bishop's colour and where the defending king stands all matter.

steps.text: **A testable checklist [I].** A *fortress* is a position the stronger side cannot break however long it tries. Ask three questions. (1) Can a check also attack a second piece? If so, no fortress (the queen boards with the king on f8 and on e8). (2) Is every defending unit guarded by another or out of reach? (3) Does the defender have a safe spare move, or can zugzwang bite (the two pawn boards later)?

steps.text: **Other families [H].** Locked pawn chains can also form fortresses. This course has no tablebase-checked board for them yet, so treat that as an idea to test, not a result.

**What 'depth' counts [R].** In engine settings, depth N means the search looks N half-moves (plies) ahead along its main lines, and good engines look further on promising lines. From here on, 'depth N' always means that setting.

steps.prompt: Why might a shallow search rate this position above zero, while the tablebase says draw?

steps.text: **What the engine does [I].** An engine adds up material and piece activity at the end of its search. To see a draw it must see that every winning try fails, which can take many moves. A tablebase simply stores the answer for positions with few pieces.

**What we found [V].** In the queen-versus-rook fortresses, depth 4 to 8 gave +1 to +1.5 and depth 16 to 20 gave 0.00. In the bishop and rook-pawn position the score rose with depth, from +0.01 at depth 4 to +1.09 at depth 30, while the tablebase says draw. [I] A second depth helps in some families, not all; the tablebase is the check when it applies.

**Horizon effect.** The name comes from computer chess: a search that stops at a fixed depth cannot see what lies beyond it [R]. [I] Our fortress numbers are a related problem, the search stopping before the draw is visible, not the classic horizon effect, which is about delaying an unavoidable loss. Treat every number as 'this engine, this depth'.

steps.text: **Reading a score honestly [H].** A rough guide many players use, not tested here: 0.0 to +0.5 level, about +1 a small edge, +3 and above often winning. Whether +3 wins depends on the position type: fortress positions can read +3 at shallow depth and be drawn. Always note the engine and the depth.

**From score to chance [I].** 'Win probability' curves turn a score into a chance. One public formula, recalled and not re-checked [R], gives 50 + 50 x (2 / (1 + e^(-0.00368 x score in hundredths)) - 1) per cent. Worked here: +1.00 gives about 59%, +3.00 about 75%. The curve is a model fitted to games, not a fact about your position.

steps.text: **Disagreeing with the engine [H].** Where compensation comes from pressure and activity, a human's feel may beat a short search or fall short of a deep one. We do not know how often. steps.text: **Why the pawn step matters [I].** In the f7 board the only saving rook moves went to g6 and e6, squares the pawn on f7 guards. On f6 the pawn no longer guards them, so the rook has no safe shelter and the queen's checks fork it. The tablebase confirms the loss [V].

steps.prompt: In one sentence: why did moving Black's pawn a single step flip the result?

steps.text: **Common mistakes.** Three to watch. Trusting a plus score in a locked position. Giving up material in a fortress because it feels passive: the shelter needs those pieces where they are. Resigning a drawn game because the number looks big. [H] The last is the costliest, because nobody can punish it; you only lose the chance to learn the position.

**A real model case [H].** We have not yet read and checked a famous game where a misread evaluation or a mistaken resignation decided the result, so none is claimed here. Until that is done, the constructed example below is a teaching device, not history.

steps.text: **Three questions before you believe a number.** (1) Which engine and which depth, and does a second depth agree? (2) Is the position locked, or built on a few precise moves, so counting is the wrong tool? (3) What would a person need to do next, and could they? A number answers none of these. [H] Writing the three answers down is a habit worth building.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did I say when a big score can mislead (a fortress, a short search)? Did I say when it does not (a score over +3 that a tablebase also agrees with)? Did I give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did I name one mistake? Nothing here is graded; compare your answer with the lesson, not with a mark.

**Recap.** A big score can hide a fortress, and a small or rising score can hide one too. Bishop colour, the file of the pawn and where the defending king stands decide the corner. A second depth is one check, not a guarantee. Compensation is not in the count. A 0.00 can hide five only-moves. Write your view down before the engine's.

title: Engines and humans 3: using an engine to learn
outcomes: Writes a one-sentence verdict (move, threat, plan) for a position before asking an engine, then compares ideas before numbers
Reads an engine score with its sign, its depth and a mate score, and says in plain words who is better and by roughly how much
Reads an engine line by saying what each move threatens and what it stops, and says why the first move is advice and the rest evidence
Shows with two boards why the engine's best move is not always the best teaching move
Names one pattern behind three blunders (the capturing piece was a guard) and asks what a piece was doing before it captures or trades
Uses the app's Analysis page (lines, depth, whole-game analysis, next mistake, learn from your mistakes, show threats) inside a small review routine

steps.text: **Two moves, two ideas.** At depth 16 the engine put Re1 first, with h3, b4 and Nbd2 each within a tenth of a pawn [V, one run]. A gap that small is invisible in play. [I] Both are ordinary here: the number cannot choose, your reason can.

steps.text: **The question and the method.** Can you review a game engine-last, find the pattern behind a blunder, and read a score and a line the way a teacher would? Engine-last means: one, look and name a threat, a weak spot and a plan; two, write one sentence of why; three, only then ask the engine; four, compare ideas before numbers. That order is our own design decision, not a tested result.

steps.text: **Reading a score.** The number is pawns from White's side: plus one (100 centipawns) means White is about a pawn ahead, minus one means Black is. 'M3' means mate in three. 'Depth 16' means the main lines reached about sixteen half-moves; some go deeper, some shallower [R]. [I] Rough words: under half a pawn level, up to one and a half a small edge, up to three a clear edge, beyond that decisive.

**What a pawn is worth to a person.** The score assumes both sides play perfectly from here. *Win chance* turns it into odds: in the app's formula plus one pawn is about 59 per cent for White and plus three about 75 [V, arithmetic checked]. [I] For club players the practical chances are probably closer to level, since nobody plays perfectly. The marks ?!, ? and ?? later measure lost win chance.

In 26,506 (about 12 per cent of all hangingPiece puzzles) the reply takes a different piece the capturing piece had been guarding [V, our count]. Puzzles are chosen because a tactic exists: a catalogue of mistakes, not a frequency in play.

steps.text: **One question for all three.** Before a capture, a trade or a 'free pawn', ask: *what was this piece doing before it moved?* If the answer is 'guarding something', keep guarding, or make sure the guarded piece is safe another way. [I] The habit works because attention follows the prize; the question moves attention to what you give up.

**The Analysis page, step by step** [V, read in the app source on 30 Oct 2026]. Load a game as text, or set up a position. Choose how many lines and what depth. *Analyse whole game* scores every position at depth 12 and marks moves: ?! loses 10 to 20 points of win chance, ? 20 to 30, ?? 30 or more. *Next mistake* and *Learn from your mistakes* visit the ? and ?? moves only.

steps.text: **What others say.** As summarised on pages we could read, Jeremy Silman puts a tactical check first and treats engine output as the what, not the why [S]. Jacob Aagaard argues that serious errors often start at the very beginning of a calculation, when a candidate move is never considered [S, a reviewer's account]. Mark Dvoretsky's school stressed analysing your own games [R, from memory]. None of this tests engine-last review; they are directions to try.

steps.text: **Three habits that waste an engine.** One, shown above: playing its line without knowing why. Two: trusting a small plus in a quiet position; a score near plus one half is within what both sides can reach with sensible play [I]. Three: analysing only your losses. [H] Wins hide errors too. [H] Reading the engine's answer before trying may feel like learning without being so; this is our conjecture.

steps.prompt: Which of the three habits is yours? Write one sentence about the last time you did it.

fields.label: my habit, and the last time:

steps.text: **Where engines mislead.** Three cases. Depth: the same position gave -1.3 at depth 2 and a forced mate at depth 6 [V, earlier board]. Perfect play: the score assumes both sides play exactly, so a plus that needs ten precise moves may be worth little to you [I]. Fortresses: when the side ahead cannot make progress against best defence, a large number can hide a draw [R, endgame books; we did not check a position here].

**Compare ideas with several lines.** The Lines setting in Analysis shows more than one engine choice. Set it to 3 on the Ruy Lopez position from earlier and hide the scores in your mind. For each of the three first moves, write what it is for in one sentence. Then compare the ideas. [H] Choosing between ideas for your own reasons trains judgement more than reading which number is largest.

steps.prompt: Open the Ruy Lopez position in Analysis with Lines set to 3. Write the idea of each first move before you look at its score, then say which idea you prefer and why.

steps.text: **A weekly routine [H].** After a game that mattered: replay it without the engine and mark the moments you felt unsure (ten minutes). Run whole-game analysis and open only the three biggest swings, writing your sentence before each answer (ten minutes). Name the pattern in one word and add it to a list (two minutes). Once a week, pick one pattern to watch for. Cut any step you will not do.

steps.text: **Teach-back checklist.** Did you (1) ask your listener for a sentence before showing the engine, (2) name the pattern, (3) give one example they could set up on a board, (4) give one warning? A missing item is the one to practise.

**Recap.** Write before you ask; compare ideas, then numbers. The first move is advice, the rest is evidence. Before a capture ask what the piece was guarding. [H] Keep one habit: a sentence of why before the engine. **Check yourself:** minus means Black is better; depth is how far the search looked; for a line, say what each move threatens and stops; drop the habit you named.

title: Engines and humans 4: how people actually play and lose
outcomes: Explains why a model trained on human games can predict human moves, and names one limit of the claim
Tells the best move, the popular wrong move and the practical move apart in a position, with an engine check
Counts the good replies a move leaves the opponent and says why that is not the same as the evaluation
Names the kinds of error in his own games (piece left capturable, missed capture, quiet slip) and the phase where he makes most
States what the January 2013 sample can show and cannot show (no clocks, depth 8, online play)

steps.caption: Black to move after five moves of a well-known opening. Black can take the pawn back with the knight on f6, or send the other knight to a5. Which do most players choose, and which does the engine prefer? Decide first.

Taking the pawn back is at least 70 centipawns worse than the best move.

steps.prompt: Before the numbers: out of every 100 Black players rated under 1500, how many took the pawn back on d5?

steps.text: **Same position, three rating groups** [V]. In our January 2013 Lichess file (online games, not master chess), Black took the pawn back in 69 of 107 games under 1500, and in 71 of 128 between 1500 and 1899. At 1900 and up, 23 of 28 played the knight to a5; one took the pawn. The top group is small. [I] The capture looks like a free recapture: the choice of someone who looks one move ahead.

steps.caption: The popular move, and what it allows. White does not need the pawn; White offers a piece to pull Black's king out.

The king takes. Later boards show that declining the knight is worse.

steps.caption: The engine's move. Black does not take the pawn back at once; first the knight attacks the bishop.

White checks.
Black blocks the check with a pawn.
White takes.
Black recaptures, opening the b-file.
The bishop retreats.

steps.text: **Count the material** [V]. After the check, the pawn trade on c6 and the recapture, Black has not retaken on d5, so Black is one pawn down. [R] The move 5...Na5 is the Polerio Defence. The line 5...Nxd5 6.Nxf7 is the Fried Liver Attack. Search either name to find the theory.

**What Black gets for the pawn** [I]. Quick development of the remaining pieces, an open b-file after the recapture on c6, and a later push of the central pawn that hits the white knight. The engine rates the result about level, which is why it prefers this to the quick recapture. Material alone does not decide a position.

steps.caption: After the knight move and the check, Black has two good replies. A position with several good moves is forgiving: a small slip costs little here.

claims.statement: Both c6 and Bd7 are within 40 centipawns of the best move.
Nd7 is at least 100 centipawns worse than the best move.

steps.text: **The question.** Engines show the best move. People choose by habit, by what looks safe, by what they saw last week. This lesson asks three things: what does a *human-like* player look like, how does practical play differ from perfect play, and where do club players actually lose games? At the end you name your own two most common kinds of error.

**Perfect versus practical.** *Objective* play asks what happens if both sides play perfectly. *Practical* play asks how hard the next move is to find and how likely an error is. [H] A move that is slightly worse on the engine scale but leaves the opponent exactly one good reply can be the better choice against a person. The engine does not count how hard a move is.

steps.caption: Black to move after the knight sacrifice. The engine says White is only about one pawn better, not winning. Count how many accurate moves Black needs in a row.

line.say: The engine's choice; other tries, such as the queen to h4, lose far more.
White's queen checks.
The king must walk forward again.
White brings another piece.
Black attacks c2 and keeps the knight on d5 defended.
The bishop retreats to b3 and still eyes d5.

claims.statement: Taking the knight is the engine's choice.
Moving the queen to h4 instead is at least 250 centipawns worse.
White's edge is modest: between +0.6 and +1.8 at depth 16.

steps.caption: Black in check. The engine prefers Ke6 by a wide margin: every other legal reply costs at least 1.6 pawns more. [I] The king on e6 defends the knight on d5, which the queen and bishop attack.

claims.statement: Ke6 is the engine's choice.
Ke8 is at least 100 centipawns worse.
Qf6 is at least 100 centipawns worse.

steps.caption: Black to move, the third accurate move in a row: king capture, king walk, and now this. The natural knight move to d4 is about a pawn worse. Ncb4 threatens a knight check on c2 that forks the king and the rook on a1 [V by line].

claims.statement: Ncb4 is the engine's choice.
Nd4 is at least 80 centipawns worse.

Our file does not show how often defenders found them, so this is a guess about people. Would you play it as White against a 1200 player? Against a 2200 player? Give a reason that is not the engine number.

steps.title: Two different questions, one structure
steps.prompt: These two positions differ in White's last move (bishop to d2, or the pawn push), so this is not a one-feature test. Predict first: in which can Black afford a careless move? Then check.

steps.text: **Choosing a practical move** [H]. When two moves are within 0.4 pawn of each other on the engine scale (our threshold, not a law), count the replies that keep the balance after each. One reply means a real question. *Conditions:* both moves must be sound by the engine, the pawn push must not weaken your own king, and you must be able to meet the best defence. [H] Against a strong opponent the extra difficulty buys little.

**The Maia idea** [S]. McIlroy-Young, Sen, Kleinberg and Anderson (KDD 2020, arXiv 2006.01855) trained a network on online human games to predict the move a person would choose, not the best move. Their abstract says it predicts human moves much better than standard engines. As I recall, "human-like" means the model's top move matches the move played [R, not in the abstract]. The app's Maia covers 1100 to 1900 only [V: maia.ts].

steps.text: **Why a human-like model can work** [I]. In the positions you stepped, a large share of players chose the same move: 69 of 107, 40 of 70, 47 of 54 [V]. If one move gets 60 percent, a model that only guesses that move is right 60 percent of the time. That is the pattern Maia learns. [H] Test it yourself: play the Maia opponent and see whether its mistakes match the popular ones.

**What a human-like opponent offers.** This app has one: on the Play page, choose the Maia opponent and a rating from 1100 to 1900. It picks a move from what players near that rating would choose (it can also be set to take the most likely move) [V: Play page]. The first use downloads about 18 MB [V: maia.ts]. [H] That may be better practice than a weakened engine, whose moves no person would pick.

steps.prompt: [H] Play one game against the Maia opponent at your own level. Afterwards write one mistake it made that you recognise from human games.

steps.text: **How club players lose: the method** [V for the counts]. I took 600 games from the January 2013 Lichess file with both players rated 1000 to 1499, and 142 with both at 2000 or more. An engine rated each position at depth 8, a rough setting. An error is a drop of 200 centipawns or more. Only the first 50 moves; games under 20 moves and time forfeits left out; opening = first 10 moves; endgame = 30 points of pieces or fewer; lost positions (below -5) not counted.

steps.prompt: Predict: in which phase do 1000 to 1499 players make the most errors per move: the opening, the middlegame or the endgame?

steps.text:
**Errors per 1,000 moves, by phase** [V at depth 8, noisy]
Opening ▇▇▇ 60
Middlegame ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇ 156
Endgame ▇▇▇▇ 77
All phases: 104 for the 1000 to 1499 group (3,853 errors in 36,871 moves). The 2000-plus group: 46 (459 in 9,925): opening 7, middlegame 70, endgame 43. Only 142 games, so these swing more. Whether the middlegame lead holds at greater depth is untested.

**Kinds of error, 1000 to 1499** [V] (depth 8; rule-based labels, not hand-checked; they overlap)
Reply captures a piece ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇ 1,202
Quiet slip: all the rest ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇ 1,068
Best move was a capture or check ▇▇▇▇▇▇ 915
Reply captures a pawn ▇▇▇ 530
Allows mate ▇ 138
(3,853 errors, so 31, 28, 24, 14 and 4 percent, rounded.) Predict which fits your games best.

steps.caption: Pattern one, from a real game in our sample (both players under 1500): moving a piece that blocks a line. White to move. The two queens are on one diagonal with White's knight between them. Predict what happens if the knight moves.

line.say: The knight attacks the queen, but it was blocking the line between the two queens.
Black takes the white queen: nothing defended it.

claims.statement: Bd3 is the engine's choice.
Ng3 is at least 700 centipawns worse than the best move.
After Ng3 the queen on c2 is loose and White has no other loose piece.

steps.caption: The repair: Bd3 is the only move that keeps the balance (about +1.3 at depth 16; every other move is about 2 pawns worse). The bishop defends the knight and stands between the queens.

line.say: The bishop defends the knight and stands between the queens.
Black retreats the bishop, the engine's main reply.
The knight leaves the diagonal and opens the bishop's line to the black queen.
Black takes the knight.
The bishop takes the queen.
Black recaptures the bishop.

claims.statement: Bd3 is the engine's choice.
Nh4, the next-best move, is at least 150 centipawns worse than Bd3.

steps.text: **Why it happens** [I]. A piece that blocks a line is easy to forget. Before moving any piece, ask what it stands in front of. [S] Jacob Aagaard, as summarised by a reviewer of *Excelling at Chess Calculation* (2004), says serious errors often start when a key candidate move is overlooked. His point is the overlooked candidate; ours is the forgotten blocker, a related slip.

steps.caption: Pattern two, also from our sample: capturing with the wrong piece. White's queen has just checked on d7, and Black can take it two ways. The rook on d8 is defending the rook on f8. Predict which capture is wrong.

line.say: The rook takes, and the rook on f8 loses its defender.
White takes the rook with check.
Black blocks.
White takes the second rook.
Black recaptures: both of Black's rooks are gone, for a queen and a rook.

claims.statement: Kxd7 is the engine's choice.
Rxd7 is at least 700 centipawns worse than the best move.
One black piece (the rook on d8) defends the rook on f8.
One white piece (the rook on f1) attacks the rook on f8.

steps.caption: The right capture. Same queen, same file, different piece. Before taking, ask what the capturing piece is doing now.

line.say: The king takes the queen, and the rook on d8 still defends the rook on f8.
White takes the rook on f8 anyway.
Black recaptures: Black has taken a queen and a rook for one rook.

claims.statement: Kxd7 is the engine's choice.

steps.caption: Pattern three, also from our sample: a won position, then one careless move. Black is far ahead and the engine agrees. The knight on b8 is attacked. Predict the natural move, then step what it allows. Qb7 looks natural: it defends the knight and attacks the rook.

line.say: The queen defends the attacked knight and attacks the rook.
A knight fork of the king and the queen.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: Nd7, Ke7 and Qh2 are all within 110 centipawns of the best move.
Qb7 is at least 900 centipawns worse than the best move.
Before Qb7, Black stands at least +4 on the engine scale (White's view -4 or lower).

steps.caption: After the careless move: White to move. The knight check is the engine's move, and the evaluation has swung from Black far ahead to White far ahead.

claims.statement: Nd6+ is the engine's choice.
After Qb7 White stands at least +2 on the engine scale.

steps.caption: The repair. Before you move, list every check and capture White has: the knight on c4 can check on d6. That makes a queen on b7 unsafe, and the knight on b8 must still be saved. Step the safe move.

line.say: The knight leaves the attack and no white check wins anything.

claims.statement: Nd7 is within 110 centipawns of the best move.

steps.text: **Winning positions lose too** [V]. After one of its own moves, a side stood at +3 or better 849 times (counted per side per game) in the 1000 to 1499 sample: it won 575 (68 percent), drew 36, lost 238. At 2000 and up the same figure is 129 of 163 (79 percent). Depth 8 is noisy, so some of these +3 scores are false. In 567 of the 600 games one side made a 300-centipawn error first; that side lost 360 times (63 percent).

**The leader drifts** [S]. Capablanca's Havana example in his book (sections 27 and 28) shows a side ahead drifting into inaccurate moves [V-sheet]. The habit that helps: when ahead, keep asking what the opponent threatens, as you did when behind.

**Time pressure: what the data cannot say.** The 2013 file records the time control, not the clock on each move [V]. Fast games (3 minutes or less per side, estimated as the clock plus 40 moves of increment) against slow ones (8 minutes or more): 102 against 106 errors per 1,000 moves. Time forfeits are not in the sample. [H] Time pressure probably matters, but a game-level label cannot show it. [S via Wikipedia, original unread] Kotov described a calculation trap: too many lines, then too little time.

steps.text: **Common mistakes about engines and your errors.** First: believing every red mark means you are bad at chess. [I] Most players have two or three recurring error types, and a long list of flagged moves hides them. Second: ignoring the errors that repeat and studying the one-off blunders. [H] Fixing the top two repeating types probably gains more than learning a new opening. Test it: after ten games, count the kinds again in Games review.

steps.prompt: Teach it back, second part. In three sentences, explain to a friend why the most popular move is sometimes not the best move. Then compare with the model answer on the next card.

steps.text: **Model answer** [I]. The popular move is what many people see first, often a quick recapture or a natural developing move. The best move comes from looking deeper, where the natural move can hide a sacrifice or a fork. So popular tells you what people see; best tells you what holds up.

**Self-check, then recap.** Did you name the phase where you lose most, separate a piece left capturable from a quiet slip, give a position for each, and write one question for every move?
**Remember:** players of different strength choose differently [V]; difficulty matters [H]; errors repeat by kind [I]; the middlegame holds most errors [V at depth 8, noisy]; winning positions get lost [V]; review the first big error.

title: Engines and humans 5: top players, centaurs and your own habits
outcomes: Explains how preparation, advanced chess, freestyle and correspondence chess use engines, naming the source for each fact
Reads a Berlin endgame structure and says why the position limits attacks
Chooses between equal engine moves by asking what plan each starts, and says what to do when the opponent leaves the prepared line
Shows a fortress where material misleads, using a tablebase result

steps.text: **What the data says [V].** Of 4,911 games in which White castled on move four, 4,874 saw Black take the e-pawn. Then 2,263 pushed the d-pawn, 2,240 reached the knight retreat, 1,270 took on c6, and 1,243 reached the queenless position: about one in four of the castling games. Several later moves are forced recaptures, so repeating a line does not prove preparation [I]; that strong players chose it so often suggests it [H]. What is left for a human to decide?

steps.text: **The wall.** With the queens off, nobody has a direct mating attack on Black's king, and White's four-against-three kingside majority needs many moves to create a passed pawn [I]. Black's bishop pair is a lasting asset [I], and the engine rates the position as level [V]. The setup is nicknamed the Berlin Wall [R]. Wikipedia's page on the Berlin Defence says Kramnik played it in four games of his 2000 match with Kasparov, all drawn [R: recalled, not rechecked here].

steps.text: **Preparation is memory plus a reason.** Players keep files of engine-checked lines, and a *novelty* is the first move that leaves the files [R]. If you only remember moves, you have nothing to ask; if you know what each side wants, you can still make a plan.

steps.text: **What this lesson does and does not claim.** It gives a formula you can compute, and a few dates, each with its sources. It makes **no** claim about chess positions, and it says nothing about whether faster time limits made play better or worse: we have no two sources for that. Where sources disagree, we say so.

**The Elo expected score.** According to Wikipedia's article on the Elo rating system, player A (rating R_A) against B (rating R_B) has expected score E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B - R_A)/400)); a win counts 1, a draw 0.5. The FIDE Handbook (section 8.1.2) tabulates .64 for the higher-rated player at about 100 points difference and .76 at about 200. The formula gives 0.640 and 0.760: they agree there.

steps.text: **Dates for ratings.** According to Wikipedia's article on the Elo rating system and to the World Chess Hall of Fame's page on Arpad Elo, the US Chess Federation adopted his system in 1960 and FIDE adopted it in 1970. Wikipedia's article on the FIDE rating gives 1970 as well. Neither source is used here for how the calculation has changed since.

**Dates for clocks.** According to Wikipedia's article on the chess clock and to a Chess.com user blog post (GeneralSalesTax), a clock was first used in a tournament at London in 1883, and Bobby Fischer's increment clock was first used in the 1992 Fischer-Spassky match. Google Patents lists his application as filed on 5 August 1988. An **increment** is time added after each move. Both are secondary and may share a source, so treat 1883 and 1992 as less firmly established than the dates above.

title: How the rules took shape: reading dates with care
outcomes: Names three rule changes (queen and bishop, stalemate, fifty-move rule) with each date's source, and whether one source or two give it

steps.text: **What this lesson does and does not claim.** It reports a few dates about the rules, each with its source. Where two sources I read agree, I say so; where only one gives a date, the card says so. It gives no stories, no quotes and no opinions on whether a rule is better. Historical claims cannot be checked by the engine, so you will practise asking: who says this, what do they actually show, and what is missing?

**The queen and bishop.** According to Wikipedia (History of chess), they stayed weak until between 1475 and 1500, when their modern moves started in Spain, in the Kingdom of Valencia. According to the Valencia Chess History Society, the poem *Scachs d'amor*, composed around 1475 in Valencia, is the earliest known text describing the modern rules. Neither source dates the bishop's change separately. Both are secondary sources. The sources I read give no shared date for castling or en passant, so none is given.

steps.text: **Stalemate: the old rule.** According to John McCrary (US Chess, 2021) and Edward Winter (chesshistory.com), Arthur Saul's 1614 book treated stalemate as a loss for the player who gives it. Pratt still defended that view in 1805 (McCrary) or 1806 (Winter): the sources differ by a year, so I give both.

**Stalemate: when it changed.** Winter alone gives about 1807 for clubs dropping the loss rule, and McCrary alone gives 1808 for English books proposing a draw. McCrary adds that it was a draw everywhere by the mid-1800s. Treat each of those dates as a lead, not a settled fact.

steps.text: **The fifty-move rule.** Wikipedia and chessbio.com agree that FIDE abolished the longer-limit exceptions in 1992. Only Wikipedia gives 1561 (Ruy López) for the rule's introduction. A separate automatic 75-move draw also exists; the only date I found for it, 1 July 2014, comes from chessprogramming.org alone.

steps.text: **How to read such claims.** A date from one source is a lead, not a fact. Two sources that copy each other count as one. 'Around' and 'between' mark real uncertainty, so keep them when you repeat a claim. Where sources disagree, say so. For further reading, the Library holds public-domain chess books from the 1800s and early 1900s; they are old sources, so read them as evidence of what was written then.

title: Down material: what are you getting for it?
outcomes: Counts material first, pawns and pieces for both sides

steps.text:
A **gambit** gives up a pawn or more. It can be sound if it buys **compensation**: something durable such as a lead in development, open lines toward the king, a safer king or the initiative.
Name what you got, and how long it lasts. In this course 'sound' means the engine at depth 16 rates the side within half a pawn of level; 'practical chances only' means more than half a pawn behind but less than three; anything worse is simply bad.

steps.caption: Black to move. White is two pawns down (6 pawns against 8) and has castled; White gave one pawn on move four and another on move six.

cxd4 wins a pawn back. The b- and c-files are now half-open for White's rooks.
Black strikes in the centre at once. If White cannot keep the files open and the centre alive, the compensation fades.
exd5 takes it. White's compensation is the centre and open b- and c-files, not a lead in development: Nb1 and Bc1 have not moved. Engine, depth 16: about level.

steps.text:
**Compensation runs on a clock.** A lead in development shrinks each time the opponent develops a piece or castles. Count the moves the opponent still needs to catch up, and ask whether you can make threats faster than that.
The next board shows a different gambit, also a pawn down, after slow moves by White.

Black gains space on the queenside.

steps.text:
**When it holds.** The compensation is real if what you gave buys something that outlasts the opponent's next few moves. **It fails** when lines are closed, when the opponent has already developed, or when the engine rates you more than half a pawn behind.
**Rule of thumb:** give material back only for something tangible. The engine verdict is evidence at one depth, not proof.

steps.text:
In this course a **threat** is a move that would win material or mate if the other side did nothing. The **initiative** belongs to the side whose moves carry threats the opponent must answer, while the opponent has none.
To find it, list the threats for both sides. The side to move does not automatically have it.

steps.text:
**Costs and limits.** Keeping the initiative means making a new threat soon; a move without one can hand it over. Cashing in turns the pressure into material.
**Rule of thumb:** not every move needs a threat. When neither side has any threat, as in the drawn rook ending below, nobody has the initiative.

title: Keep it, cash it or consolidate
outcomes: Chooses between keeping the initiative, cashing it in and consolidating

steps.text: In **Who is making the threats?** you listed threats and the replies they force. Now decide what to do with an initiative. You can **keep up** the threats, **cash in** by turning the pressure into material, or **consolidate** by answering his threat first. Two questions decide it: if I pass, what can he do? And is anything of his loose?

**Rule of thumb:** cash in when the material is free and the capture does not trade off your attackers. Keep up when a capture would only trade the pieces that make the threats. Consolidate when his threat is faster than yours. A quiet move that adds a threat keeps the initiative. In the next three positions the same White pieces face three different jobs.

steps.text:
A **held threat** is a capture or attack you could carry out but have not. While it hangs there, the opponent's pieces are tied to answering it. Carrying it out frees them.
So ask before every capture: do I gain something at once, or can I add pressure first? This lesson names the threat and the piece it ties down.

steps.text:
**When to hold, when to cash in.** Hold when the capture only trades and a quiet move adds an attacker. Cash in when the capture gains material at once.
**Rule of thumb:** execute a threat only if something is gained immediately. A held threat is worth nothing if the target can simply move or be defended.

steps.text: The pawn on e4 was the loose one. Finding it was the **safety scan**: two quick questions before every move. **One:** what did my opponent's last move attack or open up? **Two:** is any of my pieces loose? [H] My guess is the scan takes ten or fifteen seconds as a habit; I have not timed learners. A habit, not a law, built for plain dangers, not deep tactics.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's last move aimed a knight at the e-pawn. Answer one: defend it.

line.say: A pawn now defends the e-pawn, so a capture there could be answered.
Black develops a pawn of its own, and nothing of White's is loose any more.

claims.statement: Before the move, the pawn on e4 is loose.
After d3, no White piece is loose.
d3 and castling are both among the engine's top choices.

steps.caption: White to move. Answer two: take the attacker. Two bishops are attacked here, and the scan finds both.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight that was attacking the loose bishop on e4, and it also leaves the h6 pawn's reach.
Black retakes with the queen. The knight that threatened e4 is gone.

claims.statement: The bishop on e4 is loose.
One Black piece attacks the bishop on e4.
One Black piece attacks the bishop on g5 (the h6 pawn).
Bxf6 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: When a piece is attacked, three common answers are: **defend** it, so a capture can be answered; **remove the attacker**, usually by capturing it; or **move the piece away**. Two more come later: block the line, or make a bigger threat of your own. This is a teaching frame, not a complete list. You have now seen the first two. Next, the third.

steps.title: Same square, different attacker
steps.prompt: A rook attacks a defended knight. Then a pawn does. Predict, for each, whether White must react.

line.say: The bishop leaves the pawn's reach and keeps its diagonal.
Black pushes a pawn to attack it again.
It steps back once more, safe from the pawns for now.

claims.statement: One Black piece attacks the bishop on g5: the pawn on h6.
On h4 nothing of Black's attacks the bishop.
Bh4 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: **Defended is not the same as safe.** Counting values are a rule of thumb: pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. If a cheaper piece attacks your defended piece, it can take, you retake, and you have lost more than you won. Ask two things: what attacks it, and what would the trade cost me?

steps.caption: Same position. Suppose White ignores the pawn on h6 and plays a quiet move on the other wing.

line.say: A quiet move that does nothing about the attack on the bishop.
The pawn takes the bishop: the knight defends g5, but a pawn is the cheapest attacker there is.
The knight retakes the pawn. White gave a bishop (3) for a pawn (1).

claims.statement: The bishop on g5 is defended once, by the knight.
Ignoring the pawn is far worse than moving the bishop.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on d5 is defended once and attacked twice. Count before you capture.

line.say: The cheaper attacker, the knight, captures first.
The pawn retakes.
The second attacker takes the pawn. White gave a knight and won a knight and a pawn.

claims.statement: Two White pieces attack the knight on d5.
One Black piece defends the knight on d5.

steps.text: Count the attackers against the defenders on the square. Here two White pieces attack the knight and one pawn defends it. The cheapest attacker captures first, so White trades a knight for a knight and then takes the pawn too. The opponent's last move is the only thing that changed since you last looked, so that is where new danger can come from. [I]

steps.text: The second question has a twin: **what does my own move do?** Dan Heisman, a chess coach, calls moving without checking the opponent's forcing replies (checks, captures, threats) "Hope Chess". I know this from articles about his books, not from the books themselves. After a move, look in three places: the piece that moved, the pieces it used to guard, and any line it opens.

line.say: The rook slides along the rank, and it was the only piece defending the knight on e3.
Black takes the knight, which nothing defends now. One quiet move cost a piece.

After the rook leaves the e-file nothing defends the knight.
After the rook move the knight on e3 is loose.
Rd2 is far worse than the best move.

line.say: Black grabs the loose bishop. It looks like a free piece.
The knight on e5 was blocking the rook. Moving it uncovers check from the rook on e1, and it takes a knight on the way.
Black answers the check. With the natural block Be7, the knight on c6 now attacks the queen, and White takes it.
The knight now attacks the queen, and White takes it.

Be7 and Nxe5 are both fine (within a few hundredths of a pawn at depth 16-18), while Nxb5 loses about 7 pawns [V, SF19 lite d18].

steps.text: A loose enemy piece is a chance, not an order. Run the scan on the capture itself before you take. [H] My guess, not measured: the freer a piece looks, the more it is worth one extra look, because a gift and a bait look the same from far away. Treat "free" as a question, not an answer.

steps.text: In "The safety scan: look before you move" and "Before every move: two questions" the questions were put to you. Now they are not. In mixed positions, some with a threat and some without, ask them yourself. **Ignore a real threat** and you lose material. **Answer a threat that is not there** and you lose a move. Both mistakes cost.

line.say: The pawn on e3 defends the knight on d4. The knight on c5 is loose, so the rook takes it.

steps.text: **The question behind both mistakes:** after a quiet move from me, can the opponent win material or mate? Check loose pieces and mate threats first. An attack on a piece that is defended is usually a threat only if the attacker is worth *less* than the target, or if the target is attacked more often than it is defended (a rule of thumb; count to be sure). When there is no threat, spend the move on your plan.

steps.text: **Forcing moves** leave the opponent very few choices. There are three kinds. A **check** attacks the king. A **capture** takes a piece. A **threat** is a quiet move that will win something, or mate, if ignored. The habit this lesson builds: list these first, look at every reply, then decide. It is where to look first, not proof that one of them works.

Qg3+ forces checkmate in two.

The knight retakes.

One black piece defends g4.

The queen moves away; the rook is still attacked.

After the push, the pawn attacks b7.

steps.text: Why list them first? Because they **shrink the tree**. In 7,465 positions with the side to move in check (1,500 Lichess games, January 2013), the mean was 3.3 legal replies, and 86% had five or fewer [V]. In 88,464 positions with no check, the mean was 31.5 [V]. A capture usually invites one recapture [I]. [H] Naming the three kinds may also make an opponent's check or capture harder to miss.

steps.caption: White's queen has just checked from b3. Count Black's legal replies. A check can leave very few.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly one legal move.

line.say: Only Be6 blocks the check, and the king has no square. One legal reply.

steps.caption: Another position after a check. Now Black has four replies, of three kinds: take the checker, block, or move the king. Which is which?

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly four legal moves.

steps.caption: The three kinds of answer. The queen can take the checker. The queen or the f-pawn can block on f5. The king can step to b8.

claims.statement: Black's four legal replies are the three kinds.

steps.text: Three kinds of answer to a check: **take** the checker, **block** between the checker and the king, or **move** the king. A knight check cannot be blocked. Sorting the replies this way makes a check easy to read to the end.

Counts from Lichess games (January 2013), recalled from an earlier run that cannot be reproduced now [R]: the best move was quiet about 70% of the time, a capture about 20 to 25%, and a check 5 to 10%, depending on how a capture with a check is counted. A reviewer's recount of 18,420 Lichess puzzles [S] found 62% begin with a check. [I] Forcing moves are where tactics hide, not where most moves are.
