steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Checks, captures, threats: look at the forcing moves first. This part covers Near misses and a mixed test; A real game; Say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

A **near miss** changes one detail, and the result may flip. Study the original, then ask what the detail did. Details that matter: who can take the checking piece, how many defenders a piece has, whether the king has a flight square. Details that do not: a pawn far from the action. Predict each, then check.

steps.title: One pawn, one square
steps.prompt: The first position is a mate in two. In the second a black pawn stands on b7 instead of a7. In the third a white pawn stands on a3 instead of a2. Predict each, then check.

steps.text: Kotov's method, as summarised on Wikipedia [S], is to list candidate moves and analyse them in an organised tree. Test each forcing move against the opponent's best answer: can the checking piece be taken, what does the capture lose, can the threat be met with a bigger one? If one passes, play it. If **none** passes, say so and play a calm move.

steps.text: A forcing move limits the replies, which is why it comes first; it does not make the move good. **Rule of thumb:** test a check by asking what can capture the checking piece. steps.text: Do not play the first good-looking move. Make a short **candidate list**: two to four moves, forcing moves first. Then follow each for about three **plies** (a ply is one move by one side): your move, the opponent's best reply, your next move. Drop candidates that clearly fail. Two to four is a habit to try, not a rule.

steps.caption: White is in check. The candidate list is short: White has exactly four legal moves.

line.say: Qxc4 captures the checking bishop.
Black takes the rook with check.
Bxd1 takes the queen. Three plies show White clearly ahead.

claims.statement: White is in check.
White has exactly four legal moves: Kg1, Be2, Qxc4 and Qd3.
Qxc4 is the engine's best move.
Kg1 is far worse.
Qd3 is far worse.
Qxc4 nets White at least five points of material along the engine's line.

steps.text: To follow a line you must hold the board in your head. **Drill:** you study a position for 15 seconds, then some pieces vanish from the board. You must still say where a piece can go. This is a training exercise for seeing lines, not a chess rule.

**Short lines have limits.** Three plies are enough when every move is forcing. They can mislead when a sacrifice pays off later: a line that looks bad at ply three can be mate at ply five. And in quiet positions the candidates may not separate at all.
Ask: **is the last move of my line quiet or forcing?**

steps.text: You have met the candidate list in **Candidates and short lines**. This lesson adds one test: does a candidate **survive the opponent's best reply**? Judge it against his strongest answer, not the one you hope for. Often the first idea fails this test and a different move on the list passes. Your job is to find that move before you play.

steps.text: **When this pays.** Testing every candidate against its best reply costs time. It pays when the position is not forced and more than one plan is plausible. **Rule of thumb:** test the forcing candidate first; if it fails, move down the list. Keep a quiet move on the list: sometimes it is the only one that survives. It is wasted when the first idea is plainly right or only one move is legal.

steps.text:
Depth is a **budget**, not a virtue. Habits to try:
**Go deep** when every move in the line is a check, capture or threat: the replies are few.
**Stop** when the position is quiet and you can compare it, when you have found a refutation, or when the clock says so.
**Spend more** at critical moments, less at routine ones.

**Four stop signs:** the position is quiet; you found a refutation; no line changes the material (the moment is routine); time. And **two warning signs** that you stopped too early: your line ends on a capture, or on a check.
Depth allocation is a habit to try; nobody has measured the best split.

steps.text: **How deep? Spend calculation where it pays** gave you the signs. Now put numbers on them. First **sort** for ten seconds: *critical* (a tempting move that costs a lot), *routine* (many moves about equal), or *forced* (one legal move). Then **budget**: routine and forced positions get little, and what is left goes to the critical ones. Start with the sort.

**Budget arithmetic.** Say a set of five positions has five minutes in total, and a routine position gets 30 seconds. If three positions are routine, they use 90 seconds, and the rest is shared between the two critical ones. This split is a rule of thumb to try, not a measured optimum.

title: Cross out, then check from the other side
outcomes: Crosses out candidates one at a time with one concrete reply each
Checks the surviving move from the opponent's seat, in a different order from the one that found it

steps.text: Two steps, in this order. **Eliminate:** for each candidate, look for one concrete reply that refutes it: a capture, a check, a threat. Cross out what falls. **Verify:** for the survivor, change seats. In the position after your move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats, then find his best reply. Do not re-walk your own line in the same order: it tends to repeat the same blind spot.

steps.caption: White to move. One candidate is crossed out in two moves.

line.say: Nxe8+ takes a rook with check. It looks strong.
The rook on f8 takes the knight, and nothing of White's defends it.

claims.statement: Nxe8+ is at least 300 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is attacked by 2 black pieces.
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is loose.

steps.text: **Verifying is not recalculating.** You found the line from your side, so walking it again in the same order shows the same things. Switch sides and change the order: his checks first, then his captures, then his quiet threats. **Rule of thumb:** spend it where a mistake is costly and cannot be taken back. A position with one legal move has nothing to cross out.

**Some refutations are quiet.** A search of captures and checks crosses out the easy candidates. A candidate that survives that search may still fail to a quiet move: one that captures nothing and gives no check but makes a threat or traps a piece. That is why the survivor gets its own look from the other side. Next: find a quiet refutation.

**Test the escape squares before you trust a perpetual.** A run of checks forces a draw only if every reply Black has leads back into the same checks: no capture of the checker, no block, and no king step that gets out of them. List the king's squares first, then ask where each one leads. A free square often ends the checks, but not always.

Kh7 is forced.

Kh8 is forced. Ng6+ would now repeat the position after the first check.

title: The Alien Gambit: the idea and the first six moves
outcomes: Says why White plays Ng5 on move five and why f7 is the target: it is defended once, by the king, while h7 is defended twice
Names the six squares a knight on f7 attacks, sees that it forks the queen and a rook, and explains why Black must capture it with the king
States honestly that the sacrifice is objectively unsound (engine, depth 20: Black about two pawns ahead) yet practically testing, with our own sample sizes
Steps through the first moves and a typical continuation, with the purpose of each move, and reads two real games
Names the typical mistakes for each side (...Bg4 or ...Ke7 for Black, Qh5+ for White) and the reason each fails

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Alien Gambit gives a knight for a pawn on move six. Why would anyone do that, what does the knight attack on f7, and what does each side get? By the end you can answer in your own words, say honestly whether it is sound, and set up the first moves on a board. Marks: [V] checked, [S] source, [R] recalled, [I] inference, [H] guess.

steps.prompt: A knight for a pawn is a big price. What would White need in return for this to be worth trying? Write two things.

steps.text: **What White hopes to buy.** [I] Time: the king on f7 makes checks gain tempi. Lines: the bishop's diagonal to f7 is open. Squares: a knight on e5 gives check. And surprise: Black must find several accurate moves in a row. None of these is a pawn, so the gambit is a bet on the next few moves, not an investment with a return.

steps.chapter: Test yourself and teach it back

steps.prompt: Lichess bands average both players' ratings: White scored 46% where the two averaged 1900 or more, and 57% where they averaged below 1500. What can a result averaged over both players say, and not say, about which player should try this gambit? One sentence.

steps.text: **Say it like this.** [I] 'White's knight on g5 aims at f7. When Black attacks it with a pawn, White can give the knight for a pawn on f7: it forks the queen and a rook, and Black must take it with the king. It is playable only as a trap: the king must take on f7, so White gets the exposed king and the tempi, but the engine still has Black about two pawns ahead.'

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in a few sentences, explain the Alien Gambit to a friend who knows the rules. Say what the knight attacks on f7, why the king must take, why an engine calls it unsound, and one mistake to warn about. Self-check: did you say when it works, when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.

steps.text: **Recap.** The knight on g5 aims at f7, defended only by the king. After the pawn attacks it, White can retreat (best) or sacrifice it on f7, forking queen and rook; Black must take with the king. Engine: Black is about two pawns ahead [V, depth 20]. Results follow the rating gap [V, S]. Mistakes: ...Bg4 or ...Ke7 for Black; Qh5+ for White.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
1. 7...e6 shuts the bishop check and frees the f8 bishop.
2. Cost: the c8 bishop is shut in and e6 depends on it.
3. Plan A (Bd3, Qe2): keep e6 guarded. Plan B (knight check, fork): ...Kg8, then ...c5. Plan C (g4): ...Bd6.
4. Trap: before blocking the c8 bishop, count the guards of e6; with Kg8, Bd3 and Qe2 the block loses to Qxe6 mate.
5. Trade queens only when the count says it is safe.
6. Archive scores mix the line with the player.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The gambit looks unsound, yet strong players still lose to it sometimes. steps.text: **What the archive holds.** [V] 237 games reached this gambit: a knight sacrifice on f7 after Black played ...h6. Black won 116, White won 105, 16 were drawn: White scored about 48 per 100. Compare that with your guess: were you close?

**Where the games come from.** [V] 229 carry the site tag chess.com, 228 of them in events named Titled Tuesday or 3-0 Thursday (counted by script; time controls not checked). 98 players had White; Volen Dyulgerov supplies 33. This is one fashionable gambit in fast games, not an objective verdict.

steps.text:
**The rating gap speaks louder.** [V] White's score per 100, by Black's rating minus White's (234 games with both ratings; a gap of exactly 200 counts in the 200+ row on both sides):
Black 200+ above: 26 (n=54)

Within 50: 53 (n=39)
White 50 to 199 above: 64 (n=46)
White 200+ above: 71 (n=33)

[I] A gain of roughly 3 per 100 is the size chance alone can produce in 234 games, so it is not proof of an edge.

steps.chapter: Why a dubious gambit can score

steps.prompt: Would you play this gambit as White in a three-minute game?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** A gambit that loses about two pawns on paper can still score in fast games. Why, when does that stop being true, and how should a learner use gambit knowledge without fooling themselves? You will test three explanations against our archive and the engine, then decide for yourself. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis, [S] read in a source.

steps.prompt: Predict. In 234 games with both ratings, White averaged 2184 and Black 2234. By the standard rating formula, how many points per 100 should White score?

steps.text: **On paper and in practice.** [V] The formula expects about 45 per 100 for White; White scored about 48. A gain of roughly 3 per 100 is within the range chance alone produces, so the honest reading is: against these opponents the gambit cost White nothing measurable, which is not the same as being good. [V] Volen Dyulgerov, 33 games: 50 against about 41 expected. [I] With 33 games that is a hint, not proof.

steps.prompt: What would you need to see before you believed "this gambit works"? Write the evidence you would ask for.

steps.text: **Three explanations to test.** [H] (1) Checks leave Black few legal moves, so each reply must be found. (2) The king on f7 needs repairs, and each repair costs a move. (3) In fast games Black has little time to find the repairs while the gambiteer has prepared. The board can test the first, the engine part of the second, and nothing here can test the third: the files hold no clock times.

steps.caption: Black to move after 7.Nf3. Six sensible moves are open to Black: ...c5, ...Kg8, ...Be6, ...Bf5, ...e6 and ...Nbd7. steps.text: **What the counts say.** [V] In this game Black's legal moves fell from 39 to 3, then 5, then one, over four White moves. [I] This is one game as an example, not a measure of the gambit.

Few legal moves does not mean a lost position; it means each reply must be found, and only some of them are good. [H] This is the practical engine of a gambit in fast play: every forcing move costs White one move and costs Black a search.

**How far that count goes.** [I] By this one measure the gambit games are more forcing. It does not show that Black has fewer good replies. The comparison is rough: the gambit games are mostly online blitz, the ordinary sample is a mix of events, and part of the forcing share is plain recapture.

steps.title: Grab or consolidate?
steps.prompt: Predict, then check. The same bishop can take the same loose pawn on c2 in both positions, which differ in several ways. In one it is the best move and in the other it hands back the advantage. Which is which?

steps.text: **Same grab, opposite verdicts.** [V] In both positions Bxc2 wins a loose pawn. [I] The positions differ in several ways: a pawn or a queen attacks the bishop, the king stands on h7 or g8, and e6 is open in only one. So the pair suggests a rule but cannot isolate one cause. [H] When a pawn forces the bishop to move anyway, the grab is free; when a defence like e6 exists, it may only send the bishop to the edge. Count the attackers first.

steps.prompt: Write your own rule for "grab or consolidate?" in one or two sentences, using a count (attackers, defenders, loose pieces) rather than a feeling.

steps.text: **Three honest uses of gambit knowledge.** (1) A repertoire experiment: play it in a fixed number of games, log the results, and stop at a rule you wrote before you started. (2) King-attack practice: gambit lines are full of checks and sacrifices, so replaying them trains pattern recognition. (3) A test of defence: knowing the traps helps you meet them from the other side. None of the three needs the gambit to be sound.

steps.text: **Modern Benoni.** Moves: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 (ECO A60 in our data; 2,347 visits in our online sample). After 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cxd5 d6 6.e4 g6 the pawns are unbalanced: White has more pawns on files e to h, Black more on files a to d, and Black has no e-pawn. Each side plays where it has more. Step through one main line, then count.

Nf3 develops the knight.

Be2 prepares castling.

White castles kingside.

After ...g6 the e-file is half-open for Black (no black e-pawn, a white pawn on e4).
After Re8 the rook attacks e4.

After Nc7 the knight covers b5.

At the end Black's majority pawns are a7, b6, c5, d6.
At the end White's majority pawns are e4, f3, g2, h2.

steps.text: **What was played (results of games, not evaluations).** Masters (both players 2500 or more, 329,379 games in our file): after 5...d6, 6.e4 in 313 games and 6.Nf3 in 236. After 6.e4 g6 the seventh move was f4 in 145 games (White won 69, drew 49, lost 27), Nf3 in 57 (29, 18, 10), h3 in 49 (20, 21, 8). Online (4,752,291 games): 7.Nf3 appears in 390 games, 7.f4 in 264.

**White's plan: e5 (rule of thumb).** White's extra pawns are in the centre and on the kingside; the break is e4-e5, which attacks d6 and f6. Condition: a pawn should defend e5 after the push. After 7.f4 Bg7 8.Nf3 O-O (the Four Pawns Attack, ECO A68) the pawn on f4 does that. Masters: at 9.Be2 Re8, all 8 games continued 10.e5, a small sample. Find White's move next.

**Black's plan: ...b5 (rule of thumb).** Black's extra pawns are on files a to d; the break is ...b5, and the rook on the half-open e-file adds pressure on e4. Condition: the break needs support first, here a knight on c7. Masters, after 10.Nd2: Nbd7 49 games, Na6 30, a6 8 (87 games); after 11.f3, Nc7 in all 13. Find the preparing move next.

**Check before you push (rule of thumb).** A plan tells you which move to look for, not whether it works now. Ask what attacks the square before pushing, and count attackers against defenders. In the line you stepped through, b5 is attacked by the pawn on a4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on e2, and defended by the knight on c7. The engine's verdict on the tempting pawn push is in the next item.

**When each plan works (rule of thumb).** In the Four Pawns positions here a pawn on f4 defends e5, and e5 is within 0.7 pawn of the best move in two of three; with a black knight on d7 it is not. In one Classical position (f-pawn on f2, rook on e8) e5 is more than 0.7 pawn worse. A defender is a condition to check, not a guarantee. ...b5 needs support and a look at what attacks it. The engine decides each case. Next, three positions: predict, then check.

title: Caro-Kann Defense: the bishop outside, and three branches
outcomes: Names the Advance, Classical and Exchange branches by their move orders
Finds the break that attacks the base of the chain (...c5) and the h-pawn push that harasses a bishop on g6
Tells when ...c5 is premature (no ...e6 yet) and when it does not exist (Exchange structure)
Reads game counts from master and online data as results, not evaluations

steps.text:
**The Caro-Kann Defense** starts 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5. Black supports d5 with the c-pawn, so the bishop on c8 can still leave the pawns before ...e6 (compare the French, where ...e6 comes first).
Our opening data names three main branches: **Advance** (3.e5), **Classical** (3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5) and **Exchange** (3.exd5 cxd5). Pawn chains and breaks are taught elsewhere (the chain and breaks lessons); here we use them in one opening.

steps.caption: Advance Variation. Black to answer 3.e5 after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5; step through the usual first moves.

line.say: The pawns on d4 and e5 now form a chain. Its base is d4.
Black's bishop goes outside the chain, before the e-pawn can shut its diagonal.
White develops and adds a second defender to d4.
The pawn supports d5. The bishop is already outside it.
White brings out the last minor piece on the kingside. Think about what Black's c-pawn can do next.

claims.statement: 3.e5 is legal.
After 3.e5 the pawn on d4 is the base of a chain: it defends e5 and no pawn defends it.
After 4.Nf3 two white pieces defend d4 (queen and knight).

**Results of games, not evaluations.** Our master set (329,379 games, both players 2,500+) holds 9,271 games that reached 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5; in 9,266 of them White played a third move. Third moves: 3.e5 in 5,097, 3.exd5 in 1,693, 3.Nc3 in 1,422, 3.Nd2 in 739, 3.f3 in 315. After 3.e5 the results were 1,975 White wins, 1,757 draws, 1,365 Black wins.
Online (Lichess, September 2026, 1900-2100 band, 20,943 games at this position): 3.exd5 in 6,827, 3.e5 in 6,264, 3.Nc3 in 5,029.

line.say: White defends e4 with a knight and keeps the centre pawns.
Black takes the pawn on e4.
White retakes. No chain exists in this variation.
The bishop comes out at once, before ...e6, and attacks the knight.
The knight steps aside and keeps an eye on the bishop's diagonal.
The bishop keeps its diagonal, one square back.
White's rook pawn heads for g6: after h5 it would attack the bishop. Black to move; what should Black do about it?

claims.statement: After 4...Bf5 the bishop attacks the knight on e4.
After 4.Nxe4 no black pawn attacks the knight on e4.

steps.text:
**When these ideas hold.** In the checked pair, ...c5 is the engine's top move after ...e6 and loses at least 80 centipawns before it (depth 16). In the Classical, after h4 the engine picks ...h6; ...Nf6, ...Nd7 and ...e6 lose at least 150.
**Question to ask:** has the supporting move been played? Here ...e6 comes before ...c5. Bringing the bishop out first is a choice that keeps its diagonal open, not a law. In the Exchange structure the c-pawn is gone, so ...c5 does not exist. Check the position first.

steps.title: Is the c5 break sound yet?
steps.prompt: Predict, then check.

Which part is least clear: the base of the chain as the target, the order of ...e6 and ...c5, or the h-pawn push in the Classical? Then, if you like, open the Openings explorer at 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5, switch the rating band chips, and compare how the share of 3.e5, 3.exd5 and 3.Nc3 changes. (The explorer shows online games only; the master counts above are not in it.)

title: Catalan Opening: the long diagonal and the open and closed plans
outcomes: Names the move order of the Catalan Opening (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2) and the two branches that Black's choice on c4 creates
Opens the bishop's long diagonal with a knight move only after checking that the b7 square and the rest of the line are empty
Before taking a pawn on c4, counts the white pieces that attack c4, and finds that a knight on d2 changes the answer
In the closed branch, counts the defenders of the e4 break for White and finds a pawn move that frees the bishop on c8 for Black

steps.text: **Catalan Opening** (ECO E00 to E09, the standard codes; the name comes from our opening data): 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2. The bishop on g2 looks along the long diagonal towards d5. In our online data (4,752,291 games, September 2026, all 8 rating bands) 1,530 games reach 3.g3 and 1,241 reach 4.Bg2. Black's choice between taking the pawn on c4 and keeping the pawn on d5 splits the opening into *open* and *closed* plans. This lesson shows one of each.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Source: our masters data, 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After 4.Bg2, Black played Be7 in 563 games, Bb4+ in 532 and dxc4 in 408. After 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3 O-O 6.O-O, Black played dxc4 in 2,764 games (White won 678, 1,618 were drawn, Black won 468) and c6 in 466. Samples are small; results also reflect the players.

**White's two ideas in the open lines (rule of thumb, not a law).** In the next position the engine (depth 16) rates Qc2, Qa4 and Ne5 within 0.4 pawn of its best move, so attacking c4 is one sound idea and opening the diagonal is another. A bishop on g2 attacks a8 only if every square between them is empty. Ask first: what stands between my bishop and a8?

**Black's side of the long diagonal (rule of thumb).** In the next position a Black bishop can step onto the diagonal that White's bishop on g2 looks along. The engine (depth 16) names a first choice; check which squares and pieces lie on the diagonal before you move.

**The closed branch.** After 6.O-O c6 our data names the position *Catalan Opening: Closed* (E06): 849 online games reach it. In the masters data c6 was played in 466 games against 2,764 for dxc4. No pawn has been taken on c4 here. The next two items give one position for each side; the claims are engine claims at depth 16 (within 0.4 pawn of the best move).

**A typical mistake.** In the open branch after 4...dxc4 5.Nf3 Nc6, our data names a line *Open Defense, Modern Sharp Variation* (40 online games). Before that, White has a tempting pawn move that attacks the knight. The next item tests whether you check what a move costs before you play it.

title: Why the Dragon exists: ...g6, the bishop on g7 and the pawn on d6
outcomes: Explains in own words why Black answers 5.Nc3 with ...g6: the long diagonal for the bishop, with the d6 pawn and the c-file as the setting that makes it work, and what ...g6 costs
Predicts how far a bishop on g7 sees when the diagonal holds a knight, a pawn or nothing
Steps through the first six moves and says what each is for
Says why 6.e5 does not refute ...g6, and reads opening counts as results of games, not verdicts

steps.caption: White to move after 5...g6. Black's dark-squared bishop is still on f8. Look along the long diagonal from h8 to a1. Where could the f8 bishop aim once it reaches g7, and what is in its way?

claims.statement: A black pawn stands on g6.
The c-file is half-open for Black and the d-file half-open for White.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: once Black's bishop reaches g7, what do you think it aims at, and what stands in its way first?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Why does Black answer 5.Nc3 with ...g6, and what do the bishop on g7 and the pawn on d6 make possible for the whole game? By the end you will explain it in your own words and could teach it to a friend. Marks you will meet: [H] is a hypothesis (a guess worth testing), [I] an inference (reasoned, not proven), [V] checked here.

**Three ways to answer 5.Nc3.** [I] 5...a6 keeps every plan open and stops Bb5 and Nb5, but commits to nothing. 5...Nc6 develops and hits d4, but gives the c-pawn's file plan less clarity. 5...g6 prepares Bg7: a clear plan and a clear diagonal, at a price, shown on the next card. So the reason for ...g6 is the diagonal; the d6 pawn and the c-file are the setting in which it works.

steps.prompt: Before the boards: which of the three answers to 5.Nc3 would you pick, and what do you think it gives up?

steps.text: **What ...g6 costs.** [I] Three prices. The light squares around the king (f6, h6) rely on the g7 bishop. The king depends on that one bishop, so trading it is White's regular plan. And the bishop needs time: ...a6 or ...Nc6 develop faster. [I] The gain, a strong long diagonal, outweighs these prices only while the diagonal stays open.

steps.caption: Position A (edited: the knight on f6 is removed so the diagonal is clear of Black's own pieces). White's pawn is on e4 and White's knight on d4. Predict: how far does the bishop on g7 see along the diagonal?

claims.statement: The bishop on g7 attacks exactly these squares.

steps.caption: Position B (edited): same as A, but White's e-pawn has advanced to e5; the knight still stands on d4, behind the pawn. Predict first: shorter or longer than position A?

claims.statement: The bishop on g7 attacks exactly these squares.

steps.caption: Position C (edited): White's knight has left d4 (traded off). The knight on c3 and the pawn on e4 remain. Predict: how far now?

claims.statement: The bishop on g7 attacks exactly these squares.

steps.text: **What decided the range?** Not the bishop, which stood on the same square in all three. What stood on the diagonal decided it: nothing of Black's own, a white pawn on e5, a white knight on d4. Capablanca noted that the bishop is usually stronger than the knight except in blocked positions [V-sheet 8.4]. [I] With its diagonal blocked, the Dragon bishop loses that edge.

**Idea 1: the long diagonal.** Play ...g6 and the bishop can go to g7, from where it looks through f6, e5, d4 and c3 to b2 and a1. It is a distant centre-control piece, influencing the middle without a pawn there: a thought the hypermodern school pushed [S].

steps.caption: Black's bishop arrives on g7. Its own knight on f6 is first in line, then White's knight on d4.

line.say: The g6 pawn made room; from g7 the bishop looks down the long diagonal toward b2.

claims.statement: Black's knight stands on f6, the first piece on the diagonal.
White's knight stands on d4, the second piece.

steps.text: **Idea 2: the pawn on d6.** It guards e5 and c5, so a white pawn on e5 can be captured, and it keeps White's e-pawn from advancing for free. It is not on the long diagonal, so it blocks nothing there. [I] It also fixes Black's centre until ...d5 becomes possible.

steps.caption: The pawn on d6 watches e5 and c5. White's e4 pawn would like to advance; the pawn stands guard.

claims.statement: Black's pieces attack e5 (the d6 pawn).
White has no piece attacking e5 yet.

steps.text: **Idea 3: the half-open c-file.** After ...cxd4 Black has no pawn on the c-file, but White's c2 pawn is still there. A black rook on c8 would press on that file and on the knight on c3. [I] In most Dragon games Black's rook pressure goes down this file, because White's c-pawn is the only pawn left on it. The d-file is White's: White has no d-pawn, Black has d6.

steps.caption: After the knight trade on d4 the c-file is open to Black's rook on c8, and White's knight on c3 stands in front of its c2 pawn. [I] This is why Black's rook often goes to c8.

claims.statement: The c-file is half-open for Black, the d-file for White.
One black piece (the rook on c8) attacks c3.

steps.text: **The first six moves, with reasons.** A move order is a chain of small purposes. Emanuel Lasker pointed out that first moves leave lasting marks on a game [V-sheet 1.12]; he used the French as his example, and we borrow the idea. Watch what each move leaves behind. Step through the boards and say each purpose aloud before reading it.

steps.caption: Move 1. Why not copy with ...e5? [I] After ...c5 White cannot build a pawn centre on d4 and e4 for free: the c-pawn is traded for White's d-pawn, which gives Black a half-open file. ...e5 would leave Black's e5 pawn needing protection at once.

Black fights for d4 with a wing pawn. Leaves behind: unbalanced pawns and a trade that opens the c-file.

Guards e5 and c5 and opens the road for the bishop. Leaves behind: a pawn on d6 that fixes the centre.
White challenges the c5 pawn and opens the centre.

steps.caption: Moves 4 to 6: the Dragon takes shape.

Develops the bishop, guards the knight on d4 and prepares Qd2 and long castling [S: standard plan]. It also gets the bishop out before f2-f3 shuts it in.
The bishop takes the long diagonal at last.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The pawn on g6 lets the bishop reach g7 and look down the long diagonal; what stands on that diagonal decides its range. The d6 pawn guards e5, so a white e-pawn push can be met by a capture. The c-file is half-open for Black, the d-file for White. ...g6 costs light-square weakness and a dependence on the g7 bishop. Counts show what was chosen, not what is best. Next lesson: the pawn structure and the breaks.

**Typical mistakes.** [I] First, grabbing the e4 pawn with the knight: after 6.Be3 the capture ...Nxe4 loses a piece for a pawn, because White recaptures (see the board). Second, letting the bishop be traded on h6 with no plan for the king. Third, blocking your own bishop with a knight that never moves, so the diagonal stays closed.

title: The Dragon structure: pawn skeleton, half-open files and the breaks each side wants
outcomes: Names the half-open files of the Dragon (c for Black, d for White) and says which pawn trade created each
Finds each side's pawn lever (d, b and a for Black; g and h for White) and says which file it opens

steps.caption: White to move, twelve moves into the Yugoslav Attack. The kings stand on opposite wings. Do not calculate: look at the pawns, the open file and the bishop on g7.

claims.statement: White's king is on the queenside.
Black's king is on the kingside.

steps.prompt: Whose attack do you think arrives first, and why? Write the reason, not just the name of the side. You will come back to this at the end.

steps.text: **Today's question.** Both kings are castled, but on opposite wings. A rule of thumb from Edward Lasker: with kings on opposite wings, speed counts more than material, because pawns stop being a shield and become a battering ram. We will test it. By the end you will say, for each side, which pawn lever it wants, which file it opens, and what to do when it is blocked or early. First, three small positions.

So the race is decided by tempo: who gets the file open one move earlier.

steps.text: **Six shapes decide most Dragon games.** The bishop trade on h6. The h-file. The knight jump to d5. The exchange sacrifice on c3. Queen-and-rook pressure on the c-file. King hunts near the back rank. By the end you can look at a position you have never seen and say which shape is in the air and what it needs. You are learning conditions, not lines. Each shape is shown working and failing.

**The trade on h6.** Black's bishop on g7 guards the dark squares around the king. A white bishop on h6 attacks it. If Black trades, White's queen lands on h6; if Black retreats to h8, the queen gets the h-file. Either way a defender is gone. The price: the bishop on e3 and the queen on d2 are the two guards of the knight on d4, and this plan spends both. Three boards follow, each with a different answer.

steps.text: **Conditions, not a rule.** The trade tends to work when the h-file is open or opening and when taking on h6 is worse for Black than declining. It fails when the bishop and the queen are the only guards of a loose knight, here on d4. [I] The queen leaving d2 also loosens c2, but d4 decides this position. [H] Many amateur Dragon games are lost by playing the trade because it looks aggressive, without counting the guards. Test this on your own games.

**The h-file.** White pushes the h-pawn to h5 to trade it for the pawn on g6, the shield of Black's king. When the file opens, a rook stands behind and the other pieces join: the bishop removes the g7 defender, the queen lands on h6 or h4. Capablanca noted that sacrifices on a castled king work through coordination [S]; I apply that to h-file attacks [I]: cover stripped, then queen, rook and a minor piece finish.

steps.text: **The exchange sacrifice on c3.** Black gives a rook for the knight. In the common case a pawn recaptures, White's king (usually on the queenside) has lost its cover, the queen reaches a5, and the bishop on g7 stands behind the knight on f6. [I] The general principle: the rook is paid for by a target the pawn recapture exposes: a king without cover, a loose pawn, a long diagonal. Nimzowitsch argued for giving material to open a line, but only after quieter attacks have been tried [S].

steps.text: **What the six shapes share.** Each removes or overloads a guard: the bishop on g7, the pawn on g6, the guards of d4, the knight on c3. Before a forcing move ask who guards what and what leaves. Edward Lasker's rule applies too: every pawn move leaves something behind [S]. Nimzowitsch spoke of giving material to clear the way [S]; Petrosian used the positional exchange sacrifice [S], a different purpose from a quick attack [I].

Did you name the common case of the exchange sacrifice (bishop on g7, king on the queenside, a queen ready to arrive) and the general principle (a target the recapture exposes)? Did you name one mistake, such as spending both guards of the knight on d4? The app grades nothing. Compare with a friend or coach.

**Recap.**
- The trade on h6 works when the h-file is ready; it fails when the bishop and queen are the only guards of a loose knight on d4.
- The h-file attack is a team job and a race.
- Count attackers and guards before the jump to d5.
- The exchange sacrifice needs a target the recapture exposes: often a queenside king, sometimes a loose pawn.
- Queen and rook on the c-file make c3 the square to count.
- Ask who guards what before every forcing move.

steps.text: **Kings on one wing.** Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*), and Philidor in a lighter-read source, noted that when kings castle on opposite wings, pawns are cheap and speed decides. steps.text: **Diagnose before you defend.** Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*) advises: find your chief weakness and the opponent's chief threat, then choose a long plan, not a single parry; when you stand worse, defend and win back freedom. Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*, Lecture 9) advises vacating weak points and supporting them when compromised. In the Dragon, ask: whose pawns are nearer the enemy king, which file is open, and which trade removes an attacker?

steps.text: **Dutch Defence** (ECO A80): 1.d4 f5. Black grabs control of e4 with the first move. In the set-up this lesson follows, Black adds pawns on e6, d5 and c6 to make the **Stonewall**: pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5. Chains and good and bad bishops are core lessons and are not re-taught here; this lesson asks what this structure gives each side. Step through one main line.

steps.text: **Chains have a base (rule of thumb).** In a pawn chain the base is the pawn that defends another pawn and has no pawn defending it. An attack on the base undermines the whole chain; an attack on the head only wins or trades one pawn. Find the bases in the Stonewall.

**White's plan: use e5 (rule of thumb).** With black pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5, no black pawn attacks e5 now, and none can reach d6 or f6 by moving forward, so e5 is a hole. A knight there cannot be kicked out by a pawn, but a piece can still trade it (for example a bishop on d6). Condition: a black pawn on d6 or f6 takes the hole away. In the next item tap the square that fits.

**Black's plan: the e4 square (rule of thumb).** The pawn on f5 guards e4, so a black knight there is supported by a pawn. In the position after Qc2 the engine rates Ne4 and Qe7 about equally (a few hundredths of a pawn apart at depth 16), but this is one position, not a law. Condition: White has pieces (Nc3, Qc2) that attack e4, so Black needs the supporting pawns. In the next item several moves are sound.

**The price (rule of thumb).** Black's pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5 stand on light squares, so the bishop on c8 has few moves: the bad bishop. The bishop on d6 is the good one, and the hole on e5 is the other cost of advancing the f-pawn. Tap the squares the bad bishop can reach.

**Count before you push (rule of thumb).** A plan tells you where to look, not whether a move works. White may be tempted to fight for e4 with the e-pawn. Count the pieces and pawns that attack e4 and the ones that defend it. In the next item e4 is tempting; find a better move.

**Both plans depend on the pawns (rule of thumb).** The e5 plan needs a hole, so one black pawn move can remove it. Black's e4 plan needs the f5 pawn and a square White cannot easily attack. Next you predict Ne5 in three positions; they differ by one pawn move each.

Explains why 4.Qe2 matters (the pawn on e4 is pinned to the king) and finds Black's defending moves
Avoids the typical mistakes: taking back on d5 too early and defending with a pawn move
Reads engine numbers and online counts as evidence of different kinds, with their sample sizes

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Elephant Gambit offers a pawn on move two. What does Black give, what does Black get, and why does one White reply matter so much? Afterwards you can explain the opening to a friend, give the engine's honest verdict and avoid the traps on both sides. Marks: [V] checked here, [S] a source, [I] inference, [H] a guess to test.

steps.text: **What Black gives and gets.** [I] Black gives a pawn for now, and spends three of the first three moves on pawns while White has one piece out. Black gets time: the pawn on e4 hits the knight, controls d3 and f3 and cramps White's development. Whether that is worth a pawn depends on one reply, so we look at it next.

steps.text: **The idea behind 4.Qe2.** [I] A pin means a piece cannot (or should not) move because a more valuable piece stands behind it. Here the queen pins the black pawn to the king, so the threat against the knight disappears and White's queen attacks the pawn. That is why this reply matters most. Black needs a move that adds a defender to e4. Which one?

steps.text: **Do not take back on d5 too early.** Black can win the pawn back with the queen at once, but then the knight comes to c3 and attacks the queen. After 4...Qxd5 5.Nc3 the queen has to move, and wherever it goes only the queen defends e4 while the queen and the knight attack it. The videos repeat this rule too [S-video, unverified]; the engine confirms it on the board below.

steps.text: **Plans for both sides.** [I] White: take the pawn back only when the queen cannot be hit with tempo, develop the queenside knight, castle, and use the extra pawn after the queens are traded. Black: develop with threats on the e-file, castle, and look for the exchange that regains d5 or e4. [H] The gambit works best against a White player who forgets the queen move.

steps.title: Is the pawn pinned?

steps.text: **A pin ends when the line is blocked.** The pinned pawn can still step forward along the file but can no longer capture, so the knight on f3 is safe from it. The pin lasts only while nothing else stands between the queen and the king. A piece on e7, e6 or e5 releases it; whoever releases it must check the result first.

steps.caption: The release of the pin, and the price of ignoring it. [V] After the quiet queen move to e7, White's natural central push loses a piece by force. The capture on f3 comes with the queens facing each other.

steps.text: **Why the queen move is different.** It does two jobs at once: it attacks the pawn on e4 and pins it, so Black cannot use the pawn to attack the knight on f3. The three knight moves each leave the pawn on d5 for the black queen to take. [I] The pin is what the other moves lack, which is why only this move keeps a clear edge in the engine's list.

steps.text: **Black's plan after the queen move.** Black cannot attack the pinned knight, so the plan is to develop with threats: defend e4 with a piece, bring out the bishop, castle off the e-file, and take back the pawn on d5 when it costs nothing. [S] Lichess sample: the knight to f6 in 1,623 of 2,310 games, the queen to e7 in 184.

steps.text: **How big a sample?** [V] The score of a player over 20 games has a margin of error of about plus or minus 11 percentage points (one standard error, the square root of 0.25 over 20). Over 100 games it is about 5. [I] So ten games of your own tell you almost nothing. The Lichess samples are large, so three points there is not noise; but the players who choose 2...d5 are not the same players who choose 2...Nc6, so it still does not prove the move is better.

**When to play it.** The honest case for the Elephant Gambit is practical: opponents who know the queen move and the pin will keep an edge, and most players will not. [H] It suits fast games, a player who likes initiative, and a learner who wants to study king safety by doing; it suits badly someone who wants a sound repertoire for the long term. Decide by your own results, not by anyone's boast.

steps.text: **The French Defence** starts 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 (ECO C00). After 3.e5, the *Advance Variation* (C02), White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain, and Black's pawns on e6 and d5 answer it. This lesson is about that one structure: where each side plays, and why. It assumes you know a chain's base and head (*Pawn chains: hit the base, not the head*) and why a bishop can be bad (*Good and bad pieces*).

steps.text: **What strong players chose.** In our master data (329,379 games from The Week in Chess and Lichess broadcasts, both players rated 2,500 or more, 2012 to 2026), 11,236 games reached 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. White then played 3.Nc3 in 5,659, 3.Nd2 in 2,681, 3.e5 in 1,806 and 3.exd5 in 957. After 3.e5, Black chose 3...c5 in 1,751. These count games; none is an evaluation.

**White's plan.** The pawn on e5 attacks f6 and d6, so a black knight on f6 would be attacked by a pawn. In this line White usually keeps the base d4 defended with the pawn on c3, the knight on f3 and the queen along the d-file. Before any other idea, count the attackers and the defenders of d4.

**Black's plan.** Black's pawns on e6 and d5 stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop, so that bishop is hemmed in. Black's counterplay is elsewhere: the lever ...c5 and then ...cxd4 hit the base, and bring the knight and the queen to bear on it. The bishop stays a problem until Black finds it a square or a trade; if ...c4 closes the queenside, it gets worse.

**When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* in a chain, attack the base, not the head. It works here because a chain exists and d4 needs defenders against c5 and the knight. It does not apply when no chain stands: after 3.Nc3 or 3.exd5, ...c5 is rated at least 0.6 and 1 pawn worse at depth 16. And a bad bishop is bad *now*, not forever. Ask first: is there a chain, and who attacks and defends its base?

**Who chooses the bishop on c4?** Our data, at the moment White picks a bishop square. Masters (both players 2500+): b5 in 26,563 of 46,776 listed games, c4 in 13,320. Online 1500-1700 (47,772 games): bishop 15,037 (31%), knight 14,696 (31%), pawn to h6 7,300 (15%), pawn to d6 3,547 (7%). Masters play the pawn moves in under 2% of games. These are counts of games, not proof of strength.

**White's fourth move against the bishop.** Masters (7,112 recorded): c3 44%, d3 28%, castling 22%, Nc3 3%, b4 3%. Online 1500-1700 (15,626 games): c3 29%, d3 21%, castling 21%, Nc3 13%, b4 6%, d4 6%, the jump to g5 0.7% (108 games, White scores 22%). [H] Online players try more different things; the jump is the one our engine check says loses a piece.

steps.text: **What a retreat has to keep: a checklist.** Does the bishop keep a useful diagonal? Does the rook keep its guard of e4? Is the d-pawn free to move? Bb3 passed all three. Bf1 gave up the diagonal but passed the other two. Each of the other retreats failed one. [I] This is my reading of a few positions, a checklist of trade-offs, not a law. Once d3 is played the structure itself picks the retreat.

steps.text: **Reading the skeleton.** Edward Lasker argued that pieces can retreat but pawns cannot, so the pawn skeleton is what lasts and the pieces should be placed around it. [S] Nimzowitsch advised removing a strong enemy centre pawn by a *prepared* pawn break. [S] Here White's break is d4, which needs support. Black's break is ...d5, which needs e4 overloaded. Both breaks stay in reserve while pieces are placed.

steps.text: **How to judge a gambit.** Emanuel Lasker (Common Sense in Chess, lectures of 1895) treats a gambit as a pawn traded for time and open lines, to be judged by whether the compensation survives the first accurate reply [V-sheet]. A modern engine puts the main line near level, about +0.08 at depth 22 [V], so we test his view instead of trusting it.

Our engine check puts the main line near level, so the strong form of that claim does not survive. [V] One engine, one depth, not a verdict on the opening.

Did you say when it works (White gains time) and when it fails (the pawn is already on d3, or a knight attacks e4)? Did you give a position a friend could set up? Did you name one mistake? Then revisit your first two guesses and change one word. Last, did the gambit make tempo easier to see than the quiet structure did?

**What to remember.**
- A gambit pays a pawn for time, centre and lines.
- Judge it by whether the compensation survives the accurate reply. [V-sheet]
- Black accepts and hits back, or declines.
- Pawn c3 first makes a push; b4 first makes a gambit.
- With d3 played or a knight on f6, the offer fails. [V]
- The rare third moves are met simply; the pawn grab is a trap. [V]
- Count defenders before offering or accepting a pawn.

steps.title: Does the pinned-knight trick work?

steps.text: **Before you grab or sacrifice.** Ask four things. How many pieces guard the target square, and how many attack it? Which pieces are pinned and cannot move or recapture? What would a check hit besides the king? What can the opponent's queen reach next move? [H] If you cannot answer all four, you are playing on hope.

Then go back to your first guess in the hook and rewrite it in one better sentence.

steps.prompt: Did your teach-back pass the self-check? Which of the five sentences was the weakest?

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
- A trap is a pattern with conditions: count guards, find pins, ask what a check hits.
- The f7 sacrifice needs a lone guard, a check with tempo and a second target.
- A pinned knight may jump if its threat is bigger than the queen.
- A free pawn is bait: ask what the queen can do next.
- Change one piece and the trick fails.
- [H] In three counted positions masters differed from the online crowd; a hint, not a rule.

In each you will name the plan, choose at the decision points, and find the slip. [I] Model games show typical play, not best play: strong players may deviate, and so may you.

**The quiet Italian.** The family after 3...Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano, 'quiet game'; the version with c3 and d3 is nicknamed Pianissimo, 'very quiet' [R]. White's plan: castle, rook to e1, knight round to f1 and g3, pawn to h3, bishop to b3, pawn to a4. [I] Reasons: c3 prepares d4, d3 guards e4, h3 stops a pin on g4, and the bishop on b3 avoids hits from ...d5 and ...b5. It is slow, but nothing hangs.

steps.text: **The Italian in five lines.** [I] Idea: develop fast, aim the bishops at f7 and f2, build c3 and d3, break with d4 when the pieces are placed. Works when: e4 stays guarded and the centre can stay closed while you improve. Fails when: a pawn hangs, the break comes before the pieces, or a plan ignores the weak point. Warning: count the guards first. Repair: hit the intruder.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A beginner who knows how the pieces move has five minutes. Write (1) the idea of the Italian Game in one sentence, (2) when it works, (3) one position they could set up on a board, (4) one warning: a typical error and its cheapest repair.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Compare with a model answer. (1) Develop fast, aim at f7 and f2, break with d4 when ready. (2) It works while e4 stays guarded. (3) Set-up: pawns on c3 and d3, both sides castled. (4) Warning: an unguarded e4 costs a pawn, so play d3 before castling. Did you say when it fails? The app grades nothing; you judge. [H] Teaching exposes gaps faster than a test.

**What to remember.**
- Count the guards before you castle, break or grab.
- Errors are cheap, costly or beyond repair.
- Cheap: hit the intruder. Costly: limit the damage, then develop.
- A break usually needs the queen's file open and no fewer attackers than defenders [H].
- A plan starts from structure, weak point and worst piece.
- Surprise: what does it threaten, what is undefended, which plan changes?
- The Italian: develop, aim at f7 and f2, break when ready. It fails when a pawn hangs [I].

steps.text: **White's plan: c5 (rule of thumb).** In the locked centre White has more room on the queenside. The break is c5, which attacks the pawn on d6. Condition: the pawn should be supported, here by a knight on d3, and Black's kingside play must not be faster. In the next item, find the move and check what the pawn on c5 attacks.

**Black's plan: f5, f4, g5 (rule of thumb).** Black has more room on the kingside. The break ...f5 challenges e4; ...f4 and ...g5 follow to attack White's king. Condition: the centre must stay locked, and it is a plan, not a guarantee. It is a race, and a tempting capture can cost more than it gains. Masters (329,379 games, both 2500+): after 9.Ne1 Nd7 10.Be3, all 50 games went ...f5; a small sample. Next, the pawn has reached f4.

**Check before you push (rule of thumb).** Your plan tells you which moves to look at; it does not tell you what the opponent's last move attacks or whether a capture works. Here White has just played c5, which attacks the pawn on d6. Black can capture on c5 (dxc5), or take on e4 with the knight. The engine's verdicts on both are shown in the next item. Check what each capture leaves behind, then decide.

steps.text: **The question.** The centre is closed, so where does the game happen, and how does each side break it open? You will read the pawn skeleton, find which squares are safe for pieces, and learn the break each side wants, with the conditions that make it work or fail. Evidence: engine claims at depth 16 [V], exact pawn facts [V], and our master data (329,379 games, both players rated 2,500 or more) with sample sizes.

**What the skeleton fixes.** No file is open and no pawn can capture another, so neither side can open the centre without a pawn move on a wing. A chain is the line of pawns that defend one another: White's pawn on d5 is held by c4 and e4, Black's pawn on e5 is held by d6. [I] A chain base is a pawn that defends another pawn but is defended by none; it tells you where the weak points are.

steps.caption: The same position. Because White has no pawn on c3 or e3, the square d4 is a hole in White's camp: a black pawn on e5 holds it and no white pawn can ever challenge it. [V] These are exact facts about the pawns. Whether a piece on d4 matters depends on the pieces, which is [I].

claims.statement: White's chain bases are the pawns on c4 and e4: each defends a pawn and no pawn defends them.
Black's chain bases are the pawns on c7, f7 and h7.
White has two holes, the squares d3 and d4, which no white pawn can ever cover.
Black has exactly one outpost, d4: a black pawn defends it and no white pawn can attack it.

steps.text: **The breaks.** Each side has one main break. White's is c5, which attacks the pawn on d6, the guard of e5. Black's is ...f5, which attacks the pawn on e4, the guard of d5. [I] Both are blows at a guard, not at the pawn that stands in front. The other pawn moves (a4, b4, a5, ...) prepare a break or answer one. The lesson now takes the breaks one at a time, Black's first.

steps.text: **Why ...f5.** [I] The pawn attacks e4, the guard of d5. If e4 falls or is traded, d5 loses a guard and White's grip on the centre loosens. The f-file also opens for Black's rook and supports the g-pawn storm. If White answers exf5, Black recaptures with the knight and reaches d4. So count the attackers and defenders of e4 once the pawn lands: the board after f3 shows the count.

**Conditions for ...f5.** The knight must leave f6. Black must be ready for exf5, so check what the recapture does. And the centre must stay closed: if White can open it, Black's pieces are slower than White's. [I] These are checks, not guarantees. One easy test: count the attackers and the defenders of e4 once the pawn lands.

steps.text: **Two plans, one race.** White opens the queenside with c5, supported by a knight on d3 or a pawn on b4. Black opens the kingside with f5, f4 and g5, supported by the knights. Neither side can stop the other's plan cheaply. [H] The side that keeps its king safe and times its lever correctly wins the race; the moves above show the timing in outline, not as a rule.

**Why each side plays on its own wing.** In a locked centre the only pawns that can still move are on the wings. A lever is a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn. White's lever is c4-c5, which attacks d6, supported by Nd3 or b4. Black's lever is ...f5, which attacks e4, supported by the knights, and later ...f4 and ...g5. Each lever opens lines toward the other side's king or pieces. [I]

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Most King's Indian games leave the main line early. Five sidelines each put a different question to Black: a solid centre (Sämisch), extra space (Four Pawns), pressure on f6 (Averbakh), a quiet fianchetto, and a queen trade (Exchange). For each you will say **what White buys, what it costs, and Black's best reply**, and you will see how two move orders can reach one position.

**The Sämisch pawn move (f3).** The pawn on f3 gives e4 a second guard, so a black knight cannot simply win it, and it prepares Be3, Qd2 and long castling. The price [I]: the f3 square is no longer free for the knight, and the pawn has left the g1-a7 diagonal open. The move appears 654 times in 5,565 master games after 4...d6 [V]. steps.text: **The rule behind it.** Count who takes first and what each capture gives up. A capture pays when you gain more than you give over the whole exchange; equal numbers of attackers and guards do not settle it. The gambit removes a guard (the knight) by offering it a pawn. This is the first of the three counts: **attackers, guards, recaptures**. [H] A pawn sacrifice that deflects a guard pays off best when your pieces already aim at the same square. Name another square where you could try it.

**A trade that loads a guard.** Black pushes ...h6 and ...g5 to drive the bishop back, then the knight jumps to h5 and takes on g3. White recaptures with the h-pawn. The trade works for Black only when it leaves d4 with one guard too few, so ...exd4 wins a pawn. The next count is **recaptures**: who retakes after each capture? steps.text: **What decided game C.** Black's attack was working: the engine had Black ahead until the queen took the pawn on c4 [V, depth 16]. [I] A good attack can be thrown away by a greedy capture: ask what the capture does to the piece that was making the threats. In games B and C one capture did. **What the games share.** Each side had a plan: a queenside break and knight play, a pawn storm. In game A White lost the e6 pawn, then slipped with the king. In game B Black's extra sacrifice failed. In game C Black's attack worked until a greedy capture. Masters tree, after the b-pawn push: Black played the knight to h5 in 138 games (White won 58, drew 53, lost 27) and the a-pawn push in 122 (52, 39, 31). Small samples: popularity, not best play. steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Source: our masters data, 329,379 games, both players 2500 or more. After 1.d4 d5 (30,060 games with a next move) White played 2.c4 in 22,757, 2.Nf3 in 5,216 and 2.Bf4 in 1,094 (White won 452, 339 drawn, Black won 303). After 2...Nf6 3.e3, Black played ...c5 in 626 games (268 White wins, 177 draws, 181 Black wins) and ...e6 in 356 (144, 124, 88). Samples are small; results also reflect the players.

**White's plan (rule of thumb).** The bishop on f4 defends e5, so a knight can go there when Black's setup allows it. In the masters data, after 4.Nf3 Bd6 White played Nbd2 in 330 games, Bg3 in 211, Ne5 in 116 and Bxd6 in 57. A plan can fail when Black's last move creates a new threat. Check the exact position: the contrast step shows one Black move that flips it.

**Black's plan (rule of thumb).** The bishop on f4 is defended by the e3 pawn, so Black cannot win it, but Black can offer a trade with ...Bd6 or ...Nh5. Another try is ...c5 with ...Nc6, pressing on d4. The next item is a position from that setup.

**A typical mistake.** A setup move can be so automatic that you stop checking. With Black's queen on b6, the usual c3 leaves b2 attacked and lets Black take the pawn at no cost. Before any setup move ask what the opponent's last move attacks, and whether your move deals with it.

steps.chapter: After 8.Ne5: what White is paying for

steps.text: **What White hopes to buy.** Three ideas, all my readings [I]. **Time:** Black's bishop must move again while the other kingside pieces stay at home. **Light squares:** with the f7 pawn gone, e6, f7 and g6 are easy targets for a light-squared bishop. **The king:** it has lost its f-pawn and faces a half-open file. The boards and the engine are the checks, not these sentences.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** After the knight jump the bishop must move. Black has three natural retreats, to f5, h7 or f7, and one extra on e4 that we treat as an aside. Which keeps the extra piece safest? What does each do for e6 and f7? steps.text: **Two kinds of mistake.** [I] The first trap loses by force: a count of attackers and a mate. The second gives back the whole advantage without any blunder, which is why it is easy to play. The remedy is the same question in both cases: which of my pawns has no defender, and which of my squares does the other side's next piece reach?

**Recap: what to remember.** The knight on e6 forks queen and bishop; taking it keeps Black a piece up. A queen move costs the castling right, and some squares cost the queen: c7 and d5 at once, b6 and a5 after a quiet knight move with two threats. A fork needs the targets on the knight's squares, and a knight never attacks the next square. Count the reply before a tempting move.

steps.text: **Two set-ups.** After 6.Be3, Black's two most common pawn moves in our master data are ...e5 and ...e6 (see the counts later). With **...e6** no black pawn attacks White's knight on d4 and the pawn on e6 guards d5. With **...e5** the pawn attacks that knight, and d5 becomes a square that no black pawn guards and none is likely to, because Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn has moved past it. steps.text: **A plan belongs to a structure.** A move from one set-up can be a mistake in another. Two questions before you borrow a move: what does Black's last pawn move attack, and does my plan still make sense there? Next, a mistake for each colour. **When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* the f3, Qd2 and g4 plan goes with ...e6, where no black pawn attacks the knight on d4. steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Najdorf is played with the same first six moves and then two different pawn skeletons. A skeleton tells each side where it can break open the position and where it cannot. After this lesson you can read a Najdorf position from its pawns, name the break each side wants, and say when that break fails.

steps.text: **What each skeleton gives.** [H] The ...e5 skeleton buys space and a firm grip on d4 and f4, and it costs a backward d6 pawn and a hole on d5. The ...e6 skeleton keeps d6 healthy and leaves d5 covered, and it costs space and the e5 square. In these two lines neither is clearly better: both scores are close to level [V, depth 16]. Which one you play is a choice of weaknesses.

steps.text: **What a pawn break is.** A break is a pawn move that challenges the enemy pawn structure, usually by offering a trade: ...d5 and e5 are breaks. A pawn storm, such as ...b5-b4 or g4-g5, pushes pawns at pieces to win time. [H] A break or a storm works when it comes before the opponent's pieces are ready for it: a hypothesis from the three positions here, and ...d5 is still slightly worse for Black even when it works. Test it on the central break first.

steps.text: **Reading a skeleton.** [H] Three questions. Which break is mine, and has the other side's piece placement let it work yet? Which break is theirs? Which square is the pawn structure giving away for free? Answer these before you choose a plan, then check the plan against a count of attackers and defenders.

**Before the test.** No labels from here. 'Sound' for a find-the-move item means within about half a pawn of the engine's best at depth 16; 'playable' for a break means the score stays within about a pawn of equal. Both are proxies, noisy by about 0.2. Expect new positions and no hints that name the idea.

steps.text: **The Najdorf skeleton in five lines.** [I] The skeleton fixes where each side can break. With ...e5: space for Black, a hole on d5 and a backward d6 pawn, and an outpost for White. With ...e6: a healthier d6 pawn, no outpost, and the central break ...d5 while White's pieces are not ready. White's levers: the storm g4 and g5 when a pawn or piece can recapture, and the break e5 only after the pieces are placed.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A beginner knows how the pieces move. In five minutes explain (1) the two Black skeletons, (2) what a pawn break is, (3) one break that works and why, (4) one break that fails and what it ran into.

steps.text: **Self-check.** (1) ...e5 and ...e6: one pawn, two different sets of weaknesses. (2) A pawn move that challenges the enemy pawns, usually by offering a trade; a storm pushes pawns at pieces. (3) ...d5 right after f3: the white queen and pawns are not ready. (4) ...d5 after Qd2 and g4: the pawn on g4 hits the knight with tempo. Did you say when each fails? The app grades nothing; you judge. [H] Teaching exposes gaps faster than a test.

steps.prompt: Optional. Play one game from this Najdorf position as Black (or as White) and try to steer toward the skeleton you chose. You pick the level; the app marks it as a quiet record, never a gate.

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
- A skeleton fixes where each side can break.
- ...e5: space, a hole on d5, a backward d6 pawn.
- ...e6: no hole, a flexible chain.
- A break works while the other side's pieces are not ready [H].
- g5 needs a recapture; e5 needs the pieces placed.
- Read the pawns first, then count attackers.

steps.prompt: After your game: which skeleton did you reach, and which break did you play or stop? How sure are you now that you could teach the Najdorf pawn structures in five minutes? Which of the four parts is your weakest?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Every opening move does two jobs: it answers what the opponent just did, and it makes a later move possible. We follow both sides of the Najdorf and ask of each early move: *what does this make possible, and what does it cost?* By the end you can build either set-up piece by piece and give a reason for every step. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.text: **When the push gains time.** A push gains time when it attacks a piece and a pawn guards it. Both parts matter. With White's bishop on e2 the pawn on b5 would attack nothing: it is a space move that leaves c6 less covered and costs a tempo. It is good only when it prepares ...b4 against the knight on c3 or ...Bb7 [I]. So before pushing, ask: what does the pawn attack, and what guards it? The next three positions share one base and change one thing each.

steps.text: **A set-up is a list of jobs.** Our opening file names the position after White's bishop goes to e3 the *English Attack* [V]. Its list: a pawn to f3 (guards g4), the queen to d2 (clears the first rank), long castling (king far from the storm) and the g-pawn push (the storm itself). None of these wins anything alone; each makes the next possible. First question: why can the g-pawn not go at once?

steps.text: **Queen out, then the king.** The queen on d2 clears the squares between the king and the rook, and long castling puts the king on c1, far from the g-pawn push. The rook lands on d1, facing the d6 pawn on a half-open file. The cost [I]: Black's pieces (the bishop on e6, a knight heading for c5) now aim at the queenside, and the king faces Black's queenside pawns, so the game becomes a race with the kings on opposite wings.

steps.text: **Black's list.** Black has jobs too. The pawn to e5 takes space and attacks the knight. The bishop goes to e6: it guards d5, where White's knight wants to land, and eyes the white knight on b3. The other bishop comes to e7 and the king castles. Last come the knight to d7 and the pawn to b5 for counter-play. The two bishop moves can come in either order; the next two boards reach the same set-up both ways.

steps.text: **What to remember about the race.** [I] In the English Attack each side's attack uses pawns on the wing where the enemy king stands. The side that makes threats first forces the other to answer. The engine rates the line we stepped through between level and slightly better for White, so neither wing wins by itself [V]. To test it yourself: in your own games, count how often each side's first attack move is a pawn move.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** After 5...a6 White has more than a dozen reasonable sixth moves, and each asks Black something different. steps.text: **Three questions to ask of any sixth move [I].** First: does it allow or stop ...e5? Second: where does the other bishop go, and does that cost time? Third: after a knight leaves c3, who still guards the e4 pawn? The boards ahead put these questions to Be2, h3, Bc4 and Be3, one move at a time.

**6.Be2: wait, then castle.** The bishop steps in so White can castle at once, and the c1 bishop can still choose e3 or g5 later. It does not stop ...e5, so White is ready to meet that pawn with Nb3. [I] A player who wants a calm structure first chooses it.

Black: develop the c8 bishop to e6, put a knight on d7 or c6, and use the open c-file with a rook. Neither plan is forced; they are what the pawns point to.

steps.text: **What Nd5 does [I].** It trades one of Black's pieces for a knight, and the recapture on d5 leaves White with a pawn that restricts the e6 and c6 squares. **The Poisoned Pawn.** After 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Black's queen can go to b6. White's bishop has left c1, so b2 has no guard; White keeps the queen on the d-file to defend the d4 knight and offers the pawn as bait. steps.text: **Why it holds, and when it does not [I].** The sacrifice works because the recapture bxc3 removes the knight and leaves e4 with no guard, while the knight on f6 already attacks it. If a second white piece guarded e4, for example a bishop on d3, then ...Nxe4 would lose a piece. So count the guards of e4 first, then offer the rook. [H] The engine treats the sacrifice as one of several equal choices, so it is a way to unbalance the game, not a necessity.

steps.text: **Typical mistakes and where they come from [I].** (1) Moving the guard of a pawn without a bigger threat. (2) Grabbing a pawn that is still guarded. (3) Sacrificing a rook without counting what the recapture leaves behind. All three are the same error: not asking which piece guards the key square. Our data cannot say how often these errors occur; they are what the boards above show.

**Recap.** Count the guards of the key square before you jump, grab or sacrifice. A knight jump from c3 leaves e4 loose unless f3, a bishop or another piece guards it. Nd5 works in the English Attack because f3 holds e4. ...Rxc3 works because it removes the guard of e4. Grabs fail while the guard stands. The Poisoned Pawn is not a guard count: queen escape squares and development decide it, and draws are common in our data.

steps.text: **What decided game 2.** The position was level at move 23 [V]; one queen move then lost the game. The mistake did not come from the opening or from a bad plan: it came from not checking what was attacked. **Game 3: the poisoned pawn.** In the Bg5 Najdorf Black plays ...Qb6 and, after Qd2, takes the b2 pawn. In 162 master games with 8.Qd2, Black took in 149: White won 26, 104 were drawn, Black won 19 [S: stats.json]. White scored 52%, Black 48%. steps.text: **What decided game 3.** Not the poisoned pawn: the engine rates the position after the capture as roughly equal [V]. White left the engine's first choice with 10.Be2 (about 0.6 pawn behind f5); Black's ...Nc6 was within 0.2 of the best, and the game stayed balanced until Black's recapture on d5. One recapture decided it: ...exd5 instead of ...cxd5 [V]. [I] The structure after the capture mattered more than the pawn. White then converted over twenty more moves.

**Three games, three decisions.** Game 1 turned on two slips after Black found the best defence; game 2 on one queen move after a balanced middlegame; game 3 on one recapture. [H] In all three, the swing came within a few moves of a forcing line and the opening itself did not decide. That may be true only of the games I picked: a larger sample would test it. steps.text: **A rule with an exception.** Nimzowitsch, in *My System*, wrote: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" [V-quote: citable-views 1.7]. He allowed an exception for a central pawn taken without great danger. That is a rule of thumb, and rules of thumb have conditions. steps.text: **Nimzo-Indian Defense** (ECO E20 for the first position): 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4. The bishop pins the knight on c3 against the king, and the knight on f6 attacks e4. Black can later take on c3, which gives White the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns. This lesson covers the opening's plans only; the doubled-pawns and bishop lessons explain those ideas.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Our masters file: 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After 3...Bb4 White played 4.e3 in 5,563 games (1,857 won by White, 2,349 drawn, 1,357 won by Black), 4.Qc2 in 3,501 (1,014, 1,725, 762), 4.f3 in 713 and 4.a3 in 384. Our online sample (Lichess Blitz, Rapid and Classical, 4,752,291 games, first 16 moves, all rating bands): 11,641 reach 3...Bb4, 2,203 reach 4.Qc2 and 1,786 reach 4.e3.

**White's plan (rule of thumb).** After ...Bxc3 and bxc3, White has two bishops and often advances e4 to open lines for them. Condition: count what attacks e4 first. Only the knight on f6 attacks it in the next position; an extra black attacker can turn the same advance into a lost pawn. Find the move, then compare the two cases.

**Black's plan (rule of thumb).** White's pawn on c4 has no b-pawn beside it, so only pieces can defend it. Black adds attackers: ...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Na5. In the masters data, after 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3, Black played ...c5 in 174 games, ...b6 in 88 and ...Nc6 in 42 (results of games, not evaluations). Condition: this asks White's pieces to defend; it wins nothing by itself.

**When the plans apply.** Both plans are rules of thumb for positions where Black has taken on c3 and White has recaptured with the b-pawn. Check that the structure is there: with the bishop still on b4 White has no doubled pawns. Then count attackers and defenders on the square you aim at. In the next three positions, only one feature differs.

title: Pirc Defence: let White build the centre, then strike at it
outcomes: Names the Classical (4.Nf3), Austrian Attack (4.f4) and Byrne (4.Bg5) branches by their move orders

steps.text:
**The Pirc Defence** starts 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6. Black lets White build a centre of pawns on e4 and d4, then attacks it from the sides: the bishop on g7 and pawn breaks such as ...c5 and ...e5 (breaks are taught in the breaks lesson).
Our opening data names the next move: 4.Nf3 is the **Classical Variation**, 4.f4 the **Austrian Attack**, 4.Bg5 the **Byrne Variation**.

**White's plans (rule of thumb).** Two common set-ups in our data. **Austrian:** pawns on e4, d4 and f4; develop with Nf3 and a bishop, and keep e5 as a space-gaining push. **Quiet (Classical):** Be2, castle, then slow moves. In both, the centre pawns are the asset to keep. Step through the Austrian, then find White's move.

steps.text: **Queen's Gambit Declined** (ECO D30, the standard code for this opening): 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6. In our online data (4,752,291 games, September 2026) 63,292 games reach this position, and 6,259 reach the position named the *Exchange Variation*, after 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.cxd5. This lesson follows the Exchange Variation, where both sides have clear plans to test. Its pawn structure (White d4 and e3, Black c6 and d5, no e-pawn) is the book form of the Carlsbad structure from the Carlsbad lesson: Black has no e-pawn, and White has no c-pawn.

After 3.Nc3 Nf6, White played 4.cxd5 in 4,184 of 5,794 games (Bg5: 813, Nf3: 739). Of those 4,184 games White won 1,493, 1,700 were drawn and Black won 991. **When the minority attack fits (rule of thumb).** White has two pawns against three on the a-, b- and c-files, the pawn pushed to b4 can be supported (here the rook on b1 defends it), and Black has no quicker threat. It does not fit when something of yours is attacked. Ask first: what did my opponent's last move attack? The next item shows what skipping that question costs.

**Black's side (rule of thumb).** Black often looks to exchange minor pieces, for example a knight against a bishop that has come to g5 or g3. Condition: the exchange must be safe in the position in front of you. In the next item two knight moves both attack the bishop, and the engine rates them very differently. Check the move, not just the idea.

steps.text: **The minority attack, in plain words.** On the a, b and c files White has two pawns where Black has three. Pushing the b-pawn to b5 offers a trade. It fits when the pushed pawn is supported, Black has no faster threat, and White's pieces can reach the new target.

White's own a-pawn is also isolated, and the open b-file serves both rooks. [I] Engines usually rate such positions as a small plus, not a win. - A half-open file belongs to the side with no pawn on it.

**What to remember.**
- Each fourth move commits to something: take (structure), pin (pressure), develop (options).
- After the exchange Black may retake with the pawn or the knight; the engine calls them level.
- A pinned piece cannot move or recapture: look along the line to the king.
- Many roads lead to the same position; the first moves decide which doors stay open.
- Before a pawn push, count attackers and defenders.

steps.chapter: A retreat into a pawn fork

steps.text: **When a pawn fork works.** Two valuable pieces stand on the two squares a pawn attacks from one step ahead. The square in front of the pawn is empty. The pawn is guarded, or taking it costs more than it wins. And you have no in-between answer, such as a check. Before a retreat, ask which enemy pawn could advance and attack this square, and what else stands beside it.

outcomes: Explains in a sentence why the c8 bishop is the problem piece of the Orthodox Declined, and names two ways to repair it (trades then a central break; the b6 route to the long diagonal)

steps.text: **The question.** How does the Queen's Gambit Declined go wrong, and how do you repair it? Usually slowly: the engine drifts by a quarter or half a pawn and nobody notices. A few mistakes lose a pawn at once. You will meet four kinds, see what each costs at depth 16 [V], and learn the repair. At the end you diagnose positions with no labels, then teach the whole thing back.

**Error one: the sleeping bishop.** Black's pawns on d5, e6 and c6 stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop, and with the knight on d7 they hold it in. [I] That is why the Declined is called solid but passive. The repair is not speed: it is choosing a way out (a trade, a break or a new diagonal) before the opponent adds pressure.

steps.text: **Closed does not mean quiet.** In this position no file is open, because every file still holds a pawn. [I] So play happens in two places: behind the pawns, where pieces regroup, and at the pawn levers. A lever is a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn and can change the structure. This lesson lists the levers, what each one costs, and when a side should take or keep the tension.

**Holes.** A hole is a square that none of your pawns can guard any more. [V] Black has two here, a5 and c6; White has one, d3. A hole is only a weakness if an enemy piece can settle there. [I] So ask who can reach the hole, not only whether you have one. Black's knight on c6 stands on one of its own holes, which is safe while it stays there.

**The lever d4.** The pawn on d4 attacks e5, so e5 now has two attackers. The pawn on c3 is what makes the lever work: it guards d4, so a black capture would be met by a recapture with a pawn. [I] The price is that e4 and d4 become targets, and Black's pieces can go after them. Watch what Black does with the knight that stood on c6.

A capture is a decision about who gets the tempo; the side that recaptures with a gain wins that decision.
