A move can free a piece, defend a pawn so another piece may leave, take a square away from the opponent, or prepare a lever. We go through White's set-up with that question, then Black's, then ask how the order of the moves matters.

**Castling does not defend e4.** [V] After 4...Nf6, masters castled in 10,556 games and played d3 in 1,414. [I] Castling puts the king in safety and the rook on f1. If Black takes e4, White regains the pawn with d4 and dxe5 (the Open Ruy Lopez). The calmer path is to defend e4 first. Both exist; the next board shows the most popular route.

steps.text: **What makes the cage.** [I] Three features work together. One: a Black pawn on b5 covers both a4 and c4, so one pawn guards both exits. Two: White's own pawns on a2 and c2 shut off the other two diagonal squares. Three: the pawn on c5 hit the queen with tempo, so White never had a free move to rescue the bishop. Remove one feature and there is a hole. Count the exits and who guards each.

**How often do players walk into it?** [V] The Week in Chess files hold 3,370,649 games (2012 to 2026, not de-duplicated, all strengths). about 132,000 begin with the Ruy Lopez, and 285 of them reach this position. White then chose c3 in 106, Bd5 in 98, the queen grab in 43 and a4 in 22. After the grab Black won 35, drew 4 and lost 4. In only 2 of the 43 were both players rated 2500 or more.

steps.text: **A tie to the queen is a tie of cost, not of law.** [I] The black knight on e7 may legally move, because the king is not behind it. But if it moves, the bishop takes the queen. So the knight is tied to e7 as long as the queen stands on d8 and the bishop stays on g5. Check the line behind a piece before you move it. The tie disappears when the queen leaves the diagonal, or when the bishop is traded off.

**Recap.**
- A free pawn is an offer: look at what the capture leaves behind.
- Count the exits of any piece you are about to leave; one pawn can guard two.

steps.prompt: Three games, one move each: Game 1 (23...f4, attacking the queen), Game 2 (25...Kd7, defending c7), Game 3 (24...f5, attacking the rook). What do Games 1 and 3 have in common? Does Game 2 fit?

steps.text: **One possible answer [I].** In Games 1 and 3 the losing move was natural and active: a pawn push with a threat that gave up a defender or a square that a tactic then used (a swing of about 2.1 and 1.9 pawns). Game 2 does not fit: White was already clearly better, and the king step only made it worse. Before a natural move, count what it leaves undefended. This is a hypothesis from two fast games, not a rule.

**Plans in the three games [I].** White tried a slow kingside build-up (Game 1), a queenside and open-file build-up in a Berlin ending (Game 2), and the bishop pair with a changed structure (Game 3). Black tried a central break, solid defence, and counterplay by trades. Quiet plans take many moves: about fifteen in Game 1, about twenty in Game 2. One slip can end them.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did your five lines name a plan for each side and a move number? Did you say what the slip gave up? Could a friend set up your idea on a board? The app grades nothing; a stronger player or a friend can read it.

**Recap.**
- The Ruy Lopez fights over e5 and e4; the plans follow the structure.
- Quiet plans (a knight to f5, a rook lift, the bishop pair) need many moves.
- A rare move order tests the opponent more than the position.
- A push that hits a piece can give up the squares behind it (Games 1 and 3); in Game 2 the slip only made things worse.
- Count with your own eyes first; the engine is a ruler.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Ruy Lopez has many sound moves, but a few natural-looking ones cost real material. So where do games go wrong? You will meet six instructive errors [I], three for each colour, learn to tell cheap errors from costly ones, repair what can be repaired, and then build plans from quiet positions.

steps.text: **Three kinds of error.** [H] Sort an error by what it gives up. *Cheap*: no piece or pawn is lost at once; the price is time or structure, and the repair may offer a pawn. *Costly*: a pawn lost and kept. *Beyond repair*: a piece lost for nothing. steps.text: **The Ruy Lopez in five lines.** [I] Idea: pressure the knight that guards e5, keep e4 guarded by a rook, and build c3 and d4. Works when: e4 is guarded and the centre can stay closed while you improve. Fails when: a pawn is grabbed without counting, d4 comes before c3, or a knight leaves e5 undefended. Warning: count the guards first. Repair: limit the damage, then develop.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A beginner who knows how the pieces move has five minutes. Write (1) the idea of the Ruy Lopez in one sentence, (2) when it works, (3) one position they could set up on a board, (4) one warning: a typical error and what it costs.

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
- Count the guards before you grab, break or move a defender.
- Errors are cheap, costly or beyond repair.
- Cheap: no material lost. Costly: a pawn. Beyond repair: a piece.
- A pinned knight cannot count as a defender: the same break is an error with the king on e8 and only a gambit once it has castled [H].
- A plan starts from structure, weak point and worst piece.
- Surprise: what does it threaten, what is undefended, which plan changes?

title: The Scandinavian Defence: tempi against open lines
outcomes: Finds the developing move that attacks the queen after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5

steps.text: **The Scandinavian Defence** starts 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 (ECO B01). Black removes White's e-pawn at once, so lines open: the e-file for White, the d-file for Black, and the c8 bishop is free. The price: after 3.Nc3 the queen must move. This lesson is about that trade. It assumes *Tempo: choosing the move that gains one* and *An opening is a route to a structure and its plans*.

steps.caption: The Main Line of the Scandinavian, step by step.

line.say: White takes space in the centre.
Black attacks the e-pawn at once. This is the Scandinavian Defence (ECO B01).
White captures the pawn.
Black recaptures with the queen. The e-file is now half-open for White, the d-file for Black.
White develops and attacks the queen. Black must spend a move on it.
The queen moves again. It has now moved twice, and the queen on a5 attacks the knight on c3.
White takes the centre and opens the bishop on c1.
Black develops a knight.
White develops a second piece.
Black plays a pawn move that covers b5 and d5 and leaves c7 free for the queen.
White develops the bishop with a free diagonal.
Black's c8 bishop comes out; its diagonal was open since the d-pawn left.

After 2...Qxd5 the bishop on c8 has 5 legal moves: its diagonal is open.
After 3.Nc3 one white piece, the knight, attacks the queen on d5.
After 4.d4 one black piece, the queen on a5, attacks the knight on c3.
After 6...Bf5 the engine (depth 16) rates the position between level and 1.1 pawns in White's favour.

steps.text: **What strong players chose.** In master data (329,379 games, both players 2,500 or more), 1,687 of the 142,147 games that began 1.e4 went on with 1...d5. After 3.Nc3, Black played ...Qa5 in 598 games, ...Qd6 in 379, ...Qd8 in 207 and ...Qe5+ in 87. Online (a sample of 4,752,291 Lichess blitz, rapid and classical games, September 2026): ...Qa5 35,176, ...Qd8 33,957, ...Qe6+ 12,969. These count games; none is an evaluation.

**White's plan.** After the queen retreats, White has one piece developed and Black none besides the queen. White's job is to keep developing and take the centre before Black catches up. *Rule of thumb:* when you are ahead in development, make moves that develop; do not chase. On a5 the queen attacks the knight on c3, so the c3 knight needs care.

**Black's plan.** Black has spent two moves on the queen, so the job is to catch up: a knight to f6, ...c6 or ...Bf5, then castling. Black's gains: the c8 bishop has open diagonals and the d-file is half-open. In the 3.Nc3 lines of this lesson the engine rated ...Bg4 and the queen checks below the quiet moves; after 3.Nf3 it is different (see the contrast).

**When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* an early queen often costs a tempo when a developing move can attack it. Here that is 3.Nc3. It does not apply when nothing attacks the queen: after 3.Nf3 the engine's first choice at depth 16 is a developing move, not a queen move. Ask: is my queen attacked, and who has more pieces out?

steps.text: **They left the book: three questions** gave you the questions with labels. Now there is no label, and the first job is a sorting job. Does the odd move attack something of yours, so that a piece is loose? Then answer it. Does it threaten nothing? Then your habits are free again. A quick test: *if I passed, what could they take?*

Not every odd move is a threat. An early queen move or an edge pawn can look alarming and threaten nothing at all. Treat 'harmless' as a claim to test, not a feeling. Pass in your head, then look at every capture and check the opponent would have: does any of them win material or give mate? If none does, the move is harmless. Even then, ask what the move gave up.

steps.text: **An odd move: answer it or ignore it** sorted odd moves into threats and harmless ones. Some odd moves are neither: they invite your natural reply, and the natural reply is the mistake. When a capture or a developing move seems obvious right after an odd move, calculate it two moves deep before you play it. Ask what your move leaves loose and what it opens.

Now name the habit. In the position you just met, Black has moved the same knight three times (...Nf6, ...Ng4, ...Nxe5), brought the queen out and put a bishop on b4. Naming the habit tells you *where to look*: the knight that keeps moving and the king still in the middle. But a broken habit is not a refutation. *Rule of thumb:* name the habit, then calculate.

steps.text: **Moves that help and moves that wait** sorted moves into helping and waiting. Now you choose with no label. A rook-pawn move (a move of the a- or h-pawn) is rarely best, and it is right when it has a concrete job: it attacks a piece that pins, takes a square the opponent wants, or stops a plan. *Rule of thumb:* ask what the pawn will attack, then compare it with the best developing move.

The job has to be real. A pin does not make every pawn move the best one: compare it with the developing moves. And a plan has to be a plan the opponent can carry out. If you cannot name what the pawn attacks, it is a waiting move, and waiting moves cost time when the opponent can use it.

title: When the position makes a quiet move right
outcomes: Predicts that a pinned knight or a settled centre can make a quiet pawn move the right move

steps.text: **Develop, wait or answer: choosing without a label** gave rook-pawn moves a concrete job. Here the *character* of the position decides. A pinned knight lets a pawn ask the pinning bishop a question. A settled centre, where neither side has a profitable break (a pawn push that opens lines), takes the rush out of the game. Each such move overrides a default; name it.

The default to name is the one the move overrides. Against a pin, the default is *develop a piece first*. steps.text: A **novelty** is a move that leaves known play where it is at least as good as the old move, and is new to the person you play. 'Known' means known to someone: a book, a database, your opponent. Two tests: is it new where it matters, and can you say why it works? The engine's first choice is often already known.

steps.text: **What this app can check, and what it cannot.** Its items were checked offline with Stockfish 19 Lite, depth 16, one thread (roughly 16 half-moves). Nothing here can check that a move is new to theory: the Openings page holds online games, not master games. So 'new' here means rare at your opponent's rating. An engine score (100 centipawns is about one pawn) is evidence under those limits, not proof.

A **written justification** has three lines. The concrete reason: a capture, check or threat that the old move allows and yours stops. The evidence with its settings: engine, depth, centipawn gap. What remains unproven: deeper lines, untested replies. **Rule of thumb:** a gap of a few centipawns is not an improvement. If you cannot write the first line, you have an engine move, not a novelty.

steps.text: Preparation has two jobs. **Exact recall** is for forcing lines, where one slip loses at once: you remember the move. **Understanding** is for flexible positions, where many moves work: you know the plan and the structure. Real games show which lines are worth the memory. On the Openings page, after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4, Black plays 3...Bc5 in 21% of games at 1100-1300 (869 of 4,100). The engine prefers 4.Nxe5, yet only 29% of White players take it in that band. The line is forcing, and each reply needs its own move. Watch it once.

title: Opening habits: one checked failure each
outcomes: Gives one checked position where taking the centre fails, one where moving a piece again is right, and one where castling is not the move

steps.text: **When the opening habits fail: reasons and conditions** showed that a habit gives way to a threat. Here each habit gets its own checked failure. Start with the centre. A centre pawn is only as good as the square it lands on, so before you push, count the enemy pieces that attack that square and your own pieces that defend it. This is a *rule of thumb*: count first, then push.

Second habit: do not move a piece twice before the others are out. The reason is time, and time is worth little when a piece of yours is loose (attacked and not defended). If the piece that has already moved is the one in danger, moving it again is the development that counts. *Rule of thumb:* a loose piece comes before a new piece.

Third habit: castle early. Castling puts the king away, but it does not defend anything else. Before you castle, ask what a trade could leave loose. A pawn defended only by a piece that can be traded off is the usual case. In the next pair, a position where the d6 pawn defends e5 is set against one where only the c6 knight does.

steps.text: In **Punishing an opening mistake: find it, or develop calmly** you decided whether a punishment exists. A punishment rests on conditions: a target guarded only once, a check that works. Change one feature and it can vanish. Your skill now is prediction: say what the plan needs, then look for the one feature that gives it away. First, a position where nothing important changed.

**What each plan needs.** Taking on e5 with the knight is a sacrifice: the f-pawn already guards e5, and after ...fxe5 the queen's check on h5 has to do the work. So the plan needs two things: no *second* guard of e5, and a check on h5 that works. Ask: who else guards e5? Can a pawn block the check? *Rule of thumb:* a defender that adds a second guard of e5 usually ends the punishment; a pawn move on the far wing usually does not. Predict, then check.

It stops applying when taking the pawn wins material at once and the other side gets nothing back. Two positions follow in which Black offers a pawn. Ask what your pieces want, not what the pawn wants.

title: An opening is a route to a structure and its plans
outcomes: Explains that different move orders can reach one pawn structure, and that the structure suggests plans

steps.text: An opening is a route to a **structure**: the shape of the pawns. Pawns cannot go back, so the shape changes only slowly, by pushes and captures, and it says where pieces belong and which pawn pushes matter. Different move orders can reach the same structure. Learn a few structures and their usual plans, and many openings become one problem.

steps.caption: Route A. White's c-pawn is gone from the board and Black has no e-pawn.

line.say: 3.Nc3

steps.caption: Route B starts with a different first move but ends in exactly the same position.

line.say: 2.Nc3
4.cxd5

steps.text: **Carlsbad:** White has no c-pawn, and Black has a pawn on d5 and usually one on c6 (it may still stand on c7). White often pushes the queenside pawns (b4, then b5) to create a target on c6, or trades pieces. Black often repositions a knight toward the kingside or trades pieces. These are usual plans, not laws.

**Isolated d-pawn:** a pawn on d4 with no friendly pawn on the c or e file. Pawns cannot defend it, but it gives space and open lines. The owner usually keeps pieces on and aims them at the king. The other side adds pressure, blockades d5 and trades pieces. Tendencies, not laws.

steps.title: The same push in different structures
steps.prompt: A plan belongs to a structure. Predict where a queenside pawn push fits, then check.

steps.text: **Open centre:** the central pawns are traded and files and diagonals are open. Speed and king safety count most. Put rooks on open files and develop before you attack. These are tendencies; check what the opponent's last move attacks first.

steps.prompt: Pick an opening you play. Which structure does it usually lead to, and what is the usual plan for each side? Write one sentence for each.

**Five traps, four shapes.** [I] This sorting is ours. The f-pawn capture **opened a line**. The knight capture ignored a **counter-threat**. The captures on e7 and b4 each met a **check in between** (Bxf2+, exf2+). The last was a **promotion**: a pawn near the end is a piece in disguise. Légal combines a check with mate. Name the shape and the reply is easier to find.

steps.text: In **Sure material, or a trap?** you were told a position held a trap. Now nobody says. Before a capture, ask two things: *what does it open or take away?* and *what can the other side do next?* If the honest answer is 'nothing', or a reply that you have checked fails, take. If a piece loses its duty or the opponent gets a strong reply, decline with a quiet developing move.

**Rule of thumb for club players:** take sure material. It fails when the capture drags a defender away, or the piece you win is the bait. Just as important, the habit works both ways: when the capture is sure, take it, because declining free material is also a mistake. steps.text:
A **passed pawn** has no enemy pawn in front of it on its file or a neighbouring file. A **blockade** puts a piece on the square directly in front of it, so the pawn cannot advance.
**Rule of thumb:** the default blockader is a **knight**, because it loses no strength standing in front of the pawn. A queen there tends to be driven off; the king belongs in the endgame.

**Rule of thumb:** a blockade works when the blockading square is **safe** and the pawn is dangerous (passed, advanced or central). Check who attacks the square, above all pawns. A piece on a square an enemy pawn attacks will simply be taken.

steps.text: A **pawn break** (or lever) pushes a pawn so that it can be exchanged for an enemy pawn. It opens a file or diagonal, or changes the pawn structure. It is also how you attack a chain of pawns: strike at the **base**, the pawn at the back that protects the rest. Judge a break by what it opens and who is ready to use it.

steps.text: A break is ready when pieces stand behind it. Count the defenders of the break square against the attackers, check that no pin punishes the move, and look at what the push uncovers: a pawn that leaves its square can open a diagonal or file for the opponent. In an undeveloped position a break can give the opponent targets. As a *rule of thumb*, finish development first.

outcomes: Chooses between playing the break and a preparatory move by counting attackers and defenders of the break square
Rejects a break when an enemy piece newly attacks the break square
Names the files a break opens and the rooks that could use them
Tells a pawn advance that attacks nothing from a real break

steps.text: In **Pawn breaks: ready or premature?** you tested whether one break was ready. Now you choose between two moves: the break itself, or a **preparatory move** that adds a defender of the break square or takes an attacker away. Count the attackers and defenders of the square the pawn lands on. Then ask what the break opens, and **who** can use the opened line first.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d3 can step to d4 and offer an exchange against c5.

line.say: The break: the pawn attacks c5 and offers an exchange.
Black takes.
White recaptures. Now White has no d-pawn and Black has no c-pawn.

claims.statement: d4 is among the engine's top two moves.
After the exchange the d-file is half-open for White and the c-file is half-open for Black: the break opens a line for both sides.

steps.text: Preparation is cheap when the count is against you. *Rule of thumb:* if the break square is attacked more often than it is defended, add a defender or remove an attacker first; if the count is level or better and no pin or capture on the opened line punishes the push, break. A break opens a line for **both** sides, so look at his rooks as well as yours.

steps.title: Same break, one piece different
steps.prompt: In the first position White can play d5 now. In the second only the Black knight differs (on b6 instead of f8): break, or prepare? The third position asks a different question: does the pawn attack anything? Predict, then check.
Think of the two positions where White could play d5: the Black knight stood on f8 in one and on b6 in the other. What did you count, and which side's rooks would have used the opened files?

title: Controlling the centre: count the attackers
outcomes: Counts the attackers of d4, e4, d5 and e5 for both sides
Picks the move that adds the most attackers to the central squares and names the pieces involved
Checks whether a central pawn can be held, and what is attacked, before playing for the centre

steps.text:
To **control** a square means your pawns and pieces attack it, and can win the fight there. A pawn standing on e4 or d4 *occupies* a central square; it controls only the squares it attacks.
Count attackers: for d4, e4, d5 and e5, how many pawns and pieces does each side have? More attackers is a first sign of control, not a verdict.

steps.caption: White to move. Watch the attackers on e5.

line.say: Nf3 attacks e5 (and d4). White has one attacker on e5.
Nc6 defends e5. Black has one defender of e5 and also attacks d4.
The d-pawn attacks e5 too. White now has two attackers on e5 against one defender.

claims.statement: After Nf3 White attacks e5 once.
After Nc6 Black defends e5 once.
After d4 White attacks e5 twice.
Black still defends e5 once.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** a central pawn controls squares only while it can be **held**. Count its attackers and defenders; if the count is against you, the pawn is a target, not control.
Capturing the enemy's central pawn is not automatic either: check what lines it opens. And what is attacked comes first: no plan beats losing a piece.

steps.title: Same pawns, one defender fewer
steps.prompt: In the next position White's bishop stands on e2, not d3. Does the pawn on e4 still hold? Predict first, then check.
In the last positions, before you moved: did you count the attackers on the central squares, or look first at what was attacked? What would you check first next time?

title: A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it
outcomes: Recognises a free enemy centre pawn: on d4 or e4 (d5 or e5 if the enemy is Black), attacked by none of your pawns and able to advance
Chooses between a prepared break and a quiet set-up of pieces for a given free pawn
Counts defenders and attackers of the break square before breaking
Says when there is no free centre pawn

steps.text: A **free centre pawn** is an enemy pawn on d4 or e4 (d5 or e5 if the enemy is Black) that none of your pawns attacks and that can advance. You have two answers. **Break** it with a prepared pawn move that attacks it, or **restrain** it: place pieces so that the square in front is covered, and wait. Neither answer always works.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn on d4 is free: no Black pawn attacks it and it can advance.

line.say: The break e5 attacks d4. Two Black men defend e5 and two White men attack it.
White takes.
Black retakes, and White's free pawn is gone. The d-file is open.

claims.statement: No Black pawn attacks d4.
The pawn on d4 can advance.
After e5 the pawn attacks d4.
Two Black men defend e5.
Two White men attack e5.
After the exchange there is no White pawn on d4.
The d-file is open.
e5 is among the engine's top moves.

steps.text: Both answers cost something. A break needs the pieces behind it: count the defenders of the break square against the attackers. Restraint takes several moves and ties pieces to their squares, so it is slow; that is a *rule of thumb*, not a law. Sometimes the break is not ready, and sometimes there is no free pawn at all. Check which case you are in.

steps.title: Break now, or not?
steps.prompt: In the first two positions Black can play ...c5 against White's free d4 pawn. They differ by one Black knight (on d7 or on g8). Predict each before you check. In the third, the Black c-pawn has already moved to c5.

Think of the two positions without hints before the practice set: White had a free pawn on d4 in one and none in the other. What did you check first: whether White had a free pawn, or which move to play? Write what you looked at, and what you would check next time.

title: The free centre pawn: break, set up, or neither?
outcomes: Decides in an unlabeled position between the break, the piece set-up and neither
Rejects a break that an enemy rook or piece on the open line has made premature
Tells that a pawn that is already attacked, or blocked, is not a free centre pawn

steps.text: In **A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it** you met the free pawn and its two answers. Here nobody names the answer. For each position ask three questions. Is the pawn free: no enemy pawn attacks it, and it can advance? If so, is the break ready: count its attackers and defenders. If not, which set-up of pieces watches the square in front?

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn on d4 is free. Black's pieces are developed behind the c-pawn.

line.say: The break: the pawn attacks d4.
White takes.
The bishop recaptures and the free pawn is gone.

claims.statement: No Black pawn attacks the pawn on d4.
After c5 the pawn attacks d4.
c5 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: A break needs a clear line. A rook on the file behind the break square adds an attacker, and a pawn that has moved cannot come back. *Rule of thumb:* when the count is not in your favour, play the set-up and let the enemy pawn come to you. A pawn that is already attacked, or blocked, is not free: there is nothing to prepare, and neither answer applies.

steps.title: The same free pawn, one rook different
steps.prompt: In both positions Black can break against the free pawn on d4 with e5. In the second position only a White rook differs (on e3 instead of d1). What is best in each, and why? Predict, then check.
In the last two positions you were asked whether the pawn on d4 was free. Which of the two parts did you check first, the attackers or the pawn's ability to move?

title: Connecting the rooks: a step, not a goal
outcomes: Names the pieces that stand between the rooks and the moves that clear them
Connects the rooks when development is otherwise finished
Checks for threats and tempo moves before connecting, and sees when the rooks are already connected

steps.text:
Rooks are **connected** when they stand on one rank or file with no piece of either colour between them. Then each rook defends the other, and they can share a file. At the start the knights, bishops, queen and king are in the way, so connecting is usually the **last step of development**, not the first.
*Which pieces are in the way, and where can they go?*

steps.caption: White to move. Only the queen stands between the rooks on a1 and f1.

line.say: The queen leaves d1. Nothing stands between the rooks on a1 and f1 now: they are connected.
Black strikes in the centre. This changes nothing about the rooks.
One rook goes to the d-file. The rook on f1 still defends it, because nothing stands between them.

claims.statement: At the start the rooks are not connected.
After Qc2 they are connected.
After Rad1 the rook on f1 defends the rook on d1.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** connect the rooks once your other pieces are out and nothing is pending. It is a step, not a goal.
Before you do, ask: *is any piece loose, mine or theirs? Is there a move that makes a threat?* Connecting can also wait on purpose, for instance when castling is delayed. And connected rooks on files that still have pawns on them do little until a file opens.

steps.title: Same position, one rook moved
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's a8 rook stands on d6. Does castling long, which connects White's rooks, still look best? Predict first, then check.
In the last positions, what did you check first: whether the rooks were connected, or whether anything could be attacked? Which should come first?

title: Connect the rooks, or something sharper?
outcomes: Checks first whether anything of his is attacked and loose, and whether an enemy piece can be taken
Chooses between a connecting move and a move with a threat or a tempo
Sees when the rooks are already connected and no connecting move is needed

steps.text:
In **Connecting the rooks: a step, not a goal** you saw which pieces stand between the rooks. Here you decide **when**. Ask in this order.
**Is anything of mine attacked and loose? Can I take something loose? Does a developing move also make a threat?**
Connecting the rooks is the answer to none of these; it is what you do when they are all quiet.

steps.caption: Black to move. No Black piece is loose, and the rooks on a8 and h8 do not yet see each other.

line.say: Black castles. The rooks on a8 and f8 now see each other along the back rank.
White plays f4, attacking the pawn on e5.

claims.statement: No Black piece is loose.
Before castling the king stands between the rooks.
After O-O the rooks are connected.
Castling is among the engine's first choices.

steps.text:
Connecting comes last on the checklist. **Skip it** when a piece of yours is attacked and loose, when an enemy piece can simply be taken, or when a developing move also makes a threat. Castling may be delayed on purpose.
And when the squares between the rooks are already empty, there is nothing left to connect.
**Rule of thumb:** finish development unless something sharper pays.

steps.title: Same position, one change
steps.prompt: In the first position castling queenside is the move. In the next two, one thing has changed. Predict whether connecting is still the question, then check.
Think of a recent game of yours. At which move did you last connect the rooks, and was a piece of yours attacked or a tempo available at the time?

title: Square control: the whole board at once
outcomes: Reads the n-m counts and the blue or orange tint of the control map on any square
Explains what the map adds (x-rays, pins, the exchange result, safe value) and what it still cannot see (sacrifices, tactics, king safety)
Glances at the map before moving, starting with the landing square

steps.text: Under a lesson board, the **Control map** button paints every square at once. Each square shows two numbers, **White-Black**: how many White pieces and how many Black pieces attack it. **Blue** means White's number is higher, **orange** means Black's. Tap any square to see which pieces they are. Counting attackers is taught in its own lessons; here you learn to read the picture.

steps.caption: White to move. Turn on the map and tap f7.

line.say: The knight joins the bishop. The map on f7 changes from 1-1 to 2-1.

steps.text: The map does more than count. It adds **x-rays** (a rook behind a rook, a bishop behind its own pawn), skips a piece **pinned** to its king unless the capture stays on the pin line, and plays out the exchange with piece values to show who wins a capture there and each side's **safe value**. It still cannot see sacrifices, tactics, or king safety beyond that exchange. Read it as a strong hint, not a verdict.

steps.title: Same map, different truth
steps.prompt: Both boards have a black knight on e5 that looks at f3. Only one rook has moved. A plain count gives f3 as 0-1 in both. Can the knight really capture on f3? Predict first, then check. (The current map already knows about the pin.)

steps.text: Make the map a **habit before you move**, in this order. First, the square you want to land on: is Black's number above zero, and does the exchange favour Black? Second, your own pieces: any whose Black number is higher than yours? Third, look for what the map cannot see: a sacrifice, a fork, a threat to your king. Note that opening the map during a test or game counts as a hint.

steps.caption: White considers the knight jump to d4. What would the map say there?

line.say: On d4 the map would read 0-2: no White support, two Black attackers.
Black can take with the pawn.

steps.prompt: Which of the three map limits (pins, x-rays, a number is not a verdict) would you have forgotten in the last position? Name the square it would have misled you about, then rate your confidence (low / medium / high).

title: Converting an advantage: take, exchange or stay quiet
outcomes: Lists the kinds of move available when clearly ahead: take material, exchange pieces, make a threat, make a quiet move
Asks what the opponent's best reply would be before taking a pawn
Chooses among the kinds in positions the engine rates as clearly better, and names what the engine's line shows
Does not treat 'clearly ahead' as a reason to stop calculating

steps.text: When you are clearly ahead, the advantage has to be turned into something that cannot slip away. Your kinds of move: **take material**, **exchange pieces**, **make a threat** (a pawn push or piece move that attacks something), or play a truly **quiet move** that keeps his counterplay small. Before you choose, ask: after my move, what is his best reply? The strongest move is not always the one that wins the most.

steps.caption: White to move and clearly ahead. The rook can take the pawn on b7.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and attacks the queen and the bishop.
The queen steps away.
The rook takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position at least 300 centipawns in White's favour.
After Rxb7 the rook attacks a7 and e7.
Rxb7 is the engine's best move.
Qxb7 is at least 300 centipawns worse than Rxb7.

steps.text: Which kind of move is best depends on the position, so this is a *rule of thumb* and not a recipe. Taking is often best when the capture is also the strongest line. An exchange can be best when it leaves an ending you can judge. A threat can be best when it forces a concession. A quiet move can be best when a capture would give him counterplay. Being clearly ahead still needs moves: check his forcing replies first.

steps.title: Take, threaten, wait or trade
steps.prompt: The engine rates all three positions as clearly better for the side to move. Predict which kind of move is best in each, then check.

Think of a game of yours where you were clearly ahead and the win slipped. Which kind of move (take, exchange, threaten or quiet) did you play, and what was your opponent's best reply at the moment you chose? Write the move and the reply.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has made four moves: one bishop and three pawn moves. Look at the pieces still on their first squares. What would you try?

claims.statement: Black's queen's knight has not moved.
Black's king's knight has not moved.
Black's king's bishop has not moved.

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: what would you play here, and what makes you think it works? A guess is fine.

steps.text: **Development** means bringing your pieces off their first squares to places where they do something. A **tempo** is one move of time. If you spent your moves on pieces and the opponent spent his on other things, you hold a **lead**. This lesson teaches you to count a lead, use it, notice when it is gone, and build it or defend against it.

**Why a lead matters.** A piece at home can neither attack nor defend. Where the fight begins, the side with more pieces out has more of them there, and the other side has fewer defenders and fewer attackers. Edward Lasker's rule of thumb, which I restate in my own words from his *Chess Strategy*: a lead in development permits an attack, and a deficit forbids one. Look at f7 on the first board and ask who can reach it.

steps.caption: Count after every move: pieces brought out, not moves made. This is how the first board arose.

line.say: White opens a path for the queen and for the bishop on f1. Nothing is out yet, but two pieces are freed.
Black does the same for his c8 bishop and his queen. Level.
The first piece comes out and eyes the centre. White: one piece out.
Black develops too. His bishop looks at the knight on f3. One piece each.
A second White piece, aimed at the square f7. White: two pieces out.
Black spends a move on a pawn. No new piece, so White now leads by one.
A third White piece. The count is three pieces to one.
Black makes a threat against the bishop, but adds no piece. Four Black moves, one of them a piece.

claims.statement: Black's queen's knight is still on b8.

steps.caption: Not every position has a lead. Here both sides used their moves on pieces, and the count is level.

line.say: A knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and defends the pawn.
The bishop comes out toward the f7 square.
Black mirrors it and aims at f2.
A modest pawn move that opens the c1 bishop and defends e4.
A third Black piece. Black attacks the pawn on e4.
Castling moves the king to safety and brings the rook toward the middle. White: three jobs done.
Black frees his c8 bishop. Three pieces each: the count is level.

claims.statement: After castling the rook stands on f1.

steps.caption: Pawn moves can be useful, but they only count when they free a piece. White leads by two pieces to one.

line.say: A knight comes out.
Black copies it.
The c1 bishop leaves its post behind the pawns, before the pawn move that would block it.
A rook-pawn move. It may stop a bishop check on b5 later, but it brings out no piece.
A solid move that also frees the f1 bishop.
Another rook-pawn move. Black has made four moves and only one is a piece.

claims.statement: Black's c8 bishop has not moved.

steps.caption: The count is a tool, not a law. A bishop that moved twice and a pawn move that asked a question cancel out here.

line.say: A knight comes out and defends the e5 pawn.
The bishop attacks the knight that guards e5.
Black asks the bishop what it will do. It is a pawn move, not a piece.
The bishop retreats and keeps the pressure. It has now moved twice.
A second Black knight.
White castles.

Black develops his bishop. Each side has made five moves (the first pawn move frees pieces) and three jobs are done, so the count is level: White's bishop spent two moves, Black's a6 spent one on a pawn.

steps.text: **How to count.** Count the pieces off their first squares that do something, plus castling. Pawn moves are not counted themselves; they matter only because they let a piece count. A piece that moves twice has spent a move for no new job, and the early queen often does too. [I] These are habits with exceptions: you will see an early queen work in the real game below. Nimzowitsch argued that development belongs to the whole army, so [I] a stuck rook counts too.

steps.caption: White to move. Three White pieces are out against one, and the c4 bishop aims at f7.

line.say: The bishop gives itself up on f7, a square only the king guards. Black has no developed piece nearby to take or block.
The king must take. It leaves its shelter and stands where the knight can check it.
The knight checks the king and also opens the queen's line to the bishop on g4.
The king steps back. The check is answered, but the second threat is not.
The queen takes the loose bishop. White gave a bishop for a pawn and a bishop, and Black's king is exposed.

claims.statement: Bxf7+ is legal.
At depth 16 the engine's best move is Bxf7+.
Bxf7+ wins material along the engine line.
Only the king defends f7.
After the knight check the bishop on g4 is Black's only loose piece.

steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

steps.text: The shot worked for three reasons you can check beforehand. Your pieces can reach the target quickly. The target has few developed defenders: here only the king. And giving up a piece drags the king into the open, where the knight check wins a second piece. Remove one reason and the sacrifice can lose a piece: the look-alike a few boards on shows it. [I] I expect that to hold more often than not, but I have not counted.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, one more defender
steps.prompt: Original first: Black has moved only pawns. Then Black has also played ...Nf6. Predict whether Bxf7+ still works.

steps.caption: The Légal trap, first half: what happens if Black declines the bait. White to move.

line.say: The knight takes a pawn and leaves f3, so the bishop on g4 now attacks White's queen. This is the bait.
If Black takes the knight instead of the queen, the queen has a target of her own.
The queen takes the bishop. White ends a pawn ahead with the queen still on the board.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is Nxe5.
Nxe5 wins material along the engine line.
Only the c4 bishop attacks f7 now.

steps.caption: The Légal trap, second half: Black took the queen. White to move; the queen is gone, but White has two attackers on f7.

line.say: The bishop checks. Black cannot take it: the knight on e5 also guards f7.
The king has one legal move.
The knight gives checkmate. Black's own pieces on d8 and f8 block the king's escape.

claims.statement: Bxf7+ leads to forced mate in two.
The bishop and the knight both attack f7.

steps.text: A lead is a chance, not a promise. It stops working when a developed piece guards the target, when the king has a safe square, when the opponent can trade your attackers, or when you wait and the lead shrinks. [I] A locked centre probably slows an attack because the lines stay shut; this lesson does not test it. Before sacrificing, ask: *what has changed since the last time this worked?* The next pair of positions changes exactly one thing.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the hypothesis [H]? Name one thing in your own games that would count as evidence against it.

steps.caption: The failing look-alike. Black's knight developed, so the king has a square and no second attack follows.

line.say: The same sacrifice.
The king takes.
The knight checks, but no Black piece is left loose behind the king.
The king retreats to g8, the square the knight on f6 left empty. White has given a bishop for a pawn.

claims.statement: At depth 16 Bxf7+ is at least two pawns worse than the best move.
After the knight check Black has no loose piece.
A Black knight stands on f6.

steps.caption: The lead fades if you wait. The bishop was attacked by the b5 pawn, so White lost time retreating. The sacrifice is gone and only a small edge is left (about +0.6, depth 16).

line.say: White retreats. No piece is added and the pressure on f7 is gone.
Black opens a diagonal for the f8 bishop.
White asks the bishop on g4 to decide.
Black trades his developed bishop for the attacking knight.
White recaptures. The pieces are coming off.
A Black knight develops. Only a small White edge is left.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the quiet retreat is at least two pawns worse than Bxf7+.
Bxf7+ is still the engine's best move here.

steps.text: **Hypothesis [H], not tested here.** Below master level the lead may be worth more than the engine says, because defenders miss one-move threats and the engine assumes the best defence. The test is yours: in your next ten games, count development at move ten and note who won. If the count never matters, the hypothesis is wrong.

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Development: a lead you can spend. This part covers Build it, or stop it; Near misses and a mixed test. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Build a lead.** Make each move do a job. Develop with a threat, so the opponent must answer instead of developing. Castle early. Early queen moves usually lose time unless each carries a threat. **Defend against one.** Develop a defender, trade the attacker, give the king a square. [I] Closing the centre may help, but the test position below is a case where capturing is best. Capablanca and Emanuel Lasker both urged bringing the pieces out quickly; see the sources.

steps.text: **What decided it.** Before the first sacrifice White had four pieces out and Black two, with a knight and a bishop at home. [I] Black's early bishop trade did not change the count, but the recapture put White's queen on f3 with tempo. After that nearly every White move carried a threat, while Black's replies developed little. Early queen moves are fine when each one makes a threat. Go back through the game and list which White moves threatened something.

[I] Here developing a piece was worse than guarding the target. The sacrifices only cashed in these small slips; compare both boards with your own answer above.

claims.statement: Qf6 and Qd7 are the engine's best moves, within 40 centipawns.

steps.text: **What to remember.** Count pieces that do something, plus castling, on both sides. A lead is the difference. A sacrifice needs a lead, a target few pieces defend, and a king with no safe run. A developed defender or a safe king square cancels it. Waiting shrinks a lead. Build one with threats; defend one by trading the attacker.

**Self-check before you teach it.** Did you say when a lead works and when it fails? Did you give one example a beginner could set on a board? Did you name one mistake, such as grabbing a pawn or leaving a bishop to be fed a trap? Did you say what you counted and how? Say it in your own words; the app does not grade it.

steps.text: A rule of thumb is a default with conditions. "Put a rook on an open file" gives a good move in many positions and a poor one in others. To learn the condition, change one feature of a position that fits the rule and see whether the rule still gives a good move. One failure does not cancel the rule; it shows where its limit lies.

steps.text:
A trade changes two things: **the piece you give up** and **the piece you keep.** Before trading, ask what the enemy piece is doing for him (holding an outpost, attacking, defending) and what your recapture will look like.
Trading just because you can does neither job.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on c5.
White recaptures with the pawn.

steps.text: When two trades are possible, compare them. **Rule of thumb:** give up the piece that matters less, keep the one that fits your pawns and plans, and prefer the trade that removes his most active piece. Always look at the recapture before you take.

title: Trade or keep the tension?
outcomes: Chooses between trading and keeping the tension in unlabeled positions
Names which piece a trade gives up and which it removes

steps.text:
In **Trades: which piece goes, which stays** you compared two trades. Now the choice is *whether to trade at all*.
A trade needs a purpose: remove an active piece, remove a defender, settle a point. A trade without one can give away your best-placed piece, or relieve a cramped opponent.
**Rule of thumb:** ask before each trade which of the two pieces matters more. The list of purposes is a guide, not a law.

Keeping the tension (leaving both pieces able to capture each other) is a move too. Before you capture, name the piece you give up and the piece you remove, and see how well each is placed.
The next three positions differ by a single feature. Predict each, then read the check. The engine's verdict is evidence at a fixed depth, not a proof.

steps.text: A **freeing move**, usually a pawn break, offers an exchange of pawns to open lines. It helps the side whose pieces can use the lines. So the same pawn move can be good in one position and bad in another. Before you play a break, count which of your pieces still stand at home, and which pieces of his guard the squares the break aims at.

steps.text:
A piece is **good** or **bad** by what it can do now: squares, targets, a useful job. Bad means few useful squares: hemmed in by its own pawns, shut out, or passive.
It can be bad *now* and good later. Before you give up on it, ask: **can it do a job where it stands? can it move with a threat? can I trade it for the enemy's best piece?**

steps.text: *Good and bad pieces: now, and later* taught you to find the worst piece. This lesson asks what to do about it. Three tools: **retreat** it to a better square, **reroute** it so it also threatens something, or **trade** it for a piece that matters more. Sometimes the answer is none of them.

steps.text: **When each tool fits.** *Retreat* when the new square is better, not only safer. *Reroute* when no enemy pawn attacks the new square and the piece gains squares or a target. *Trade* when the enemy piece is the stronger one. **Rule of thumb:** first ask whether the piece already has a job where it stands, then ask what the new square costs. Sometimes the engine's best moves leave the cramped piece alone: another move matters more. Several moves can be right.

steps.text:
A **pawn majority** is more pawns than the opponent on one wing (files a-d or e-h). Its job is to make a **passed pawn**. The pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it on its own file is the **candidate**; it usually leads and the others follow.

**Rule of thumb:** the candidate leads, the middle pawn waits. It holds only while the majority is healthy and nothing else interferes. Counting is the first step, not the last: **king position and tempo can decide**.

steps.text: An **obstruction** is a pawn or minor piece that blocks the line of a rook, bishop or queen: a file or a diagonal. It can be the enemy's or your own. steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* an enemy obstruction is easier to remove than one of your own, because you can bring many attackers against it. **Count first:** attackers against defenders, including pieces that join after the first capture; the cheapest man should capture first. With more attackers, taking or exchanging the obstruction can open your line. Without them, leave it alone. An obstruction only troubles the side whose line it blocks.

steps.text: **Today's question.** An open file is a road with no pawns on it. Roads lead somewhere, or nowhere. By the end you will look at a position and say which file is worth a rook, which square the rook will land on, who can stop it, and what each side does about it. First, learn to see the road at all.

steps.text: **A road, not a prize.** A rook on an open file with no way in still ties pieces down; it just does not win material by itself. What matters is where it can *land* in the enemy camp: its **entry square**. A common best landing [I] is the seventh rank, where the enemy pawns start and the king is boxed in. Aron Nimzowitsch's *My System* treats a file as a way to reach a point [S]. Ask: which square, and who watches it?

steps.text: **When it usually works.** Three things usually need to hold [I]. Your rook reaches the file before the enemy contests it. The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece. And something is waiting there: loose pawns, or a king with no room to move. If one is missing, ask what else makes up for it; a landing with tempo or a forcing follow-up can still work.

steps.text: **Why the seventh rank? [I]** Three reasons, in our reading. No enemy pawn can guard a square there, because pawns never stand on their own back rank; only pieces can. The pawns still at home can be attacked from the side. And the king is often boxed in behind them, so two rooks there can threaten mate. Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, says the side whose rooks reach the file first gets the raids on the seventh [S].

**When the landing is a trap [I].** A rook on the seventh can be cut off. If a bishop or knight attacks it, its retreat squares are covered, and the king or a pawn guards the squares beside it, the rook may be lost for a piece. Before you land, ask not only who attacks the square now but where the rook goes if it is attacked next. [H] This may cost club players more rooks than a slow arrival does. steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Open files: find the entry square. This part covers When it fails; Set it up, prevent it, test it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Four things a defender can try [I].** Cover the entry square with a piece. Put a rook on the file and offer a trade. Take the file first: the mirror board below is the same road seen from the other side. Or ignore the file and threaten something bigger; we show no board for that one here. [H] I suspect club players lose more games by landing on a covered square than by arriving late; we have no count. The next boards show the first two.

steps.text: **Opening the road, being first.** Files open by trades: a pawn exchange, or a capture that removes the pawn. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*) advises being the side that puts rooks on the file first [S]. Znosko-Borovsky adds a question to ask before opening any line: who benefits? As a rule, opening a line tends to help the stronger side, or the side with the stronger part of the position [S]. A rule of thumb, not a law.

steps.text: **A pawn on the road.** Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) separates a *protected* blocker from an unprotected one [S]. Undermine a protected one with a pawn lever. Besiege an unprotected one: bring more attackers than it has defenders, and capture with the cheapest piece first, so you give up the least if the exchange goes on. Sacrifices to clear the file come last.

steps.text: **The answer: not yet a landing.** The bishop and queen watch e7, and the queen, knight and rook watch e8, so a rook that jumped in would be taken. White may still put a rook on e1 to contest the file and tie pieces down; the engine counts that among its better moves (depth 16). The file here is a road to be fought for, not a landing.

**What to remember.** An open file is a road, not a prize. Find the entry square and count who watches it. Pawns never guard a seventh-rank square. Reach the file first, or contest it. A blocking pawn is protected or unprotected: treat them differently. A rook on an open file with no entry still ties pieces down. [H] Keep a list of the files you used in your own games and the squares you landed on; the pattern will teach you more than this page.

In **Open files: find the entry square** you were told to use a file. Now decide for yourself. For each open or half-open file ask three things.

steps.text:
A file is worth taking when you have a rook for it and something to aim at: a pawn or an entry square. It is worth little when pawns of both colours close it, or the enemy covers the entry square. An open file is open to both rooks, so ask who gets there first.
**Rule of thumb:** name the entry square first; enter only when nothing covers it.

steps.text:
In **Open files: find the entry square** you counted attackers and defenders on a blocking pawn. This lesson picks the method.
**Capture:** more attackers than defenders, no pawn protecting it, cheapest piece first.
**Lever:** a pawn protects it, so attack it with a pawn.
**Sacrifice:** a piece for the entry square. A last resort; this lesson names it but has no checked example.

A pawn of yours defends the square, and no enemy pawn on a neighbouring file is still able to advance and attack it. *Rule of thumb:* no enemy pawn can attack the piece by simply advancing, so pawns usually cannot drive it away. The test ignores pawn captures that change file, and pieces can still trade it off.

steps.text: **Over-protecting** means giving an important point more defenders than the attack on it needs. The idea comes from a master's writing and is *practical, not proven*. The point should be strong, central and under lasting pressure. The hope is that the defenders stay close to the point and keep their moves. For an ordinary pawn it is simply a lost tempo. In the examples here the extra defender is also a developing move, so the engine's agreement does not show that over-protection itself helps.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on e4 is attacked once, by the knight on f6, and defended once, by the rook on e1.

One White piece defends e4.

After Nbd2, ...Bb7 and Bc2 three White pieces defend e4.
Nbd2 and Bc2 are the engine's two best moves.

steps.text: Ask three questions before adding a defender. Is the point strong and likely to stay under pressure? Does the defending piece keep useful moves where it stands? Is there a developing or active move that does the same job or more? As a *rule of thumb*, if the answer to the first is no, or if a developing or active move does the same job, leave the point alone.

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Passed pawns: blockade early, if you can arrive in time**. A passed pawn gives you three choices: **push** it, **support** it (with the king or a piece), or **hold back** and improve something else. The pawn is an asset, not a duty. **Can a pawn of his protect it?**
**Can my pieces reach it,** for example along an open file?
**Do I attack it more often than he defends it?**
A pawn that fails these tests is just a pawn.

steps.text: A pin need not be won at once; it can shape an opening. When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, you have four policies: **put the question** (a flank pawn attacks the bishop), **ignore** the pin and play in the centre, **bring up reserves** so the knight is no longer pinned, or **hold the choice** with a useful move and decide later. (No exercise in this lesson trains 'hold the choice'.)

The engine's first choice is h6.
The queen stands behind the knight.
The bishop on g5 attacks the knight.
e7 is empty, so the knight is pinned to the queen on d8.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* the question is good when the bishop's retreat leaves it few squares and the centre cannot be opened with profit, so the bishop cannot come back to life. It is bad when the centre can open, or when the pawn advance leaves your king facing a break. It does not always win a tempo, and it can weaken the side that asks.

steps.text: You know the four policies from *A pin can last: four ways to meet it*. Here you decide, from a bare position, whether to ask. Check one thing first: **can the centre open?** As a *rule of thumb*, if your centre pawn (here d5) is already pressed, by a pawn or by a pawn and pieces, it can. Then the bishop may come back to life.

The question is a *rule of thumb*, not a law. It works best when the centre stays shut: the driven bishop finds few squares and cannot return. It fails when the centre can open, or when no pin exists, because then there is nothing to ask. Often several moves are sound, so asking is one option, not a duty.

steps.text: Before you look for moves, list the **differences between the two sides**: material, king positions, open lines, weak squares. Each difference suggests a possibility. steps.text: Before you choose a plan, decide **who stands better**. Then match the kind of game to the label (a *rule of thumb*): if you are better, **play actively**, so the advantage is not wasted; if worse, **defend and restore freedom** by bringing pieces into play; if equal, **manoeuvre**: improve your worst piece and do not force matters. steps.text: **Prophylaxis** is a question you ask before you move: what does my opponent want to play next? If the answer is a real freeing move, a quiet move that makes it unattractive can be worth a tempo. It is not passivity. It is also not always needed: when his plan is not real, the question has a quick answer and you carry on.

Imagine you pass and look at his best move. Name what it would do: which pawn it attacks, which line it opens. Then find the quiet move that attacks that square or removes its support. As a *rule of thumb*, stop the break when, if he played it next move, you would lose a pawn or piece or be left cramped. If you would not, carry on with your plan. If he has no break, there is nothing to stop.

steps.text: **Restraint** means stopping an enemy pawn break before it happens. Find the pawn and the square it would advance to. If one of your pieces attacks that square, the push is no longer free; whether it costs him material depends on how many defend it. Nimzowitsch's order is a *rule of thumb*: restrain first, blockade next, destroy last. Free centre pawns have their own lesson, "A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it".

It fails when his advance is already supported, or when the pawn cannot move at all. Adding an attacker is also not automatically good: the engine's rating of the move still decides. steps.text:
A rook on the **seventh rank** (the rank next to the enemy back rank) attacks pawns from behind, since they often stand on their starting squares, and it can keep the enemy king on the back rank.
To get there you need a safe **entry square** (the square where the rook lands) on an open file (a file with no pawns on it). Then look at what the rook can **attack** from the rank.

steps.text: In this app, **space** is counted from pawns only: the squares in the opponent's half of the board that your pawns attack. title: Restrict first, threaten later
outcomes: Prefers a quiet move that denies the freeing break over a showy pawn push when the opponent is cramped

steps.text: In *Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever* you counted space. Now choose moves. A *rule of thumb*: when the opponent is cramped, first cover the square of his freeing break with pieces, and only then think about threats. A showy pawn push can hand him the freedom you were denying. Restriction is not passivity: it is a plan.

A space edge helps most when the other side's pieces really lack squares and no pawn lever frees them. If a lever exists, the edge does not bind. In an open position with no pawn space at all, space is not the question; piece activity is. Space also does not grow without limit: breaks and exchanges can undo it.

steps.text: In **Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever** you counted space. Now ask what space costs. steps.text: A **pawn chain** is a line of pawns that defend each other diagonally. The **base** is the pawn at the back that no pawn defends; the **head** is the pawn at the front. steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Attacking the base works best when the lever is supported and your pieces are ready; attacking the head leaves its defender where it is. steps.text: In this app, **hanging pawns** are two pawns side by side on the 4th or 5th rank, alone on their files and flanks, with no enemy pawn on their files. No pawn can defend them (a static weakness), yet they control squares and can advance (a dynamic strength). Rule of thumb: the plans are to hold them, advance one, or exchange them off.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Advancing tends to work when the advanced pawn gains something concrete, such as attacking a piece, and the pieces that could stop it can be hit. A well-placed enemy piece can make the same advance fail. This lesson tests the advance only; holding and exchanging are named, not drilled. Choosing the safest plan is not a rule.

steps.text: In *The hedgehog: waiting until the break is ready* you met the structure and the idea of waiting. This lesson trains the decision itself, with nobody naming the plan: **break now, wait with a useful move**, or, for the space side, **hold or strike**. Start by counting who can recapture on the break square. Counting is a rule of thumb that rules breaks out; you will check each verdict against the engine.

steps.caption: Black to move, in the hedgehog. The break b5 looks natural, and White's c4 pawn attacks it. Count first: who can recapture on b5?

c4 holds the white pawn.

steps.text: **Conditions.** No recapture usually means *wait*: improve a piece, or play ...a6 first so that ...b5 has a pawn behind it. A recapture is necessary, not sufficient: pieces matter too, so the engine can still reject a break the count allows. Rule of thumb: break when the count is level, your pieces cover the break square and no tactic punishes it; otherwise a quiet move costs little.

steps.text: An **isolated queen's pawn** (IQP) in this app is a pawn on the d-file with no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file. No pawn can defend it, and the square in front of it suits an enemy piece. In return its owner gets space and open lines. Rule of thumb: the owner keeps pieces on and attacks; the other side trades pieces and blockades.

**Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The owner's attack tends to work while pieces are still on and the opponent has not pulled back the defenders. Trading pieces can make the pawn harder to defend; one example below shows the verdict moving; it does not show why. A blockade must also be safe: check the square. The next pair of positions differs mainly in the trades, and in the rook placement too. One pair is an example, not a proof.

steps.text:
The app's **King's Indian chain**: pawns on c4, d5 and e4 against pawns on d6, e5 and g6 (colours may be reversed). This is the app's own definition.
The centre is locked, so each side attacks on its own wing. Rule of thumb: attack the base, not the head. White plays c4-c5 against d6, the base of Black's d6-e5 pair; Black plays ...f5 against e4.

steps.text:
**Maroczy bind** (app's own definition): White pawns on c4, e4, none on the d-file; Black pawns on d6, g6, none on the c-file (colours may be reversed).
c4 and e4 attack d5, c4 also b5: Black needs preparation before ...d5 or ...b5. The price: d4 is a **hole**, a square no White pawn can attack now or by advancing, so an advancing pawn cannot drive a Black piece from it.

steps.caption: Black to move. Two White pawns (c4, e4) attack d5, and d4 is a hole in White's camp. Here Black's pieces are ready, so the break works.

line.say: d5: three attackers against three defenders, and the pawn on e6 can recapture.
White pushes e5; now only the pawn on c4 still attacks d5.

claims.statement: c4 holds the white pawn.
e4 holds the white pawn.
d6 holds the black pawn.
g6 holds the black pawn.
Open files: none. Half-open for White: d. Half-open for Black: c.
Two White pawns (on c4 and e4) attack d5.
No White pawn can attack d4 now or by advancing: d4 is a hole.
After d5, three White pieces attack d5.
After d5, three Black pieces defend d5.
After d5, one Black pawn (on e6) attacks d5.
After d5 and e5, only the White pawn on c4 still attacks d5.
At depth 16 d5 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The bind holds while both breaks stay unready. The cramped side trades pieces and plays ...d5 or ...b5 when the square has enough defenders and a pawn can recapture; counting is the first check, not the whole answer. As pieces come off, it tends to get more room. The owner keeps c4 and e4: pushing either gives up part of the grip on d5.

title: Switching wings: can the heavy piece cross, and should it?

steps.text: A **switch of wing** has three parts. First a demonstration: a pawn advance or threat on one wing. Second, the opponent's pieces move across to meet it. Third, your own rooks or queen swing to the other wing, where fewer defenders now stand. In this lesson the kingside is files e to h. Rule of thumb: it works when your heavy pieces can change wings in a move or two and the opponent is slow to bring defenders back.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black has pushed a pawn to b4 on the queenside, where it attacks a3 and c3: that is the demonstration. White's king is on the kingside. The rook on a8 has not moved yet; the e-file is the first kingside file in this lesson (files e to h).

The pawn on b4 attacks a3 and c3.
White's king is on the kingside.
Rae8 is legal: the squares between a8 and e8 are empty.
At depth 16 Rae8 is among the engine's accepted moves (Rae8), all within 0.4 pawns of the best.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A swing needs mobile pieces and an opponent who is slow to answer. It fails if the path is blocked, if a pawn guards the landing square, or if you act on the first threat too early. The app can check legal moves and engine ratings but not the opponent's intentions. steps.text: Aim at what cannot get away. A **backward pawn** whose front square an enemy pawn controls cannot simply step forward, so you can bring more attackers. A piece **pinned** to its king cannot leave the line of the pin (the pin itself is taught in "Pins: cannot move, or should not move"). A piece that can move away is a poor target for a pawn kick (a pawn push that attacks it): it moves, and the pawn that kicked it can never go back.

steps.text: You can find a target that cannot move (see the lesson *Aim at what cannot move away*). Now compare two ways to use a pawn. You can **chase** a piece, which makes it move, or you can **fix** a target and attack it. As a *rule of thumb*, a chase gains time only if the piece has no good square to go to; otherwise you spend a pawn move and the piece steps aside.

steps.text: A **transformation** changes what the position is made of: an exchange or a break turns one structure, or one kind of advantage, into another. A trade that leaves his pawns doubled or isolated can be worth it, but it has a cost, such as your bishop. Name both before you trade. Which piece to trade is taught in "Trades: which piece goes, which stays"; here the question is what it does to the pawns.

steps.caption: White to move. White can trade the bishop for the knight. Look at what the recapture does to Black's pawns.

A Black knight stands on c6.
Before the exchange Black's doubled pawns are: none.
After Bxc6 bxc6 Black's doubled pawns are: c5, c6.

steps.text: A transformation is only as good as the structure it leaves. The recapture may not be forced, the damaged pawns may be easy to defend, and your own pieces may be the ones that pay. *Rule of thumb:* damaged pawns justify a trade only if you can attack them. title: Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard
outcomes: Marks the holes in one side's camp: squares on its 3rd to 5th rank that none of its pawns can guard by moving forward
Names the enemy piece that could move onto a given hole
Checks that a piece can reach a hole and stay there, not only that the hole exists

steps.text: A **hole** is a square on your 3rd, 4th or 5th rank (counted from your own side) that none of your pawns can guard by moving forward, because pawns never move backward (a pawn changes file only by capturing). A hole is a weakness only if an enemy piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. It is a fact about *your* pawns; your opponent decides whether it matters.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has no e-pawn and his c-pawn stands on c5, so d5 is a hole in his camp.

line.say: The knight settles on d5. No Black pawn can ever attack it, and no Black piece attacks it now.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack d5.
After Nd5 no Black piece attacks the knight.
Nd5 is among the engine's top two moves.

steps.text:
Before you call a hole a weakness, ask three things.
**Can a piece reach it?** A knight can get there in time; a bishop only squares of its colour.
**Can it stay?** If an enemy knight or bishop attacks it, it can be traded off.
**Is there something to aim at from there?**
This is a *rule of thumb*: the more answers are yes, the more the hole matters.

title: Holes you can use and holes that only look good
outcomes: Judges whether a hole is usable (reachable and not challenged) or challenged (worth less)

steps.text: A hole is a square your pawns can no longer guard (see the lesson *Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard*). It helps the opponent only if a piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. So a hole gets one of two verdicts: **usable** (reachable and not challenged) or **challenged (worth less)** (a pawn or piece can challenge it, or no piece can get there).

Check three things. **Is it a hole?** None of the pawns of the side whose half of the board it lies in can ever guard it. **Can a piece reach it?** **Can an enemy pawn or piece attack that piece on the square?** As a *rule of thumb*, a hole is strong for one side only when its piece can land and stay; the same hole can be worth more in one position than in the next, so check it each time.

steps.text: In **Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard** you found holes already on the board. Now look ahead. A pawn push in front of your castled king makes holes for good, because pawns never move backward. With the e-pawn gone from e7, the push **g6** leaves f6 and h6 unguarded by any pawn. steps.text: A push does not always cost you. If the e-pawn still stands on e7, it guards f6, so g6 leaves only h6. title: A budget, not an equal share
outcomes: Splits a 15-minute game into an opening share, a middlegame share, an endgame share and a reserve that add up to the whole
Works out how many long thinks a middlegame share allows once routine moves are paid for
Tells a routine, a critical and a forced position apart and says whether a flat share is enough

steps.text: A **time budget** is a plan for where the clock goes: a share for each phase, a reserve for the end, and room to think longer on the few moves that matter. **The same time on every move is not a budget**: it pays as much for a forced reply as for a decision. Every number here is a first guess to test against your own clock.

steps.prompt: A 15+0 game gives each player 15 minutes and adds nothing. Say the reserve is 2 minutes, the opening 3 and the endgame 3. The middlegame is moves 13 to 30, which is 18 moves. Work these out before you read on.

fields.label: If each middlegame move costs a routine 10 seconds, how many one-minute thinks fit in what is left of the middlegame share?

steps.text: **Pay for routine moves first.** Give routine moves a small price and keep the rest of the phase share for critical moments, such as a tempting capture that may cost material (here you only price such a move, you do not calculate it). Forced replies cost almost nothing. The prices (10 seconds, one minute) are a rule of thumb to adjust, not a measured optimum.

steps.title: How much of the budget does it deserve?
steps.prompt: Each position comes with the same budget: a routine move gets about 10 seconds. Decide for each: is it critical, so it needs extra from the pool, or routine, so the usual price is enough? A forced move, with one legal move, gets almost nothing; you meet one in the next exercises. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **When a budget works.** It works if you check it: compare your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end with the plan after each game. It fails when rigid: on a critical move, take the minute and pay it back from the share. It barely binds with a big increment (seconds added after every move; 60+30 is about 120 seconds a move over 40 moves). Treat it as a rule of thumb.

steps.prompt: Sort each case. Does a time budget work, fail, or not apply? Choose, then save to see my answer. The answers are my judgement, not a measurement.

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: The clock is a budget. This part covers The clock in numbers; When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Games are timed with two numbers, like **10+5**. The first is the minutes each player starts with. The second is the *increment*: seconds added to your clock after every move you make. If your clock reaches zero you usually lose, whatever the board shows.
Worked example, 15+10 and 30 moves: 15 minutes is 900 seconds, the increment adds 30 × 10 = 300, total 1,200. Divide by the 30 moves: **40 seconds a move** on average.

steps.prompt: Now you try. Time control 10+5, and you play 40 moves. How many seconds do you have in total, and how many seconds per move on average?

steps.text:
An average hides a problem. [H] Hard decisions tend to arrive late, when the clock is lowest; test that on your own games. So keep a **reserve**, a block of seconds you promise not to touch until the end.
Example, 5+0, reserve 60 seconds, 35 moves: (300 − 60) ÷ 35 is about 6.9 seconds a move. Forced moves cost almost nothing, so they add to what is left for the hard ones. Treat these numbers as a first guess to test, not a law.

steps.text: Each phase asks for different thinking. In the opening you mostly recall, until the opponent leaves your preparation. In the middlegame you choose plans. In the endgame a few moves can decide the game. So the shares differ. But **where your critical decisions fall is a fact about your own games**: read it from the record, not from a guess.

steps.text: **Mark the boundaries from the record.** Rules of thumb to try: the opening ends at the first move you did not know from your preparation; the endgame starts when queens are off or few pieces remain. Your own opening matters: a line you know costs little until the opponent leaves it, a sharp line can need clock early. A critical decision can fall in any phase. The routine, critical and forced prices come from *A budget, not an equal share*.

title: When you are worse: make it hard, and decide with a reason
outcomes: Lists the resources a worse position can have: a repeated check, a stalemate trick, a fortress, a move that sets a problem

steps.text: **Worse is not lost.** When you are behind, aim for the line that is hardest for the opponent, not the slowest loss. Your resources: a repeated check (a perpetual), a stalemate trick, a fortress (a position the stronger side cannot break into), a move that sets a problem. Each has exact conditions and each can be tested against the opponent's best reply. Whether to give up the game is a different question: no source gives evidence, so we call it a judgement.

**Exact conditions.** A perpetual needs a safe check at every turn: count the king's squares. A stalemate trick needs two things: the stronger side has no better reply than taking the offered piece, and after that capture the weaker side has no legal move at all. A fortress needs its key squares held. A trap is worth setting only if the right reply costs you nothing (our rule of thumb).

steps.title: A fortress, and one change

steps.text: No labels now. In each position the side to move is behind in material. Name the drawing resource it offers, or say there is none. Then check it against the opponent's best reply. The perpetual and the stalemate trick are taught in *Perpetual check: the draw you can force* and *Stalemate as a rescue*. The next two exercises are silent.
**Resign or play on?** Our working hypothesis, not a fact: play on while a resource exists and the game still teaches you something; resign when none is left.

steps.text: Players often relax when they are ahead, and a classic slip follows: taking the first gain on offer without asking what the opponent threatens, or whether something stronger exists. **Feeling safe is a risk.** A habit to try: when you are ahead, run the safety scan and look at the opponent's best reply before every move, for ten moves in a row.

title: Anand and Kramnik: what the numbers show
