steps.text: **What this lesson claims, and what it does not.** It compares two world champions on a few counted measures, taken from games in our own data: both players rated 2400+, standard games, de-duplicated (The Week in Chess and Lichess broadcasts). It does *not* say who played better, and it gives no verdict on style. A number shows what happened in this sample, nothing more.

**Evidence 1: sample and openings.** Viswanathan Anand: 1,513 games in our data, 1987 to 2026. Vladimir Kramnik: 1,626 games, 2012 to 2025. The windows differ, so the two samples are not the same era. With White, Anand opened 1.e4 in 672 of 762 games (88.2%); Kramnik opened 1.e4 in 277 of 817 (33.9%), 1.Nf3 in 205 (25.1%), 1.d4 in 180 (22.0%) and 1.c4 in 154 (18.8%). Source: our own game data (counts from the games described in the first card).

steps.text: **Evidence 2: results and length.** Draws: Anand 794 of 1,513 games (52.5%); Kramnik 553 of 1,626 (34.0%). Average game length: Anand 41.8 moves, Kramnik 47.8 moves. Average opponent rating in the sample: Anand 2729, Kramnik 2663. Draw share depends on opponents, tournament format and the years covered, which differ here. Source: our own game data (counts from the games described in the first card).

**Evidence 3: queens at move 30.** Among games that reached move 30, queens were still on in 689 of 1,233 for Anand (55.9%) and 807 of 1,468 for Kramnik (55.0%). That is a difference of under one percentage point in samples of this size, and we have not tested whether it is meaningful. *Similar here* is the honest reading. That is about the same share as Nakamura's 61.2% in 6,635 games, but 183 games could move several points on a few events.

steps.text: **Evidence 2: draws, opening choice, colour.** Share of all games drawn, in our data: Carlsen 1,671 of 5,654 (29.6%), Caruana 1,574 of 4,963 (31.7%), Aronian 1,596 of 3,796 (42.0%), Nakamura 2,226 of 7,612 (29.2%). **Evidence 3: colour changes the picture.** Carlsen won 1,769 of his 2,869 White games (61.7%) but 1,368 of 2,785 Black games (49.1%). Caruana won 1,229 of 2,507 as White (49.0%) and 976 of 2,456 as Black (39.7%). Aronian: 816 of 1,919 (42.5%) and 578 of 1,877 (30.8%). Nakamura: 2,329 of 3,946 (59.0%) and 1,806 of 3,666 (49.3%). steps.text: In **Giving the exchange: name what you get back** you named the reason for giving a rook for a minor piece. Now decide for yourself whether the sacrifice works. There are three verdicts: **sound** (testing it with the engine shows it wins), **unsound** (testing shows it fails) and **unnecessary** (a simpler move wins as well). Always test the plain move too.

**What decides it.** The counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 are a rule of thumb: a rook for a bishop costs about two points, so the gain must last. One change can flip the verdict: a defender arrives, or a simpler move does the job. Call a sacrifice *sound* only after you have tested it; otherwise call it *practical* and say you have not checked it.

title: Why give material: the job a sacrifice does
outcomes: Names the job of a sacrifice (decoy, or removing a guard) and states the payoff that pays for it

steps.text:
A **sacrifice** gives up material for something you can name. Two jobs to look for first.
**Decoy:** lure a piece to a square where it hurts its own side.
**Remove a guard:** take or drive off the piece that guards a key square.
Some sacrifices do both jobs at once; say which one you would name first. No named job and payoff means you are guessing. Opening lines against a king: 'The Greek gift: when the bishop sacrifice on h7 works, and when it does not'.

steps.caption: White to move. A decoy: the queen is given up to pull the rook onto g8.

line.say: The queen goes to g8 with check. The knight on h6 guards g8, so the king cannot take it.
The rook takes the queen and now stands next to its own king.
Knight to f7 is checkmate.

claims.statement: Qg8+ Rxg8 Nf7 is a forced mate in two.
After Qg8+ one white piece (the knight) guards g8.

steps.prompt: Name the job in your own words, then pick the closest option, and give the payoff.

fields.label: The job:
options: Decoy: a piece is lured to a bad square
Remove a guard: a defender is taken or driven off

steps.text:
**When a sacrifice holds.** The payoff must survive Black's best reply, including declining. *Rule of thumb:* count the king's flight squares and the pieces that can recapture before you give anything.
**When it fails.** One flight square, or one extra recapturing piece, can turn a mate into a lost queen.
**When it is not needed.** If the material can be won without giving anything up, win it that way.

steps.text: You already know how to **count** a square from the lesson "Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting": list every piece that can capture there, start with your cheapest, and stop when carrying on would lose material. Here is that count once more, then the cases where it **lies**.

A black pawn recaptures.

The rook takes the knight. White has won two pawns and a knight for a pawn and a knight.

steps.text:
A count is only as good as its pieces.
**Order matters.** With the same numbers, a cheap piece that captures first can win what an expensive one would lose.
**Every counted piece must really be able to capture.** A pinned piece cannot recapture if that would expose its king, and a piece with two jobs may be needed elsewhere.

title: Take it or leave it: the running balance
outcomes: Keeps a running balance (won minus lost) while playing a capture sequence through

steps.text: You have met counting in "Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting". Here you make the **decision**. Play the captures out and keep a **running balance**: what you have won minus what you have lost after each capture. Start only if the balance ends above zero at the best place to stop.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on d5 is attacked twice and defended once. Keep the balance.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight. Balance: +3.
The pawn takes back. Balance: +2.
The knight takes that pawn. Balance: +3. Black has nothing left to take with.

claims.statement: Two White pieces attack d5.
One Black piece defends d5.
Starting with the pawn, White comes out at least 3 points ahead along the best defence.

steps.text: **When the balance can mislead.** Counting values are a *rule of thumb*. You may stop an exchange early, so read the balance at your best stopping point. Usually the cheapest capturer goes first. A count can lie when a defender cannot really recapture (for example, it is pinned, meaning it cannot move without exposing its king) or is busy defending something else; a later lesson looks at those cases. If a piece has no defender, there is no balance: check that taking it leaves nothing of yours loose.

title: Counting what can arrive
outcomes: Lists the pieces each side can bring to a pawn's square with one move, and counts again

steps.text:
Counting the attackers and defenders of a square tells you the position **now**. A pawn you push, or one that stays where it is, is also reached by pieces that **arrive**.
So count twice. First count what attacks and defends the square. Then list the pieces of each side that can move to a square from which they attack or defend it, one move each, and count again.

steps.caption: White to move and about to push d4-d5. Watch the count on d5 change as pieces arrive.

line.say: The pawn goes to d5. The knight on e7 attacks it, the rook on d1 defends it: one against one.
Black brings a second attacker: the rook moves to d8.
White brings a second defender: the knight moves to c3. Two against two.
Black takes first with the knight, its cheaper attacker.
The knight takes the knight.
Black could take again with the rook.
The rook takes the rook. Black took a pawn and a knight; White took a knight and a rook.

After the push one white piece, the rook, defends d5.
Black can bring the rook to d8: two attackers.

steps.text:
Three conditions for the second count.
**The target stays.** A piece whose side is to move can step away.
**The arrival is effective.** Not boxed in, and not attacked on its landing square by a piece of lower counting value.
**It arrives in time.** **Rule of thumb:** two-move arrivals usually come too late.
Treat the count as a first estimate: a bigger threat can pull a defender away.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Five ways to meet an attack. This part covers The five ways. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

To **defend** a piece is to put a friend where it could capture back. Then the attack is no longer free: if the enemy takes, you take back, and the trade decides. Use the counting values you learned. As a rule of thumb, defending works when the attacker is worth more than the piece it attacks. Count attackers against defenders too: two attackers beat one defender.

steps.caption: The first position again, second answer: defend. The rook goes to d1.

line.say: Defend: the rook on d1 now guards the knight along the d-file.
Suppose Black takes the knight anyway.
The rook takes back. Black gave a rook, worth five, for a knight, worth three.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Rd1 one white piece, the rook, defends the knight on d4.
After Rd1 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.text: To **capture** the attacker is to remove the problem. First ask whether the attacker is defended. If it is, your capture starts a trade, so count it with the values. As a rule of thumb, capturing works best with a piece worth less than the attacker: a pawn that takes a knight wins the difference.

steps.caption: White to move. The black knight on e5 attacks the bishop on c4, and nothing defends the bishop. Third answer: capture the attacker.

line.say: Capture: the pawn takes the knight. The attack is gone, and the pawn is worth less than the knight.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is attacked and nothing defends it.

steps.text: To **block** is to put a piece on a square between the attacker and your piece. It cuts the line, so it only works against a bishop, a rook or a queen. A knight jumps over pieces, and a pawn or king attacks the next square, so nothing can go in the way. The blocker is now in the line of fire, so check it is safe.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the white rook on c1 along the open file, and nothing defends it. Fourth answer: block.

line.say: Block: the bishop steps between the rooks. The rook on c1 is not attacked now.
Suppose Black takes the blocker (not Black's best reply).
The rook takes back. Black gave a rook for a bishop.

claims.statement: The rook on c1 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Bc2 no black piece attacks the rook on c1.
After Bc2 the rook on c1 defends the bishop on c2.

steps.caption: A knight jumps, so you cannot block it. White to move: the black knight on b3 attacks the rook on a1, and nothing defends the rook.

line.say: Move with a threat: the rook leaves, and now attacks the knight.

One black piece, the knight, attacks the rook.
After Rb1 none of White's pieces is loose.
After Rb1 the rook attacks the knight on b3.

steps.text: To **counterattack** is to ignore the threat and make a bigger one. It works when the piece that could take yours is also the only guard of your target, so taking drops the target. Ask: does the capture remove a defender of my target? Znosko-Borovsky argued [S, via synthesis sheet] that a counterattack needs a sound position, and that a half-measure is the worst choice.

line.say: Counterattack: the rook attacks the black queen. Only the rook on c8 guards that queen, so if it takes the bishop, it drops the queen.

steps.text: Edward Lasker warned, in *Chess Strategy*, that a defender can be an illusion [S, via synthesis sheet]: a cheaper piece may take it, a bigger threat may draw it away, or it may be pinned. [I] My broader reading: a defender can also be tied to another job, like the knight above. [H] My guess: the question "what else does it guard?" may catch many errors.

An attacked piece is not always in danger. A threat is **real** if the capture gains something against best defence. It is **fictitious** if the capture fails. steps.text: Your rook just took a knight, and Black could not take back. In this course that knight was **loose**: an enemy piece attacked it, and none of its own side's pieces defended it. A loose piece can be taken for free. Missing a free piece, yours or theirs, is one of the most common ways a game swings. [H] I suspect it is the most common cause below club level, but I have not measured it.

steps.text: In this course a piece is **loose** when two things are true: an enemy piece **attacks** it, and no friendly piece **defends** it. Attacked but defended is not loose: they take back. Undefended but not attacked is not free yet, and the next board shows why it still matters.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?. This part covers Try it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Sometimes two pieces are loose at once, and you can take only one now. A good default is to take the **higher-value** piece first, then see whether the other can run. [I] That default comes from these two boards, not from a law. Both orders are shown, so you can compare. Two boards after them show when the order matters less.

steps.caption: Two loose pieces: the rook on b8, attacked by the bishop, and the knight on d4, attacked by the rook.

Taking the rook first is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: The other order: the rook takes the knight first.

The black rook runs. White won only the knight.

claims.statement: Taking the knight first wins only the knight.
It is worse than taking the rook first.

steps.text: The default bends when the smaller piece cannot run. A knight **pinned** to its king cannot move, so both orders win both pieces. [I] The reverse case: if the bigger piece cannot run but the smaller one can, take the smaller one first, before it escapes. Always ask which piece can actually get away.

[H] My guess is that players miss their own loose pieces more than the enemy's, because after your own move your mind is on your plan. [I] An unchecked scan fails most often on your own side. I have not measured either.

steps.text: Your answers to an attacked piece: **capture** the attacker, **move** away, **block** the line, **defend** the piece, or **counterattack** with a bigger threat. Defending works well when the attacker is worth as much as your piece or more. A cheaper attacker, such as a bishop against a rook, still wins value even against a defended piece. A counterattack must really be bigger.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?. This part covers When it does not apply. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

A loose piece is free only if no defender can take back, and a defender can stand far away. A rook or queen guards along a whole file or row. A bishop or queen guards along a whole diagonal. A knight guards by its jump, a pawn the two squares diagonally ahead of it, and the king the squares beside it. Before you capture, trace lines back from the piece. Here is a defender that is easy to miss.

steps.caption: The bishop in the corner is far from the knight, but nothing stands between them on the long diagonal.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The bishop takes back from across the board. White lost a rook for a knight.

claims.statement: No black piece is loose.
The bishop on a8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses the rook for a knight.

steps.caption: A rook standing behind the piece guards it just as well. Here the rook on d8 defends the knight.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The other rook takes back along the file. Rook for knight.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses a rook for a knight.

steps.text: A defender can also fail while it still stands there. Edward Lasker's *Chess Strategy* names three ways: a cheaper piece can capture the defender, a bigger threat elsewhere can pull it away, or it can be **pinned** (my paraphrase, from our reading notes). Look at a pinned one: it guards on paper but cannot take back.

steps.caption: Defended on paper. The bishop on e6 guards the knight, but the rook on e1 pins it to the king, so it cannot take back.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
Black cannot recapture: the pinned bishop may not leave the e-file.

claims.statement: On paper the bishop on e6 defends the knight.
The rook still wins the knight.
Taking the knight is the engine's best move.

steps.text: The second question is what the capture costs. A piece that guards something important may be needed where it stands. Look at the first row of the next board: White's rook is the only piece keeping the king safe.

steps.text: Two questions before every capture. **Is any piece defending it, even from far away, or only on paper?** **What does my capturing piece stop doing, and what is my opponent's most forcing reply: a check, a capture or a threat?** That scan has its own lesson in the loop course. If the answers are no and nothing, the piece really is free. Then a case where a defender exists, but the capture is still good.

steps.text: So **defended** means *not free*, but not always *safe to leave alone*: a cheap piece can attack an expensive defended one. Rule of thumb, from the counting values. A later lesson makes this exact by counting every attacker and defender. For now, one more fact. Attacking a loose piece does not win it if your opponent can move it.

steps.text: Part 4 of 4: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

A habit, as a rule of thumb. After each opponent move: **list their loose pieces, list yours, then count defenders before you take.** A loose piece is free on your move, not after you only attack it. Now the tests give no hints about which idea to use, and sometimes nothing is free.

Two named views, rephrased. Edward Lasker's *Chess Strategy* treats a defender as something that must itself be checked: it can be captured, pulled away or pinned. Znosko-Borovsky's *The Middle Game in Chess* separates threats that really win something from ones that would gain nothing if carried out (both from our reading notes, [S]). [I] My conjecture: the scan fails most often on your own pieces.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A piece is loose when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side defends it. After every move I check both sides, and I trace long lines for far-away defenders. Before I take, I ask whether a defender is real, and what my capturing piece stops doing.

steps.text: In "Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?" someone told you to find the loose pieces. Now nobody does. After a move, go through **your own pieces one by one** and end with a number: how many are loose? Zero is a real answer. Remember: a piece is loose only when it is attacked **and** no piece of its own side defends it. *Undefended* (nothing guards it, even if unattacked) and *hanging* (attacked without enough defence) are related, not the same.

steps.text: **Two look-alikes.** A piece that is attacked but defended is *not* loose, although the exchange can still go wrong (see the counting lessons). A piece that is undefended but not attacked is *not* loose either; one move can change that. Defenders count from far away, along a file or a diagonal.

steps.text: A **threat** is the strongest thing your opponent could start with their *next* move if you did nothing: win something loose, give checkmate, or attack two pieces at once. It can be a short forcing line, not only one capture. Ask it after **every** opponent move, before your own plan. Why: your plan was made for the position before their move, and their move is the only new fact, so look there first. [H] I think skipping this look causes many club blunders; I have not measured it.

steps.text: After each opponent move, look at four things. **Where did the moved piece go, and what does it attack now?** **What line did it open?** A piece that steps aside can unmask one behind it. **Is any piece of mine loose?** Attacked and undefended: check it first. **Does it give check or pin something?** A pinned piece cannot move freely. With two threats at once, look for one move that answers both, such as capturing the attacker.

steps.text: Three kinds of threat come up again and again. You have met the first: **winning a piece** that is loose. The second is **checkmate**. The third is **attacking two things with one move**, such as your king and a piece, so that you can only save one. People call that last one a **fork**.

The square h7 is empty, so the king can go there.

steps.text: A piece standing **behind** another on the same line backs it up. A queen with a bishop behind it on a diagonal is guarded through the queen: if the queen captures, the bishop covers that square. That can turn a capture the king could answer into one it cannot. [I] This idea sits behind many mating threats against a castled king.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen and bishop line up towards h2. Is that a threat?

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The queen takes h2 with check. The bishop behind it guards the square, and the rook blocks the king's last exit: checkmate.

claims.statement: If White passes, Qxh2 is checkmate.
Only the king guards h2.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight has just jumped to d4. Nothing of White's is attacked yet.

line.say: White sees nothing attacked and plays an unrelated move.
The knight jumps to e2 with check. From there it also attacks the rook.
White must answer the check first, so the rook cannot be saved.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: No white piece is attacked right now.
No white piece covers e2.
From e2 the knight attacks both the king on g1 and the rook on c1.
If White passes, the knight wins the rook.

steps.caption: Black to move. White spotted the jump and put the rook where it covers e2.

line.say: Black tries the fork anyway.
The rook covers e2 and simply takes the knight.

claims.statement: The rook on e1 covers e2.
Ne2 just loses the knight.

steps.text: Eugene Znosko-Borovsky, in *The Middle Game in Chess* (1922), split threats into direct ones, which act at once, and distant ones, which show only over several moves, and said the decisive role belongs to the distant ones. [I] My reading: a fork is a direct threat, so the distant kind is what later lessons train.

steps.caption: White to move. One pawn move has attacked two knights at once.

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The pawn takes one knight.
White saves the other knight, but a piece is gone.

claims.statement: A black pawn attacks the knight on c4.
The same pawn attacks the knight on e4.
If White passes, Black wins a knight.

steps.text: Part 2 of 5: What did their last move threaten?. This part covers Answer it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Once a threat is real, you have four basic answers. **Move** the target away. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line it uses; that works only against a bishop, rook or queen, never a knight or a pawn. **Guard** the target so taking it costs something. A fifth, **counter-threat**, works only if their capture would be met by mate or a bigger capture of yours, so count first. [H] Beginners may reach for 'move away' by habit; I have not measured it.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop attacks a loose rook. The attacker itself can be captured.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop that carried the threat. The threat disappears with it.
Black has lost a whole piece and nothing is threatened any more.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the bishop, it wins the rook.
The pawn on h3 attacks the bishop.
Capturing the bishop wins at least a piece.

steps.caption: White to move. A rook attacks the loose bishop along the d-file. Put something in the way.

line.say: The knight steps between the rook and the bishop, and the e-pawn guards it.
If the rook took the knight, the pawn would take the rook, so Black looks for something else.

claims.statement: The bishop on d3 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the rook, it wins the bishop.
After the block, no black piece attacks the bishop.
The blocking knight is guarded once.
After the block, no white piece is loose.

steps.caption: White to move. One knight attacks both the bishop and the knight. Look for one move that answers both.

line.say: Capturing the attacker removes both threats at once, and wins the knight.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
Taking the knight wins a piece.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop attacks the loose knight. This time guard it.

line.say: A pawn now guards the knight.
If the bishop takes, the pawn takes back. The swap is even, so nothing is lost.
The pawn recaptures and White has lost nothing.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the bishop, it wins the knight.
After the pawn move, no white piece is loose.
The knight is now guarded once.

steps.caption: The fifth answer. White to move. The bishop attacks the loose knight, but White has a bigger idea.

line.say: The rook makes a threat of its own: the back rank is open, and the rook now aims at d8.
Black needs to deal with the mate threat on d8, for example by making room for the king. The counter-threat bought only one move.
The knight still had to be saved, and now it is safe.

claims.statement: The knight on c4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
After the rook move, the rook attacks d8.

steps.caption: What if Black grabs the knight instead? White to move.

line.say: The back rank is open and nothing covers d8: checkmate. The bigger threat won.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 is checkmate.

steps.caption: An answer that fails. White blocks with the knight, but nothing guards it.

line.say: The knight steps between the rook and the bishop.
The rook simply takes the blocker. The block was loose, so it only moved the loss.

claims.statement: After the block, the knight on d4 is attacked and unguarded.
The block is a clear mistake.

steps.text: After you pick a reply, ask the question again about the reply itself. A block can leave the blocker loose, and a retreat can land on an attacked square. [I] A habit worth trying: before you let go of the piece, say aloud what your move leaves loose.

steps.text: Part 3 of 5: What did their last move threaten?. This part covers Is the threat real?. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Not every attack is a real threat. Before you worry, ask three questions. **What would they take?** **After my recapture, who is ahead?** Count points: pawn 1, knight or bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9 (a rough convention). **Can they really play it?** A covered square, or an escape square for my king, can cancel a threat. If they gain no material and no mate, there is no immediate threat. [I] Positional threats exist but are outside this lesson.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the bishop, but a pawn defends it.

line.say: White ignores the attack.
The rook takes the bishop.
The pawn takes the rook. Black gave 5 points for 3.

claims.statement: The rook attacks the bishop.
The pawn on b3 defends the bishop.
Rxc4 bxc4 loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Since nothing is threatened, White can use the move for its own plan.

line.say: [I] One plan: bring the king nearer the middle if the game is heading for an ending.
Black still has no way to win anything.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose.

steps.text: Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*, 1922) called a threat fictitious when carrying it out would gain nothing, yet he held that it still ties the opponent down and turns real if they forget it [V-sheet]. [I] Limit of this lesson: it covers threats that act within one move. Deeper ones come later.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.prompt: The black bishop stands on b6 in all three. First nothing guards the knight. Second, a pawn guards it. Third, only a far-away white pawn has moved. Predict each verdict, then check.

steps.caption: White to move. Now a pawn does the attacking. The knight is defended, yet this threat is real.

line.say: White ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
White takes the pawn back. White gave 3 points and won only 1.

claims.statement: A black pawn attacks the knight.
The pawn on b3 defends the knight.
If White passes, Black comes out two points ahead.

steps.caption: Same position. White spots the pawn and moves the knight away from it.

line.say: The knight steps to e5, a square no black pawn attacks right now.
Black has no capture, so the threat is over.

claims.statement: No black pawn attacks e5 after the knight arrives.

steps.text: Here is a **rule of thumb**, not a law. An attack by a cheaper piece on a more valuable one needs an answer, even if the target is defended. A pawn attacking a knight is a threat. A rook attacking a bishop that a pawn defends usually is not. Check the recapture, count the points, then decide.

A swap on one square is a count. Say two black pieces attack a pawn that two white pieces guard. Each side stops as soon as the next capture would lose material. [I] A rule of thumb, not a law: capture with the cheapest piece first, and count before the first capture.

steps.caption: Black to move. Two black pieces attack e5 and two white pieces guard it. Count before capturing.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
The rook takes the pawn.
The rook takes the rook. Black has lost a knight and a rook for two pawns.

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack e5.
Two white pieces guard e5.
Starting the exchange loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's rook sits on the open e-file. Does it threaten checkmate?

line.say: Black ignores the rook, because the bishop on d7 already covers e8.
The rook gives check on e8.
The bishop takes the rook. White gave a whole rook for nothing.

claims.statement: The bishop on d7 covers e8.
Re8 loses the rook for nothing.

steps.text: Now one position, changed one piece at a time. Predict first: in each version, is the bishop's attack a real threat, and why? Then step through the boards, which also show a pin.

steps.caption: The original. White to move. Black's bishop looks at the knight.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The bishop takes the knight and nothing takes back.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White passes, the bishop wins the knight.

steps.caption: Change one: a white pawn now stands on e3. Is the knight still in danger?

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The bishop takes the knight.
The pawn takes the bishop. A knight for a bishop is an even swap.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose now.
One white pawn guards the knight.
If White passes, the capture gains Black nothing.

steps.caption: Change two: instead of a pawn, a white rook stands on b1. The bishop's king is behind it.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
Black cannot play the capture: the bishop is pinned to its king and may not leave the b-file.

claims.statement: The bishop has no legal move at all.
The bishop does attack the knight, but only on paper.

steps.text: Two common ways a real-looking threat fails, and you can check both in seconds. The target is **guarded**: count the points after the recapture, and if the capture gains nothing or loses material, there is no threat. Or the attacker is **pinned**: the capture would be illegal. [I] These are not the only ways; an in-between check can also change the count. Ask before you spend a move on a defence.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's bishop on e6 looks towards the a2 pawn. Is that a threat?

line.say: White makes a quiet move of its own.
The bishop takes the pawn.
A defender takes the bishop. Black gave 3 points for 1.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks the a2 pawn.
The rook on a1 and the knight on c3 both defend it.
No white piece is loose.
Bxa2 Rxa2 loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Because nothing is threatened, White uses the move to improve a piece.

line.say: The rook comes to the open d-file, where it has more room.
Black takes the same file, and play goes on.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose.

steps.text: Part 4 of 5: What did their last move threaten?. This part covers Make it, stop it, see it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

You make threats too, and every threat costs your opponent a move. The best ones are quiet: they improve your position *and* ask a question your opponent must answer. [H] At our level people often make a threat by accident, then forget to follow it up. Saying 'my move threatens...' aloud may fix that. I have not tested this.
steps.chapter: Make it, stop it, see it

steps.caption: White to move. Nothing is attacked on either side. Make a threat with a developing move.

line.say: The rook takes the open file and now attacks the loose pawn on d5.

claims.statement: At the start, Black threatens nothing.
After the rook move the pawn on d5 is attacked and unguarded.

steps.caption: The position after the rook move. Black to move. What if Black ignores it?

line.say: Black plays an unrelated move.
The rook takes the pawn that nothing guarded.

steps.text: The same question protects you from your own moves: *what would they threaten after I play this?* Dan Heisman, as reported in a chess.com article [S], uses 'hope chess' for moving and hoping the reply is harmless, and suggests looking at forcing replies first. A move can leave a piece loose that it used to guard.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the bishop, and the knight is its only guard. A developing move tempts.

line.say: The knight develops, and that takes away the bishop's only guard.
The rook takes the bishop and nothing takes back.

claims.statement: Now no white piece is loose: the knight guards the bishop.
After the knight leaves, the bishop is loose.
The developing move is a clear mistake.

steps.caption: Same position. Ask the question first, then pick a move that keeps the knight where it is. Kf1, b3 and a3 all do.

line.say: The king steps towards the centre, and the knight keeps guarding the bishop.
Black has found nothing to take.

claims.statement: After the king move, no white piece is loose.
After b3 no white piece is loose either.
The knight still guards the bishop.

steps.text: Part 5 of 5: What did their last move threaten?. This part covers Mixed test, say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Now mixed positions with no labels. Some hold a real threat; in others nothing is threatened, and 'nothing' is a correct answer. Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*, Lectures 1 and 6) criticises rook-pawn moves played out of fear of a threat that does not yet exist. [V-sheet] [I] My reading: asking is cheap, but inventing a danger costs you a move.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: Black's rook is on the open file. Black has just moved, and one piece differs each time. In which versions is there a real threat?

steps.text: A famous old trap is usually credited to a game of Légal against Saint Brie, Paris, 1787 [R: from memory, no source checked here]. The trap itself is taught in the opening-traps lessons; here it is only practice for the question. White has just made a surprising move. What does it threaten?

steps.caption: Black to move. Black sees a free queen and takes it. The bishop was giving a mating threat, and taking the knight on e5 would have removed it.

line.say: Black takes the queen, the biggest prize on the board.
White does not recapture. The bishop takes f7 with check.
The king has only one square.
The knight gives checkmate. All the king's squares are covered.

claims.statement: If Black takes the queen with Bxd1, then Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5 is checkmate.
Taking the queen is legal.

steps.caption: The same position. Black asks what the last move threatened and takes the knight instead.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight, so the bishop's check on f7 no longer comes with a mating net.
White takes the bishop that had been attacked, and is still about two pawns ahead (Stockfish 19 lite, depth 18 [V]).

claims.statement: Taking the knight is Black's best move (engine, depth 16 [V]).
White is still about two pawns ahead after best play (Stockfish 19 lite, depth 18 [V]).

steps.prompt: Black took the queen at once. Name the first question Black skipped, and describe one moment in your own games where you are most likely to skip it.

fields.label: Where I am most likely to skip it

steps.text: [H] A guess, not a tested fact: many lost pieces at your level come from one-move threats you could have seen by asking the question once. I have no data on this. Test it on your own games: find a loss, and look for the first opponent move whose threat you did not answer.

**What to remember.** A threat is what they could do next if I passed. Look at where the moved piece went, what line it opened, and which of my pieces are loose. Answer a real one by moving, capturing, blocking or guarding. Check it is real: guarded target and recapture count, pinned attacker. Then ask the same question of my own move before I play it.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a beginner who has just lost a piece to a move they did not see coming. Write what you would tell them. title: Threat or no threat?
outcomes: Imagines a free move for the opponent and lists checks, captures and double attacks

steps.text: In "What did their last move threaten?" there was always something to find. Now there often is not. Pretend your opponent gets a **free move** and list what they could do: **checks, captures, and moves that attack two things or threaten mate**. If every move on the list fails, the answer is **none**, and you do not spend a move on it.

steps.caption: White to move. What if Black got a free move?

line.say: Suppose White plays a quiet move.
Re1 is checkmate: the king has no square and nothing can take or block.

claims.statement: If White passes, Re1 is checkmate.

steps.text: A threat must gain something next move: material or mate. **Rule of thumb** for the list: is a piece of mine attacked and short of defence, can a check lead to mate, can one move attack two things? A covered square stops a fork (one piece attacking two things at once). An attacked piece that is also defended may still be a threat: a pawn attacking a defended knight is one. Count to be sure.

steps.caption: A position from a Lichess game [R, not rechecked], White to move. Before any opinion, just look. The black knight on d4 is marked.
The knight attacks eight squares. Two of them hold White pieces: the queen on f3 and the pawn on c2. A careful count gives the same answer every time.

steps.text: **Look first.** What you just did is an **observation**: something you can point to on the board, so a careful count gives anyone the same answer. A **guess** is a prediction or a judgment, such as 'I am winning' or 'he will take my pawn'. Guesses are fine. The skill is knowing which of the two you are writing down.

**Why bother separating them?** A misread board and a misjudged future need different fixes: recount the first, test the second. Even a count can slip, such as calling a pawn twice defended when it is defended three times, so recount. Untested guesses become mistakes, as the f7 trap will show. [H] Labelling a guess may slow you enough to look for the reply you hoped would not come.

steps.caption: Observation one. The knight attacks the queen on f3. One White pawn, on g2, defends that square. You can count both on the board.

Observation two. The knight also attacks the pawn on c2, and no White piece defends it. A piece that is attacked and has no defender is **loose**. (Books often use 'loose' for any undefended piece; here we use the narrower sense.)

Observation three. The pawn on e4 is attacked once, by the knight on f6, and defended three times. That is the count. Whether the pawn is safe is a guess; you would test it. [I] The count changes if a defender, such as the queen, is taken.

steps.text: Now the other kind. 'I am lost' feels like a fact because the feeling is strong, but it is a judgment about the future. So is 'my queen is safe, because a pawn defends it'. Write guesses down too, but **label them as guesses**. Next you will see how a guess can be tested, with a worked example first.

steps.caption: Three notes about this position. One: the knight attacks my queen. Two: my queen is safe, a pawn defends it. Three: I am lost. Only the first can be read straight off the board. Notes two and three are guesses.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Observe: one unsure moment, and what you actually saw. This part covers Test the guess; Feelings are different; Test the guess, once more. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: A worked test of note two, 'my queen is safe'. Play it out: let White ignore the knight with a quiet move, and see what happens.

line.say: White ignores the knight and plays a quiet pawn move.
The knight takes the queen and attacks the king.
The pawn takes the knight. White gave a queen for a knight, so the guess failed.

steps.text: **Three ways to test a guess.** Count the attackers and defenders. Play the line out and add up what each side takes. Or ask an **engine**, a chess program that calculates far deeper than you can. One warning from the last board: a defended piece is not always safe, because a cheaper attacker can still win a dearer piece.

steps.caption: Another guess: 'I can move the queen anywhere, it will be fine.' Test one square, g3.

line.say: The queen steps away, but c2 stays loose.
The knight takes the pawn with check and also attacks the rook on a1.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the rook. White has lost a pawn and a rook so far; the engine rates it about -3 pawns for White at depth 18.

steps.caption: The test of that guess. The bishop takes the pawn with check, and the king takes the bishop.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn and gives check.
The king takes the bishop. White gave 3 for 1.

steps.caption: Now test the guess 'the queen to d1 is my best move'. The engine agrees, and the move does two jobs.

line.say: The queen leaves the knight's reach and guards the pawn on c2, so no White piece is attacked and unguarded any more.
Black makes a quiet move.
White castles: the king is safe and the rook joins in.

steps.caption: The guess 'I am lost' tested: the engine rates this position as close to level. [H] A queen under attack is vivid, and a vivid danger may make the whole position feel worse than it is. That is a hypothesis, not a result.

steps.title: Guesses can be tested
steps.prompt: Compare a confirmed guess, a refuted guess and an observation. For a guess, predict whether a test will confirm it, then check.

steps.caption: A quiet moment in the same game, one move earlier. 'I can castle now' is an observation, because the board allows it. 'Castling feels scary' is a feeling. It is real, but it is about you, not about this board.

steps.text: **Three boxes.** Some notes are observations, settled by looking. Some are guesses you can test. Some are feelings the board cannot answer, such as 'I feel nervous'. [I] A feeling is still worth one line in your notes, because it shows where you were unsure. Just do not write it in the observation box.

steps.caption: Testing the note 'Black will win my e4 pawn'. White actually played d3 here, adding a third guard. Black takes the pawn anyway.

line.say: White adds a third guard to the pawn on e4.
Black takes the pawn with the knight.
The pawn takes the knight, which nothing defends. Black gave a knight for a pawn, so this try fails.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Observe: one unsure moment, and what you actually saw. This part covers Why test: a trap; Write your note. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: A beginner trap. White's queen and bishop both look at the pawn on f7. Black to move.
Suppose Black replies with a knight move that attacks the queen, thinking 'she must run' [I] a typical beginner thought. That is a guess, and nobody tested it. Now White moves.

line.say: The queen takes f7. The bishop guards her, so the king cannot take her and has nowhere to go: checkmate.

steps.text: Dan Heisman called this **Hope Chess** [S: Heisman, chess.com article on Hope Chess]: you make a move and hope the opponent has no strong reply, without first checking their forcing replies: checks, captures and threats. Black's note was a guess, 'she must run', and it was never tested. Before you move, name your guess, then look at every forcing reply the other side has.

steps.caption: What testing would have found. The pawn move attacks the queen first, so Black keeps control.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen and gives her a reason to move.
The queen steps back and still eyes f7.
The knight develops and blocks the f-file, so only the bishop still looks at f7.

steps.caption: More than one answer works. The queen to e7 adds a second defender, so f7 is now attacked twice and defended twice.

line.say: The queen becomes a second defender of f7, next to the king.

steps.caption: A model note. Move 9. I could see: the knight attacks my queen, one pawn defends the queen, the pawn on c2 is loose. I guessed: the queen is safe, because it is defended. What would settle it: let the knight take the queen and count what each side loses.

Another model note, from the black side. Move 3. I could see: two white pieces attack f7, one black piece defends it. I guessed: if I attack the queen she must run. What would settle it: list White's checks and captures after my move.

steps.text: **One unsure moment per game.** After a game, pick one move where you felt unsure and write four lines: the move number, what you could see, what you guessed, and what would settle it. Skip the engine for now. One short note beats a long review you never finish. [H] Keeping to one moment may make the habit easier to keep. It is a habit to try.

steps.caption: Where the first model note came from, so you can find its move number. White's eighth move adds a guard of e4. Black's reply puts the knight on d4, and the next move is the unsure moment: move 9.

line.say: White's eighth move: another guard for the pawn on e4.
Black's eighth move: the knight jumps to d4, attacking the queen and the pawn on c2.

steps.text: **Be honest in the note.** Capablanca (Chess Fundamentals, Part II) openly names ways his own thinking failed, such as judging a combination unsound and then losing to it. Silman, as reported on chess.com [S] and not checked in his own books, says an engine shows what to play but not why: test a guess with it, then explain the result yourself. Both are paraphrases.

steps.text: **Explain, and say how sure you are.** Before you see an answer, commit to it and rate your confidence: low, medium or high. Afterwards compare. Over many answers you can see whether your 'high' is right more often than your 'low'. That match is called *calibration*. It is a habit to try; evidence for it in chess is thin.

steps.title: Confidence and evidence
steps.prompt: Answer each position and mark your confidence (low, medium or high) before you check. Then compare confidence with the result.

steps.text: Look at your three answers. A confident wrong answer (the trap) teaches more than a lucky right one. If your 'high' answers are wrong about one time in four or more, treat 'high' as 'check once more'. That cut-off is a guess, not a measured threshold.

fields.label: Of those, how many were right:

title: Diagnose: which kind of mistake, and how do you know?
outcomes: Names four kinds of mistake: not seen, seen but miscalculated, misjudged, time pressure
Labels a mistake tentatively from the player's own note
Reads an error log and tests a diagnosis against it
Says honestly that a diagnosis can be wrong

steps.text:
When you lose material, ask which box it belongs in.
**Not seen:** you never looked at the reply.
**Seen but miscalculated:** you looked and the count was wrong.
**Misjudged:** the count was right, your verdict on the position was wrong.
**Time pressure:** the clock decided.
The label is tentative: only the player knows what happened.

Different boxes may need different practice: not seen suggests a scan habit; miscalculated suggests practice with lines and counting; misjudged suggests comparing positions; time pressure suggests a clock plan. This pairing is a hypothesis to test, not a proven rule.

**An error log** lists each mistake with the game, the clock and a box. A diagnosis is a claim the log can test. Fictional log of 8 errors, clock left in brackets: 1 not seen (9:40); 2 miscalculated (7:15); 3 not seen (8:05); 4 time pressure (0:48); 5 not seen (6:30); 6 misjudged (9:10); 7 time pressure (0:35); 8 not seen (7:50).

steps.prompt: Test two diagnoses against this log: 'I lose because I run low on time' and 'most of my mistakes are things I never looked at'.

fields.label: How many of the 8 errors happened with more than 5 minutes left?
Does the log support 'I lose because I run low on time'?
In your own games, what would you check to test a diagnosis? (one line)

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The app supplies the boxes (these four, and out of book as a fifth) and the log layout. The plan is that after you have filled in the log for five games you name the boxes yourself and the app stops showing them (a first guess). The log is plain text you can keep outside the app; exporting it is planned.

steps.prompt: Start your own log. After your next game add up to three mistakes. Silent practice: do it with the app closed, then bring the log back.

fields.label: Which of these labels am I least sure of?

title: Plan a training block, test it, and revise it
outcomes: Writes a training block with a goal, practice, baseline and a later check
Explains why the check must use tasks that were not practised
States what result would change the plan
Says honestly that a plan can fail

steps.text: A **training block** is a plan you can test: a **goal** (one specific thing), **practice** (what, how often, how long), a **baseline** (a measure before you start) and a **later check on tasks you did not practise**. Plans can fail, and a failed plan that you measured teaches more than a plan you never tested.

steps.prompt: Choose one goal for a block. Use your error log or unsure moments as evidence, not a feeling.

fields.label: The evidence it matters (games, log entries):

steps.text: In a real block, practice runs for days with many positions. Here it is compressed: one practice position, then a check position that is new. The baseline above was your first attempt at the same skill, answering the opponent's last move.

steps.title: A fair check
steps.prompt: Two positions could be used as the check. One is new; one is the practice position flipped left to right. Which makes a fair check?

steps.text: **Revise from evidence.** At the check date compare with the baseline. Then change one thing: keep the plan, change the practice, or change the goal. If the check is no better than the baseline, the plan may be wrong, the check may be too noisy, or the block too short. With a few items you cannot tell which; say so.

steps.prompt: Write the block. The check must use positions or games you have not practised.

fields.label: Baseline: how I will measure before starting:
What result would make me change the plan?

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Now it gives you the template, a baseline item and check items from families you have not practised. The plan is that you choose the block length and write your own check, and the app only keeps the check items sealed until your check date. Silent practice: do your block with the app closed and return on the date.

steps.prompt: Revision, to fill in at the check date. Compare with your baseline and change one thing.

fields.label: The one thing I will change:
Could the plan have failed because of the plan, the check, or the length of the block?

title: Experiment: change one thing, check fairly, decide by a rule written first
outcomes: Designs a two-way comparison of training methods that changes one thing and keeps the rest fixed
Writes a prediction and a decision rule before any data
Chooses a fair check: new positions, no idea named, some look-alikes where the practised idea fails
Reads two small scores with their ranges and says whether they can be told apart

steps.text: An **experiment** changes one thing and keeps the rest the same, so a difference can be blamed on the change. *Example:* practise forks **blocked** (all forks in a row) for two weeks, then forks **interleaved** (mixed with other themes) for two weeks, same minutes, with a check on new mixed positions after each. Two good sessions prove nothing. You need a measure, a check on positions you did not practise, and a decision rule written *before* you look.

In a block of forks you know the idea before you look; a **fair check** does not tell you. Rules of thumb: (1) positions you did not practise, not a mirror of one; (2) no idea named; (3) some positions where the practised idea fails, or 'always fork' scores full marks; (4) the same check for both methods. Compare two methods on one skill, not forks against pins; the order can also fool you (by the second fortnight you know more). Four silent positions follow as a tiny check.

steps.title: The same fork, one change
steps.prompt: A check made only of the first kind of position cannot tell skill from habit. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **How much does a score show?** The My plan page prints a rough range for each score. With 8 items: 2 right is 7%-59%, 4 right 22%-78%, 6 right 41%-93%, 8 right 68%-100%. A start of 3 of 8 and a check of 6 of 8 sounds like a doubling, yet the ranges overlap. 'Cannot tell' means not enough data, not 'no effect'. A plan that shows nothing, or goes down, is still data.

steps.prompt: Press Save note to see the answers. Ranges for 8 items: 1 right 2%-47%, 2 right 7%-59%, 7 right 53%-98%, 8 right 68%-100%. With 4 items, 3 right is 30%-95%. Your four silent answers form a tiny check.

fields.label: How many of the four silent positions did you get right on the first try, with no hints?
Baseline (your starting score) 2 of 8. What is the smallest check score out of 8 whose range lies completely above the baseline range (above 59%)?
Baseline 1 of 8, check 8 of 8: can the two ranges be told apart?

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** My plan keeps one skill, your goal, a 'what would tell you it worked' box and the check date. The silent baseline and check use up to 8 positions of that skill (the check from new families), with ranges. For tactics like forks, nearly all are positions where the idea works, so add look-alikes yourself. It cannot compare two methods: keep a paper log. Write your rule in the success box first. Do not delete a failed plan.

steps.prompt: Design your own experiment. Write the prediction and the decision rule now, before any data. A plan that fails is a result, not a mistake.

title: Lead: your own manual, silent sessions, and handing a skill back by evidence
outcomes: Tells an exercise that shows unprompted skill from one that names the idea
Runs a silent session and records first-try results and which habits he used unprompted
Decides from a small ledger which skill to hand back to coached mode and which has too little data
Writes a one-page manual for a month: routine, evidence, hand-back rule, one thing done with another person

steps.text: To **lead** is to run the routine yourself while the app only keeps the record. Help should fade on **evidence** that you do something unprompted, session after session. A rating summarises game results; it does not show which habits you use without being asked. A **silent session** turns hints off so that what you do alone shows. Solving an exercise that names the idea shows less than solving one that does not.

steps.title: Same position, the idea named or not
steps.prompt: The board you just saw is the unprompted version of the position you solved, shown with its answer marked. Predict about the named version.

steps.text: **What the record can and cannot see.** The Progress page counts your first attempts at unlabeled exercises (nothing names the idea or the theme): hints used and right without hints, by week, with all skills pooled. Its skill table gives running totals, not weeks. It does not show your habits, your thinking time, or games played elsewhere. So your manual needs a second record, your own: after a silent session, note which habits you used unprompted, and tally results per skill.

steps.prompt: Session note: four silent positions, no hints.

fields.label: How many of the four did you get right on the first try?
Did you run your own routine (for example: list checks, captures and threats) without anything telling you to?
One thing I did that no prompt asked for, or one thing I skipped:

steps.text: **Hand back on evidence.** Handing a skill back to **coached mode** (hints on, named exercises again) should follow your record, not a mood. The Progress page shows, week by week, how often you used hints and how often you were right without them; for one skill, keep your own tally as in the ledger below. **Rule of thumb** (a first guess): judge a skill after 8 or more hint-free attempts, and send it back if accuracy without hints stays under half in both weeks.

steps.prompt: Press Save note to see the answers. Fictional ledger, two weeks, first attempts at exercises that do not name the idea. Hints is the share of attempts where you opened a hint; right counts only attempts without a hint. Forks: hints 50% then 10%; right 4 of 6, then 8 of 9. Pins: hints 20% then 20%; right 3 of 8, then 3 of 8. Skewers: right 2 of 2, then 1 of 2. Rule of thumb (a first guess): judge a skill after 8 or more hint-free attempts in all; send it back to coached mode if accuracy without hints stays under half in both weeks.

fields.label: Which skill has too little data to judge?
By the rule, which skill goes back to coached mode?
Forks: hints fell from 50% to 10% while accuracy rose. What does the rule say?
One way this rule could mislead me:

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Silent practice is a checkbox on the Practice page: hints off, answers shown afterwards. Today lets you set your own aim first, and Progress keeps the weekly record. The thinking prompts for loop levels 1-3 retire after five mixed solves in a row with them closed (five is a first guess). Nothing hands a skill back for you. Saved notes export from Settings, but there is no manual page: keep your manual in your own file.

steps.prompt: Write your manual for one month, with no system prompts: the app only keeps the record. Working alone is not automatically good practice; one study of chess players (reported second-hand, not re-checked here) found practice with others mattered in its sample. So include one thing you do with someone else.

title: Investigate: a claim, a test that could fail, and the limits written down
outcomes: Turns a claim with a source and a year into a question a test could answer, with a result that would show it false
Chooses a tool (engine, tablebase, Openings page, own games) and says what it can and cannot show
Plans the limits and a failing look-alike to write beside a conclusion
Tells a research question from one that a tablebase lookup answers

steps.text: An **investigation** starts with a claim you can name, with its source and year: a book, a video, or a 'rule of thumb' in these lessons. Turn it into a question a test could answer. What would I see if the claim is true, and what would show it false? Pick a tool, write its **limits**, and look for a **failing look-alike**. Checking an old claim counts as research; a novelty is not required.

steps.prompt: Choose a claim to investigate: something you have read, heard or been taught. Write only the claim for now.

fields.label: Where it comes from (author or title):

steps.text: **A worked question.** Claim (made up here, so no source or year): a move that scores well on the Openings page must be sound. If so, moves with equal results should be about equally sound. Data (September 2026 online games, band 1300-1500) after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4: 4.Nxd4 (10,125 games) White won 53%, drew 4%; 4.Ng5 (2,519 games) won 53%, drew 2%. A draw counted as half a win gives about 54 to 55% for both. Now ask the engine.

steps.caption: White to move after 3...exd4. Written beside this result: tool Stockfish, depth 16, one position; data from the Openings page, September 2026 sample, band 1300-1500. At depth 16 the engine ranks 4.Nxd4 first and rates 4.Ng5 at least 1.5 pawns lower. Failing look-alike: 4.Ng5 is a common move (14% of games here) that wins as often as 4.Nxd4 (53% each), yet it is the move the engine rates lower.

claims.statement: Nxd4 is legal.
Nxd4 is the engine's best move.
Ng5 is at least 1.5 pawns lower than the best move.

steps.text: **What each tool can and cannot show.** *Openings page:* what players of a band chose and how those games ended (one month, online); not why, and not strength. *Engine:* a fixed-depth rating of one position; not what people will do. *Your games:* real mistakes, but few. *Tablebase* (seven pieces or fewer; the Analysis page can look a position up online): exact for each position, so one position is a lookup, not research; a claim about many positions takes many lookups. Write tool, sample, depth and band beside every result.

steps.title: One position, two kinds of question

steps.text: A conclusion is worth keeping when the test could have failed, the result sits beside its tool, sample, depth and band, and one **failing look-alike** is named. It breaks when you keep only the cases that agree, when the sample is tiny (a **rule of thumb**: under about 30 games in a band is noise; the Openings page hides such results), or when a lookup would have answered. A result that contradicts the source is a finding.

steps.caption: Black to move. Look at the white king on h1: two pawns in front of it, and the white queen far away on h5. Black's rook can give check on the first rank. White's last move captured the black queen on b1. Guess before you read on: mate, or only a check?

claims.statement: The rook can go to e1.
Black is not in check and can move.

steps.prompt: Black's rook goes to the first rank with check. Pick a guess and give one reason. The lesson comes back to this position, so write what you actually think.

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Look at any position and decide, with nobody naming the idea, whether a back-rank mate exists, for either side. Refute a mate that is not there. Make your own king safe in the cheapest way. And say plainly when there is no back-rank mate at all. The test near the end mixes positions with and without mates, and nothing in it is labelled.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's rook is on the other side of the board, but the d-file is open. Count the squares the white king could step to.

claims.statement: The king can go to f1 and h1 only.

steps.text: **Shield and cage.** The three pawns shield the king from checks coming from the front, yet they also fill three of its squares. An edge king has at most six squares (its own and five neighbours), and here the pawns take three. Emanuel Lasker's reminder for any attack is to count the squares you must control and to make sure the checking piece cannot be taken.

steps.caption: The same position, Black to move. Step through and count which squares one rook covers. [H] Counting the squares before hunting for checks may find mates faster; untested.

line.say: One rook check covers e1, f1 and g1. The king cannot step to h1 either: that square lies on the same line.

claims.statement: Rd1 is checkmate.
The rook on d1 covers f1.
The rook on d1 gives check on g1.

steps.caption: An uncastled king is shut in the same way. White to move: which squares are free for the king?

claims.statement: The king can go to d1 and f1 only.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's rook stands on the e-file, which has no pawns on it.

line.say: The rook checks along the first rank. The pawns hold the king in, and nothing white covers e1.

claims.statement: ...Re1 is checkmate.
No white piece covers e1.

steps.text: **Three conditions.** A check along the first rank is mate only if all three hold. **One:** the king has no flight square. **Two:** nothing can capture the checking piece. **Three:** nothing can step between the checker and the king. Look at them in that order. Remove any one and it is only a check.

steps.title: What turns a mate into a check?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position: mate, or only a check? Then say what changed.

steps.caption: Back to the opening position. Compare with your guess at the start: what did you miss or get right? Then check the three conditions one by one.

line.say: The rook checks. g2 and h2 fill the king's squares, nothing covers e1, and nothing can step in.

claims.statement: Re1 is checkmate.
No white piece covers e1.

steps.text: **Only a rook?** No. Any piece that gives check along the rank can mate there: a queen as well as a rook, or two pieces working together. The three conditions never change. What changes is how you meet the second one: when a defender can take the checking piece, you may need a second piece behind it. The next three boards show each case.

steps.prompt: In positions B, C and D, which condition failed? Which of the three questions do you usually forget to ask?

steps.caption: White to move. A queen can do the rook's job. Look for the check on the eighth rank.

line.say: The queen checks along the eighth rank. Nothing can take it or step in, and the pawns hold the king.

claims.statement: Qd8 is checkmate.
No black piece covers d8.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has two rooks guarding the eighth rank; White has two rooks aimed at it.

line.say: The first rook takes the guard on e8 with check.
The other black rook has to recapture; nothing else can.
The second rook takes again, and now nothing is left to take it.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves, starting with the capture on e8.
The rook on e2 attacks e8.

steps.caption: White to move. A knight guards e8, so a lone rook check would simply be taken. The queen stands behind the rook.

line.say: The rook goes to e8 with check, backed by the queen behind it.
The knight must take it; there is no other reply.
The queen takes the knight with check, and the guard is gone.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves.
The knight on f6 covers e8.

steps.caption: Position A. White to move. Predict before you step: mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks along the eighth rank. Look at each of the three questions.

claims.statement: Re8 is checkmate.
No black piece covers e8.

steps.caption: Position B: one black pawn has moved from h7 to h6. Same question: mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks. The pawn move gave the king a square.
The king steps to h7 and the check is over.

claims.statement: Re8 is not checkmate.
No white piece covers h7.

steps.caption: Position C: the black bishop has moved from b7 to d7. Mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks, but the bishop covers e8.
The bishop takes the rook, so the check does not mate.

claims.statement: Re8 is not checkmate.
A black piece covers e8.
The rook is lost along the engine line.

steps.caption: Position D: the black bishop stands on d6 and the h-pawn is back on h7. Mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks. This time a piece can step in.
The bishop interposes on f8, and the check is parried.

claims.statement: Re8 is not checkmate.
Two black pieces cover f8: the bishop and the king.

steps.text: **The checklist.** Before you call a check on the first rank mate, ask three questions in order. Where can the king go? Who can take the checker? Who can step in between? If the answers are 'nowhere', 'nobody' and 'nobody', it is mate. If not, say aloud which question failed: flight, capture or block. [H] Naming the failure may help you diagnose your own mistakes faster; this is untested.

steps.text: Part 2 of 2: Back-rank mate, and luft as the cure. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**How the mate gets there.** [I] From the examples below, three things often come before the mate: pieces developed away from the back rank; a rook that was the only piece able to reach the rank goes elsewhere; and a pawn move that opens a file for the enemy rook. Dan Heisman's remedy [S] is to list the opponent's forcing replies (checks, captures, threats) before each move. A check on your first rank is one of them.

steps.caption: White to move. Black threatens Rd1+. Even the rook's return to e1 would only be taken with mate. White needs air. Predict what happens if the rook grabs the pawn on c7, then step through.

line.say: The grab ignores the threat.
Black's rook checks along the first rank. The pawns hold the king in and nothing can step in: mate.

claims.statement: The pawn grab loses to a forced mate.
If White passes, Black already wins by force: Rd1+, and the rook's return to e1 is taken with mate.
The engine prefers a king step to the pawn grab.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d4 blocks the d-file for now. What might a natural pawn capture do?

line.say: The pawn takes on e5 and leaves the d-file.
The file is open, Black's rook reaches the first rank, and the white king has nowhere to go: mate.

claims.statement: The capture loses to a forced mate.
While the pawn stands on d4, Black's rook does not attack d1.

steps.caption: White to move. Black threatens a rook check on d1 that would be mate. First try: the h-pawn.

line.say: Luft with the h-pawn: the king gets the square h2. The price is that g3 loses one pawn guard.
Black checks anyway, but now the check is only a check.
The king steps to h2. The threat is gone. A king step to f1 also holds here, but it needs a free, safe square and is not always available.

claims.statement: The h-pawn move holds, like the g-pawn move and a king step.
Before the move, two white pawns guard g3.
After h3, only the f-pawn guards g3.

steps.caption: The same position. Second try: the g-pawn. Ask what it leaves behind.

line.say: Luft with the g-pawn: the king gets g2, and the pawn leaves the long diagonal. The price is f3 and h3.
Black checks, but the king has a square.
The king steps to g2.

claims.statement: Before the move, a white pawn guards f3.
After g3, no white pawn guards f3.
After g3, no white pawn guards h3.

steps.caption: A different setup: the pawn stands on c2 instead of a2, so the rook can return to a1. Third try: guard the first rank instead of making luft. [I] I guessed the guard would be best; Stockfish 19 at depth 16 rates it about 0.1 pawn below the best move here. One position proves nothing.

line.say: The rook returns to guard the rank. Now a check on d1 would simply lose a rook.
Black makes a waiting move. [I] The rook is now tied to the first rank.

claims.statement: The rook retreat holds, like the luft moves.
The engine rates the retreat at least a tenth of a pawn below the best move here.
After the retreat, the rook covers d1.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has no rook and no queen, so nothing can use White's back rank. Would a quiet luft help, or does it only cost a move?

line.say: The knight checks the king and also attacks the bishop on a5.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the bishop. White has won a piece.

claims.statement: The fork wins a piece for White.
Playing h3 first throws the win away.
The knight on c6 would attack the bishop on a5.

steps.text: **When to give luft.** Edward Lasker notes that every pawn move leaves something behind, and advises against a luft made as a precaution before a mate threat shows it is needed. [I] His advice is stated more strongly than modern practice follows: many strong players make h3 or a3 early for other reasons. The practical test is one question: can an enemy rook or queen reach my back rank soon? [H] Beginners may still gain from an early, cheap luft.

steps.title: Does White need luft now?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position: does White need to spend a move on luft now? Then name the one thing that differs.

Do you agree with the rule of thumb that luft waits until a threat shows? Think of your own games: did you lose more by giving luft too early, or by giving it too late? [H] I suspect beginners lose far more by waiting; I have not tested this.

steps.caption: Decoy: the king is pulled to g1. Black to move. White's only protection against a second black rook is the king itself. Predict how Black can use that.

line.say: The rook takes the knight with check and forces the king to take it.
The king recaptures. It now stands on the first rank.
The second rook checks along the rank. The king is shut in by its own pawns: mate.

claims.statement: Black mates in two moves.
The rook on c1 attacks g1.

steps.caption: Deflection: the knight is pulled off c7. White to move. Two black pieces guard e8: the rook and the knight on c7. What happens if the knight is made to move?

line.say: The queen takes the rook with check and offers herself.
The knight takes the queen. It had to, and it has left c7.
The knight no longer guards e8, so the rook checks and nothing can answer.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves.
Two black pieces cover e8.

steps.caption: Exchange: rooks trade until none is left. White to move. Black's queen stands between White's two rooks, and Black's rook guards the eighth rank. Predict how many captures White needs.

line.say: The first rook takes the guard on d8 with check.
The queen must recapture. That clears the d-file for the second rook.
The second rook takes the queen with check, and nothing can answer.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves.

steps.text: **Three ways to remove the last guard.** You have just seen a decoy (a sacrifice drags a piece onto a square), a deflection (a forcing move pulls a guard away) and an exchange (a trade removes it). Each has its own lesson: L-TAC-DECOY-1, L-TAC-DEFLECT-1, L-TAC-REMOVE-DEFENDER-1 and L-TAC-OVERLOAD-1. Here, learn one habit: count the defenders of the key square first.

steps.title: Does the exchange work?
steps.prompt: Count the defenders of d8 before you decide. In the second position a black bishop has been added.

steps.text: **A mate threat wins material too.** A piece tied to guarding the first rank has less freedom, so it is often a worse defender elsewhere. [I] Edward Lasker lists a mate threat that ties a piece down among the ways a defender can be an illusion. Znosko-Borovsky's point about threats applies as well: a threat can pay off even if you never carry it out. The next boards show a poisoned piece and a forced loss.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's bishop on d3 is attacked by the black queen and nothing defends it. Is it free?

line.say: The queen takes the free bishop, leaving the job of guarding the eighth rank.
The rook checks and the king has nowhere to go: mate.

claims.statement: The bishop on d3 is attacked and undefended.
Taking the bishop loses to a forced mate.

steps.caption: The same position with White to move. Black's queen is the only piece that can answer a check on e8.

line.say: Check along the eighth rank. Only the queen can step in, on f8.
The queen interposes. It has no other choice.
The rook takes the queen with check.
The king takes the rook. White gave a rook for a queen.

claims.statement: The rook check wins material for White.
Nothing can take the rook on e8.

steps.caption: White to move. Both kings are shut in by their pawns and the rooks face each other. Who benefits from having the move?

line.say: White takes first, with check. Nothing can retake and the king has no square: mate.

claims.statement: White mates in one.

steps.caption: The same position with Black to move. Predict the result.

line.say: Black takes first, with check. The same pattern gives mate to the other side.

claims.statement: Black mates in one.

steps.text: **Two questions, every move.** Can I check on his first rank, and is it mate? Could he do it to me? [I] Looking at both kings every move is cheap and may catch these mates on both sides. This mirrors Heisman's looking-for-trouble routine [S]: find his threat, then the prevention. Asking 'what rook could check there?' before a quiet move is its practical form. More mixed practice: L-TAC-BACKRANK-2.

steps.caption: From a Lichess puzzle record (eSn5l, CC0), tagged as a master game in that database. White to move. Black's rook on e1 attacks the white rook on g1. In the game White took the pawn on a6 with the queen. What could go wrong with that?

claims.statement: Black's rook on e1 attacks White's rook on g1.
The queen capture on a6 loses to a forced mate.
A knight move is best.
White stands clearly better (engine, depth 16).

steps.caption: In the game the queen took on a6. Black to move. Predict Black's forcing move before you step: the white king has only its own pawns for cover.

line.say: A rook sacrifice: the capture on g1 forces the king to recapture.
The king takes the rook. Its shelter is now the first rank, with no air.

claims.statement: Black mates in two moves.
The rook on e1 attacks g1.

steps.caption: Black to move again. The second rook is still on e8. Predict the finish.

line.say: The second rook checks along the rank. The pawns hold the king in: mate. One sacrifice dragged the king where the other rook could reach it.

claims.statement: Black mates in one.

steps.text: **Recap.** A back-rank mate needs three things together: no flight square, nothing to capture the checker, nothing to block. Any piece that can check along the rank will do. The cure is cheap: a luft, a guard, or noticing that no heavy piece can arrive. Count defenders before an exchange. Look at both kings on every move. Positions with no mate are common, so ask the three questions every time.

**Self-check.** Before you write, test yourself. Did I say when it works (all three conditions)? Did I say when it fails (flight, capture, block)? Did I give an example a beginner could set up with a few pieces? Did I name one mistake, such as grabbing a pawn with the only guard? Nothing here is graded; the list is only for you.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Explain back-rank mate and luft to a beginner who knows how the pieces move. Use your own words.

outcomes: Finds the back-rank mate for either side when no theme is named
