steps.text: You know the pattern from **Back-rank mate, and luft as the cure**. Now it has to work for both sides, with nobody naming it. Before each move ask two questions. Can I check on the enemy first rank, and is that mate? Could the opponent do it to me: does my king have a free square, and does a piece of mine guard my first rank? Look at both kings, every time.

steps.caption: White to move. What does Black threaten, and how can White answer?

line.say: White makes a luft with the h-pawn, so the king gets the square h2.
Black checks on the first rank.
The king steps out. It was only a check.

claims.statement: If White passed, ...Re1 would be checkmate.

steps.text: A back-rank mate needs three things together: **no flight square**, **nothing that can capture the checking piece**, and **nothing that can block**. For your own king the same list is a checklist: one guard on the first rank, or one free square, removes the threat. As a **rule of thumb**, make air once a threat appears rather than on every move, because it costs a move and loosens the pawns. Predict before you look.

steps.title: Is there a threat to the black king?
steps.prompt: Only one feature changes each time. Predict whether White threatens mate.
Think of the position where you were slowest. Which king did you look at first, and did you check the other king's escape square? Which one did you skip? Rate your confidence (low / medium / high).

title: Clearance: step aside with a threat
outcomes: Finds the vacating move that carries a threat when told to clear a line
Checks what the cleared piece attacks once the line is open
Rejects a vacating move that has no threat, or that opens a line leading nowhere

steps.text:
A **clearance** is a move that takes a piece off a square or a line so that another piece can use it. It usually works only when the vacating move **carries a threat of its own**, such as a check or a capture: the opponent must answer it and has no time to cover what you opened.
Opening a line is not enough by itself.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f2 stands on the f-file between the rook on f8 and the first rank. The knight on e3 covers f1 and g2.

line.say: The knight moves with check and leaves f2 at the same moment. The f-file opens for the rook.
White takes the knight. (If the king steps to h1 instead, Rf1 is mate as well.)
The rook goes down the open file. Rf1 is checkmate.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Nh3+ (depth 16).
Nh3+ forces checkmate in 2 or fewer against the engine's best defence.
While the knight stands on f2, the rook on f8 does not reach f1.
After the knight has left f2, the rook on f8 attacks f1.
The knight on e3 covers f1 and g2.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the vacating move makes a threat, and the cleared line leads somewhere that matters, such as a square the queen can use.
**When it fails:** the target square is defended, or the line is blocked further on, or the piece behind is not on the line at all. **Rule of thumb:** a vacating move with no threat gives the opponent time to close the line again.

steps.title: Same clearance, one change
steps.prompt: Same position, one change: the pawn on h6 is gone. Predict, then check.

In the silent positions, which of your pieces did you see as being in the way, and did you check that the vacating move made a threat? (The practice puzzles carry Lichess's automatic theme label, which is not always an exact fit for this lesson.)

title: Clearance: win, mate, or only retreat?
outcomes: Finds the vacating move that opens a line and wins material or mates, in a mixed set
Tells a forcing vacating move from one that only retreats

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Clearance: step aside with a threat**. Many moves open a line; few are worth playing. Ask three things.
**1. Is the vacating move forcing?** A check, or a capture with check, leaves the opponent no time.
**2. What does the opened line reach?** It should lead to mate or to material.
**3. Is the king's flight covered?** A free square can make the attack fizzle.

steps.text: A **combination** is a chain of forcing moves in which each move is justified by the next. It usually joins ideas you already know: a fork (*Forks: one move, two targets*), a pin (*Pins: cannot move, or should not move*) or removing a defender (*Removing the defender*), ending in a mating pattern or a won piece. The first move may look bad. The last move pays for it.

steps.text:
Check the whole chain, not only the first move. Play it to the last position. At every step ask what else the opponent can do: a quiet reply, a check, or declining the capture.
A combination that beats weak defence can fail against the best defence. *Rule of thumb:* if a simple move wins, play it; a complicated course adds risk.

steps.text: A **decoy** is a sacrifice that lures a piece, often the king, to a square where it can be hit. The opponent is better off taking, and the capture puts the piece where you want it. Ask: which piece do I want on which square, and what makes it go there?

steps.caption: Black to move. The white queen on e4 is defended by the king on e3. Other king moves lose to mate, so taking is White's best try.

steps.text: A lure needs two things. **The capture must be forced**, or at least better than every other reply. **The follow-up must win at once** on the new square. If the opponent can decline, or another piece can take the offer, the sacrifice is just a lost piece.

steps.title: Another piece can take

steps.text: **When it holds:** the offered piece must be taken and the lured piece lands where the follow-up wins. **When it fails:** the offer can be refused, the follow-up line is blocked, or the lured piece has a flight square. As a rule of thumb, check every reply that does not capture.

title: Deflection: forcing a defender away

steps.text: A defender can be **forced away** rather than captured. A check, a capture or a threat that it must answer pulls it off its key square, and what it was guarding falls. This is *deflection*. Ask: what is the piece guarding, and what forces it to leave?

Deflection works when the defender has no good alternative. Before you play it, ask two questions. **What if the defender refuses?** A check cannot be refused, but a capture or threat can be, so see what you win then. **Does another piece take over the duty once the first has gone?** If yes, the idea fails.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the move forces the defender, and the square or duty it leaves is unguarded the moment it goes. **When it fails:** the defender can decline without losing anything, or a second piece covers the same square. As a rule of thumb, list every guard of the target before you start.

steps.text: A **discovered attack** needs three pieces on one line. A *front piece* stands in the way. Behind it stands a *back piece*: a rook, bishop or queen. At the far end is a *target*. When the front piece moves away, the back piece suddenly attacks the target. Because the front piece also moves, one move can make two threats at once, and the opponent has only one move to answer both.

steps.chapter: Set it up or stop it

steps.text: **Building a discovery.** Put a slider on a line, put your own piece in front of it, and aim the line at something that matters: a king, a queen, a loose piece. Now the front piece can move whenever it has a good move, and the opponent must keep watching that line. [H] Such a battery may be worth more as a standing threat than as a quick strike; I have not measured this.

steps.text: **Stopping one.** Before you move, scan the lines through your king and queen. Is an enemy slider aiming along one, with his own piece in front? steps.text: **Why only the king can answer.** A single check can be met three ways: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. A capture or a block deals with one checker, and the other check is still there. So the king must move. That includes the king *capturing* a checker, if the checker stands next to the king and nothing protects it.

steps.text: **What a double check needs, and what makes it win.** It needs an open line once the front piece leaves, and a front piece that checks from its new square. Miss either and you have one check, which can be blocked or captured. It wins when the king cannot take the checker and every flight square is covered. Even then the forced king move buys a free move, because the king had to answer. That free move can bring mate, a fork or an undefended piece.

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Double check: how to see it, set it up and stop it. This part covers Set one up, stop one; Look-alikes and a mixed test; Mixed test. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Setting one up, and stopping one.** [I] Two ways to set one up, from the boards in this lesson: put a long-range piece behind a piece that has a checking square, or use a first check to drive the king onto the line. Dan Heisman advises listing the opponent's checks, captures and threats before each move [S, paraphrased]. [I] The question this theme adds: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check my king?

steps.text: **Many defences work.** [V] At depth 16 the engine rates stepping the king off the rank, advancing a pawn and capturing with the rook within about a pawn of each other. What fails is leaving the king on the line. [I] So ask before each move: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check me? The king, the back piece or the front piece can move, or the line can be blocked.

**Two look-alikes and one failed double check.** (1) The line is blocked, so the move gives one check. (2) The front piece lands where it does not attack the king: a *discovered* check, which can be blocked. And a real double check can still fail: the king takes the checker, or has a safe square (the third condition). Ask: which check is missing, or which king answer exists?

steps.text: **What others say.** Nimzowitsch (*My System*, chapter on discovered check) describes double check as leaving the king nothing but flight, and calls it purely tactical [V-sheet: paraphrased from our own notes, not the book page]. Jacob Aagaard argues that many calculation errors start with a candidate move that was never considered [S, a reviewer's account, paraphrased]. [I] So the habit: put the double check on your candidate list before you calculate.

**What to remember.**
1. Double check: two checkers, so only the king can move.
2. A back piece, a front piece, an open line.
3. The front piece must check from where it lands.
4. The king may take a checker next to it, if nothing covers that square.
5. Count the flight squares: mate, or a free move.
6. Look-alikes: blocked line, or no front check.
7. Defence: ask what long-range piece stands behind a piece that could check you. Move the king or either piece.

steps.prompt: A model answer [I], in the author's words. Idea: one move makes two pieces check at once, so only the king can answer. When it works: the line is open, the front piece checks where it lands, and the king cannot take the checker or reach a safe square. Example: White rook e1, bishop e5, pawn c5, Black king e7; the bishop to d6 is mate. Warning: without the pawn on c5 the king takes the bishop. Compare with yours.

**This lesson, as four tests you can take yourself.**

steps.text: **The idea, with its conditions.** A fork is one move that attacks two targets at once. It usually wins material when the opponent has no single reply that deals with both; you will test four kinds of reply later. Check the landing square first, because a forker that is simply captured for nothing is a classic failure. [I] Znosko-Borovsky separated real from fictitious threats [V-sheet]; treating a fork as two threats and asking about each is my own use of that idea.

**[H] Which forks get missed?** Hypothesis, not finding: the knight fork is the one people miss most, because its jump leaves no line between it and its targets, and eyes look for lines. Our own puzzle bank cannot test this. [V, reviewer's recount] Among the 81 single-move fork puzzles in the bank (filter: fork theme, find the move), 30 start with a knight move and 24 with a queen move. That shows what the bank contains, not what players miss.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Forks: how to see them, set them up and stop them. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**A seeing routine.** Search in a fixed order. The Steps method is reported to teach a search routine for each tactic [S, secondary description; manuals not seen]:
1. List enemy pieces that are loose or worth more than yours.
2. Find one square that touches two of them.
3. Can your piece reach it, ideally with check?
4. Run the four answers.
[H] I suspect starting from targets beats starting from your own checks. Test both orders later.

steps.text: **A fork usually wins when none of the four answers works:** capture the forker, check first, defend both, or move one and defend the other. [I] These four cover the usual replies, not every reply: a bigger counter-threat, such as a mate threat, is a fifth thing to look for. If you find one, write it down; it is a new answer.

**Is the guard real?** Edward Lasker warned that a defender can be an illusion: it may be capturable by a cheaper piece, pulled away or pinned [V-sheet]. The same goes for the pieces a fork attacks. Before you rely on a fork, ask who can capture the forker and whether the target is worth more than your piece. Count what can arrive, not only what is there.

Ask of each forcing move: where must the reply land, and does that square touch a fork?

steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Forks: how to see them, set them up and stop them. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Royal and discovered forks.** When the king is a target, the check must be answered first, so the other target cannot simply move away. [I] That makes a check fork the cleanest kind; each board below is checked, the generalisation is my inference. A discovered attack adds a free second threat: a piece moves with a threat of its own and uncovers a line behind it.

steps.text: **Stopping a fork against you.** Before you move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats that your move allows. Heisman calls skipping this *Hope Chess* [S]; he also pairs it with finding the threat, then preventing it [S]. For forks, look for squares an enemy knight can reach that touch two of your pieces. Aagaard (as a reviewer of his book reports it) says serious errors often begin when a key candidate is overlooked [S].

**Mixed test.** Eight unlabelled positions: some forks, some other tactics, some where no fork works. Aim for 6 of 8; that threshold is our choice, not a research finding. steps.text: Part 4 of 4: Forks: how to see them, set them up and stop them. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Three typical mistakes.** Grabbing a fork without testing the replies: the fork square can hide a bigger counter-threat. Forking a target that is defended and cheap. Forgetting that the forker can be taken. Each is a way a fork fails. How common each is in real games is [H]: we have not counted. For each position, find the move that avoids the trap.

**What to remember**
1. A fork is two threats from one move.
2. Any piece can fork; the knight is easiest to miss [H].
3. Find one square that touches two targets.
4. Check the four answers first.
5. Forcing moves can set one up.
6. [I] A king among the targets cannot be saved by moving the other.
7. Scan the opponent's checks, captures and threats first.
8. Test yourself unlabelled; retest.

Any piece can fork. A **pawn** fork is the hardest to meet, because the forked pieces have a higher counting value than the pawn. A **queen** can fork a king and a loose piece with one check.

Not every fork works. Before you play one, ask:
**Can the forking piece be captured?** By a piece, or even by one of its own targets.
**Does taking the second target gain material?** If it is defended and the forking piece has the higher counting value, the fork wins nothing.
Then check what your opponent can do instead.

steps.text:
**Interference** puts a piece on the line between two enemy pieces, so that one of them no longer protects the other or no longer guards a square. The piece that lost its protector may become a **loose piece**: attacked and not defended.

steps.text: A forced mate is found by **listing**, not by hoping. List every check. For one check, list every reply: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. The check starts a **mate in two** only if you have a mating move against *every* reply. Here we test checks only: if every check fails, a quiet first move may still mate (next lesson).

steps.text: **Why the list matters.** A check can fail in three ways: the defender takes the checking piece, a block spoils your next move, or the king has a step you did not count. *Rule of thumb:* before you call a check a mate in two, try to take the checking piece with each enemy piece, king included. A capture is fine only if you still have a mating move after it.

steps.text: When no check works, look for a **quiet move**: not a check, but a threat of mate that no reply can meet. Search in this order: every check, then captures next to the king, then quiet moves. For a quiet move ask: how many moves does the king have? Can the defender check, or take my attacking piece? After your first move, test the defender's forcing replies first: a check, the capture of your attacking piece, a move that gives the king a square. *Rule of thumb:* count the replies after the first move. If there are only one or two, follow each to the end.

steps.text: **Where the search breaks.** The defender has more chances: a check, the capture of your attacking piece, or a king square you did not count. One extra square can end the line. *Rule of thumb:* after the first move, count the king's squares and the defender's checks before following any line. steps.text: A piece with **two jobs** can be beaten. If one defender guards two targets, attack one: when it answers there, the other is left alone. This is an *overloaded defender*. Ask: which piece guards two things, and can it keep both?

title: Perpetual check: the draw you can force

steps.text: A **perpetual check** is a series of checks that the king cannot escape, so the same position keeps returning. When a position occurs three times, a player can claim a draw. When you are worse, a perpetual can save half a point. It needs every reply to lead back into more checks, so **test the king's squares** first.

steps.caption: White to move. Black is ahead (a queen and three pawns against a queen), so White looks for checks.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn with check. The king has only one legal move.

Forced. The queen can go back to f7.
The position after the first check is back, for the second time. A third time allows a draw claim.

claims.statement: Qxf7+ is the engine's first choice.
The engine rates the position as equal (depth 16).
After Qxf7+ the king on h7 has exactly one legal move.
No black piece attacks the queen on f7.
After Qxf7+ Kh8 Qf8+ the king on h8 again has exactly one legal move (h7).
After five moves the queen is on f7 again.
And the black king is on h7 again.

steps.text:
Three tests before you rely on a perpetual.
**Where can the king go?** Count its flight squares after each check.
**Can the checker be captured, or the check blocked?**
**Is the draw really your best result?** If another move wins, or the perpetual is not there, a draw may be a mistake. *Rule of thumb:* take the perpetual only when the alternatives are worse.

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Perpetual check: the draw you can force**, where you were told to find the perpetual. Now nobody tells you. You are the side that is behind, and you must look for the checks yourself.
A row of checks is not yet a perpetual. It becomes one only if the king cannot leave the checks, nothing can block or capture the checking piece, and the position repeats.

**Test before you rely on it.** (1) List your checking moves. (2) For each one, count the king's squares and ask whether anything can block or capture the checker. (3) Find your next check: is its square guarded? Only if every answer leaves you another check do the checks repeat.

steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Pins: cannot move, or should not move. This part covers What a pin costs; Ways out of a pin. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Cannot, or should not.** If the screened piece is the king, the pinned piece can move only along the line: an **absolute** pin. If it is anything else, moving is legal but costs what stands behind: a **relative** pin. Nimzowitsch spoke of whole and half pins: a piece that can slide along the line is only half pinned. The price is one comparison: what is behind, against what moves.

steps.prompt: Before you step on: can the black king capture or step onto d6? Say why in a few words.

fields.label: Can the king go to d6?

line.say: Suppose the knight retreats. The move is legal.
The bishop takes the queen, which the knight was shielding.

steps.text: **A pinned piece still bites.** It cannot leave the line, but it keeps attacking the squares it attacks, so the enemy king may not step onto them. A pinned knight is stuck completely, because a knight never moves along a line. Look at the board, then answer before you step on.

line.say: The pawn attacks the pinned bishop.
The bishop leaves anyway. The rook behind it is defended, so taking it wins nothing.

claims.statement: The pawn push wins nothing along the engine line.

steps.text: **Why a pin bites.** A pinned piece cannot leave, so it can be attacked again and again. If it leaves, it pays. Nimzowitsch (*My System*, pin chapter) held that a pinned piece defends only on paper, and that a pawn is the best attacker, because it cannot be chased away. E. Lasker listed pins among the ways a defender is an illusion. [I] Cheaper attackers are usually better, but check the position.

steps.text: **Five ways out of a pin.** The pinned side can **block** the line, **capture** the pinner, **step aside** (move the screened piece, or swap it for a cheaper one), **hit the pinner**, usually with a pawn, or **counter-attack** harder. [I] This sorting is mine. Nimzowitsch listed related policies: ask the pinner a question, ignore the pin, bring up reserves, or keep your options open. Check each answer before you lean on a pin.

steps.text: From **Pins: cannot move, or should not move** you know what a pin is. Now judge whether it is real and how to win the piece. A knight pinned to the king cannot move at all. A pinned rook or bishop may still slide along the pin line, even capture the pinner. The best attacker of a pinned piece is usually a **pawn**: it is the cheapest, and a piece pinned to the king cannot run.

steps.text: Not every winning move is a check or a capture. A **quiet move** gives no check and takes nothing, yet it prepares a threat the opponent cannot meet, or it removes their last defence. Look for one when the forcing moves have run out. It is a move to find, not one to play by habit.

A quiet move gives the opponent a free move. Before you play one, ask:

This lesson builds on **The quiet move: no check, no capture, still decisive**. There you were told a quiet move existed. Now nobody tells you. Use a fixed order:
1. List your checks.
2. List your captures.
3. List your direct threats.
4. Only if none of these wins, look for a quiet move.
5. Then give the opponent a free move and find their best check and capture.

title: Removing the defender
outcomes: Finds the capture that takes away the only defender of a piece

steps.text: A defended piece is only safe while its defender stays. If one piece does all the defending, **capture that defender** and the target is left without protection. This is *removing the defender*. It is a capture, so it is the plainest of the ways to attack a defence. Look for the defender first, then ask what captures it.

Taking the defender is a trade, and a trade can go wrong. Before you capture, count: **who else defends the target?** And **what can recapture on the square you capture on?** The idea works only if the target ends up with no defender after the exchange.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the target has one defender and you can capture it; after the trades the target is still unprotected. **When it fails:** a second piece defends the target, or the defender is guarded so that your capture loses more than it wins. As a rule of thumb, count both before you take.

A **skewer** attacks a valuable piece with a second piece lined up behind it. If the front piece is the king, it must move, so the piece behind is lost. If the front piece is a queen or rook, the owner can move it, but only by giving up the piece behind or paying something else. In a pin the order is usually reversed: the cheaper piece stands in front. Most boards so far begin with a check; a quiet one comes later.

steps.text: **Why it works, part one: a king in front.** A check must be answered, and the king cannot stay on the line, so its step is forced. That forced step is the whole trick: the owner has no spare move to rescue the piece behind, because the turn is used up answering the check. A king in front is the strongest case.
steps.chapter: Why it works and when it fails

steps.text: **Part two: a queen or rook in front.** Nothing forces the owner here, so the owner picks the cheaper loss. Count it: a bishop attacks a queen with a rook behind it. The queen steps away and you take the rook, five points for the price of one move. The owner never gives up the queen to save the rook. [I] That is why the front piece should be worth more than what stands behind it.

steps.caption: The same line, reversed order: the knight stands in front of the king, so it is pinned. White to move. White has exactly one good reply, Ke2, which defends the knight, and Black's bishop earns at most a trade.

line.say: The king steps up behind the knight and defends it.
The bishop takes the knight.
The king takes back. An even trade: nothing is won.

claims.statement: The knight on d3 has no legal move: it is pinned to the king.
The engine rates the position as roughly level (depth 16).
After the king steps to e2, it defends the knight.

steps.text: **Part three: swap the order.** Put the cheaper piece in front and the same line becomes a pin or nothing: the owner defends the cheap piece or lets it go and loses only that. So the order of values, not the line itself, decides whether material is won. [H] Skewers may turn up more in endings, where kings are exposed and few pieces can block. We have not tested this.

**Four ways out.** Before you play a skewer, ask what the defender can do. One: take the attacker. Two: step in between, cutting the line. Three: guard the piece behind, so that taking it is only a trade. Four: move the front piece with a threat of its own. [I] These four cover most of what goes wrong. If none of them works and you have checked for a stronger reply, the skewer very likely wins. Keep a place for a fifth: a forcing reply you did not list.

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Skewers: the king moves, the piece behind falls. This part covers Set it up, or stop it; Near misses. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Where skewers come from.** Sometimes both pieces already stand on one line and you need only a safe attack on the front one. Otherwise you build the line: a check drives the king to a square where something stands behind it. [H] Skewers that need a preparing check may be common in practice; we have not counted them. A check from a distance cannot be answered by taking the checker, which is why queens and rooks suit it. A checker next to the king works if something defends it.

steps.text: **What coaches say.** Dan Heisman teaches listing the opponent's forcing replies (checks, captures, threats) before each move [S], and treating the opponent as someone who will find the best one [S]. Jeremy Silman puts a look for tactics ahead of positional analysis [S]. [H] One extra question may catch skewers sooner: do my king and another valuable piece share a line? [H] Beginners may see pins before skewers because a pin is easier to picture. Untested; your games are the test.

**Look-alikes.** A **fork** attacks two pieces from one square. A **pin** has the cheaper piece in front. A **discovered attack** moves one piece to unmask another. A skewer needs a line with the *more valuable* piece in front and something worth taking behind. If the line is blocked, or nothing is behind, the check is only a check.

steps.text: **Recap.** A skewer attacks the more valuable piece first, with something behind it on the same line. Check four answers: take the attacker, block, guard the piece behind, or move with a threat. Build skewers with checks that push the king onto a line. Guard against them by keeping valuable pieces off shared lines. Many checks line nothing up: say no tactic when that is so.

**Before a skewer, three questions.**
1. Is the piece behind on the line, with nothing between?

title: Stalemate as a rescue
outcomes: Finds the sacrifice that forces a stalemate when told to look for one

steps.text:
In **stalemate** the side to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is a **draw**: neither side wins.
So a side that is clearly losing can sometimes save the game by giving up a piece, usually with check, so that the capture leaves it with no legal move. The stronger side must check, before each quiet move, that the opponent still has a legal move.

Rc7 loses (tablebase).
The black king has no legal move even now.
The rook on a7 gives check to the king on a8.
After Kxa7 the black king still has no legal move.
After Kxa7 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the capture is forced, and afterwards your side has no legal move and is not in check. That usually needs your king boxed in, often on the edge or in a corner, and no pawn or piece able to move.
**Check:** if your side has any legal move left, there is no stalemate. Count your own legal moves after the capture.

steps.text:
A piece is **trapped** when it is attacked, or can be attacked, and every square it can go to loses it. Knights on the rim and bishops that grabbed a pawn are the usual victims.
To trap a piece, count its escape squares and ask which of them you cover.

Trapped is not the same as cut off. A piece that is **cut off** from the action still has a safe square, so you cannot win it. Before you attack, ask:
**Which squares can it reach?**
**Which of them do I cover?**
**Can it capture something, or can its friends help?**

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank, you choose its new piece. The queen is the usual choice because it is strongest. Sometimes another piece is better. A **knight** can give check and attack a second piece at once. A **rook** can win where a queen would leave the opponent with no legal move and no check: **stalemate**, a draw. Choosing a weaker piece on purpose is **underpromotion**.

steps.text:
Check the queen first. Ask two questions.
**Does the queen promotion fail?** It might stalemate, or a knight's check and fork might win more.
**Does a knight on that square give check and attack a second piece?** As with any fork, ask whether the knight can be captured and whether the second target is worth taking.
*Rule of thumb:* the queen is the default. These questions find the exceptions.

outcomes: Counts attackers and defenders of a square including the pieces behind
Finds the capture sequence in which the rear piece joins in

steps.text:
Two of your pieces on one line form a **battery**. The rear piece attacks, or defends, *through* the front one: once the front piece captures or moves away, the rear piece joins in. This is called an **x-ray**.
When you count attackers and defenders, include the pieces behind. Two rooks on a file are two attackers, not one.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on b1 stands behind the queen on d3, on the same diagonal as h7.

line.say: Qxh7 is checkmate. The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop behind it guards h7.

Only the king attacks h7.
Before the capture the bishop does not reach h7: the queen is in the way.
After the queen has gone to h7, the bishop guards it.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the front piece can capture and leave the line, and the piece behind moves along that line. **Rule of thumb:** count attackers and defenders including the pieces behind, cheapest capture first, and remember that either side may stop trading.
**When it fails:** the front piece is pinned and cannot capture, or nothing stands behind it, so there is only one attacker.

title: X-ray: count every piece on the line
outcomes: Counts the attackers and the defenders of a square, including the pieces behind others
Plays out the exchange in order of counting value and says who comes out ahead
Finds the winning capture sequence in a mixed position

steps.text:
This lesson follows **X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in**. There you were told that an x-ray existed. Now you count it yourself.
On the square in question list your attackers, including each piece standing behind another on the same line, and then the defenders. Play the exchange with the cheapest piece first. Either side may stop, so ask who runs out of pieces first.

**The count works** when the rear piece stands on the same line and the front piece will leave by capture or by moving. **It fails** when the front piece cannot capture, or when a second defender arrives. **Rule of thumb:** counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 only guide the order; check the last capture, because the side that makes it must not be recaptured.

title: X-ray: predict how the count changes
outcomes: Predicts how the count changes when a defender is added, the front piece is pinned or the rear piece is missing
Verifies a capture sequence square by square before playing the first capture
Says which changes to a position leave the count as it was

steps.text:
This lesson follows **X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in** and **X-ray: count every piece on the line**. Here the count is not given; you predict it after a change.
Start from a battery that wins. Change one thing: a defender arrives, the front piece becomes pinned, or the rear piece leaves the line. Predict whether the count still wins, then check it square by square.

**Three changes that matter:** a new defender of the target square; a front piece pinned to its king, so it cannot capture and the rear piece never joins in; a rear piece that no longer stands on the line.
**A change that does not matter:** a move that touches neither the line nor the target. **Rule of thumb:** recount after every change; never carry the old count over.

title: In-between moves: a check or capture first
outcomes: Asks, before a capture or recapture, whether a check or capture can be played first
Finds the in-between check or capture when told one exists
Re-counts the exchange to see that the original capture still wins what was expected
Recognises a position where the plain recapture is simply best

steps.text:
An **in-between move** (German: *Zwischenzug*) is a forcing move you play *before* the reply your opponent expects, such as the recapture. It is usually a **check**, which the opponent must answer, or a **capture**.
The question to ask before any capture or recapture: **is there a check or capture I can play first, and does my original capture still work afterwards?**

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4, and Black's bishop on a6 attacks the white rook on b5. The expected move is to take on d4.

line.say: The attacked rook moves with check along the c-file. Black has to answer the check first.
The king steps aside. The white rook has left b5, so the bishop can no longer take it there.
Now the pawn takes the rook on d4. Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rc5+ (depth 16).
Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.
Taking at once with cxd4 is at least 600 centipawns worse (engine).
Black's bishop on a6 attacks the rook on b5.
The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the in-between move forces a reply, and afterwards the capture you wanted still wins what you expected. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** for example when a pawn defends the target, so the follow-up capture wins nothing. After the forcing move, count the exchange again, and ask whether the opponent has an in-between move of their own.

steps.title: Same exchange, one change
steps.prompt: The black rook on d8 and the white rook on d1 face each other on the d-file. In the next position a white pawn stands on f4 instead of f2. Predict, then check.

In the silent positions, what did you expect your opponent to do next, and did you check that your capture still worked after your forcing move? (The practice puzzles carry Lichess's automatic theme label, which is not always an exact fit for this lesson.)

title: In-between moves in exchanges: yours and theirs
outcomes: Finds the in-between check or capture in a mixed exchange
Re-counts an exchange after the forcing move before relying on it
Does not rely on a recapture that the opponent can sidestep with a forcing move
Recognises an exchange where the plain recapture is best

steps.text:
In *In-between moves: a check or capture first* you found the forcing move before a recapture. In exchanges both sides can play one.
**Before you rely on a recapture:** can the opponent play a check or capture first?
**Before you play your own in-between move:** after it, does the original capture still win what you expected?
Count again after every forcing move.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rooks on b7 and f7 attack each other, and the bishop on f3 defends the rook on b7. The knight on d4 attacks that bishop.

line.say: The knight takes with check, an in-between move.
Suppose White takes the knight.
Now the rook takes the rook on b7.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Nxf3+ (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line Nxf3+ nets Black at least six points of material.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the forcing move leaves your original capture available and the target cannot move away with a threat of its own. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** a pawn or piece now guards the target, so the capture wins nothing, or the opponent has a forcing move of their own. Recount after the forcing move.

title: In-between moves: recount with their check
outcomes: Lists the checks and captures of both sides before trusting an exchange count
Predicts which side gains once the best in-between move of each side has been played
Tells a position where a check changes the count from one where it does not

steps.text: This lesson follows **In-between moves: a check or capture first** and **In-between moves in exchanges: yours and theirs**. Before you trust a count such as 'I take, he takes, I take again', list the **checks and captures of both sides** at each step, then recount. The question is not only 'do I have a check?' but 'who gains once every check has been played?'

steps.caption: White to move. Both white rooks are aimed at the black rook on a1 and the bishop on g8.

line.say: Rxg8+ is check, so the rook takes the bishop with tempo.
Black takes the rook back.
Now the second rook takes the black rook: a rook and a bishop for a rook.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rxg8+ (depth 16).
The rook on a7 attacks the black rook on a1.
Along the engine line White ends material ahead.

steps.text:
**The check pays** when your second capture is still there afterwards and the opponent has no check of their own. **Rule of thumb:** before relying on a count, list both sides' checks.
**It fails** when the target is no longer attacked, or when the opponent's check wins back enough to level the count.
Recount after every forcing move, for both sides.
